
See [Environment Variables](/configuration/env-vars/) for what each one does.

## Request limits

Fixed limits that apply whatever the configuration:

| Limit | Value | Over the limit |
|---|---|---|
| Request head (request line + headers), HTTP/1.1 | 64 KiB | `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` |
| Header list, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 | 64 KiB | stream reset |
| Concurrent streams per HTTP/2 connection | 250 | stream refused |
| Idle time between reads | 30 s | connection closed |
| HTTP/2 connection with nothing running and nothing received | 30 s | `GOAWAY(NO_ERROR)`, connection closed |
| HTTP/2 stream resets, the client's or provoked by it (rapid reset, MadeYouReset) | 1000 per 10 s | `GOAWAY(ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM)` |
| Whole request head, from its first byte (HTTP/1.1) | 30 s | `408 Request Timeout` |
| TLS handshake | 10 s | connection closed |

The request body limit is `max_body_size_in_bytes` above. On HTTP/1.1, bodies
may be sent with `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`; a request
that carries both, or two different `Content-Length` values, is rejected with
`400` so `rws` and a proxy in front of it can never disagree about where a
request ends.

For the same reason an HTTP/1.1 request head is read strictly (17.113.2) and
answered `400` when it has no `Host` or more than one, a method not in upper
case (`get`), a version other than `HTTP/1.0`/`HTTP/1.1`, a folded header
line (starting with a space or tab), whitespace before a header's colon, or a
header name with characters a token can't have. `Connection` is read token by
token: `Connection: close, TE` closes the connection after the response.

## `[[virtual_host]]`

Repeat this section for each domain that needs its own TLS certificate. The SNI
resolver selects the right certificate automatically at handshake time.

```toml
[[virtual_host]]
domain    = "example.com"
cert_file = "/etc/ssl/example.com.pem"
key_file  = "/etc/ssl/example.com.key"

[[virtual_host]]
domain    = "api.example.com"
cert_file = "/etc/ssl/api.example.com.pem"
key_file  = "/etc/ssl/api.example.com.key"
```

## `[[upstream]]`

Defines a named backend pool. Upstreams are referenced by name from routes.

```toml
[[upstream]]
name      = "api"
backends  = ["localhost:3000", "localhost:3001"]
strategy  = "round_robin"   # "round_robin" | "random" | "ip_hash" | "least_connections" (default: round_robin)
# tls_ca_file = "/etc/rws/internal-ca.pem"  # TLS backends: trust this CA instead of the public roots
# tls_client_cert_file = "/etc/rws/client.pem"  # TLS backends that require a client certificate (mutual TLS),
# tls_client_key_file  = "/etc/rws/client.key"  #   with its private key — since 18.3.0
# protocol = "h3"        # HTTP/3 (QUIC) to the https:// backends, TCP fallback — since 18.13.0

[upstream.health_check]
path                = "/health"  # HTTP path polled on each backend (default: /health)
interval_secs       = 30         # Poll interval (default: 30)
timeout_ms          = 5000       # Connect + read timeout per poll (default: 5000)
healthy_threshold   = 2          # Consecutive passes before marking healthy (default: 2)
unhealthy_threshold = 3          # Consecutive failures before marking unhealthy (default: 3)
```

When the health checker removes all backends, the route returns `502 Bad Gateway`
until at least one backend recovers.

## `[authz]`

Relationship-based authorization for routes with `[route.middleware.authz]`
(since 18.14.0) — see [Authorization](/features/authorization/#in-the-config-file).

```toml
[authz]
store  = "memory"                        # or "sql": RWS_DB_* (a model-* feature)
tuples = ["doc:42#owner@user:olga"]      # written at start and on reload; may span lines

[authz.type.doc]                         # one table per object type
owner  = "user"
viewer = "user | group#member | owner"   # terms: type, type#relation, relation, rel->rel
```

## `[[route]]`

Each `[[route]]` entry maps a set of match criteria to an action and an optional
per-route middleware stack. Routes are evaluated in declaration order; the first
match wins.

### `[route.match]`

All criteria are optional. A request must satisfy every criterion that is set.

```toml
[[route]]
name = "api-proxy"

[route.match]
host         = "api.example.com"  # SNI hostname or Host header (exact match)
path         = "/api/*"           # Prefix match when ending with *; exact match otherwise
method       = "POST"             # HTTP method (case-insensitive; matches any if omitted)
content_type = "application/json" # Content-Type prefix match
```

### `[route.action]` — proxy

Forward requests to a named upstream pool.

```toml
[route.action]
type = "proxy"

[route.action.proxy]
upstream            = "api"          # Must match a [[upstream]] name
connect_timeout_ms  = 5000           # (default: 5000)
read_timeout_ms     = 30000          # (default: 30000); 504 past it (502 before 18.27.0)
strip_path_prefix   = "/api"         # Strip this prefix before forwarding (optional)
add_path_prefix     = "/v2"          # Add this prefix after stripping (optional)
preserve_host       = true           # Send the client's Host upstream (default: false)
upstream_host       = "app.internal" # Send this Host upstream (optional; wins over preserve_host)
```

The upstream gets the backend's address as its `Host` unless the route says
otherwise: `preserve_host = true` passes on the client's (nginx's
`proxy_set_header Host $host`, for an application that builds its links from
the host it's asked for), `upstream_host` sends a fixed name. Over HTTP/3
upstreams they set `:authority`. The proxy writes `Host` itself, so a
`header_set` rewrite of `Host` doesn't reach the upstream — `rws --check`
warns about one. The client's host also goes upstream as `X-Forwarded-Host`
either way.

### `[route.action]` — grpc

Forward gRPC traffic over HTTP/2 to a named upstream.

```toml
[route.action]
type = "grpc"

[route.action.grpc]
upstream           = "grpc-backend"
connect_timeout_ms = 5000
read_timeout_ms    = 30000
```

### `[route.action]` — static

Serve static files from a directory on disk.

```toml
[route.action]
type = "static"

[route.action.static]
root  = "./public"
index = ["index.html", "index.htm"]
```

### `[route.action]` — redirect

Issue an HTTP redirect.

```toml
[route.action]
type = "redirect"

[route.action.redirect]
location = "https://new.example.com$path"  # $path is replaced with the request URI
status   = 301                             # (default: 301)
```

### `[route.action]` — respond

Return a fixed response body without proxying.

```toml
[route.action]
type = "respond"

[route.action.respond]
status       = 200
body         = "{\"ok\":true}"
content_type = "application/json"   # (default: text/plain)
```

### `[route.action]` — mcp

An [MCP gateway](/mcp/gateway/): one MCP endpoint in front of several upstream MCP servers, their tools prefixed, with per-caller access rules, rate limits and an audit log (since 18.9.0; before, `mcp` was accepted and not served). The route needs an exact `path`. Secrets stay out of the file: caller tokens and upstream header values come from the environment variables named.

```toml
[[route]]
  [route.match]
  path = "/mcp"

  [route.action]
  type = "mcp"

  [route.action.mcp]
  name            = "gateway"             # announced to clients (default rws-mcp-gateway)
  refresh_secs    = 300                   # re-read upstream tools; 0 = only at start
  audit_log       = true                  # one JSON line per tool call in the access log
  allowed_origins = ["https://app.example.com"]

  [[route.action.mcp.upstream]]
  prefix      = "github"                  # tools appear as github__<tool>
  url         = "https://mcp.github.example/mcp"
  timeout_ms  = 30000
  headers_env = { Authorization = "GITHUB_MCP_AUTHORIZATION" }   # header = env var with its value

  [[route.action.mcp.openapi]]             # an HTTP API's operations as tools (since 18.19.0)
  prefix      = "billing"
  spec        = "https://billing.internal/openapi.json"
  base_url    = "https://billing.internal"
  include     = ["getInvoice"]            # operationIds; default: every GET
  headers_env = { Authorization = "BILLING_API_AUTHORIZATION" }

  [[route.action.mcp.caller]]             # who may connect: their bearer token
  identity  = "alice"
  token_env = "ALICE_MCP_TOKEN"

  [[route.action.mcp.allow]]              # what they may use
  identity = "alice"
  tools    = ["github__*"]                # full names, prefixes ending in *, or *

  [[route.action.mcp.limit]]              # per caller and tool
  tools       = "github__create_issue"
  max_calls   = 5
  window_secs = 3600
```

The gateway lists its upstreams in the background at start: until it has, and while an upstream is down then, the route answers `503` and the build is retried every 10 s. `rws --check` reports unknown keys, bad prefixes and URLs, and unset token and header variables.

### `[route.action]` — a2a

An [A2A gateway](/mcp/a2a/#gateway): a public address for an A2A agent running elsewhere (since 18.18.0). Its card is served at `<path>/.well-known/agent-card.json` with the JSON-RPC interface pointing at this route, and JSON-RPC `POST`s to `<path>` go to the agent, streams included. Use the route's middleware for auth and rate limits; the caller's `Authorization` isn't passed on.

```toml
[[route]]
  [route.match]
  path = "/agents/billing/*"

  [route.action]
  type = "a2a"

  [route.action.a2a]
  upstream    = "http://10.0.0.7:9000"   # the agent's base URL (its card at /.well-known/agent-card.json)
  timeout_ms  = 300000                   # default; SendMessage may wait for its task
  audit_log   = true                     # one JSON line per call: client, method, status, duration
  headers_env = { Authorization = "BILLING_AGENT_AUTHORIZATION" }  # sent to the agent, from the environment
```

### `[route.action]` — llm

An [LLM proxy](/proxy/llm-proxy/) in front of OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic providers: virtual keys, fallback, token usage, budgets (since 18.9.0). Provider keys, virtual keys and the Redis password come from the environment variables named.

```toml
[[route]]
  [route.match]
  path = "/v1/*"

  [route.action]
  type = "llm"

  [route.action.llm]
  audit_log          = true
  redis              = "127.0.0.1:6379"   # budgets shared between replicas (default: in memory)
  redis_password_env = "REDIS_PASSWORD"
  redis_prefix       = "rws:llm:"
  connect_timeout_ms = 10000
  read_timeout_ms    = 300000
  allow_anonymous    = false

  [[route.action.llm.provider]]           # tried in order, per API
  name    = "openai"
  api     = "openai"                      # or "anthropic"
  url     = "https://api.openai.com"
  key_env = "OPENAI_API_KEY"              # optional (local servers)

  [[route.action.llm.key]]                # a virtual key clients send
  identity      = "alice"
  key_env       = "ALICE_LLM_KEY"
  budget_tokens = 2000000                 # optional, with window_secs
  window_secs   = 86400
```

### `[route.middleware]`

Per-route middleware applied before the action. All sub-sections are optional.

```toml
[route.middleware]
timeout_ms    = 5000      # 504 Gateway Timeout past this (0/unset = none)
max_body_size = 1048576   # 413 above this many bytes (0/unset = only the global limit)
early_hints   = ["</app.css>; rel=preload; as=style"]   # sent as a 103 before the route answers (18.12.0)

[route.middleware.rate_limit]
max_requests = 100
window_secs  = 60

[route.middleware.cache]
ttl_secs = 300
vary_by  = ["Accept-Encoding", "Authorization"]
# dir      = "/var/cache/rws/api"   # on disk instead of in memory (18.11.0)
# max_size = "512M"                 # disk bound, default 256M
# purge_token_env = "RWS_PURGE_TOKEN"  # accept HTTP PURGE with this bearer token (18.11.0)

[route.middleware.authz]                 # caller needs relation on object (18.14.0)
relation = "viewer"
object   = "doc:{path:2}"

[route.middleware.auth]
type      = "bearer"        # "bearer" | "jwt" | "basic"
token_env = "API_TOKEN"     # env var name holding the expected token (bearer)
# secret_env = "JWT_SECRET" # env var name holding the JWT secret (jwt)
# previous_secret_env = "JWT_SECRET_OLD" # also accepted while rotating (jwt, 18.20.0)
# htpasswd_file = "users.htpasswd" # path to htpasswd file (basic)

[route.middleware.ip_filter]
allow = ["10.0.0.0/8", "192.168.1.0/24"]
deny  = ["10.0.0.5"]

[route.middleware.wasm]             # a WebAssembly plugin (feature wasm-plugins, 18.10.0)
module    = "plugins/tag.wasm"
fuel      = 50000000                # CPU per hook call
memory_mb = 16
config    = "region=eu"             # passed to the plugin's rws_init
```

See [WebAssembly plugins](/features/wasm-plugins/) for the plugin ABI and sandbox.

A top-level `[middleware]` table (same keys and sub-tables as
`[route.middleware]`) wraps every route and the static fallback.

#### Request rewrite rules

```toml
[[route.middleware.rewrite.request]]
type  = "header_set"
name  = "X-Forwarded-Proto"
value = "https"

[[route.middleware.rewrite.request]]
type   = "uri_strip_prefix"
prefix = "/api"

[[route.middleware.rewrite.request]]
type   = "uri_add_prefix"
prefix = "/v2"

[[route.middleware.rewrite.request]]
type  = "header_remove"
name  = "X-Internal-Secret"

[[route.middleware.rewrite.request]]
type  = "uri_set"
value = "/health"
```

#### Response rewrite rules

```toml
[[route.middleware.rewrite.response]]
type  = "header_set"
name  = "X-Powered-By"
value = "rws"

[[route.middleware.rewrite.response]]
type  = "header_remove"
name  = "Server"

[[route.middleware.rewrite.response]]
type   = "status"
code   = 200
reason = "OK"

[[route.middleware.rewrite.response]]
type = "body_replace"
from = "old-domain.com"
to   = "new-domain.com"
```

## `[[tcp_proxy]]`

Standalone L4 TCP proxy. Binds its own port and relays bytes bidirectionally
between the client and a backend. Runs in a background thread and is independent
of the HTTP server.

```toml
[[tcp_proxy]]
name               = "db-proxy"
listen             = "0.0.0.0:5433"               # Address to bind
backends           = ["db-primary:5432", "db-replica:5432"]
connect_timeout_ms = 5000                          # (default: 5000)
```

## `[[udp_proxy]]`

Standalone UDP datagram proxy. Each datagram is forwarded to a backend and the
reply is relayed back to the originating client.

```toml
[[udp_proxy]]
name              = "dns-proxy"
listen            = "0.0.0.0:5353"
backends          = ["8.8.8.8:53", "8.8.4.4:53"]
reply_timeout_ms  = 5000    # How long to wait for a reply (default: 5000)
buffer_size       = 65536   # Datagram buffer in bytes (default: 65536)
```

## `[[ws_proxy]]`

Standalone WebSocket proxy. Handles the HTTP upgrade handshake then relays raw
bytes bidirectionally between client and backend.

```toml
[[ws_proxy]]
name               = "ws-backend"
listen             = "0.0.0.0:8080"
backends           = ["localhost:8081"]
connect_timeout_ms = 5000    # (default: 5000)
read_timeout_ms    = 30000   # (default: 30000)

[ws_proxy.health_check]       # optional, same keys as [upstream.health_check]
path = "/health"
```

## Complete example

```toml
ip                 = "0.0.0.0"
port               = 443
http_redirect_port = 80

[acme]
domains = ["example.com", "api.example.com"]
email   = "ops@example.com"

[cors]
allow_all = false
allow_origins = "https://app.example.com"
allow_methods = "GET,POST,PUT,DELETE"
allow_headers = "content-type,authorization"
max_age       = 86400

[rate_limit]
max_requests = 500
window_secs  = 60

[[virtual_host]]
domain    = "example.com"
cert_file = "/etc/ssl/certs/example.pem"
key_file  = "/etc/ssl/private/example.key"

[[upstream]]
name      = "api"
backends  = ["localhost:3000", "localhost:3001"]
strategy  = "round_robin"

[upstream.health_check]
path                = "/health"
interval_secs       = 15
healthy_threshold   = 2
unhealthy_threshold = 3

[[route]]
name = "api"

[route.match]
path = "/api/*"

[route.action]
type = "proxy"

[route.action.proxy]
upstream          = "api"
strip_path_prefix = "/api"

[route.middleware.rate_limit]
max_requests = 100
window_secs  = 60

[[route]]
name = "health"

[route.match]
path = "/ping"

[route.action]
type = "respond"

[route.action.respond]
status = 200
body   = "pong"
```

---

# CLI Arguments

<https://rws8.tech/docs/configuration/cli-args/>

Command-line arguments are the highest-priority configuration layer — they
override defaults, system environment variables, and `rws.config.toml`. Every
flag maps directly to a `RWS_CONFIG_*` environment variable; setting the flag is
exactly equivalent to setting that variable before the process starts.

Flags use the `--long-form=value` syntax. A single-character short form is also
supported with `-x=value`.

```bash
rws [--flag=value ...]
```

## Server

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Maps to |
|------|-------|------|---------|---------|
| `--ip=<addr>` | `-i` | string | `0.0.0.0` | `RWS_CONFIG_IP` |
| `--port=<n>` | `-p` | integer | `7878` | `RWS_CONFIG_PORT` |
| `--thread-count=<n>` | `-t` | integer | `200` | `RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT` |
| `--request-allocation-size-in-bytes=<n>` | `-r` | integer | `10000` | `RWS_CONFIG_REQUEST_ALLOCATION_SIZE_IN_BYTES` |

```bash
# Listen on all interfaces on port 443 with 500 worker threads
rws --ip=0.0.0.0 --port=443 --thread-count=500
```

## TLS

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Maps to |
|------|-------|------|---------|---------|
| `--tls-cert-file=<path>` | `-s` | path | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE` |
| `--tls-key-file=<path>` | `-k` | path | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE` |

Setting both `--tls-cert-file` and `--tls-key-file` enables HTTPS, HTTP/2, and
HTTP/3. The server falls back to plain HTTP/1.1 when either flag is absent.

```bash
rws --tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem
```

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Maps to |
|------|-------|------|---------|---------|
| `--http-redirect-port=<n>` | — | integer | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT` |

:::note[mTLS]
`RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE` has no CLI flag. Set it via the environment
variable or `tls_client_ca_file` in `rws.config.toml`.
:::

## ACME

Long form only (`acme` feature). See [Automatic HTTPS](/features/acme/).

| Flag | Type | Default | Maps to |
|------|------|---------|---------|
| `--acme-domains=<list>` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DOMAINS` |
| `--acme-email=<addr>` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_EMAIL` |
| `--acme-staging=<bool>` | bool | `false` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_STAGING` |
| `--acme-directory=<url>` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DIRECTORY` |
| `--acme-ca-file=<path>` | path | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CA_FILE` |
| `--acme-challenge-port=<n>` | integer | `80` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CHALLENGE_PORT` |
| `--acme-cert-path=<path>` | path | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CERT_PATH` |
| `--acme-key-path=<path>` | path | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_KEY_PATH` |
| `--acme-profile=<name>` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_PROFILE` |

Settings not listed on this page have no flag; set them through the
environment or `rws.config.toml`.

## CORS

| Flag | Short | Type | Default | Maps to |
|------|-------|------|---------|---------|
| `--cors-allow-all=<bool>` | `-a` | bool | `false` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL` |
| `--cors-allow-origins=<list>` | `-o` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` |
| `--cors-allow-methods=<list>` | `-m` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS` |
| `--cors-allow-headers=<list>` | `-h` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS` |
| `--cors-allow-credentials=<bool>` | `-c` | bool | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS` |
| `--cors-expose-headers=<list>` | `-e` | string | `` (empty) | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS` |
| `--cors-max-age=<seconds>` | `-g` | integer | `86400` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_MAX_AGE` |

`<list>` values are comma-separated strings. Header name lists should be
lowercase.

```bash
# Disable the allow-all default and restrict to specific origins
rws \
  --cors-allow-all=false \
  --cors-allow-origins=https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com \
  --cors-allow-methods=GET,POST,PUT,DELETE \
  --cors-allow-headers=content-type,authorization \
  --cors-allow-credentials=true \
  --cors-expose-headers=x-request-id \
  --cors-max-age=3600
```

:::caution[allow-all takes precedence]
When `--cors-allow-all=true` (the default), the specific `--cors-allow-origins`,
`--cors-allow-methods`, and `--cors-allow-headers` flags are ignored. Set
`--cors-allow-all=false` to activate fine-grained CORS control.
:::

## Informational flags

These print and exit without starting the server.

| Flag | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `--version`, `-V` | Print `rws <version>` |
| `--help` | Print usage and every flag with its environment variable |
| `--check[=<file>]` | Validate the config file (default: `RWS_CONFIG_FILE`, else `./rws.config.toml`); exit `0` if no errors, `1` otherwise |
| `--format=json` | With `--check`, print the report as JSON |

`--windows-service=<directory>` (Windows) runs rws as a service of the Service Control Manager, serving `<directory>` — see [Windows](/deployment/windows/).

## Quick-start examples

### Development server (HTTP only)

```bash
cargo run -- --ip=127.0.0.1 --port=7878
```

### HTTPS with HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

```bash
cargo run -- --tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem
```

### Locked-down CORS for production

```bash
rws \
  --port=443 \
  --tls-cert-file=/etc/ssl/server.pem \
  --tls-key-file=/etc/ssl/server.key \
  --cors-allow-all=false \
  --cors-allow-origins=https://app.example.com \
  --cors-allow-methods=GET,POST \
  --cors-allow-headers=content-type,authorization \
  --request-allocation-size-in-bytes=65536
```

### Override a single value from the config file

CLI flags always win over `rws.config.toml`. Use this pattern to temporarily
change a setting without editing the file:

```bash
# rws.config.toml has port = 7878; override to 9090 for this run only
rws --port=9090
```

## Full flag reference

```
rws [OPTIONS]

OPTIONS:
  -i, --ip=<addr>
        IP address to bind (default: 0.0.0.0)

  -p, --port=<n>
        TCP port to listen on (default: 7878)

  -t, --thread-count=<n>
        Worker thread pool size (http1 build only; default: 200)

  -r, --request-allocation-size-in-bytes=<n>
        Read buffer size per request in bytes (default: 10000)

  -s, --tls-cert-file=<path>
        Path to PEM certificate chain; enables TLS when set

  -k, --tls-key-file=<path>
        Path to PEM private key; enables TLS when set

  -a, --cors-allow-all=<bool>
        Allow all CORS origins (default: true)

  -o, --cors-allow-origins=<list>
        Comma-separated allowed origins

  -m, --cors-allow-methods=<list>
        Comma-separated allowed HTTP methods

  -h, --cors-allow-headers=<list>
        Comma-separated allowed request headers (lowercase)

  -c, --cors-allow-credentials=<bool>
        Allow credentials in CORS requests

  -e, --cors-expose-headers=<list>
        Comma-separated response headers exposed to the browser (lowercase)

  -g, --cors-max-age=<seconds>
        Preflight cache duration in seconds (default: 86400)

      --http-redirect-port=<n>
        Plain-HTTP port that 301-redirects to HTTPS (and answers ACME HTTP-01)

      --acme-domains, --acme-email, --acme-staging, --acme-directory,
      --acme-ca-file, --acme-challenge-port, --acme-cert-path, --acme-key-path,
      --acme-profile
        ACME settings (see above)

  -V, --version          Print the version and exit
      --help             Print usage and exit
      --check[=<file>]   Validate the configuration and exit (--format=json for JSON)
      --windows-service=<dir>
                         (Windows) Run as a service serving <dir>
```

# Building Apps Overview

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/overview/>

## Request lifecycle

Every request travels the same path regardless of which routing style you use:

```
main.rs
  └─ Server::setup()        — bind TCP listener
       └─ Server::run_tls()  — accept loop (plain HTTP via run_plain when no certificate);
            │                  TLS handshake; ALPN picks HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1
            └─ one task per connection — keep-alive loop; Request::parse()
                 └─ app.execute()  — your routing logic returns Result,
                 │                   run on tokio's blocking thread pool (or inline, see below)
                 └─ compression, metrics, Connection header, write response
```

The connection handler calls `app.execute(request, connection)` where `app` is any value that implements the `Application` trait. `execute` is synchronous and may block (read files, call a database or upstream): the server runs it on tokio's blocking thread pool, so a slow handler never stalls other connections. Requests for which `Application::runs_inline` returns `true` (the built-in `App`'s GET/HEAD — health, metrics, static files) skip that handoff and run directly on the event loop; see [Middleware](/building-apps/middleware/#running-on-the-event-loop-runs_inline). (The `http1`-only build has no async runtime; there each connection is served by `Server::process()` on a fixed-size worker thread pool.) The three routing styles differ only in how you implement or compose that `Application`.

`Server::setup()` reads the IP, port and thread count from the layered configuration (defaults → env vars → `rws.config.toml` → CLI args; see [Configuration](/configuration/overview/)) and returns the bound listener plus a thread pool. The async builds then pass your app to `Server::run_tls` (see [Quick Start](/getting-started/quick-start/)); the `http1`-only build uses the blocking `Server::run`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::server::Server;

fn main() {
    let (listener, pool) = match Server::setup() {
        Ok(v) => v,
        Err(e) => { eprintln!("{}", e); return; }
    };
    let app = MyApp::new();          // any type implementing Application + Clone
    Server::run(listener, pool, app);
}
```

## Three ways to add routes

### 1. Controller trait

The lowest-level option. Implement two static methods on a unit struct and register the struct in `App::execute`.

```rust
use rust_web_server::controller::Controller;
use rust_web_server::request::{METHOD, Request};
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::range::Range;
use rust_web_server::mime_type::MimeType;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;

pub struct PingController;

impl Controller for PingController {
    fn is_matching(request: &Request, _conn: &ConnectionInfo) -> bool {
        request.method == METHOD.get && request.request_uri == "/ping"
    }

    fn process(_req: &Request, mut response: Response, _conn: &ConnectionInfo) -> Response {
        response.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
        response.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
        response.content_range_list = vec![
            Range::get_content_range(b"pong".to_vec(), MimeType::TEXT_PLAIN.to_string())
        ];
        response
    }
}
```

Controllers are checked in declaration order inside `App::execute`; the first `is_matching` that returns `true` wins.

Use this style when you need precise control over matching logic that path patterns cannot express, or when you are extending the built-in controller chain.

### 2. Router

A fluent, path-based router with named parameters and wildcards. Call `router.handle(request, connection)` from inside any `Application::execute` implementation.

```rust
use rust_web_server::router::{Router, PathParams};
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::range::Range;
use rust_web_server::mime_type::MimeType;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let router = Router::new()
    .get("/hello", |_req, _params, _conn| {
        let mut r = Response::new();
        r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
        r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
        r.content_range_list = vec![
            Range::get_content_range(b"hello".to_vec(), MimeType::TEXT_PLAIN.to_string())
        ];
        r
    })
    .get("/users/:id", |_req, params, _conn| {
        let id = params.get("id").unwrap_or("unknown");
        let mut r = Response::new();
        r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
        r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
        r.content_range_list = vec![
            Range::get_content_range(
                format!("user {}", id).into_bytes(),
                MimeType::TEXT_PLAIN.to_string(),
            )
        ];
        r
    });
```

Use `Router` directly when you need to compose multiple routers (for example, one per virtual host) inside a custom `Application::execute`.

### 3. App::with_state (recommended for new code)

The highest-level option. `App::with_state(S)` creates an `AppWithState` that carries your state in an `Arc` and exposes `.get()`, `.post()`, `.put()`, `.patch()`, `.delete()` builder methods. Handlers receive `&S` directly.

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::routes;

struct Db { url: String }

let app = routes! {
    App::with_state(Db { url: "postgres://localhost/mydb".to_string() }),
    GET  "/users"     => list_users,
    POST "/users"     => create_user,
    GET  "/users/:id" => get_user,
};
```

Unmatched requests fall through to the built-in `App` controller chain (static files, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics`, 404).

## When to use which approach

| Situation | Recommended style |
|---|---|
| New CRUD endpoints with shared state | `App::with_state` + `routes!` |
| Virtual-host routing or path conditions | `Router::with_host` |
| Extend or override built-in behaviour | `Controller` trait |
| Add cross-cutting concerns | Middleware via `.wrap(layer)` |

## Application variants at a glance

- `App` — zero-config built-in app; `App::new()`.
- `AppWithState` — state-aware sync router; `App::with_state(S)`.
- `AsyncAppWithState` — same but handlers are `async fn`; requires the `http2` feature.
- `WithMiddleware` — wraps any `Application` with a middleware stack; `app.wrap(layer)`.
- `McpServer` — serves the MCP Streamable HTTP protocol; `app.mcp(name, version)`.

---

# Project layout and rws.app.toml

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/project-layout/>

Since 18.28.0 an rws application has one conventional layout, so a person or
a coding agent can find (and add) a route, a model or a migration without
reading the project first. The [starters](/getting-started/ai-agents/#start-from-a-starter)
use it; the [dev MCP endpoint](/mcp/dev-tools/)'s `layout` tool reports it,
and [`rws gen`](/building-apps/generators/) (18.29.0) writes models, routes,
migrations and tests into it:

```sh
rws gen model Post title:String       # src/models/post.rs + migrations/0001_create_posts.sql
rws gen route posts                   # src/routes/posts.rs, registered in app()
rws gen test posts                    # tests/posts.rs
rws db migrate                        # apply migrations/ (rws db status|rollback|seed)
```

```text
my-app/
├── rws.app.toml          the manifest: the app's name, paths that differ
├── Cargo.toml
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs           wiring only: settings, dev_mcp, Server::run_tls
│   ├── lib.rs            app(): the routes and middleware, built in a function
│   ├── routes/           typed handlers (#[get] …), one module per resource
│   │   ├── mod.rs
│   │   └── posts.rs
│   ├── models/           #[derive(Model)] types, one module per table
│   └── jobs/             background jobs and scheduled tasks
├── migrations/           0001_create_posts.sql, 0001_create_posts.down.sql, …
├── templates/            Tera templates
├── tests/                integration tests against app() (TestClient)
└── static/               files served as they are
```

| Role | Path | What goes there |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | `src/main.rs` | Wiring only: `Server::setup()`, `app().dev_mcp_with(…)`, `Server::run_tls`. Nothing a test needs. |
| `lib` | `src/lib.rs` | `pub fn app() -> …` building every route and layer, so `tests/` can call it; the state type; `dev_tools()` |
| `routes` | `src/routes/` | One module per resource: its [typed handlers](/building-apps/routing/#typed-handlers-get-with-extractors) and a `register(app) -> app` that adds them (`app.route(list).route(show)`) |
| `models` | `src/models/` | [`#[derive(Model)]`](/database/model-derive/) types, one module per table |
| `jobs` | `src/jobs/` | [Jobs](/features/jobs/) and scheduled tasks |
| `migrations` | `migrations/` | `NNNN_name.sql`, applied in order, each with an optional `NNNN_name.down.sql` for rollback ([migrations](/database/migrations/)) |
| `templates` | `templates/` | [Tera templates](/building-apps/templates/) |
| `tests` | `tests/` | Integration tests: `TestClient::new(my_app::app())` |
| `static` | `static/` | Static files |

A binary-only crate can't be tested from `tests/`, hence `src/lib.rs`: the
binary is a few lines that serve what the library builds.

```rust
// src/main.rs
use rust_web_server::dev_mcp::DevMcpExt;
use rust_web_server::server::Server;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().expect("server setup");
    let app = my_app::app().dev_mcp_with(my_app::dev_tools());
    Server::run_tls(listener, pool, app).await;
}
```

```rust
// src/lib.rs
pub mod routes;

use rust_web_server::dev_mcp::DevTools;
use rust_web_server::prelude::*;
use rust_web_server::state::AppWithState;

#[derive(Clone, Default)] // the server clones the app per worker
pub struct Db {
    pub posts: std::collections::HashMap<u64, String>, // or a DbPool
}

pub fn app() -> AppWithState {
    routes::posts::register(App::with_state(Db::default()))
}

pub fn dev_tools() -> DevTools {
    DevTools::new().app_dir(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"))
}
```

```rust
// src/routes/posts.rs
use rust_web_server::error::AppError;
use rust_web_server::handler::{Json, Path};
use rust_web_server::state::AppWithState;
use rust_web_server::get;

use crate::Db;

#[get("/posts/{id}")]
pub fn show(Path(id): Path<u64>, db: &Db) -> Result, AppError> {
    db.posts.get(&id).cloned().map(Json).ok_or_else(|| AppError::NotFound(format!("no post {id}")))
}

pub fn register(app: AppWithState) -> AppWithState {
    app.route(show)
}
```

## rws.app.toml

The manifest sits at the project root. It names the app and says where the
project differs from the layout; every key is optional, so an empty file —
or none — means "conventional":

```toml
[app]
name = "blog"              # default: Cargo.toml's [package] name, else the directory's

[paths]
static = "frontend/dist"   # only what differs; the rest keep their defaults
```

| Key | Default |
|---|---|
| `[app] name` | `[package] name` from `Cargo.toml`, else the directory's name |
| `[paths] main` | `src/main.rs` |
| `[paths] lib` | `src/lib.rs` |
| `[paths] routes` | `src/routes` |
| `[paths] models` | `src/models` |
| `[paths] jobs` | `src/jobs` |
| `[paths] migrations` | `migrations` |
| `[paths] templates` | `templates` |
| `[paths] tests` | `tests` |
| `[paths] static` | `static` |

- Values are TOML strings (`"…"` or `'…'`); `# comments` are allowed;
  `paths.static = "…"` at the top level is the same as the key in `[paths]`.
- Paths are relative to the project root and stay inside it: a leading `/`,
  a drive letter or a `..` is an error, as is a key set twice. Errors name
  the line: ``rws.app.toml line 3: `routes` = "/srv/x" is absolute; paths
  are relative to the project root``.
- Unknown keys and tables are warnings, not errors, so a manifest written
  for a newer release still loads.
- The manifest describes the project; rws doesn't move files or change
  routing because of it. `rws gen` writes where it says. The `mcp` starter, whose "routes" are MCP tools,
  says `routes = "src/tools"`.

Read it in code with `app_manifest::AppManifest`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app_manifest::AppManifest;

let manifest = AppManifest::load(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR"))?; // conventional when absent
println!("{} keeps its models in {}", manifest.name, manifest.paths.models);
for entry in manifest.layout(env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")) {
    println!("{:<10} {:<14} {}", entry.role, entry.path, if entry.exists { "ok" } else { "missing" });
}
```

`AppManifest::parse(text)` (or `text.parse::()`) reads a
manifest from a string; files over 64 KiB are refused.

---

# Generators (rws gen)

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/generators/>

Since 18.29.0 `rws gen` writes the four things an app gets more of — a
model, a resource's routes, a migration, a test — into a project in the
[conventional layout](/building-apps/project-layout/). What it writes is
pinned to the API of the rws release you run (CI generates into every
[starter](/getting-started/ai-agents/#start-from-a-starter) and runs the
generated tests), and it never overwrites a file: running a generator twice
changes nothing the second time, and a file that is in the way is a conflict,
shown as a diff. There is no `rws new` — new projects start from a starter.

```sh
rws gen model Post title:String views:i64 published:bool 'note:Option'
rws gen route posts            # the model's fields; or: rws gen route posts title:String
rws gen test posts
rws gen migration add_index_to_posts
cargo test
```

Use the `rws` binary of the release the project depends on
(`cargo install rust-web-server --version <x.y.z>`, or any of the
[installation](/getting-started/installation/) packages): its output names
that release in each file's header and is written against its API.

The same generators are tools of the [dev MCP endpoint](/mcp/dev-tools/#generators)
(`gen_model`, `gen_route`, `gen_migration`, `gen_test`), and a library
module, `rust_web_server::generator`.

## What each generator writes

| Command | Creates | Adds a line to |
|---|---|---|
| `rws gen model  field:type…` | `src/models/<name>.rs`, `migrations/NNNN_create_<table>.sql` and `.down.sql` | `src/models/mod.rs` (`pub mod post;`, `pub use post::Post;`; created when missing), `src/lib.rs` (`pub mod models;`), `Cargo.toml` (the `model-<db>` feature) |
| `rws gen route <resource> [field:type…]` | `src/routes/<resource>.rs` | `src/routes/mod.rs`, `app()` in `src/lib.rs` (the routes are registered) |
| `rws gen migration <name>` | `migrations/NNNN_<name>.sql` and `.down.sql` | — |
| `rws gen test <resource>` | `tests/<resource>.rs` | — |

The paths are those of `rws.app.toml` (`[paths] models`, `routes`,
`migrations`, `tests`, `lib`), so a project that keeps its routes elsewhere
gets them there. A line is added only where it can be placed safely — beside
the other `mod` lines, inside the existing `register(…)` call of `app()`, in a
one-line `rust-web-server = { … }` dependency; otherwise the plan ends with a
`note:` saying what to add by hand.

### Models

```sh
rws gen model Post title:String views:i64 published:bool 'note:Option'
```

```rust
// src/models/post.rs
//! `Post`: the `posts` table (migrations/0001_create_posts.sql).
//!
//! Generated by `rws gen model Post title:String views:i64 published:bool note:Option` (rws 18.29.0).

use rust_web_server::Model;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Model)]
#[table(name = "posts")]
pub struct Post {
    #[primary_key(auto_increment)]
    pub id: i64,
    pub title: String,
    pub views: i64,
    pub published: bool,
    pub note: Option,
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    // maps_to_the_posts_table: the table, columns and primary key;
    // round_trips_through_sqlite (SQLite only): the migrations applied to an
    // in-memory database, then save, find_by_id, delete_by_id.
}
```

- The name may be `Post`, `BlogPost` or `blog_post`: the module is
  snake_case (`blog_post.rs`), the type CamelCase, the table the snake_case
  plural (`blog_posts`). Every model gets `id: i64`, auto-increment.
- Field types are a fixed list: `i64`, `i32`, `f64`, `bool`, `String`, and
  `Option` of those (a nullable column). Anything else is refused with that
  list.
- The database is `--db sqlite|postgres|mysql`, else the `model-*` feature
  the project's `Cargo.toml` already enables, else SQLite; the feature is added
  when missing. The migration's column types follow it:

| Rust | SQLite | PostgreSQL | MySQL |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` | `BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY` | `BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY` |
| `i64` | `INTEGER` | `BIGINT` | `BIGINT` |
| `i32` | `INTEGER` | `INTEGER` | `INT` |
| `f64` | `REAL` | `DOUBLE PRECISION` | `DOUBLE` |
| `bool` | `INTEGER` | `BOOLEAN` | `BOOLEAN` |
| `String` | `TEXT` | `TEXT` | `TEXT` |

  Columns are `NOT NULL` unless the field is an `Option`.
- The migration is numbered after the highest `NNNN_` in `migrations/`; the
  down file drops the table.
- To list the model in the dev MCP endpoint's `models` tool, add
  `.model::<models::Post>()` to your `DevTools` (the plan's note says so).
- `--timestamps` and `--soft-delete` (18.30.0) add the repository's
  [conventions](/database/conventions/): `#[timestamps]` with
  `created_at: Timestamp` and `updated_at: Timestamp` (columns `NOT NULL`),
  `#[soft_delete]` with `deleted_at: Option` (nullable). The
  columns are `TEXT` on SQLite, `TIMESTAMPTZ` on PostgreSQL, `DATETIME(6)` on
  MySQL; the `serde` feature is added for `Timestamp`'s `Serialize`. A field
  of the same name is refused — `save` and `delete_by_id` write these columns.

  ```sh
  rws gen model Comment body:String post_id:i64 --timestamps --soft-delete
  ```

  ```rust
  #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Serialize, Deserialize, Model)]
  #[table(name = "comments")]
  #[timestamps]
  #[soft_delete]
  pub struct Comment {
      #[primary_key(auto_increment)]
      pub id: i64,
      pub body: String,
      pub post_id: i64,
      pub created_at: Timestamp,
      pub updated_at: Timestamp,
      pub deleted_at: Option,
  }
  ```

### Routes

```sh
rws gen route posts title:String views:i64 [--methods list,show,create,update,remove] [--prefix /api]
```

writes typed handlers — `#[get("/posts")] list`, `#[get("/posts/{id}")] show`,
`#[post("/posts")] create` (201), `#[put("/posts/{id}")] update`,
`#[delete("/posts/{id}")] remove` — a `Post` and a `NewPost` (the request
body) type, and

```rust
/// Add these routes to the app.
pub fn register(app: AppWithState<crate::Store>) -> AppWithState<crate::Store> {
    app.route(list).route(show).route(create).route(update).route(remove)
}
```

The app type and its state come from `pub fn app(…) -> AppWithState` (or
`AsyncAppWithState`) in `src/lib.rs`, and `app()`'s existing
`routes::…::register(…)` call is wrapped:
`routes::posts::register(routes::todos::register(App::with_state(…)))`. A
project whose `lib.rs` has no such `app()` — the `mcp` starter builds an
`McpServer` — is refused.

Without fields, the routes take the fields of `src/models/<singular>.rs` when
there is one, else `name: String`. The handlers keep the items in memory, in
the module (`static STORE`): they work and are tested as they are; replace the
store with the app's state or the model's repository when the data must outlast
the process. Unknown ids answer `404`, ids that aren't numbers `400`, bodies that
aren't JSON of the right shape `400` — problem details, as every rws error.

### Migrations

```sh
rws gen migration add_index_to_posts
```

writes `migrations/0002_add_index_to_posts.sql` and `.down.sql`, each holding
a statement that changes nothing (`SELECT 1;`) under a comment, so the files
apply as they are until you replace it. `DbPool::migrate` splits a file at
semicolons — keep them out of comments ([migrations](/database/migrations/)).

### Tests

```sh
rws gen test posts [--app-expr 'app(Store::memory())']
```

reads the routes `src/routes/posts.rs` declares (`#[get("…")]` and the like)
and the fields of its `NewPost`, and writes `tests/posts.rs`: a round trip
through every route there (create, show, list, update, remove, then `404`),
and the errors (`404` for an unknown id, `400` for a non-numeric id and for a
body that isn't JSON) — through `TestClient`, no socket. The test builds the
app with `app()`; when `app` takes arguments, with what the existing tests in
`tests/` pass to `TestClient::new`, or `--app-expr`.

### Migrations from the models

`rws gen migration <name> --from-models` writes the migration that brings the database up to the `#[derive(Model)]` structs in `src/models/` (18.35.0): a `CREATE TABLE` for a model whose table isn't there, an `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` for a field whose column isn't. It reads the database like [`rws db`](/database/migrations/#from-the-command-line-rws-db) (`--database-url`, else `DATABASE_URL`, else `RWS_DB_*`) and writes SQL for the `model-*` feature in `Cargo.toml` (or `--db`):

```sh
rws gen model Post title:String          # later: add `pub summary: Option` to the struct
rws gen migration add_post_summary --from-models --dry-run
# migrations/0003_add_post_summary.sql:  ALTER TABLE posts ADD COLUMN summary TEXT;
```

It is **additive only**: nothing is dropped, renamed or retyped. Columns the database has and the model doesn't, fields whose type has no SQL mapping (anything but integers, floats, `bool`, `String`, `Timestamp`, `Uuid`, `Attachment` and their `Option`s) and a missing primary key are listed as notes to write by hand. A new required column gets a `DEFAULT` (`0`, `FALSE`, `''`) so existing rows can take it; `#[column(name = …)]`, `#[ignore]` and `#[table(name = …)]` are followed. When the database already matches, nothing is written. As a library: `generator::plan_model_migration(dir, name, &existing_columns, db)`.

## Conflicts, dry runs, JSON

```text
$ rws gen model Post title:String          # after the one above
conflict   src/models/post.rs
unchanged  src/models/mod.rs
…
--- a/src/models/post.rs
+++ b/src/models/post.rs
@@ -11,9 +11,6 @@
     #[primary_key(auto_increment)]
     pub id: i64,
     pub title: String,
-    pub views: i64,
…
rws gen: not written — a file above exists with other content (the diff is what the generator would write). Move it aside or merge by hand.
```

- A file the generator creates is never replaced. If it exists with exactly
  what the generator would write, it is `unchanged`; with anything else it is
  a `conflict`, the diff goes from the file to what would be written, and
  **nothing** of the plan is written. Re-running the same command is safe.
- `--dry-run` prints the plan with every diff and writes nothing.
- `--json` prints the plan for agents:
  `{"command":"rws gen model Post title:String","status":"written","written":true,"changes":[{"path":"src/models/post.rs","action":"create","diff":"--- /dev/null\n+++ b/src/models/post.rs\n…"}],"notes":[…]}`
  — `status` is `written`, `planned` (dry run), `unchanged` or `conflict`;
  errors are `{"status":"usage"|"refused","error":"…"}`.
- `--dir <project>` runs against another directory (default: the working
  directory, which must hold the project's `Cargo.toml`).

Exit codes: `0` written (or nothing to do), `1` a conflict or a project the
generator can't work with (no `app()`, no route module for `gen test`), `2` a
usage error (a bad name or type, an unknown option).

Names are identifiers — letters, digits and single `_`, starting with a letter,
at most 64 characters, not a Rust keyword — so no generated path leaves the
project; a resource whose type would clash with a name the generated code
imports (`paths` → `Path`, `values` → `Value`) is refused.

## From Rust

```rust
use rust_web_server::generator::{plan, Field, Generate};

let request = Generate::Model {
    name: "Post".into(),
    fields: vec![Field::parse("title:String")?],
    db: None,
};
let plan = plan(".", &request)?;    // reads only
print!("{}", plan.render(true));    // one line per file, then the diffs
if !plan.has_conflicts() {
    plan.apply(".")?;                // writes; refuses if a file changed since
}
```

`Plan` has the `changes` (`FileChange { path, kind, content, original, diff }`,
`kind` one of `Create`, `Edit`, `Unchanged`, `Conflict`), the `notes`, and
`to_json(written)`; `generator::run(args, out, err)` is the command line.

# Controllers

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/controllers/>

## The Controller trait

`Controller` is defined in `crates/rws-server/src/controller/mod.rs` and has two static methods:

```rust
pub trait Controller {
    fn is_matching(request: &Request, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> bool;
    fn process(request: &Request, response: Response, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Response;
}
```

- `is_matching` — called in declaration order inside `App::execute`; the first controller that returns `true` wins.
- `process` — receives the partially-built `response` (already populated with standard headers from `Header::get_header_list`) and must return it with a status code and body.

## Complete minimal example

```rust
use rust_web_server::controller::Controller;
use rust_web_server::request::{METHOD, Request};
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::range::Range;
use rust_web_server::mime_type::MimeType;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;

pub struct HelloController;

impl Controller for HelloController {
    fn is_matching(request: &Request, _conn: &ConnectionInfo) -> bool {
        request.method == METHOD.get && request.request_uri == "/hello"
    }

    fn process(_req: &Request, mut response: Response, _conn: &ConnectionInfo) -> Response {
        response.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
        response.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
        response.content_range_list = vec![
            Range::get_content_range(
                b"Hello, world!".to_vec(),
                MimeType::TEXT_PLAIN.to_string(),
            )
        ];
        response
    }
}
```

## Registering a controller

Controllers are hardcoded in `App::execute` inside `crates/rws-server/src/app/mod.rs`. To add your own, you currently need a custom `Application` implementation that checks your controller before (or after) the built-in list:

```rust
use rust_web_server::application::Application;
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::controller::Controller;
use rust_web_server::header::Header;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

pub struct MyApp;

impl Application for MyApp {
    fn execute(&self, request: &Request, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Result {
        // Check custom controllers first
        if HelloController::is_matching(request, connection) {
            let header_list = Header::get_header_list(request);
            let response = Response::get_response(
                STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n501_not_implemented,
                Some(header_list),
                None,
            );
            return Ok(HelloController::process(request, response, connection));
        }
        // Fall through to the built-in controller chain
        App::new().execute(request, connection)
    }
}
```

## Built-in controllers

These are registered in `App::execute` in this order (first match wins):

| Controller | Matches |
|---|---|
| `IndexController` | `GET /` — serves `index.html` from the static directory |
| `StyleController` | `GET /style.css` |
| `ScriptController` | `GET /script.js` |
| `DirectoryListingAssetsController` | `GET /rws-directory-listing.css` / `.js` — same-origin CSS/JS for the directory listing page below |
| `FileUploadInitiateController` | `POST /file-upload/initiate` |
| `FormUrlEncodedEnctypePostMethodController` | `POST /form-url-encoded-enctype-post-method` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` |
| `FormGetMethodController` | `GET /form-get-method` (with query parameters) |
| `FormMultipartEnctypePostMethodController` | `POST /form-multipart-enctype-post-method` with `multipart/form-data` |
| `HealthController` | `GET /healthz` — returns `200 OK` |
| `ReadyController` | `GET /readyz` — returns `200` when `SERVER_READY` is set, `503` otherwise |
| `MetricsController` | `GET /metrics` — Prometheus text format |
| `FaviconController` | `GET /favicon.svg` |
| `StaticResourceController` | Any `GET` for a file found under the static directory; a directory with no `index.html` renders a directory listing page instead of falling through to `404` |
| `NotFoundController` | Catch-all — returns `404 Not Found` |

:::note[Prefer App::with_state for new routes]
For new application routes, `App::with_state(S).get(pattern, handler)` or the `routes!` macro is less boilerplate than writing a custom `Controller` implementation and wiring it into a custom `Application`. Use `Controller` when you need matching logic that path patterns cannot express, or when you need to intercept built-in behaviour.
:::

# Routing

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/routing/>

## routes! macro

The `routes!` macro is the recommended way to declare routes for new code. It builds an `AppWithState` (or any builder that exposes `.get()`, `.post()`, etc.) from a declarative table.

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::routes;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::router::PathParams;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::core::New;

struct Db;

fn list_users(_req: &Request, _params: &PathParams, _conn: &ConnectionInfo, _db: &Db) -> Response {
    let mut r = Response::new();
    r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
    r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
    r
}

fn create_user(_req: &Request, _params: &PathParams, _conn: &ConnectionInfo, _db: &Db) -> Response {
    let mut r = Response::new();
    r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n201_created.status_code;
    r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n201_created.reason_phrase.to_string();
    r
}

let app = routes! {
    App::with_state(Db),
    GET  "/users"     => list_users,
    POST "/users"     => create_user,
};
```

Syntax:

```text
routes! {
    <builder_expression>,
    METHOD "pattern" => handler_or_closure,
    ...
}
```

Valid methods: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` (all caps). A trailing comma after the last route is optional.

## Router — direct usage

Use `Router` directly when you need to compose multiple routers or call `handle` inside a custom `Application::execute`.

```rust
use rust_web_server::router::{Router, PathParams};
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::range::Range;
use rust_web_server::mime_type::MimeType;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let router = Router::new()
    .get("/users/:id", |_req, params, _conn| {
        let id = params.get("id").unwrap_or("unknown");
        let mut r = Response::new();
        r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
        r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
        r.content_range_list = vec![Range::get_content_range(
            format!("user {}", id).into_bytes(),
            MimeType::TEXT_PLAIN.to_string(),
        )];
        r
    })
    .delete("/users/:id", |_req, params, _conn| {
        let mut r = Response::new();
        r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n204_no_content.status_code;
        r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n204_no_content.reason_phrase.to_string();
        r
    });

// Inside Application::execute:
// if let Some(response) = router.handle(request, connection) {
//     return Ok(response);
// }
```

`router.handle(request, connection)` returns `Some(Response)` on the first match, `None` if no route matches. Routes are tried in registration order.

## Pattern syntax

| Syntax | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `/literal` | Exact path segment | `/users` |
| `/:name` or `/{name}` | Named segment — captures one segment | `/users/:id`, `/users/{id}` |
| `/*name` or `/{*name}` | Wildcard — captures everything after the prefix | `/files/*path`, `/files/{*path}` |
| `/{{text}}` | Literal braces | `/raw/{{id}}` matches `/raw/{id}` |

The braced forms (since 18.7.0) are what axum 0.8 and OpenAPI use; the two syntaxes mean the same thing and can be mixed. A brace parameter takes a whole segment — `/file.{ext}` is a literal, not a parameter.

Rules:
- A wildcard (`*name`, `{*name}`) must be the **last** segment in a pattern.
- The query string is stripped before matching; only the path is used.
- Patterns are matched segment-by-segment; `/users` does not match `/users/42`.

```rust
// /users/42/posts/7 → id="42", post_id="7"
router.get("/users/:id/posts/:post_id", handler);

// /files/a/b/c.txt → path="a/b/c.txt"
router.get("/files/*path", handler);
```

## PathParams extraction

Inside a handler, call `params.get("name")` to retrieve a named segment value. It returns `Option<&str>`.

```rust
.get("/articles/:slug", |_req, params, _conn| {
    let slug = params.get("slug").unwrap_or("unknown");
    // use slug ...
    Response::new()
})
```

## Virtual-host routing

Call `.with_host("example.com")` before registering routes to restrict a router to requests whose SNI hostname (TLS) or `Host` header (plain HTTP) matches that value.

```rust
let api_router = Router::new()
    .with_host("api.example.com")
    .get("/status", api_status_handler);

let www_router = Router::new()
    .with_host("www.example.com")
    .get("/", home_handler);

// In Application::execute:
// api_router.handle(request, connection)
//     .or_else(|| www_router.handle(request, connection))
```

`handle()` returns `None` immediately when `.with_host()` is set and the incoming request's hostname does not match, so composing multiple host-scoped routers is safe and efficient.

## Relationship to `App`'s built-in routes

`App`'s built-in controllers — static file serving, `/healthz`/`/readyz`/`/metrics`, form handling, the 404 fallback — deliberately don't go through `Router`. That set is small, static, and known at compile time, so a fixed if-chain is simpler and just as fast as a segment matcher would be there. `Router` is for **your** routes, with dynamic path params and wildcards a fixed if-chain can't express cleanly.

`AppWithState` and `AsyncAppWithState` already compose the two: they hold a `Router` internally, try it first, and fall through to `App`'s built-in controller chain for anything the router doesn't match — so static files, health checks, and metrics keep working automatically even in a fully custom, stateful app.

## Typed handlers: `#[get]` with extractors

Since 18.28.0 a handler can take [extractors](/building-apps/extractors/#extractors-as-handler-arguments) as arguments and return anything that implements `IntoResponse`; the route attribute (`macros` feature) generates the adapter and the app takes the method and pattern from it:

```toml
# Cargo.toml
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["macros", "serde"] }
```

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::error::AppError;
use rust_web_server::handler::{Json, Path, State};
use rust_web_server::{get, post};

struct Db { /* pool, … */ }

#[get("/posts/{id}")]
fn show_post(Path(id): Path<u64>, State(db): State) -> Result, AppError> {
    db.find(id).map(Json).ok_or_else(|| AppError::NotFound(format!("no post {id}")))
}

#[post("/posts")]
fn create_post(Json(new): Json, db: &Db) -> Result, AppError> {
    db.insert(new).map(Json)
}

let app = App::with_state(Db { /* … */ })
    .route(show_post)
    .route(create_post);
```

- `#[get]`, `#[post]`, `#[put]`, `#[patch]`, `#[delete]` and `#[route(METHOD, "/path")]` turn the function into a unit struct of the same name implementing `handler::Handler` (and `AsyncHandler`). `.route(h)` registers it on `AppWithState`, on `Router` (handlers without state arguments) and on `AsyncAppWithState`, where `async fn` handlers go too. The function as written stays callable as `show_post::call(Path(1), State(db))`, e.g. in unit tests.
- The generated `handle` runs the extractors in argument order and calls the function: the same work as a handler that calls them by hand, behind the same route dispatch, with no extra allocation for a classic handler's path.
- The first extractor that fails answers the request with its rejection (`400`, `415`, `422`, … as problem details); the function doesn't run.
- `show_post::METHOD` and `show_post::PATTERN` (trait `handler::RouteSpec`) are the attribute's arguments.

**Checked at compile time** — the route's parameters against the `Path` argument:

| Mistake | Error |
|---|---|
| `#[get("/posts/{id}")] fn f(Path(post_id): Path<u64>)` | `` `post_id` is not a parameter of route `GET /posts/{id}` `` |
| `#[get("/posts/{id}")] fn f(Path((id, slug)): Path<(u64, String)>)` | the tuple takes 2, the route has 1 |
| `#[get("/posts/{id}/{slug}")] fn f(Path(id): Path<u64>)` | a scalar takes one parameter |
| `#[post("/posts/{id}/comments")] fn f(State(db): State)` | `{id}` isn't taken by any `Path` (or `&PathParams`) argument |
| `#[get("/posts")] fn f(Path(id): Path<u64>)` | the route has no parameters |
| a `#[derive(FromPath)]` struct whose fields aren't exactly the route's parameters | a `const` assertion naming the route |

A name bound inside `Path(…)` names the route parameter it takes (as in Rocket), so a tuple's bindings may come in any order: `Path((slug, id))` for `/posts/{id}/{slug}`. A plain binding (`p: Path<(u64, String)>`) or `_` takes them in route order. `/posts/:id` and `/posts/{id}` are the same route.

**Classic handlers are unchanged.** On a function with the classic signature — `(&Request, &PathParams, &ConnectionInfo)` plus the state for `AppWithState` (or `AsyncAppWithState`'s owned form) — the attribute only adds a `Route: METHOD /path` doc comment, as before 18.28.0, and you register it with `.get(pattern, handler)` or `routes!`.

## Route conflicts

A route registered after one with the same method that matches every path it does never runs: routes are tried in order and the first match wins. `AppWithState`, `AsyncAppWithState` and `Router` report these when the route is added — one line on stderr per distinct conflict — and list them with `route_conflicts()`:

```rust
let app = App::with_state(db)
    .get("/users/:id", show_user)
    .get("/users/me", me)          // shadowed: /users/:id answers /users/me
    .get("/users/{uid}", other);   // duplicate: same pattern as /users/:id

for conflict in app.route_conflicts() {
    eprintln!("{conflict}");
}
// rws: warning: route GET /users/me never runs: GET /users/:id, registered before it, matches every path it does
```

Each `RouteConflict` has the `method`, the `pattern` that never runs, the `earlier` one that answers instead, and a `kind` (`Duplicate`: the same pattern, parameter names aside; `Shadowed`: the earlier one has a parameter or wildcard where it has a literal). It's a warning only — the app is built and serves as before; register the specific route first (`/users/me`, then `/users/:id`). Patterns that only overlap (`/a/:x` and `/:y/b`) aren't reported. A test can assert `app.route_conflicts().is_empty()`.

## Groups and guards

`group(prefix, |g| …)` registers routes under a shared path prefix. They share guards — checks that run before the handler (`before_action`) — and, on `AppWithState`, middleware (18.35.0):

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::flash::Redirect;
use rust_web_server::error::IntoResponse;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::Response;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;

fn signed_in(request: &Request, _: &ConnectionInfo, _: &Db) -> Result<(), Response> {
    match current_user(request) {
        Some(_) => Ok(()),
        None => Err(Redirect::to("/login").alert("Sign in first").into_response()),
    }
}

let app = App::with_state(db)
    .get("/", home)
    .group("/admin", |admin| {
        admin
            .guard(signed_in)
            .wrap(RateLimitLayer)            // only these routes (AppWithState)
            .get("/", dashboard)
            .route(export_csv)               // a typed #[get("/export")] handler: /admin/export
            .group("/billing", |billing| billing.guard(is_owner).get("/", invoices))
    });
```

A guard is `Fn(&Request, &ConnectionInfo, &S) -> Result<(), Response>`; `Err(response)` answers the request. Guards apply to every route of the group, whichever order they were added in, outer groups' first. Groups nest. On `AsyncAppWithState` (`group` takes async handlers) groups have guards but no `wrap`: wrap the whole app instead.

## Resources

`resource(path, |r| …)` registers the conventional routes of a collection, each with a name for [`url_for`](#named-routes-and-url_for):

| Method | Path | Builder | Name |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/posts` | `index` | `posts.index` |
| GET | `/posts/new` | `new_form` | `posts.new` |
| POST | `/posts` | `create` | `posts.create` |
| GET | `/posts/{id}` | `show` | `posts.show` |
| GET | `/posts/{id}/edit` | `edit` | `posts.edit` |
| PUT, PATCH | `/posts/{id}` | `update` | `posts.update` |
| DELETE | `/posts/{id}` | `destroy` | `posts.destroy` |

```rust
let app = App::with_state(db).resource("/posts", |posts| {
    posts
        .index(list_posts)
        .new_form(new_post_form)
        .create(create_post)
        .show(show_post)       // params.get("id")
        .destroy(delete_post)
        .guard(signed_in)
        .extra(|g| g.post("/{id}/publish", publish_post))
});
```

Only the actions you give are registered, and `new` always comes before `{id}`. `.name("articles")` changes the name prefix (default: the path's last segment); `extra` adds routes under the resource's path with its guards. A group has `resource` too, so `/admin/posts` is `admin.resource("/posts", …)`. Handlers have the classic signature (`AsyncAppWithState`: the async one); typed `#[get]` handlers go in a group with `.route(…)`.

## Named routes and `url_for`

`.name("…")` after a route names it; `router::url_for(name, params)` builds its path, percent-encoding the values. Parameters the pattern doesn't have become the query string:

```rust
use rust_web_server::router::url_for;

let app = App::with_state(db).get("/posts/{id}", show_post).name("post");

assert_eq!(Some("/posts/7?tab=comments".to_string()), url_for("post", &[("id", "7"), ("tab", "comments")]));
assert_eq!(None, url_for("post", &[]));                      // a parameter is missing
```

Names are process-wide (registering one again replaces it) and `named_routes()` lists them. Templates call it as `url_for(name="post", id=7)` ([view helpers](/building-apps/templates/#view-helpers)); `Redirect::to_route(name, params)` redirects to one ([flash](/building-apps/forms-uploads/#flash-messages-and-redirects)).

See the [API reference](/reference/api/) for the full list of public types.

---

# Request & Response

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/request-response/>

## Request

`Request` is defined in `crates/rws-http/src/request/mod.rs`:

```rust
pub struct Request {
    pub method: String,       // "GET", "POST", etc.
    pub request_uri: String,  // "/search?q=rust"
    pub http_version: String, // "HTTP/1.1"
    pub headers: Vec,
    pub body: Body,           // the body (since 18.0.0; was Vec<u8>)
}
```

### The body

`request.body` is a `request::Body` (since 18.0.0). It dereferences to
`&[u8]`, so `&request.body[..]`, `request.body.len()` and
`String::from_utf8_lossy(&request.body)` work as before; `.to_vec()` gives a
`Vec<u8>`. Build one from bytes or text with `.into()`
(`body: b"data".to_vec().into()`, `body: "text".into()`) or `Default::default()`
for none.

The server reads the whole body before your handler runs, as it always has.
A `Body` can also be a stream (`Body::stream(reader)`, `body.is_stream()`):
read it with `std::io::Read` (`(&request.body).read(..)`), `into_reader()`,
or all at once with `body_bytes()`.

### METHOD constants

Compare `request.method` against the `METHOD` constant instead of string literals:

```rust
use rust_web_server::request::{METHOD, Request};

fn is_get(request: &Request) -> bool {
    request.method == METHOD.get
}
```

Available fields: `METHOD.get`, `METHOD.head`, `METHOD.post`, `METHOD.put`, `METHOD.delete`, `METHOD.connect`, `METHOD.options`, `METHOD.trace`, `METHOD.patch`.

### Helper methods

```rust
// Parse the query string into a HashMaplet query: Option> = request.get_query().unwrap();

// Extract just the path, stripping the query string
let path: String = request.get_path().unwrap();

// Get a specific header (case-insensitive)
let content_type: Option<&Header> = request.get_header("Content-Type".to_string());

// Extract the Host header's domain component
let domain: Option = request.get_domain().unwrap();
```

`request.header(name)` is the allocation-free variant of `get_header`: it takes a `&str` and also matches case-insensitively.

```rust
use rust_web_server::header::Header;

match request.header(Header::_AUTHORIZATION) {
    Some(h) => println!("Authorization: {}", h.value),
    None    => { /* not present */ }
}
```

### Client address

`ConnectionInfo`, passed to every controller and handler, carries the peer address. `peer_addr()` returns it as a `std::net::SocketAddr`; the raw `client.ip` / `client.port` fields are also public:

```rust
fn process(_request: &Request, response: Response, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Response {
    if let Some(addr) = connection.peer_addr() {
        println!("request from {}", addr);   // e.g. "127.0.0.1:54321"
    }
    println!("ip={} port={}", connection.client.ip, connection.client.port);
    response
}
```

This is the TCP peer. Behind a load balancer it is the balancer's address. For the
client behind it, ask `client_ip`: when the peer is one of your
[`trusted_proxies`](/proxy/reverse-proxy/#the-client-address), it reads the
client from `X-Forwarded-For` (or `Forwarded`); otherwise it returns the peer
(since 18.27.0). The rate limit, IP filter, blocklist, WAF and access log use
the same address.

```rust
let client = rust_web_server::ip_filter::client_ip(&request, &connection.client.ip);
```

## Response

`Response` is defined in `crates/rws-http/src/response/mod.rs`:

```rust
pub struct Response {
    pub http_version: String,             // "HTTP/1.1"
    pub status_code: i16,                 // 200, 404, etc.
    pub reason_phrase: String,            // "OK", "Not Found", etc.
    pub headers: Vec,
    pub content_range_list: Vec, // response body parts
    pub stream_file: Option,      // path of a file streamed from disk
    pub stream_pipe: Option>, // reader piped chunked; wins over both
}
```

### Building a response with get_response

The most concise way to build a response:

```rust
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::header::Header;
use rust_web_server::range::Range;
use rust_web_server::mime_type::MimeType;

let body = Range::get_content_range(
    b"{\"ok\":true}".to_vec(),
    MimeType::APPLICATION_JSON.to_string(),
);

let response = Response::get_response(
    STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok,
    Some(Header::get_header_list(request)), // standard response headers
    Some(vec![body]),
);
```

`Response::get_response` signature:

```rust
pub fn get_response(
    status_code_reason_phrase: &StatusCodeReasonPhrase,
    boxed_header_list: Option>,
    boxed_content_range_list: Option>,
) -> Response
```

Pass `None` for headers to get an empty header list. Pass `None` for the body list to get an empty body (useful for `204 No Content`). A `1xx`, `204` or `304` response is always sent without a body or `Content-Length`, whatever the handler put in it (`Response::drop_content_for_status`; since 17.113.2). A `HEAD` response keeps the `Content-Length` of the `GET` it stands for, without the body.

### One-line JSON / text responses

For the common case — a JSON or plain-text body with no extra headers — `Response::json`/`Response::text` skip `get_response`/`Range::get_content_range` entirely:

```rust
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};

let response = Response::json(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok, b"{\"ok\":true}".to_vec());
let error_response = Response::text(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n400_bad_request, "invalid input");
```

`Response::json` takes already-serialized bytes, so it has no dependency on the `serde` feature — build `bytes` with `serde_json::to_vec(&value)?` or hand-rolled JSON. See [JSON](/building-apps/json/) for the `serde`-backed `Json` extractor/responder, which serializes a typed value for you in one call.

### Redirects

Set a 3xx status and a `Location` header:

```rust
use rust_web_server::header::Header;
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};

fn process(_request: &Request, mut response: Response, _connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Response {
    response.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n301_moved_permanently.status_code;
    response.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n301_moved_permanently.reason_phrase.to_string();
    response.headers.push(Header::new(Header::_LOCATION, "https://example.com/new-path"));
    response
}
```

`n302_found`, `n303_see_other`, `n307_temporary_redirect` and `n308_permanent_redirect` work the same way.

### Streaming large files

For large files, set `stream_file` instead of loading bytes into `content_range_list` (the static file server does this above 256 KiB, `StaticResourceController::STREAM_THRESHOLD`). Memory stays constant: the body goes out as-is when you set a `Content-Length` header, otherwise with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. To stream from any `Read` source, set `stream_pipe` instead:

```rust
response.stream_file = Some("/var/data/large-export.csv".to_string());
```

## STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE constants

The `STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE` constant provides typed access to every standard HTTP status code:

```rust
use rust_web_server::response::STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE;

STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n201_created
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n204_no_content
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n400_bad_request
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n401_unauthorized
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n403_forbidden
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n404_not_found
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n409_conflict
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n422_unprocessable_entity
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n429_too_many_requests
STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n500_internal_server_error
// ... and all other 1xx–5xx codes
```

Each entry has `.status_code: &'static i16` and `.reason_phrase: &'static str`. Set them on a response:

```rust
response.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n201_created.status_code;
response.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n201_created.reason_phrase.to_string();
```

## Header constants

`Header` in `crates/rws-http/src/header/mod.rs` exposes string constants for all standard HTTP header names:

```rust
use rust_web_server::header::Header;

Header::_CONTENT_TYPE        // "Content-Type"
Header::_CONTENT_LENGTH      // "Content-Length"
Header::_CONTENT_RANGE       // "Content-Range"
Header::_AUTHORIZATION       // "Authorization"
Header::_CACHE_CONTROL       // "Cache-Control"
Header::_LOCATION            // "Location"
Header::_SET_COOKIE          // "Set-Cookie"
Header::_FORWARDED           // "Forwarded"
// ... all standard request and response headers
```

Create a header value pair:

```rust
use rust_web_server::header::Header;

// name and value are Cow<'static, str> (18.0.0): a &'static str is borrowed,
// a String (e.g. format!(..)) is owned. Read them as &str via deref.
let location = Header::new(Header::_LOCATION, "/new-path");
response.headers.push(location);
```

### get_header_list

`Header::get_header_list(request)` returns the standard set of response headers (CORS, `Date`, cache control, security headers; client hints only with `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS=true`) pre-populated from the request context. Call it at the start of a controller's `process` method when building a response from scratch:

```rust
let mut header_list = Header::get_header_list(request);
header_list.push(Header::new(Header::_CACHE_CONTROL, "no-store"));
```

## MimeType constants

`MimeType` (`rust_web_server::mime_type`) provides string constants for common content types:

```rust
use rust_web_server::mime_type::MimeType;

MimeType::APPLICATION_JSON          // "application/json"
MimeType::APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM  // "application/octet-stream"
MimeType::TEXT_PLAIN                // "text/plain"
MimeType::TEXT_HTML                 // "text/html"
MimeType::TEXT_CSS                  // "text/css"
MimeType::TEXT_JAVASCRIPT           // "text/javascript"
// ... and many more
```

Use `MimeType::detect_mime_type(filepath)` to derive the MIME type from a file extension at runtime:

```rust
let mime = MimeType::detect_mime_type("/assets/app.wasm");   // "application/wasm"
let mime = MimeType::detect_mime_type("/styles/main.css");   // "text/css"
let mime = MimeType::detect_mime_type("/data/feed.json");    // "application/json"
```

## Range::get_content_range

Wrap any `Vec<u8>` in a `ContentRange` for use in `response.content_range_list`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::range::Range;
use rust_web_server::mime_type::MimeType;

let body = Range::get_content_range(
    serde_json::to_vec(&payload).unwrap(),
    MimeType::APPLICATION_JSON.to_string(),
);
response.content_range_list = vec![body];
```

For multipart range responses (e.g. `Accept-Ranges` support), push multiple `ContentRange` values into the list. The framework serialises them as `multipart/byteranges` automatically, with a `Content-Length` and a boundary that occurs in none of the parts (`Range::multipart_boundary`; since 17.113.2).
