# HTTP Client

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/http-client/>

`rust_web_server::http_client` is a small outbound HTTP/1.1 client with no third-party HTTP dependency. It follows redirects (up to 10 by default; 301/302/303 become `GET`, 307/308 keep the method) and decodes chunked bodies.

| Build | What works |
|---|---|
| any build | `Client` over plain `http://` |
| `http-client` feature, or `http2`/`http3` (the default) | `Client` over `https://` (rustls + WebPKI roots) |
| `http2`/`http3` | `AsyncClient` (async `send()`) |

```toml
[dependencies]
# Only needed for HTTPS in an http1-only build; the default features already include it.
rust-web-server = { version = "18", default-features = false, features = ["http1", "http-client"] }
```

:::caution
In a build without `http-client`, `http2` or `http3`, an `https://` URL is not encrypted — the request cannot succeed. Enable one of those features before calling HTTPS endpoints.
:::

## Calling an API from a handler

```rust
use rust_web_server::http_client::{Client, HttpClientError};

fn fetch_user(id: u64) -> Result {
    let client = Client::new();
    let resp = client
        .get(&format!("https://api.example.com/users/{id}"))
        .header("Authorization", "Bearer tok_…")
        .timeout_ms(5_000)
        .send()?;

    if resp.is_success() {
        resp.text()
    } else {
        Err(HttpClientError(format!("upstream returned {}", resp.status())))
    }
}
```

`Client::new()` uses a 30-second timeout and follows up to 10 redirects; change them with `Client::new().timeout_ms(ms)` and `.max_redirects(n)`, or per request with `RequestBuilder::timeout_ms`. `https://` URLs are checked against the public roots; for a server whose certificate a private CA signed, `Client::new().ca_file("/etc/internal-ca.pem")?` trusts that CA instead (the sync `Client`, 18.28.0). `send()` blocks the calling thread — in the async servers a synchronous handler already runs on the blocking pool, so that is fine; inside an `async` handler use `AsyncClient` instead.

## Request bodies

```rust
use rust_web_server::http_client::Client;

// JSON — sets Content-Type: application/json
let resp = Client::new()
    .post("https://api.example.com/charges")
    .body_json(r#"{"amount":1000,"currency":"usd"}"#)
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer sk_…")
    .send()?;
assert!(resp.is_success());

// Form — percent-encodes each pair, sets Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
let resp = Client::new()
    .post("https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token")
    .form(&[
        ("grant_type", "authorization_code"),
        ("code", "abc123"),
        ("client_id", "my-client-id"),
        ("client_secret", "my-client-secret"),
    ])
    .send()?;
let json = resp.text()?;
```

`.body_text(s)` sends `text/plain`; `.body(bytes)` sends raw bytes with whatever `Content-Type` you set via `.header`. `.form()` is the body shape OAuth 2.0 token endpoints require — [SSO](/features/sso/) uses it for the code exchange.

## Reading the response

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| `.status()` | `u16` |
| `.is_success()` | `true` for 200–299 |
| `.is_redirect()` | `true` for 301/302/303/307/308 (returned once `max_redirects` is reached — `max_redirects(0)` disables following) |
| `.header(name)` | `Option<&str>`, case-insensitive |
| `.headers()` | `&[(String, String)]` |
| `.bytes()` | `&[u8]` |
| `.text()` | `Result` (UTF-8) |
| `.json::()` | `Result` — requires the `serde` feature |

`HttpClientError(pub String)` implements `std::error::Error` and `Display`.

## Async client

With the `http2` feature (included in the default build), `AsyncClient` has the same builder API — `get`/`post`/`put`/`patch`/`delete`/`request`, `.header`, `.body*`, `.form`, `.timeout_ms` — with an `async fn send()`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::http_client::{AsyncClient, HttpClientError};

async fn fetch_async(url: &str) -> Result {
    AsyncClient::new().get(url).send().await?.text()
}
```

See [Async Handlers](/building-apps/async-handlers/#full-example--async-http-call) for a complete handler that forwards an upstream response.

# HTML Templates

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/templates/>

`rust-web-server` integrates the [Tera](https://keats.github.io/tera/) template engine — a Jinja2-compatible HTML templating system with variables, control flow, filters, and inheritance.

:::caution[Feature requirement]
The template integration requires the `tera` feature:

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["tera"] }
```
:::

## Quick start

1. Create a `templates/` directory next to your binary.
2. Call `template::init("templates")` once at startup.
3. Call `template::render("page.html", &ctx)` from any handler.

```rust
use rust_web_server::template::{self, Context};

fn main() {
    // Initialize the global template engine once at startup.
    template::init("templates").expect("failed to load templates");

    // Start the server ...
}
```

## Initialisation

There are two ways to initialise the global engine:

### `template::init(dir)`

Loads all files under `dir` recursively (equivalent to the glob `dir/**/*`):

```rust
template::init("templates").unwrap();
```

### `template::init_from_env()`

Reads the directory from the `RWS_CONFIG_TEMPLATE_DIR` environment variable (default: `"templates"`):

```rust
template::init_from_env().unwrap();
```

Both functions return `Err` if called a second time (the engine is a `OnceLock`).

## Rendering in a handler

```rust
use rust_web_server::template::{self, Context};
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::Response;
use rust_web_server::router::PathParams;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;

fn home(
    _req: &Request,
    _params: &PathParams,
    _conn: &ConnectionInfo,
    _state: &(),
) -> Response {
    let mut ctx = Context::new();
    ctx.insert("title",  "Welcome");
    ctx.insert("items",  &["Rust", "rws", "Tera"]);
    ctx.insert("logged_in", &true);

    template::render("index.html", &ctx).unwrap_or_else(|e| {
        // render() returns Err only when the template file is missing
        // or contains a syntax error — treat as 500
        let mut r = Response::new();
        r.status_code = 500;
        r
    })
}
```

`template::render` delegates to the global `TeraEngine`, renders the named template, and returns a `200 OK` response with `Content-Type: text/html`.

## The `Context` type

`Context` is a re-export of `tera::Context`. Call `.insert(key, value)` with any `Serialize` value:

```rust
use rust_web_server::template::Context;
use serde::Serialize;

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct User {
    name:  String,
    email: String,
}

let user = User { name: "Alice".into(), email: "alice@example.com".into() };

let mut ctx = Context::new();
ctx.insert("user",  &user);
ctx.insert("count", &42_u32);
ctx.insert("flags", &["new", "featured"]);
```

## Directory structure convention

```
your-project/
├── src/
│   └── main.rs
└── templates/
    ├── base.html          <- base layout
    ├── index.html
    ├── users/
    │   ├── list.html
    │   └── detail.html
    └── partials/
        └── nav.html
```

Template names passed to `render` are relative paths within the templates directory (e.g. `"users/list.html"`).

## Tera template syntax

### Variables

```html
<h1>{{ title }}</h1>
<p>Hello, {{ user.name }}!</p>
<p>Total: {{ count }}</p>
```

### Conditionals

```html
{% if logged_in %}
  <a href="/logout">Logout</a>
{% else %}
  <a href="/login">Login</a>
{% endif %}
```

### Loops

```html
<ul>
{% for item in items %}
  <li>{{ item }}</li>
{% endfor %}
</ul>
```

Loop provides a `loop` variable with helpers: `loop.index` (1-based), `loop.index0` (0-based), `loop.first`, `loop.last`.

### Template inheritance

Define a base layout:

```html
{# templates/base.html #}
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head><title>{% block title %}My Site{% endblock %}</title></head>
<body>
  <nav>{% include "partials/nav.html" %}</nav>
  <main>{% block content %}{% endblock %}</main>
</body>
</html>
```

Extend it in a child template:

```html
{# templates/index.html #}
{% extends "base.html" %}

{% block title %}Home — My Site{% endblock %}

{% block content %}
  <h1>{{ heading }}</h1>
  <p>{{ body }}</p>
{% endblock %}
```

### Built-in filters

Tera ships many filters you can apply with `|`:

```html
{{ name | upper }}              {# ALICE #}
{{ title | truncate(length=20) }}
{{ items | length }}
{{ price | round(precision=2) }}
{{ html_content | safe }}       {# disable auto-escaping #}
{{ date | date(format="%Y-%m-%d") }}
```

Auto-escaping is enabled by default for `{{ }}` output — HTML special characters (`<`, `>`, `&`, `"`) are escaped. Use `| safe` only for trusted content.

### Macros

Define reusable template fragments:

```html
{% macro input(name, label, type="text") %}
  <label for="{{ name }}">{{ label }}</label>
  <input type="{{ type }}" id="{{ name }}" name="{{ name }}">
{% endmacro %}

{{ self::input(name="email", label="Email", type="email") }}
```

## `TeraEngine` directly

The global singleton wraps `TeraEngine`. You can also create a standalone engine when you need multiple template directories, or for testing:

```rust
use rust_web_server::template::{TeraEngine, Context};

// From a directory
let engine = TeraEngine::from_dir("templates").unwrap();

// From in-memory strings (useful in tests)
let engine = TeraEngine::from_raw(&[
    ("hello.html", "<p>Hello, {{ name }}!</p>"),
]).unwrap();

let mut ctx = Context::new();
ctx.insert("name", "World");
let html: String = engine.render("hello.html", &ctx).unwrap();
let response = engine.response("hello.html", &ctx).unwrap();
```

`TeraEngine::from_glob(pattern)` accepts any glob pattern Tera accepts, e.g. `"templates/**/*.html"`.

## View helpers

Every engine has three functions (18.35.0):

| Function | Output |
|---|---|
| `url_for(name="posts.show", id=7)` | The path of a [named route](/building-apps/routing/#named-routes-and-url_for); other arguments become the query string |
| `vite(entry="src/main.ts")` | The `<link>`/`<script>` tags of a [Vite](#vite) entry |
| `vite_asset(path="src/logo.svg")` | A built asset's URL |

Their output is already encoded, so mark it `| safe` (without it Tera writes `/` as `&#x2F;`, which browsers read back as `/`, and `vite` would show its tags as text). `template::page_context(request)` starts a `Context` with what most pages need: `flash` (a list of `{kind, text}`), `notice` and `alert` ([flash messages](/building-apps/forms-uploads/#flash-messages-and-redirects)), `csrf_token` and `csrf_field` (a hidden `_csrf` input from [`CsrfLayer`](/features/csrf/), `csrf` feature) and `path`:

```html
{% if notice %}<p class="notice">{{ notice }}</p>{% endif %}
<form method="post" action="{{ url_for(name='posts.create') | safe }}">
  {{ csrf_field | safe }}
  <input name="title">
</form>
```

```rust
let mut ctx = template::page_context(request);
ctx.insert("posts", &posts);
template::render("posts/index.html", &ctx)
```

## Vite

`vite::Vite` (`serde` feature) writes the tags for an entry point of a frontend built with Vite (`build.manifest: true`): its CSS and that of every chunk it imports, `modulepreload` links for the imports, then the module script — or, in development, the two scripts that load it from the Vite dev server:

```rust
use rust_web_server::vite::{self, Vite};

// VITE_DEV_SERVER=http://localhost:5173 → the dev server; otherwise the
// manifest at VITE_MANIFEST (default frontend/dist/.vite/manifest.json),
// assets under VITE_BASE (default /).
vite::install(Vite::from_env()?);
```

```html
<head>{{ vite(entry="src/main.ts") | safe }}</head>
```

`Vite::from_manifest_file(path, base)`, `Vite::from_manifest_str(json, base)` and `Vite::dev(url)` build one directly; `tags(entry)` and `asset(path)` answer the same as the template functions.

## Hot reload

Edit a template file and reload it without restarting the server:

```rust
use rust_web_server::template;

template::init("templates").unwrap();
// ... edit templates/index.html on disk ...
template::reload().unwrap();
```

`template::reload()`:

- **Re-globs the whole directory** — it picks up edited content in existing files *and* newly added or removed files matching the original pattern, not just a diff of what changed.
- **Is atomic.** It builds the full replacement set of templates before swapping it in. If one edited file has a syntax error (or an `{% extends %}`/`{% import %}` chain no longer resolves), `reload()` returns `Err` and the previously-loaded templates keep serving — a bad edit can't leave the live server with a half-broken template set.
- **Is wired into `SIGHUP` automatically.** [`config_reload::reload()`](/features/hot-reload/) calls it for you (as a no-op if `template::init()` was never called), so `kill -HUP $(pidof rws)` picks up edited templates alongside CORS/rate-limit/TLS-cert changes. Call `template::reload()` directly only if you want a different trigger — a file-watcher thread, or your own admin endpoint.

The equivalent method exists on a standalone `TeraEngine` too — `engine.reload()` — for the multi-directory case described above. It requires the engine to have been built from a glob (`from_dir`/`from_glob`/`init`); an engine built with `TeraEngine::from_raw` has no directory to re-read and `reload()` returns `Err` for it.

```rust
use rust_web_server::template::TeraEngine;

let mut engine = TeraEngine::from_dir("templates").unwrap();
// ... edit a template file ...
engine.reload().unwrap();
```

---

# Translations (i18n)

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/i18n/>

The `i18n` module (since 18.16.0) holds your messages in one catalog per
language, picks the language each request asks for in `Accept-Language`, and
fills in placeholders and plural forms. It needs no feature flag and no
extra dependency.

## Catalogs

One file per language, named by its language tag: `locales/en.toml`,
`locales/uk.toml`, `locales/en-GB.toml`. The format is a flat subset of TOML,
so editors and translation tools open it as TOML:

```toml
# locales/en.toml
greeting    = "Hello, {name}!"
items.one   = "{count} item"
items.other = "{count} items"
```

```toml
# locales/uk.toml
greeting    = "Привіт, {name}!"
items.one   = "{count} річ"
items.few   = "{count} речі"
items.many  = "{count} речей"
```

Values are quoted: `"…"` takes `\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\` and `é` escapes,
`'…'` is taken as written. `{name}` is a placeholder; `{{` and `}}` are
literal braces. Load them once at startup:

```rust,no_run
use rust_web_server::i18n::Catalogs;

let catalogs = Catalogs::from_dir("locales", "en")?; // "en": the default language
# Ok::<(), String>(())
```

`Catalogs::new("en").add("uk", text)?` builds them from strings instead
(`include_str!` keeps them in the binary).

## In a handler

```rust,no_run
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::i18n::Catalogs;
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};

let app = App::with_state(Catalogs::from_dir("locales", "en").unwrap())
    .get("/cart", |request, _params, _conn, catalogs| {
        let t = catalogs.for_request(request);            // reads Accept-Language
        let body = format!(
            "{}\n{}\n",
            t.t_with("greeting", &[("name", "Olena")]),
            t.plural("items", 3),                         // "3 речі" for uk, "3 items" for en
        );
        t.localize(Response::text(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok, &body))
    });
```

- `t(key)` / `t_with(key, &[("name", value)])`: the message, placeholders
  filled. A key the language lacks falls back to its base language
  (`en-GB` → `en`), then the default language, then the key itself, so a
  missing translation shows up as its key rather than an error.
- `plural(key, count)` / `plural_with(…)`: `key.one`, `key.few`, `key.many`
  or `key.other` for that count in that language, with `{count}` filled;
  `key.other` when the category has no message.
- `localize(response)` sets `Content-Language` and adds
  `Vary: Accept-Language`, so caches keep one copy per language.
- `for_language("uk")` when the user picked a language (a cookie, a profile
  setting, a `/uk/…` path) rather than the browser's.

## Choosing the language

`AcceptLanguage` (also an extractor) parses the header: ranges ordered by
`q` and then by position, `q=0` left out, at most 32 considered.
`negotiate` follows RFC 4647 lookup: each range as sent, then with subtags
cut from the end (`uk-UA` → `uk`), then a range's language matching a
regional catalog (`pt` → `pt-BR`). Nothing matching, or only `*`, gives the
default language.

```rust
use rust_web_server::i18n::AcceptLanguage;

let preferences = AcceptLanguage::parse("uk-UA, en;q=0.8");
assert_eq!(Some("uk"), preferences.negotiate(&["en", "uk"]));
```

## Plural forms

`plural_category(language, count)` covers the common families:

| Languages | Categories |
|---|---|
| Ukrainian, Russian, Belarusian, Polish | `one` (1, 21, 31…; Polish only 1), `few` (2–4, 22–24…), `many` (the rest) |
| Czech, Slovak | `one` (1), `few` (2–4), `other` |
| French, Brazilian Portuguese | `one` (0 and 1), `other` |
| Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Malay, Turkish… | `other` only |
| everything else | `one` (1), `other` (English rules) |

## Caching

`CacheLayer` caches a response whose `Vary` names a header only when that
header is part of its cache key. Add it with
`.vary_by_header("Accept-Language")` to cache localized pages
per language; otherwise they pass through uncached rather than being served
in the wrong language.

# Dependency Injection

<https://rws8.tech/docs/building-apps/dependency-injection/>

`Container` is a type-keyed service store backed by `HashMap>`. Register services at startup, then pass the container directly as `AppWithState`/`AsyncAppWithState`'s state — it's `Send + Sync + 'static` like any other state type, so it needs no wrapping.

## Registering concrete services

`register::` wraps the value in `Arc` and stores it under `TypeId::of::()`. A second registration for the same type replaces the first.

```rust
use rust_web_server::di::Container;

struct EmailService {
    host: String,
}

let mut container = Container::new();
container.register(EmailService { host: "smtp.example.com".into() });

let svc = container.get::().unwrap();
assert_eq!(svc.host, "smtp.example.com");
```

## Registering trait objects

Use `provide::<dyn Trait>(Arc::new(impl))` when the concrete type must be erased. The key is `TypeId::of::<dyn Trait>()`, so later resolution via `get::<dyn Trait>()` works correctly.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use rust_web_server::di::Container;

pub trait UserRepo: Send + Sync {
    fn find(&self, id: i64) -> Option;
}

struct PgUserRepo;
impl UserRepo for PgUserRepo {
    fn find(&self, _id: i64) -> Option {
        Some("Alice".into())
    }
}

let mut container = Container::new();
container.provide::<dyn UserRepo>(Arc::new(PgUserRepo));

let repo = container.get::<dyn UserRepo>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(repo.find(1), Some("Alice".into()));
```

## Resolving services

Both concrete and trait-object registrations are resolved with the same method:

```rust
// concrete type
let svc: Option> = container.get::();

// trait object
let repo: Option> = container.get::<dyn UserRepo>();
```

`get` returns `None` when no matching registration exists — no panics.

## Named services

Register multiple instances of the same type under distinct string names with `register_named`. This is useful for primary/replica database pools or multiple external services.

```rust
use rust_web_server::di::Container;

let mut container = Container::new();
container
    .register_named("primary", 5432u16)
    .register_named("replica", 5433u16);

assert_eq!(*container.get_named::<u16>("primary").unwrap(), 5432);
assert_eq!(*container.get_named::<u16>("replica").unwrap(), 5433);
```

`provide_named::<dyn Trait>("name", arc)` is the trait-object equivalent.

## `into_arc()` — sharing outside `App::with_state`

`into_arc()` wraps the container in `Arc`, for call sites that need to share one container across multiple hand-built `Application`s.

```rust
let arc = container.into_arc(); // Arc```

Once wrapped you cannot add more registrations — perform all registrations first.

:::caution[Don't use `into_arc()` with `App::with_state`]
`App::with_state`/`App::with_async_state` already wrap their state argument in an `Arc` internally. Passing `container.into_arc()` there double-wraps it (`Arc>`) for no benefit, and handlers end up with `&Arc` instead of the simpler `&Container`. Pass the container itself — see below.
:::

## Wiring into request handlers

Pass the container directly as application state using `App::with_state`. Each handler receives `state: &Container` and can call `state.get::()` to resolve dependencies.

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::di::Container;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::router::PathParams;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::routes;

fn get_version(
    _req: &Request,
    _params: &PathParams,
    _conn: &ConnectionInfo,
    state: &Container,
) -> Response {
    let svc = state.get::().unwrap();
    let mut r = Response::new();
    r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
    r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
    r
}

let mut container = Container::new();
container.register(EmailService { host: "smtp.example.com".into() });

let app = routes! {
    App::with_state(container),
    GET "/version" => get_version,
};
```

The same pattern works with `App::with_async_state` (requires the `http2` feature) for `async fn` handlers — pass the container directly there too.

## Complete example: UserRepository + DI wiring

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::di::Container;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::router::PathParams;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::routes;

// --- domain trait ---
pub trait UserRepository: Send + Sync {
    fn find_by_id(&self, id: i64) -> Option;
    fn count(&self) -> usize;
}

// --- in-memory implementation (test / dev) ---
pub struct InMemoryUserRepo {
    users: Vec<(i64, String)>,
}

impl UserRepository for InMemoryUserRepo {
    fn find_by_id(&self, id: i64) -> Option {
        self.users.iter().find(|(i, _)| *i == id).map(|(_, n)| n.clone())
    }
    fn count(&self) -> usize {
        self.users.len()
    }
}

// --- handler ---
fn get_user(
    req: &Request,
    params: &PathParams,
    _conn: &ConnectionInfo,
    state: &Container,
) -> Response {
    let repo = state.get::<dyn UserRepository>().unwrap();
    let id: i64 = params.get("id").and_then(|s| s.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(0);
    let mut r = Response::new();
    match repo.find_by_id(id) {
        Some(name) => {
            r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.status_code;
            r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok.reason_phrase.to_string();
        }
        None => {
            r.status_code = *STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n404_not_found.status_code;
            r.reason_phrase = STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n404_not_found.reason_phrase.to_string();
        }
    }
    r
}

// --- wiring ---
let repo = InMemoryUserRepo {
    users: vec![(1, "Alice".into()), (2, "Bob".into())],
};

let mut container = Container::new();
container.provide::<dyn UserRepository>(Arc::new(repo));

let app = routes! {
    App::with_state(container),
    GET "/users/:id" => get_user,
};
```

:::note[Thread safety]
Every type registered with `register` or `provide` must implement `Send + Sync + 'static`. `Arc` satisfies those bounds whenever `T: Send + Sync`, making it the natural wrapper for shared services.
:::

## Lifecycle hooks

Services that need starting and stopping — a pool to warm, a background thread to join — implement `Lifecycle` and are registered with `register_managed`; plain closures go in with `on_start` / `on_stop` (18.35.0):

```rust
use rust_web_server::di::{Container, Lifecycle};

struct SearchIndex { /* … */ }

impl Lifecycle for SearchIndex {
    fn start(&self) -> Result<(), String> { /* load the index */ Ok(()) }
    fn stop(&self) { /* flush it */ }
}

let mut c = Container::new();
c.register_managed(SearchIndex::open("index/")?)
    .on_start("migrations", |c| run_migrations(&c.get::().unwrap()))
    .on_stop("metrics", |_| flush_metrics());

c.start()?;           // in registration order
// … serve …
c.stop();             // in reverse order
```

`start()` runs the start hooks in registration order; if one fails, the stop hooks of those before it run (in reverse) and the error is `"<hook name>: <message>"`. `stop()` runs the stop hooks of what started, in reverse. Both do nothing when repeated; `is_started()` tells which state the container is in. A service's `stop` only runs if its `start` did. Call `start` before serving and `stop` after the server returns.

## Inspection helpers

```rust
container.contains::();           // unnamed registration exists?
container.contains_named::<u16>("primary");     // named registration exists?
container.len();                                // total unnamed registrations
container.is_empty();                           // no unnamed registrations?
```
