# CORS & Security Headers

<https://rws8.tech/docs/features/cors-security/>

Every response includes a baseline set of security headers automatically. CORS is controlled by a set of `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_*` environment variables. Client Hints are opt-in.

## CORS

### Allow-all mode (opt-in)

With no CORS configuration, `rws` adds no CORS headers: browsers keep other sites from reading its responses (since 18.0.0 — allow-all used to be the default). When `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=true`, the server echoes back whatever `Origin` the browser sends and sets `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. On `OPTIONS` preflight requests it also mirrors back the `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers` values and adds `Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400`.

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=true
```

### Explicit origins mode

List the allowed origins as a comma-separated string (`RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL` stays `false`, the default):

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=false
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=true
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS=GET,POST,PUT,DELETE,OPTIONS
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS=Content-Type,Authorization,X-Request-ID
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS=X-Total-Count,X-Request-ID
RWS_CONFIG_CORS_MAX_AGE=3600
```

When the incoming `Origin` is not one of the listed origins no CORS headers are added to the response. Origins are compared whole (ASCII case ignored): with `https://app.example.com` listed, `https://app.example.co` and `https://app.example.com.evil` don't match (`Cors::origin_is_allowed`; before 17.113.2 a substring of the list matched). `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` is sent on the actual response, where the browser reads it, not only on the preflight.

### Environment variable reference

| Variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL` | `false` | Echo any origin back, with credentials (was `true` before 18.0.0) |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` | `""` | Comma-separated allowlist (used when allow-all is `false`) |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS` | `""` | Set `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS` | `""` | Value for `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` on preflight |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS` | `""` | Value for `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` on preflight |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS` | `""` | Value for `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`, on every response to an allowed origin |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_MAX_AGE` | `86400` | Preflight cache TTL in seconds |

### Programmatic CORS (`Cors` struct)

For handlers that need fine-grained control, use `Cors::_process` directly:

```rust
use rust_web_server::cors::Cors;

let cors = Cors {
    allow_all: false,
    allow_origins: vec!["https://app.example.com".into()],
    allow_methods: vec!["GET".into(), "POST".into()],
    allow_headers: vec!["Authorization".into()],
    allow_credentials: true,
    expose_headers: vec![],
    max_age: "3600".into(),
};

let headers = Cors::_process(&request, &cors)?;
```

### Hot reload

CORS configuration is re-read on `SIGHUP` (or `POST /admin/config/reload`) without a restart.

## Security headers

Every response carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. On TLS connections
(HTTPS and HTTP/3) the server also sends:

```
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
```

The other browser-policy headers are opt-in (since 18.0.0 — before that they
were always sent): set `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true`
(`security_headers = true` in `rws.config.toml`) and every response also
carries

| Header | Value |
|---|---|
| `X-Frame-Options` | `SAMEORIGIN` |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` |
| `Permissions-Policy` | `geolocation=(), microphone=(), camera=()` |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `default-src 'self'` (unless `RWS_CONFIG_CSP` is set) |

They are off by default because most deployments set them per site (or in a
proxy in front), and each one is work on every response — over HTTP/2 every
header is HPACK-encoded.

### Content-Security-Policy

Set a policy with `RWS_CONFIG_CSP`; it is sent whether or not
`RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS` is on:

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_CSP="default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' cdn.example.com; img-src *"
```

With `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true`, an empty value suppresses the
default policy:

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_CSP=
```

### Nanosecond timestamps

`RWS_CONFIG_NANOS_HEADERS=true` (`nanos_headers = true`) adds
`Date-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` (the response time in nanoseconds since the Unix
epoch, per response) and, for static files, `Last-Modified-Unix-Epoch-Nanos`.
Off by default since 18.0.0: `Date` and `Last-Modified` carry the same
information to the second, and values that change on every response can't be
indexed by HTTP/2's header compression.

## Client Hints

Client hints are opt-in (since 18.0.0): set `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS=true`
(`client_hints = true` in `rws.config.toml`) and every response advertises
the following hints via `Accept-CH` and `Critical-CH`:

```
Accept-CH: Sec-CH-UA-Arch, Sec-CH-UA-Bitness, Sec-CH-UA-Full-Version-List,
           Sec-CH-UA-Model, Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version, Downlink, ECT, RTT,
           Save-Data, Device-Memory, Sec-CH-Prefers-Reduced-Motion,
           Sec-CH-Prefers-Color-Scheme
```

The hints also appear in the `Vary` header so caches key responses on them.
They're off by default because they add about 700 bytes to every response,
and `Critical-CH` makes Chromium retry a request that arrived without them.
A browser that already sends a hint (`Sec-CH-UA-*` low-entropy hints,
`Save-Data`) still sends it; reading an incoming hint in a handler works
either way:

```rust
use rust_web_server::client_hint::ClientHint;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;

fn handler(req: &Request) {
    if let Some(h) = req.get_header(ClientHint::PREFERS_COLOR_SCHEME.to_string()) {
        let scheme = &h.value; // "light" or "dark"
    }
    if let Some(h) = req.get_header(ClientHint::NETWORK_SAVE_DATA.to_string()) {
        // serve lower-resolution images when Save-Data: on
    }
}
```

Available hint constants in `ClientHint`:

| Constant | Header |
|---|---|
| `USER_AGENT_CPU_ARCHITECTURE` | `Sec-CH-UA-Arch` |
| `USER_AGENT_CPU_BITNESS` | `Sec-CH-UA-Bitness` |
| `USER_AGENT_FULL_BRAND_INFORMATION` | `Sec-CH-UA-Full-Version-List` |
| `USER_AGENT_DEVICE_MODEL` | `Sec-CH-UA-Model` |
| `USER_AGENT_OPERATING_SYSTEM_VERSION` | `Sec-CH-UA-Platform-Version` |
| `NETWORK_DOWNLOAD_SPEED` | `Downlink` |
| `NETWORK_EFFECTIVE_CONNECTION_TYPE` | `ECT` |
| `NETWORK_ROUND_TRIP_TIME` | `RTT` |
| `NETWORK_SAVE_DATA` | `Save-Data` |
| `DEVICE_MEMORY` | `Device-Memory` |
| `PREFERS_REDUCED_MOTION` | `Sec-CH-Prefers-Reduced-Motion` |
| `PREFERS_COLOR_SCHEME` | `Sec-CH-Prefers-Color-Scheme` |

:::note[Vary header]
With client hints on, the `Vary` response header includes the full list of hints so HTTP caches serve the correct variant per client capability; otherwise it is just `Vary: Origin`.
:::

---

# Static Files, Directory Listing & SPA Fallback

<https://rws8.tech/docs/features/static-files/>

## Serving files

Any file under the process's working directory is served automatically — no configuration, no routes to register. `StaticResourceController` handles range requests, sets `ETag` / `Last-Modified` headers, negotiates gzip, and streams files larger than 256 KiB without loading them fully into memory.

### Browser caching

Static files are sent with `Cache-Control: no-cache` (since 18.0.0; it was
`no-store`): the browser keeps the file and asks again on the next use with
`If-None-Match` (the `ETag`) or `If-Modified-Since` (the `Last-Modified`
date), and gets a `304 Not Modified` without a body while the file is
unchanged. `If-None-Match` decides when both are sent (RFC 9110 §13.1.3).
`If-Modified-Since` takes any of the three HTTP-date forms: the IMF-fixdate
rws sends, RFC 850 (`Sunday, 06-Nov-94 08:49:37 GMT`) and asctime
(`Sun Nov  6 08:49:37 1994`).
Set `RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL` to change it — e.g.
`public, max-age=31536000, immutable` for files with a content hash in their
name — or to an empty value for the old `no-store` behavior. Responses from
your handlers keep `no-store, …` unless they set their own `Cache-Control`.

Files larger than 256 KiB are streamed from disk with an exact
`Content-Length` instead of being read into memory, so serving a 1 GB file
uses a few MiB. The static root is the working directory `rws` was started
in.

The request path is percent-decoded once before the lookup, so
`/my%20file.txt` serves `my file.txt` and `%2F` is a `/` (17.113.2); `+` is a
literal `+`. A path that isn't UTF-8 once decoded gets `404`.

Only files inside the root are served — checked on the decoded path, so
`/%2e%2e/` is refused like `/../`: a path with a `..` segment is refused
(`404`), and so is a symlink in the root that points outside it. Files and
directories whose name starts with `.` (`.git/`, `.env`) are not served unless
`RWS_CONFIG_SERVE_DOTFILES=true`; `.well-known/` always is (17.113.1).
Private-key and config files — `*.pem`, `*.key`, `rws.config.toml` — are
never served.

Range requests follow RFC 9110 over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3: `bytes=2-5`,
open-ended `bytes=7-`, suffix `bytes=-500`, and multiple ranges get
`206 Partial Content` with an exact `Content-Range` (`bytes 7-9/10`); a range
ending past the file is clamped to its last byte; a range starting past the
end can't be satisfied: it is skipped, and only a request none of whose ranges can be satisfied gets `416`, with `Content-Range: bytes */<length>` (17.113.2). Full `200` responses carry no `Content-Range`. Overlapping
ranges are merged (and then sorted); more than 16 ranges are answered with
the whole file as one range, so a response never holds more than the file
(17.113.1).

Conditional requests: every file response carries an `ETag`, made from a
hash of the file's bytes and its size (`"<hash>-<size>"`, since 18.27.0;
before, its modification time), so replicas serving the same file — from one
ConfigMap or image, unpacked at different times — give the same tag, and a
revalidation through a load balancer gets its `304` from any of them. The
hash is worked out once per file version; files over 256 MiB keep the
modification time. `If-None-Match`
takes a list of tags or `*` and compares weakly (`W/"x"` matches `"x"`), as
RFC 9110 §13.1.2 requires; a match is a `304 Not Modified` (17.113.2).
A `Range` with `If-Range` is honored only while the `If-Range` tag strongly
matches the current `ETag`, or is a date equal to the file's `Last-Modified`
(at least a second old); otherwise (another tag, a weak one, another date)
the whole file is sent with `200`, so a client never splices a piece of a
newer file onto an older download.
Asking for an existing file or directory with any other method than `GET`,
`HEAD` or `OPTIONS` gets `405 Method Not Allowed` with
`Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS` rather than `404` (17.113.2).

```bash
mkdir www && echo "<h1>Hello</h1>" > www/index.html
cd www
rws
curl http://localhost:7878/          # serves index.html
curl http://localhost:7878/index.html # same file, explicit path
```

## How files are served fast

- **Open files are reused.** A static file's open handle is kept for one
  second (`open_file_cache_secs` / `RWS_CONFIG_OPEN_FILE_CACHE_SECS`, read
  at startup; `0` turns it off; Unix only) and read with positional
  reads, so a request for a hot file costs one `fstat` instead of an `open`,
  several `stat`s and a `close`. Size and modification time are read on every
  request, so a file edited in place is served correctly at once; a file
  replaced by a new one (a rename) or deleted is noticed within the second.
  At most 128 files are held open. Files up to 64 KiB also have their
  contents kept in memory (8 MiB in total), checked against the size and
  modification time on every request, so an unchanged small file costs no
  read; a file modified in the last two seconds is always read fresh.
- **One write per response.** A small response's head and body leave in one
  system call and one TCP segment.
- **Downloads use `sendfile`** over plain HTTP on Linux and macOS: the kernel
  copies the file to the socket, with the response head in the same segment
  (`TCP_CORK` on Linux, `sendfile`'s header vector on macOS) and the open
  file handle reused rather than reopened.
- **Static files and health checks run on the event loop**, without a hand-off
  to a thread pool.

## Directory listing

**On by default.** A requested directory that has no `index.html` renders a directory listing page (`200 OK`) instead of falling through to `404 Not Found`. A directory that *does* have an `index.html` is served exactly as before — this only changes what happens for the previously-404 case.

```bash
mkdir -p www/reports && touch www/reports/q1.pdf www/reports/q2.pdf
curl http://localhost:7878/reports/
# <!DOCTYPE html> ... directory listing page ...
```

The page includes:

- A breadcrumb (`~ / reports`) linking back to each ancestor directory.
- A parent-directory link (omitted at a static root, since there's nowhere to go up to).
- A table of entries — directories first, then files, both sorted case-insensitively by name — with size and last-modified columns.
- A client-side search box that filters rows without a round-trip to the server.

Entry names are HTML-escaped for display and percent-encoded in `href` attributes, so filenames containing `<`, `&`, spaces, or other special characters render and link correctly. Dotfiles (names starting with `.`) are omitted from the listing.

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

let client = TestClient::new(App::new());
let response = client.get("/reports/").send();
assert_eq!(200, response.status());
```


### Turning it off

```toml
directory_listing = false   # RWS_CONFIG_DIRECTORY_LISTING
```

A directory without an `index.html` then answers `404 Not Found` (or the site's own `404.html`), so the folder's contents stay private. Directories with an `index.html` and plain files are served as before. Since 18.8.4.

## Why the listing's CSS/JS aren't inlined

The framework's default `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'` header (see [CORS & Security](/features/cors-security/)) silently blocks inline `<style>`/`<script>` blocks — a browser enforcing that policy would render the listing completely unstyled if the CSS were embedded directly in the page.

Instead, `DirectoryListingAssetsController` serves the listing's stylesheet and filter-box script as same-origin assets:

- `GET /rws-directory-listing.css`
- `GET /rws-directory-listing.js`

Both are `'self'`-origin `<link>`/`<script src>` references, fully compliant with the default CSP — no policy relaxation needed. Just like `StyleController` (`/style.css`) and `ScriptController` (`/script.js`), a file on disk at that same relative path overrides the compiled-in default:

```bash
# Restyle the directory listing without recompiling — drop a file named
# exactly "rws-directory-listing.css" in the working directory.
echo "body { font-family: monospace; }" > rws-directory-listing.css
```

If you set a CSP (`RWS_CONFIG_CSP`, or the default one via `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS`) and excludes `'self'` from `style-src`/`script-src`, add an allowance for it or the listing will render unstyled the same way any other same-origin asset would under that policy.

## Links with punctuation stuck to them

A link copied out of prose or Markdown often brings the punctuation after it
along: `/docs/http2/):` from `[HTTP/2](/docs/http2/): …` in an llms.txt,
`/docs/install.` from the end of a sentence. When a `GET` or `HEAD` names
nothing and its path ends with `)`, `:`, `.`, `,`, `;`, `]`, `>` or a quote,
rws answers `301` to the path without them — if that is a file or
directory — keeping the query string. Anything else still gets the `404`.
Since 18.15.0.

## SPA fallback

For local development, before you have a built app to serve this way, see [Frontend Dev Server Proxy](/getting-started/frontend-dev-proxy/) for running a React/Vite dev server alongside `rws`.

**Opt-in — unset (disabled) by default.** `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK` serves a configured file for any `GET`/`HEAD` request that matches no real file, directory, or `path.html`, instead of `404` — the standard client-side-router ("SPA") fallback a React Router / Vue Router / etc. app needs for deep links to work:

```bash
# Build your React/Vue/etc. app, then serve its output directly:
cd dist && RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK=index.html rws
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:7878/dashboard/settings
# no file on disk at this path — served index.html instead of 404,
# so the client-side router can take over and render /dashboard/settings
```

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

let client = TestClient::new(App::new());
let response = client.get("/dashboard/settings").send();
assert_eq!(200, response.status());
```

A file or directory that *does* exist is always served as itself — the fallback only ever applies to what was previously a `404`, and only when the configured file actually exists on disk (a typo'd `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK` value is a silent no-op, not a broken response).

### Scoping — avoiding swallowed 404s

A blanket fallback would turn every typo'd URL and missing asset into a `200`, which is worse than the `404` it replaces. Two checks apply automatically:

1. **Extension heuristic** — only a request whose *last path segment* has no `.` gets the fallback. `/dashboard/settings` qualifies (a client-side route); `/assets/logo.png` (a missed static asset) still `404`s. This is the same heuristic webpack-dev-server's `historyApiFallback`, `sirv`, and `vite preview` use.
2. **`RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK_EXCLUDE_PREFIXES`** — a comma-separated list of path prefixes that never receive the fallback, even when it's configured:

```bash
export RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK=index.html
export RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK_EXCLUDE_PREFIXES=/api,/healthz
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:7878/api/users/999   # 404 — excluded prefix, not rewritten
curl http://localhost:7878/settings/theme  # 200 — served index.html
```

### Several apps on one server

`RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK` is one file for the whole server. When a site also hosts single-page apps under
their own paths — a marketing site with a console at `/cloud` and an admin UI at `/admin` — give each its
own fallback with `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK_ROUTES`, comma-separated `prefix=file` pairs. Everything else
keeps its real `404`:

```toml
# rws.config.toml
spa_fallback_routes = ["/cloud=cloud/index.html", "/admin=admin/index.html"]
spa_fallback_exclude_prefixes = ["/cloud/api"]
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:7878/cloud/orgs/acme/plan  # 200 — cloud/index.html
curl http://localhost:7878/admin/users           # 200 — admin/index.html
curl http://localhost:7878/pricing/old-page      # 404 — under no prefix
curl http://localhost:7878/cloudy                # 404 — /cloudy isn't under /cloud
```

A path matches a prefix when it is the prefix or below it, and the longest matching prefix wins. Paths
under no prefix use `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK` if it is set. The same rules as above still apply: files that
exist are served as themselves, a last segment with a `.` still `404`s, excluded prefixes are never
rewritten, and a missing file is a no-op (`rws --check` warns about it).

The settings are read fresh on every request, so they can be changed via `rws.config.toml` + `SIGHUP` without a restart — see [Hot Config Reload](/features/hot-reload/).

---

# Rate Limiting

<https://rws8.tech/docs/features/rate-limiting/>

`rust-web-server` ships a built-in sliding-window rate limiter in `crates/rws-server/src/rate_limit/mod.rs`. It is keyed by a string (typically the client IP) and is safe to share across threads.

## Quick start

Add `RateLimitLayer` to the middleware stack to enforce the global limit on every request:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::middleware::RateLimitLayer;

let app = App::new().wrap(RateLimitLayer);
```

`RateLimitLayer` calls `rate_limit::global().check(&connection.client.ip)` on every request. When the budget is exceeded it returns `429 Too Many Requests` without forwarding to the inner application.

## Global singleton

`rate_limit::global()` returns a `&'static RateLimiter` initialized once from environment variables:

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS` | `1000` | Requests allowed per window |
| `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS` | `60` | Sliding window length in seconds |

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS=500
RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS=30
```

or in `rws.config.toml`:

```toml
[rate_limit]
max_requests = 500
window_secs  = 30
```

The `rws` binary enforces this global limit only when `max_requests` is set
to a positive number (an unset limit means no global limit, not 1000/60s).
Turning it on needs a restart; changing the numbers later is hot-reloadable
via `SIGHUP`. In your own app, add `.wrap(RateLimitLayer)` to enforce it.

## `RateLimiter` API

### `check(key) -> bool`

Records a timestamp for `key` and returns `true` when the call is within the budget. Returns `false` — without recording — when the budget is exhausted.

```rust
use rust_web_server::rate_limit::RateLimiter;

let limiter = RateLimiter::new(100, 60); // 100 req / 60 s

if limiter.check("192.168.1.1") {
    // request is within budget — proceed
} else {
    // return 429 Too Many Requests
}
```

### `remaining(key) -> u32`

Returns the number of requests `key` may still make in the current window without being rate-limited. Useful for `X-RateLimit-Remaining` response headers.

```rust
let left = limiter.remaining("192.168.1.1");
// add to response headers:
// X-RateLimit-Remaining: {left}
```

### `retry_after(key) -> u64`

Seconds a rejected `key` should wait before trying again. The window length — a safe upper bound, since the oldest request in the window may expire sooner. The two 429 paths (`RateLimitLayer` and `PerRouteRateLimit`) attach it to every rejection:

```
Retry-After: {window_secs}
```

### `set_limits(max_requests, window_secs)`

Updates the limits on a live limiter without a restart. Called automatically by `config_reload::reload()` on `SIGHUP`.

```rust
limiter.set_limits(200, 60); // new limit takes effect immediately
```

### `reset(key)`

Clears all recorded timestamps for `key`. Useful in tests.

```rust
limiter.reset("192.168.1.1");
```

## Hot reload

Send `SIGHUP` or `POST /admin/config/reload` to update the global limiter without restarting. The new `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_*` values are read from the environment and applied atomically via `set_limits`.

## Custom per-route limiter

Create a `RateLimiter` with custom parameters and call `check` in your handler directly:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use rust_web_server::rate_limit::RateLimiter;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::Response;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;
use rust_web_server::error::{AppError, IntoResponse};

struct State {
    login_limiter: RateLimiter,
}

fn login_handler(
    state: &Arc,
    req: &Request,
    conn: &ConnectionInfo,
) -> Response {
    if !state.login_limiter.check(&conn.client.ip) {
        return AppError::TooManyRequests.into_response();
    }
    // proceed with login logic ...
    Response::new()
}

// Wire up:
let state = Arc::new(State {
    login_limiter: RateLimiter::new(5, 60), // 5 attempts per minute
});
```

Wrap the limiter in `Arc` to share it across handler invocations.

:::note[Per-route vs global]
`RateLimitLayer` uses the global singleton. For endpoints that need tighter limits (login, password reset, OTP verification), create a separate `RateLimiter` and call `check` inside the handler as shown above.
:::

## Distributed rate limiting with `RedisRateLimiter`

`RateLimiter` tracks state in process memory. Run two or more `rws` instances behind a load balancer and each one enforces its own budget independently — the effective limit for a given client multiplies by the number of replicas instead of staying constant. `RedisRateLimiter` fixes this by keying the counter on a shared Redis server, so every instance increments and reads the same value.

```rust
use rust_web_server::rate_limit::RedisRateLimiter;

// 100 requests / 60s, shared across every rws instance pointed at this Redis server
let limiter = RedisRateLimiter::new("127.0.0.1:6379", None, 100, 60);

match limiter.check("192.168.1.1") {
    Ok(true) => { /* within budget — proceed */ }
    Ok(false) => { /* budget exhausted — return 429 */ }
    Err(e) => { /* Redis unreachable — decide fail-open vs fail-closed yourself */ }
}
```

`RedisRateLimiter::from_env()` builds one from environment variables:

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `RWS_REDIS_HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | Redis server host |
| `RWS_REDIS_PORT` | `6379` | Redis server port |
| `RWS_REDIS_PASSWORD` | *(none)* | Passed to Redis `AUTH` if set |
| `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS` | `1000` | Requests allowed per window |
| `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS` | `60` | Window length in seconds |

```rust
use rust_web_server::rate_limit::RedisRateLimiter;

let limiter = RedisRateLimiter::from_env();
```

### How it differs from the in-process `RateLimiter`

`RateLimiter` records a sliding-window log of timestamps per key. `RedisRateLimiter` instead uses a **fixed-window counter**: each key lives under one Redis string with a TTL equal to the window length, and every call issues an atomic `INCR`. This is the standard distributed rate-limiting pattern — Redis guarantees `INCR` is atomic across every concurrent caller, so the count stays correct no matter how many `rws` processes are incrementing it at once.

The tradeoff versus a true sliding window: a client can burst up to `2x max_requests` across a window boundary (once near the end of one window, once right after the next one starts). For most deployments this is an acceptable price for atomic, coordination-free enforcement across a cluster.

`check`, unlike `RateLimiter::check`, returns `Result<bool, std::io::Error>` — the network call to Redis can fail. Callers decide whether an unreachable Redis server should fail open (allow the request) or fail closed (reject it); `RedisRateLimiter` does not pick one for you.

### API

- `RedisRateLimiter::new(addr, password, max_requests, window_secs)` — connect to `addr` (e.g. `"127.0.0.1:6379"`).
- `RedisRateLimiter::from_env()` — build from the environment variables above.
- `check(key) -> Result<bool, io::Error>` — atomically increments the shared counter for `key` and returns whether the call is within budget.
- `remaining(key) -> Result<u32, io::Error>` — requests `key` may still make in the current window.
- `set_limits(max_requests, window_secs)` — update limits on a live limiter; takes effect on the next `check`/`remaining`.
- `reset(key) -> Result<(), io::Error>` — deletes the Redis key for `key`. Useful in tests.

Cloning a `RedisRateLimiter` is cheap — all clones share the same underlying TCP connection, mirroring `RedisSessionStore`'s connection-sharing model (see [Sessions](/features/sessions/)).

---

# Compression

<https://rws8.tech/docs/features/compression/>

`rust-web-server` compresses text responses automatically, in the coding the
client prefers: `br` (brotli), `zstd` or `gzip` (brotli and zstd since
18.1.0). No middleware registration, no configuration.

## Which coding

The request's `Accept-Encoding` decides: the coding with the highest `q`
wins, `*` stands for any coding not listed, and `q=0` refuses one. When
several are equally acceptable — a browser sends
`gzip, deflate, br, zstd` — the server's order breaks the tie:

| Response | Order | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Static files (compressed once, then cached) | `br`, `zstd`, `gzip` | brotli's output is smallest, and it is paid for once |
| Everything else (compressed per response) | `zstd`, `br`, `gzip` | zstd costs the least CPU at a similar ratio |

A request without `Accept-Encoding` gets the response uncompressed.

Brotli and zstd are the `brotli` and `zstd` Cargo features, both on by
default (`zstd` builds the C libzstd). Without them only gzip is offered;
the `http1`-only build (`--no-default-features --features http1`) has
gzip only.

## What gets compressed

`compression::apply_compression(request, response)` runs after your
handler, before the response is written (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3). It
compresses when:

1. The response has no `Content-Encoding` already — a backend's compressed
   response is passed through, never compressed twice.
2. The body is at least 512 bytes (`compression::MIN_COMPRESS_SIZE`, the
   same minimum Caddy uses).
3. The client accepts a coding (above).
4. The `Content-Type` is compressible (below).
5. The response isn't partial: a `206` is a slice of the file and is sent as
   is (since 17.113.2).

Levels are the fast ones peers use for per-response compression: brotli 4,
zstd 3, gzip 6 (`compression::Level::Dynamic`; brotli's default, 11, is
about a hundred times slower than gzip). If the result isn't smaller than
the original, the original is sent. A compressed response gets:

- `Content-Encoding: br`, `zstd` or `gzip`
- `Vary: Accept-Encoding` (appended to an existing `Vary`, or added)
- its own `ETag` when it had one: `"x"` becomes `"x-br"` (since 18.1.0;
  each representation needs a different strong ETag)

`compression::apply_gzip` still exists and only ever uses gzip.

## Compressible content types

Only responses whose `Content-Type` starts with one of these are compressed:

| MIME type |
|-----------|
| `text/html` |
| `text/css` |
| `text/javascript` |
| `text/plain` |
| `text/xml` |
| `application/json` |
| `application/javascript` |
| `application/xml` |
| `application/xhtml+xml` |
| `image/svg+xml` |

Images, audio, video, fonts and archives are already compressed.

## Static files are compressed once

A static file is compressed once per version per coding, not on every
request: the open-file cache keeps the brotli, zstd and gzip forms of each
file up to 1 MiB, keyed by its size and modification time, within the same
8 MiB memory budget, at the higher `Level::Static` (brotli 6, zstd 6,
gzip 6). An edit is picked up at once; a file modified less than 2 seconds
ago isn't cached yet. The `ETag` carries the coding (`"<hash>-<size>-br"`),
so a client revalidating gets a `304` for the representation it holds.

### Precompressed files

If `app.js.br`, `app.js.zst` or `app.js.gz` sits next to `app.js`, is a
regular file (not a symlink) and is at least as new as `app.js`, its bytes
are sent for that coding instead of compressing — as nginx's `gzip_static`
does. Build them once with the best settings (`brotli -q 11`,
`zstd -19`):

```bash
brotli -q 11 -k static/app.js       # static/app.js.br
zstd -19 -k static/app.js           # static/app.js.zst
gzip -9 -k static/app.js            # static/app.js.gz
```

A sibling older than the file (the file was edited since) is ignored, and
the file is compressed instead. Like the cached forms, this applies to
files up to 1 MiB.

## Large files

Static files larger than **256 KiB** are sent without being read into
memory — `sendfile(2)` over plain HTTP, chunked otherwise — except that a
client accepting a coding gets a compressible file of up to **1 MiB**
compressed from the cache. Larger files are sent uncompressed.

:::note[Range requests]
Byte-range requests (`Range: bytes=N-M`) are answered with the slice,
uncompressed: compressing a slice would describe bytes that don't exist.
:::

## Dictionary compression

With a dictionary (RFC 9842), a new version of a file is sent as the
difference from a version the browser already has. The browser names the
dictionary it holds in `Available-Dictionary` (its SHA-256) and accepts
`dcz` (zstd) or `dcb` (brotli). Since 18.12.0.

### Static files

List the URL patterns of files whose next versions should go out as deltas
— typically bundles with a version or hash in the name:

```toml
compression_dictionaries = ["/js/app.*.js", "/css/site.*.css"]   # RWS_CONFIG_COMPRESSION_DICTIONARIES
static_cache_control     = "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"  # browsers only use fresh dictionaries
```

A file matching a pattern (`*` matches any characters, `/` included) is sent
with `Use-As-Dictionary: match="<pattern>"` and `Vary: Accept-Encoding,
Available-Dictionary`, and rws keeps a copy of its bytes. After a deploy,
the browser asks for `/js/app.v2.js` naming `app.v1.js` as its dictionary,
and rws sends v2 as a delta against the copy it kept, `dcz` first. In the
end-to-end test a 102 KiB bundle with a few changed lines arrives in 85
bytes (`dcz`) or 73 (`dcb`), against 13.7 KiB as `br`, and Chromium
decodes it to the exact file.

- Each version's hash is worked out once; deltas are cached per version and
  dictionary like the `br` forms, with an ETag of `"…-dcz-<hash prefix>"`.
- Files up to 1 MiB, compressible types only, `GET`/`HEAD` without `Range`.
- Kept dictionaries take up to 32 MiB, oldest out first, and are lost on
  restart: until browsers fetch a file again they get `br` or `zstd`.
- A dictionary the server doesn't have (another server, an evicted one)
  means the usual `br` / `zstd` / `gzip`.
- `static_cache_control` matters: browsers use a dictionary only while
  it's fresh in their cache, and the default `no-cache` makes it stale at
  once. Use versioned names with a long `max-age`.

### In code

`compression::dictionary` has the codec:

```rust
use rust_web_server::compression::{dictionary, Level};
use rust_web_server::request::Request;

/// `new` as a delta against `old`, when the client holds `old` and accepts
/// a dictionary coding. Send it with `dictionary::mark_encoded`.
fn delta(request: &Request, old: &[u8], new: &[u8]) -> Option<(dictionary::DictionaryEncoding, Vec<u8>)> {
    let coding = dictionary::negotiate(request)?;
    if dictionary::available_dictionary(request)? != dictionary::hash(old) {
        return None;
    }
    Some((coding, dictionary::encode(coding, new, old, Level::Static)?)) // magic + hash + stream
}
```

`negotiate` picks `dcz` over `dcb` on equal weight and only when the
client lists the coding by name (`*` doesn't count). Dictionaries and bodies
are limited to 1 MiB each (`dictionary::MAX_SIZE`), which keeps the window
inside the 8 MiB browsers support. `decode` reverses `encode`, checking the
magic and the dictionary's hash, with a cap on the decoded size.

## Checking it

```bash
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "Accept-Encoding: br" http://localhost:7878/app.js
# content-encoding: br
# vary: Accept-Encoding
# etag: "1793007086216830266-26624-br"
```

## Configuration

Compression needs none: there are no keys, environment variables or
middleware layers for `gzip`, `br` and `zstd`. Only dictionary compression
is opt-in, with `compression_dictionaries` (above).

---

# Early Hints

<https://rws8.tech/docs/features/early-hints/>

A `103 Early Hints` response (RFC 8297) carries `Link` headers ahead of the real response. A browser that gets one starts preloading the listed stylesheets and scripts, or connecting to the listed origins, while the server is still working on the page: a slow database query or upstream no longer delays those downloads. Since 18.12.0.

## In code

`EarlyHintsLayer` sends the same hints for every request it wraps:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::early_hints::EarlyHintsLayer;

let app = App::new().wrap(EarlyHintsLayer::new([
    "</app.css>; rel=preload; as=style",
    "</app.js>; rel=preload; as=script",
    "<https://cdn.example.com>; rel=preconnect",
]));
```

A handler or middleware that only knows the hints once it sees the request calls `early_hints::send` before it returns. The `103` goes out at once and the final response follows:

```rust
use rust_web_server::early_hints;

// inside a handler, before the slow part
early_hints::send(&["</product.css>; rel=preload; as=style"]);
```

`send` returns `false` and does nothing when there is nowhere to send the hint: under `TestClient`, for an app called directly, on HTTP/1.1 unless enabled (below), on HTTP/1.0, after `early_hints::MAX_PER_REQUEST` (4) `103`s for the request, or for a value that is empty or contains CR, LF or NUL. `early_hints::available()` says whether a `send` would reach the client.

## In the config file

```toml
[[route]]
[route.match]
path = "/shop/*"
[route.action]
type = "proxy"
upstream = "shop"
[route.middleware]
early_hints = ["</shop.css>; rel=preload; as=style"]
```

See [Early hints](/proxy/config-driven/#early-hints) on the config-driven proxy page. A proxy route — and `ReverseProxy` in code — also passes on a backend's own `103`, keeping only its `Link` values.

## Metrics

`rws_early_hints_total{source}` counts the `103`s sent: `configured` (`EarlyHintsLayer`, a route's `early_hints`), `upstream` (a backend's `103` passed on) and `handler` (`early_hints::send`).

## Protocols

| Connection | Sent |
|---|---|
| HTTP/2, HTTP/3 | Yes |
| HTTP/1.1 | Only with `early_hints_http1 = true` (`RWS_CONFIG_EARLY_HINTS_HTTP1`) |
| HTTP/1.0 | Never |

Browsers act on `103` only over HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and some older HTTP/1.1 clients mishandle a `1xx` they did not ask for, so HTTP/1.1 is opt-in. The `http1`-only build runs the handler on the thread that owns the socket and writes its hints just before the response. HTTP/1.1 requests with a streamed body (a large upload read while the handler runs) get no hints.

---

# HTTPS / TLS

<https://rws8.tech/docs/features/https-tls/>

## Feature requirements

TLS is available when you build with the `http2` or `http3` (default) feature.
The `http1`-only build has no TLS support.

```bash
# Default build — HTTP/3 + HTTP/2 + TLS
cargo build

# HTTP/2 + TLS only, no QUIC
cargo build --no-default-features --features http2
```

## Local HTTPS: `tls = "internal"`

For development, rws can be its own certificate authority (since 18.21.0):

```sh
rws --tls=internal          # or tls = "internal" in rws.config.toml
rws trust                   # once: browsers and curl trust https://localhost
```

On first use rws creates a CA (EC P-256, valid ten years) in your data
directory — `~/.local/share/rws/pki` on Linux (`$XDG_DATA_HOME` if set),
`~/Library/Application Support/rws/pki` on macOS, `%APPDATA%\rws\pki` on
Windows; `tls_internal_dir` (`RWS_CONFIG_TLS_INTERNAL_DIR`) moves it. It then
serves a certificate it issued for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, the
listen address, every `[[virtual_host]]` domain and the names in
`tls_internal_names`:

```toml
tls = "internal"
tls_internal_names = "app.localhost, api.localhost, myapp.test"
```

The certificate lives 7 days and is re-issued at half-life without a
restart. Browsers refuse wildcards directly under a top-level name, so list
`app.localhost` rather than `*.localhost` (`*.myapp.test` is fine).

`rws trust` adds the CA to the system trust store — `update-ca-certificates`
on Debian/Ubuntu, `update-ca-trust` on Fedora/RHEL, `trust` on Arch (with
`sudo`, which asks for your password), the System keychain on macOS, the
current user's Root store on Windows — and to the NSS database Chrome and
Firefox use on Linux (`~/.pki/nssdb`, needs `certutil` from
`libnss3-tools`). `rws untrust` takes it out; `rws trust --print` writes the
CA certificate to stdout, e.g. for a phone or another machine:

```sh
rws trust --print > rws-ca.pem
curl --cacert rws-ca.pem https://localhost:7878/
```

Only for development and private networks: the CA key sits on your disk.
If `tls_cert_file`/`tls_key_file` or `acme_domains` are set, they win and
`tls = "internal"` is ignored (with a note at startup).

## Generating a self-signed certificate

Or use `openssl` to create a certificate and key yourself:

```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem \
  -days 365 -nodes -subj "/CN=localhost"
```

## Starting the server with TLS

Pass the certificate and key on the command line:

```bash
cargo run -- --tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem
```

Alternatively, set environment variables or add them to `rws.config.toml`:

```bash
export RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE=cert.pem
export RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE=key.pem
cargo run
```

```toml
# rws.config.toml
tls_cert_file = "cert.pem"
tls_key_file  = "key.pem"
```

## TLS implementation

`rust-web-server` uses [rustls](https://github.com/rustls/rustls) with the
`aws-lc-rs` cryptography backend. There is no dependency on OpenSSL.

## FIPS 140-3

For environments that require FIPS-validated cryptography, build with the
`fips` feature (since 18.23.0) or use the release's
`rws-<version>-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu-fips.tar.gz`:

```sh
cargo install rust-web-server --features "fips acme auth sso"   # needs CMake, Go and a C compiler
rws --version   # rws 18.23.0 (FIPS)
```

TLS — the HTTPS and QUIC listeners, mTLS client verification, ACME, the
reverse proxy's upstream connections and the outbound HTTP client — then
runs on aws-lc's FIPS 140-3 validated module with only FIPS-approved
algorithms: AES-GCM suites (no ChaCha20-Poly1305), NIST curves and the
approved hybrid key exchange, RSA and ECDSA signatures. At startup rws
checks that every TLS configuration rustls builds reports itself
FIPS-compliant and refuses to start otherwise; `GET /admin/api/v1/status`
lists `fips` among the features.

Not covered by the module: HS256 JWTs and the `{SHA256}` htpasswd scheme
(RustCrypto `hmac`/`sha2`), ES256 JWT verification (`p256`), rws's own
SHA-256 for cache keys and signed cookies, and the in-crate RSA verifier
used for RS256 tokens and SAML. Where your policy needs those under the
module too, keep authentication in a FIPS-validated identity provider and
use the TLS side of rws. The FIPS build is glibc-only (aws-lc's FIPS module
doesn't build for musl), so there's no FIPS container image yet.

## Keys in an HSM or cloud KMS (PKCS#11)

Since 18.23.0 the private key can stay on a hardware security module, a
smart card or a cloud KMS: `tls_key_file` (or a virtual host's `key_file`)
takes an RFC 7512 `pkcs11:` URI instead of a path, and rws asks the token to
sign each handshake.

```toml
tls_cert_file = "/etc/rws/cert.pem"          # the certificate stays a file
tls_key_file  = "pkcs11:token=rws;object=web-key?module-path=/usr/lib/softhsm/libsofthsm2.so&pin-source=env:HSM_PIN"
```

| URI part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `token=` | the token's label |
| `object=` / `id=` | the key's label / its `CKA_ID` (percent-encoded bytes) |
| `module-path=` | the vendor's PKCS#11 library |
| `pin-source=env:VAR` | the PIN from an environment variable (or `file:/run/secrets/pin`); `pin-value=` works but puts the PIN in the config |

Keys: ECDSA P-256 and P-384, RSA (RSA-PSS for TLS 1.3, PKCS#1 v1.5 also for
TLS 1.2 clients). The module loads at startup; each key keeps a pool of up
to 8 logged-in sessions (handshakes sign in parallel), reopened if the token
drops them; a `pin-value=` is hidden in the startup output and the admin
API's config; and `rws --check` opens the
key, so a wrong PIN or label shows up before a restart. Tested with
SoftHSM2; the same works with AWS CloudHSM (`libcloudhsm_pkcs11.so`),
Google Cloud KMS (`libkmsp11.so`, with its config file in the environment),
Azure Managed HSM and YubiHSM's PKCS#11 libraries.

The token's wait doesn't hold up other connections: rustls asks for the
signature synchronously inside the handshake, so rws hands the worker's
other connections to the rest of the pool while the token works
(`block_in_place` on the shared runtime). That's why the `rws` binary keeps
the **shared runtime** when a TLS key is a `pkcs11:` URI and `runtime` isn't
set (it says so at startup). With `runtime = "per-core"` set explicitly,
each signature stalls that core's connections for as long as the token takes
(sub-millisecond on a local HSM, more over the network to a cloud KMS) and
rws warns at startup.

Needs the `pkcs11` feature: in the macOS, Windows and Linux glibc
(`…-linux-gnu-fips`) release binaries, not in the static musl ones (they
can't load a library at runtime) — or `cargo install rust-web-server
--features "pkcs11 acme auth"`. With `fips` too, TLS runs on aws-lc's FIPS
module and the key never leaves the HSM.

## ALPN negotiation

When a TLS certificate is configured, the server advertises both `h2` and
`http/1.1` via ALPN in the TLS handshake. A single port handles HTTP/2 and
HTTP/1.1 simultaneously — no extra configuration is required.

```
alpn_protocols = ["h2", "http/1.1"]
```

The HTTP/2 server (`h2_server`) turns HTTP/2 streams into the same `Request` /
`Application::execute` / `Response` pipeline that HTTP/1.1 uses.

## HTTP → HTTPS redirect

Set `RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT` to have the server also listen on a plain
HTTP port and issue `301 Moved Permanently` redirects to HTTPS:

```bash
export RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT=80
```

```toml
# rws.config.toml
http_redirect_port = "80"
```

`Server::run_redirect()` binds the redirect listener and sends every incoming
request to the HTTPS port with a `301` response.

## Alt-Svc advertisement

HTTP/1.1 TLS responses include an `Alt-Svc` header so clients learn that a
faster protocol is available:

- HTTP/3 build: `Alt-Svc: h3=":7878"`
- HTTP/2-only build: `Alt-Svc: h2=":7878"`

Browsers that support HTTP/3 will upgrade automatically on subsequent requests.

## Configuration reference

| Variable | Config key | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE` | `tls_cert_file` | Path to the PEM certificate chain |
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE` | `tls_key_file` | Path to the PEM private key |
| `RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT` | `http_redirect_port` | Plain HTTP port that issues 301 → HTTPS |

:::note[Hot reload]
Send `SIGHUP` or `POST /admin/config/reload` to reload the TLS certificate
from disk without restarting the server. This also rebuilds the TLS acceptor
for all configured virtual hosts.
:::


## Upstream TLS (proxy mode)

When using the config-driven proxy (`rws.config.toml`), prefix backend addresses with `https://` to connect to upstream services over TLS:

```toml
[[upstream]]
name     = "secure-api"
backends = ["https://api.internal:443", "https://api2.internal:443"]
```

Certificate verification uses the WebPKI root store (same trust anchors as browsers). To trust a private CA instead, set `tls_ca_file` on the `[[upstream]]` (since 18.0.0). Requires the `http-client` or `http2` feature — included in all builds except `--no-default-features --features http1`.

See [Config-Driven Proxy → TLS upstreams](/proxy/config-driven/#tls-https-upstreams) for the full reference.

---

# Automatic HTTPS (ACME)

<https://rws8.tech/docs/features/acme/>

rws gets HTTPS certificates from Let's Encrypt (or any ACME CA) by itself:
list your domains under `[acme]`, open ports 80 and 443, and it orders,
installs and renews them with no restart. HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01 and DNS-01
challenges are supported, including wildcards and on-demand TLS.

Point a domain's DNS at the server, then:

```toml
# rws.config.toml
port               = 443
http_redirect_port = 80     # HTTP → HTTPS redirects; also answers ACME challenges

[acme]
domains = ["example.com", "www.example.com"]
email   = "you@example.com"
```

```bash
rws
```

On first start `rws` requests a certificate, stores it in `.rws/acme/`
(`cert.pem`, `key.pem`, `account.key` — keys `0600`, the directory `0700`,
and never served: the working directory is the web root), and starts serving HTTPS, HTTP/2, and
HTTP/3 with it. Later starts reuse the stored certificate. Renewal happens in
the background and is hot-swapped without dropping connections.

:::note[Which binaries include ACME]
The prebuilt binaries (Homebrew, `cargo binstall`, Docker, GitHub Releases)
include it. When building from source, enable the `acme` feature:
`cargo install rust-web-server --features acme,auth`. A binary built without
it prints a warning if `[acme]` is configured instead of silently serving
plain HTTP.
:::

## Requirements

- **DNS** for every domain in `domains` points at this server.
- **One way for the CA to check you control the domains**: port 80 reachable
  from the internet (HTTP-01, the default), or port 443 (TLS-ALPN-01), or
  write access to the domain's DNS (DNS-01, also for wildcards) — see
  [Challenge types](#challenge-types).
- **Binding ports 80/443 on Linux** needs root or the capability:
  `sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep "$(which rws)"`.

IPv6 is handled: when a domain has an AAAA record, Let's Encrypt validates
over IPv6, so the challenge and redirect listeners accept both IPv4 and IPv6.

## How it works

1. **Startup.** If no certificate exists, or it is due for renewal (see 4),
   `rws` runs the ACME flow before opening the HTTPS
   port: account (key saved to `.rws/acme/account.key`), order, HTTP-01 challenge,
   ECDSA P-256 key + CSR, finalize, download.
2. **Challenges.** At startup a temporary listener on the challenge port
   (default 80) answers them. Once the HTTP → HTTPS redirect listener is
   running on that port, it answers challenges itself — so renewals never
   compete with it for port 80.
3. **First-time failures are retried**, e.g. while DNS for a new domain is
   still propagating: after 30 s, doubling up to every 15 minutes, until a
   certificate is issued.
4. **Renewal** (since 18.0.0). A certificate is renewed at two-thirds of its
   lifetime — day 60 of 90, day 30 of 45, day 4 of 6 — or earlier when the
   CA's ACME Renewal Information ([RFC 9773](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9773.html))
   suggests a window that opens sooner, e.g. after a revocation. `rws` asks
   for it at every check (every 12 hours at most, every 6 when the CA has
   renewal information, sooner when renewal is due earlier or the CA's
   `Retry-After` says so) and picks a point in the window that's fixed per
   certificate. The renewal order names the certificate it replaces, so the
   CA can exempt it from rate limits. A failed renewal is retried within an
   hour. After renewing it reloads the TLS certificate in place (on Unix, via
   the same `SIGHUP` reload used for config). `renew_before_days`, if set,
   replaces the two-thirds point (a CA window that opens earlier still wins).
5. **New names.** A name added to `domains` that the stored certificate
   doesn't cover gets a new order at the next start or check, for all the
   names (since 18.8.3); before that the old certificate was used until it
   was due.
6. **Profiles.** `profile` orders a certificate profile the CA offers —
   Let's Encrypt has `classic`, `tlsserver` and `shortlived` (6-day
   certificates). A name the CA doesn't list stops provisioning with the list
   it offers. Unset, the CA picks its default.

The ACME client (RFC 8555) is implemented in-crate. It has been tested end to
end against [Pebble](https://github.com/letsencrypt/pebble), Let's Encrypt's
test CA, including a `shortlived` profile and renewal on Pebble's renewal
information through the redirect listener.

## Testing with the staging CA

Let's Encrypt production has strict
[rate limits](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits/). Try your setup
against staging first — its certificates aren't browser-trusted, but the
limits are generous:

```toml
[acme]
domains = ["example.com"]
staging = true
```

Delete `.rws/acme/` before switching back to production.

Before 17.113.1 the defaults were `cert.pem`, `key.pem` and `acme_account.key`
in the working directory — the web root, so the keys could be downloaded.
On upgrade, files found there are moved into `.rws/acme/` (when the default
paths are in use), and the static server no longer serves `*.pem`, `*.key`
or `rws.config.toml` anywhere. Rotate a key that was exposed.

## Private ACME CAs

To use step-ca, an internal Boulder, or Pebble, set the directory URL and
trust the CA's root certificate (in addition to the public roots):

```toml
[acme]
domains   = ["internal.example"]
directory = "https://ca.internal.example:9000/acme/acme/directory"
ca_file   = "/etc/rws/internal-root.pem"
```

## Challenge types

`challenge` picks how the CA checks that you control the domains (since
18.4.0; HTTP-01 before):

| `challenge` | The CA checks | Needs | Wildcards |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http-01` (default) | `http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/…` | port 80 reachable | no |
| `tls-alpn-01` | a TLS handshake on port 443 with ALPN `acme-tls/1` (RFC 8737) | port 443 reachable — nothing else | no |
| `dns-01` | a TXT record `_acme-challenge.<domain>` | a way to change the domain's DNS | yes |
| `dns-persist-01` | a TXT record `_validation-persist.<domain>` you publish once | nothing on the server: no port, no DNS credentials | yes |

### TLS-ALPN-01

For a server that only listens on 443 — no port 80 at all:

```toml
port = 443

[acme]
domains   = ["example.com"]
challenge = "tls-alpn-01"
```

rws answers on its HTTPS port: at startup, before it has a certificate, a
temporary acceptor on the same socket serves the challenge; afterwards the
TLS listener does, beside the normal traffic. A challenge handshake gets a
special self-signed certificate and is then closed; other clients never
see it. If a port mapping forwards 443 elsewhere, set `port` to where it
lands.

### DNS-01

The CA looks up a TXT record, so nothing needs to reach the server — and it
is the only way to get a wildcard certificate (`*.example.com`). rws adds
the record, waits until the zone's server answers with it, lets the CA check,
and removes it.

```toml
[acme]
domains   = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge = "dns-01"
dns_provider        = "rfc2136"            # DNS UPDATE (RFC 2136) to the primary server
dns_server          = "ns1.example.com"    # host[:port], port 53
dns_tsig_key        = "rws-acme"           # TSIG key name the server knows
dns_tsig_secret     = "base64secret=="     # better in RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_SECRET
# dns_tsig_algorithm  = "hmac-sha256"      # or hmac-sha512
# dns_zone            = "example.com"      # found by SOA lookup when not set
# dns_propagation_secs = 120               # how long to wait for the record
```

| `dns_provider` | Adds and removes the record by |
|---|---|
| `rfc2136` | a DNS UPDATE to `dns_server`, signed with the TSIG key — BIND, Knot, PowerDNS, Windows DNS, and many DNS hosts' "dynamic DNS" endpoints |
| `cloudflare` | Cloudflare's API, with an API token (`dns_api_token`) |
| `route53` | Amazon Route 53's API, signed with the credentials in `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` (and `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`) |
| `exec` | running `dns_exec` as `<program> present <fqdn> <value>` and `<program> cleanup <fqdn> <value>`: any DNS API, in a script (exit status 0 = done) |

A BIND key and the zone permission it needs:

```text
key "rws-acme" { algorithm hmac-sha256; secret "base64secret=="; };
zone "example.com" { type primary; file "example.com.zone";
    update-policy { grant rws-acme name _acme-challenge.example.com. TXT; }; };
```

(`tsig-keygen rws-acme` prints a new key.) The secret is never printed in
rws's startup log.

#### Cloudflare

```toml
[acme]
domains      = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge    = "dns-01"
dns_provider = "cloudflare"
# dns_api_token = "..."     # better in RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_TOKEN; never printed
# dns_zone_id   = "023e105f4ecef8ad9ca31a8372d0c353"
```

Create the token under *My Profile → API Tokens* with **Zone → DNS → Edit**
for the zone. rws finds the zone by asking for `example.com`'s parents in
turn, which also needs **Zone → Zone → Read** — or set `dns_zone_id` (the
zone's overview page shows it) and the DNS permission is enough. rws
replaces the `_acme-challenge` TXT records and deletes its own afterwards.

#### Route 53

```toml
[acme]
domains      = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge    = "dns-01"
dns_provider = "route53"
# dns_zone_id = "Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ"
```

Credentials come from the environment the AWS tools use —
`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and, for temporary ones,
`AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` (instance roles and profiles in `~/.aws` aren't read:
export them, e.g. `eval "$(aws configure export-credentials --format env)"`).
The IAM policy needs `route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets` and
`route53:GetChange`, plus `route53:ListHostedZonesByName` unless
`dns_zone_id` is set:

```json
{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [
  {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets"], "Resource": "arn:aws:route53:::hostedzone/Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ"},
  {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["route53:GetChange", "route53:ListHostedZonesByName"], "Resource": "*"}]}
```

rws waits for Route 53 to report the change `INSYNC`, then for the record
to be visible, as with every provider (`dns_server`, or the system resolver
— set `dns_server` to one of the zone's name servers to skip resolver
caches).

CI tests both against a stand-in API that writes into BIND, with the
request signatures checked independently, and Pebble validating
(`ci/e2e/acme_dns_api.sh`).

### DNS-PERSIST-01

The CA looks up one TXT record that you publish once and leave in place:
it names the CA and your ACME account, so nothing on the server needs DNS
credentials or an open port, and renewals need no DNS change at all
(draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist; Let's Encrypt is rolling it out — Pebble has
it).

```toml
[acme]
domains   = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge = "dns-persist-01"
# dns_server = "ns1.example.com"   # where to look for the record (else the system resolver)
```

The first time, rws creates its ACME account and logs the record to
publish (one line):

```text
[ACME] Provisioning failed: dns-persist-01: publish this TXT record once (it stays; rws retries until it's visible): _validation-persist.example.com. TXT "letsencrypt.org; accounturi=https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/acme/acct/123456; policy=wildcard"
```

Publish it at your DNS host; rws retries on its own and issues as soon as
it sees the record. `policy=wildcard` is there because `*.example.com` is
in `domains`. The record belongs to the ACME account, so keep
`account_key_path`'s file (`.rws/acme/account.key`) — with a new key comes a
new account, and a new record to publish. Before asking the CA, rws checks
that the record is visible, so a missing one never costs a failed
validation. `dns_provider` is ignored: rws never changes this record.

## On-demand TLS

For a SaaS whose customers point their own domains at it: rws orders a
certificate at the first TLS handshake for a name nobody configured, once
your *ask* endpoint allows that name (since 18.4.0).

```toml
http_redirect_port = 80                  # answers HTTP-01

[acme]
domains       = ["saas.example.com"]     # rws's own certificate, the default
on_demand     = true                     # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND
on_demand_ask = "http://127.0.0.1:9000/allowed"   # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND_ASK
```

- Before each order rws asks `GET <on_demand_ask>?domain=<name>`; a 2xx
  answer allows it, anything else (or no answer in five seconds) refuses
  it. Answer from your list of customer domains. `on_demand` without
  `on_demand_ask` is refused: anyone could make rws order certificates for
  every name they point at it.
- The first handshake for a new name waits for its certificate (up to 90
  seconds; with Let's Encrypt usually a few). A refused name gets the
  default certificate and isn't asked about again for a minute; a failed
  order isn't retried for ten. At most four orders run at once, and one per
  name however many clients arrive together.
- Certificates are kept in `.rws/acme/on-demand/<name>/` (next to the
  `cert_path`), loaded at startup and renewed like the main one; with
  [`redis`](#several-replicas) replicas share them too.
- HTTP-01 or TLS-ALPN-01 (DNS-01 would need every customer's zone). Over
  HTTP/3 a name is served once a TCP handshake has ordered it.

CI checks it against Pebble with an ask endpoint (`ci/e2e/acme_on_demand.sh`):
an allowed name is served its certificate on the first request, a refused
one the default, five simultaneous first requests make one order, and a
restart orders nothing.

## Several replicas

Replicas of one site behind a load balancer each run ACME for the same
domains. On their own they would each order a certificate — hitting the
CA's rate limits — and each answer only the challenges they presented,
while the CA's request may reach another replica. Give them one Redis
(since 18.4.0):

```toml
[acme]
domains = ["example.com"]
redis   = "10.0.0.20:6379"       # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS
# redis_password = "..."         # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PASSWORD; never printed
# redis_prefix   = "rws:acme"    # several sites in one Redis
```

- One replica orders each certificate (a lock in Redis, held up to five
  minutes); the others wait for it and install it.
- A renewal by any replica reaches the rest at their next renewal check,
  which they hot-swap like their own.
- HTTP-01 and TLS-ALPN-01 challenges are answered by every replica, from
  Redis, wherever the CA's request lands.
- Redis down: each replica carries on alone with its own files, and says so
  in its log.

The certificate's private key is stored in Redis: keep Redis on a private
network (and set a password). CI runs two replicas against one Redis and
Pebble (`ci/e2e/acme_shared.sh`): one order per certificate, both serving
the same one before and after a renewal.

## Configuration reference

Every setting can go in the `[acme]` section of `rws.config.toml`, on the
command line (`--acme-domains=...`; not the last three), or in the environment.

| `[acme]` key | Environment variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `domains` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DOMAINS` | — | Domains for the certificate. Setting this enables ACME. |
| `email` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_EMAIL` | — | Contact email for expiry notices from the CA |
| `staging` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_STAGING` | `false` | Use the Let's Encrypt staging CA |
| `directory` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DIRECTORY` | Let's Encrypt | ACME directory URL of another CA |
| `ca_file` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CA_FILE` | — | Extra root CA(s) to trust for the directory (private CAs) |
| `challenge` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CHALLENGE` | `http-01` | `http-01`, `tls-alpn-01`, `dns-01` or `dns-persist-01` — see [Challenge types](#challenge-types) |
| `challenge_port` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CHALLENGE_PORT` | `80` | Port the CA connects to for HTTP-01 |
| `dns_provider` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_PROVIDER` | — | DNS-01: `rfc2136`, `cloudflare`, `route53` or `exec` |
| `dns_server` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_SERVER` | — | DNS-01: `rfc2136`'s primary server, `host[:port]`; otherwise optional: where to look for the record (else the system resolver) |
| `dns_api_token` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_TOKEN` | — | DNS-01 `cloudflare`: the API token (no command-line flag; never printed) |
| `dns_zone_id` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_ZONE_ID` | looked up | DNS-01 `cloudflare` / `route53`: the zone's id |
| `dns_api_url` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_URL` | the provider's | DNS-01 `cloudflare` / `route53`: another API base URL (a proxy, a test double) |
| `dns_zone` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_ZONE` | SOA lookup | DNS-01: the zone of the records |
| `dns_tsig_key` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_KEY` | — | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: TSIG key name |
| `dns_tsig_secret` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_SECRET` | — | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: TSIG secret, base64 (no command-line flag; never printed) |
| `dns_tsig_algorithm` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_ALGORITHM` | `hmac-sha256` | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: `hmac-sha256` or `hmac-sha512` |
| `dns_exec` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_EXEC` | — | DNS-01 `exec`: the program |
| `dns_propagation_secs` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_PROPAGATION_SECS` | `120` | DNS-01: how long to wait for the record to be visible |
| `redis` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS` | — | Redis `host:port` shared by replicas — see [Several replicas](#several-replicas) |
| `redis_password` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PASSWORD` | — | Its password (no command-line flag; never printed) |
| `redis_prefix` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PREFIX` | `rws:acme` | Key prefix in that Redis |
| `on_demand` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND` | `false` | Order certificates at the first handshake — see [On-demand TLS](#on-demand-tls) |
| `on_demand_ask` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND_ASK` | — | URL asked `?domain=<name>` before each such order; 2xx allows it |
| `cert_path` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CERT_PATH` | `tls_cert_file`, else `.rws/acme/cert.pem` | Where the certificate chain is stored |
| `key_path` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_KEY_PATH` | `tls_key_file`, else `.rws/acme/key.pem` | Where the certificate key is stored (`0600`) |
| `renew_before_days` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_BEFORE_DAYS` | — | Renew this many days before expiry instead of at two-thirds of the lifetime (was `30` before 18.0.0) |
| `profile` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_PROFILE` | — | Certificate profile to order (`classic`, `tlsserver`, `shortlived`, … as the CA offers) |
| `renew_check_interval_secs` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_CHECK_INTERVAL_SECS` | `43200` | Longest time between renewal checks |
| `account_key_path` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ACCOUNT_KEY_PATH` | `.rws/acme/account.key` | Where the ACME account key is stored (`0600`) |

Top-level `http_redirect_port` (`RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT`) starts the
HTTP → HTTPS redirect listener; set it to the challenge port (80) in
production.

## Using ACME from Rust

The `rws` binary does all of the above. In your own binary built on the
library, the equivalent is:

```rust
use rust_web_server::acme::{AcmeConfig, AcmeManager};
use rust_web_server::prelude::*;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().unwrap();

    if let Some(cfg) = AcmeConfig::from_env() {
        // Serve the issued certificate unless TLS paths were set explicitly.
        cfg.install_as_tls_certificate();
        let mgr = AcmeManager::new(cfg);
        mgr.provision_until_ready().await;   // retries until issued
        tokio::spawn(mgr.run_renewal_loop());
    }

    let app = App::new();
    tokio::join!(
        Server::run_tls(listener, pool, app.clone()),
        Server::run_quic(app),
        Server::run_redirect(),               // answers renewal challenges
    );
}
```

`AcmeManager::provision_if_needed()` (single attempt, returns the error) is
also available if you want to handle failures yourself.
