# Raw SQL

<https://rws8.tech/docs/database/raw-sql/>

The query builder covers most common queries, but sometimes you need raw SQL — complex joins, CTEs, window functions, or database-specific syntax. `DbPool` exposes three async methods for this.

## Typed query: `query::`

`pool.query::(sql, params).await` executes a SQL statement and deserialises each row into `T` using `T::from_row`. `T` must implement `Model` (typically via `#[derive(Model)]`).

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbPool, Value};

let pool = DbPool::from_env().await?;

let users: Vec = pool.query::(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE role = ? AND active = ?",
    &[Value::Text("admin".into()), Value::Bool(true)],
).await?;
```

For PostgreSQL replace `?` with `$1`, `$2`, etc.:

```rust
let users: Vec = pool.query::(
    "SELECT * FROM users WHERE role = $1 AND active = $2",
    &[Value::Text("admin".into()), Value::Bool(true)],
).await?;
```

## Untyped query: `query_raw`

`pool.query_raw(sql, params).await` returns `Vec` — column-name/value pairs without deserialisation. Use this for ad-hoc queries, reporting, or when no matching `Model` type exists.

```rust
let rows = pool.query_raw(
    "SELECT u.name, COUNT(p.id) AS post_count \
     FROM users u \
     LEFT JOIN posts p ON p.user_id = u.id \
     GROUP BY u.id, u.name \
     ORDER BY post_count DESC",
    &[],
).await?;

for row in &rows {
    let name: String = row.get::("name")?;
    let count: i64  = row.get::<i64>("post_count")?;
    println!("{name}: {count} posts");
}
```

## Execute: `execute`

`pool.execute(sql, params).await` runs INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, or DDL statements and returns the number of rows affected.

```rust
let affected: u64 = pool.execute(
    "UPDATE users SET last_login = ? WHERE id = ?",
    &[Value::Text("2026-07-02T10:00:00Z".into()), Value::Int(42)],
).await?;
println!("{affected} row(s) updated");
```

## Extracting columns from `ModelRow`

`ModelRow::get::(col)` performs typed column extraction by name (case-insensitive). It returns `Result`.

```rust
let name: String       = row.get::("name")?;
let age: i64           = row.get::<i64>("age")?;
let score: f64         = row.get::<f64>("score")?;
let verified: bool     = row.get::<bool>("verified")?;
let bio: Option = row.get::>("bio")?;
```

## The `Value` enum

All parameters and raw column values are represented as `Value`:

| Variant | Rust type | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `Value::Null` | — | SQL NULL |
| `Value::Bool(bool)` | `bool` | boolean columns |
| `Value::Int(i64)` | integer types | `INTEGER`, `BIGINT`, `SMALLINT` |
| `Value::Float(f64)` | float types | `REAL`, `DOUBLE PRECISION` |
| `Value::Text(String)` | `String` / `&str` | `TEXT`, `VARCHAR`, dates as strings |
| `Value::Bytes(Vec<u8>)` | `Vec<u8>` | `BLOB`, `BYTEA` |

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::Value;

let params = &[
    Value::Text("alice@example.com".into()),
    Value::Int(30),
    Value::Bool(true),
    Value::Null,                               // e.g. an optional field
];
```

## The `FromColumn` trait

Built-in `FromColumn` implementations cover `i16`, `i32`, `i64`, `u32`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64`, `bool`, `String`, and `Option` for any `T: FromColumn` (there is none for `Vec<u8>`; read a `Value::Bytes` column through a newtype with its own `FromColumn` impl).

Implement it for custom types to enable `row.get::("col")`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{FromColumn, Value, DbError};

#[derive(Debug)]
pub enum UserRole { Admin, Member, Guest }

impl FromColumn for UserRole {
    fn from_column(v: Value) -> Result {
        match v {
            Value::Text(s) => match s.as_str() {
                "admin"  => Ok(UserRole::Admin),
                "member" => Ok(UserRole::Member),
                "guest"  => Ok(UserRole::Guest),
                other    => Err(DbError::new(format!("unknown role: {other}"))),
            },
            other => Err(DbError::new(format!("expected Text for UserRole, got {other:?}"))),
        }
    }
}

// Usage
let role: UserRole = row.get::("role")?;
```

## When to use raw SQL vs QueryBuilder

| Situation | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Simple equality filters, pagination, ordering | `QueryBuilder` |
| Multi-table joins | Raw SQL |
| CTEs (`WITH …`) | Raw SQL |
| Window functions (`OVER PARTITION BY …`) | Raw SQL |
| Database-specific functions (`DATE_TRUNC`, `JSON_EXTRACT`, …) | Raw SQL |
| INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE with complex expressions | Raw SQL via `execute` |
| Schema mutations (DDL) | Raw SQL via `execute` |

:::note[Parameterise always]
Never interpolate user input directly into a SQL string. Always pass untrusted values through the `params` slice so the driver can prepare and bind them safely.
:::

---

# Transactions

<https://rws8.tech/docs/database/transactions/>

`DbPool` provides two ways to work with transactions: a closure-based helper that handles commit and rollback automatically, and a manual `begin` / `commit` / `rollback` API for more complex flows.

## Closure-based transactions

`pool.transaction(|mut tx| async move { … }).await` is the recommended approach. Pass an `async` closure that receives (and owns) a `DbTransaction`. `transaction` itself does not commit: call `tx.commit().await` before returning `Ok`. If the closure returns `Err` — or returns without committing — the transaction is dropped and rolled back automatically, so you never need to call `rollback()` yourself unless you want to roll back inside the closure explicitly.

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbPool, Value};

let pool = DbPool::from_env().await?;

pool.transaction(|mut tx| async move {
    tx.execute(
        "INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES (?, ?)",
        &[Value::Text("Alice".into()), Value::Text("alice@example.com".into())],
    ).await?;
    tx.execute(
        "INSERT INTO profiles (user_id, bio) VALUES (?, ?)",
        &[Value::Int(1), Value::Text("Hello!".into())],
    ).await?;
    tx.commit().await
}).await?;
```

The closure can return any `Ok(T)` value; `transaction` passes it back to the caller.

```rust
let new_id: i64 = pool.transaction(|mut tx| async move {
    tx.execute(
        "INSERT INTO orders (user_id, total) VALUES (?, ?)",
        &[Value::Int(1), Value::Float(49.99)],
    ).await?;
    // Retrieve the generated PK via a follow-up query
    let rows = tx.query_rows("SELECT last_insert_rowid() AS id", &[]).await?;
    let id: i64 = rows[0].get("id")?;
    tx.commit().await?;
    Ok(id)
}).await?;
```

## Manual transactions

Use `pool.begin().await` when you need explicit control — for example, when the commit/rollback decision is made outside a single closure scope.

```rust
let mut tx = pool.begin().await?;

let result = do_first_step(&mut tx).await;
if result.is_err() {
    let _ = tx.rollback().await;
    return Err(result.unwrap_err());
}

let result2 = do_second_step(&mut tx).await;
if result2.is_err() {
    let _ = tx.rollback().await;
    return Err(result2.unwrap_err());
}

tx.commit().await?;
```

## Inserting a User and Profile atomically

A common pattern is creating a parent record and a related child record together so that neither exists without the other.

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbPool, Value};

let pool = DbPool::from_env().await?;

pool.transaction(|mut tx| async move {
    // Insert the user
    tx.execute(
        "INSERT INTO users (name, email, active) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
        &[
            Value::Text("Bob".into()),
            Value::Text("bob@example.com".into()),
            Value::Bool(true),
        ],
    ).await?;

    // Retrieve the generated PK
    let rows = tx.query_rows("SELECT last_insert_rowid() AS id", &[]).await?;
    let user_id: i64 = rows[0].get("id")?;

    // Insert the profile linked to that user
    tx.execute(
        "INSERT INTO profiles (user_id, bio, avatar_url) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
        &[
            Value::Int(user_id),
            Value::Text("Software engineer".into()),
            Value::Null, // optional field
        ],
    ).await?;

    tx.commit().await?;
    Ok(user_id)
}).await?;
```

If the profile insert fails (e.g., a constraint violation), the closure returns `Err` before `commit()`, the dropped transaction rolls back the user insert as well, and the database is left unchanged.

## Error handling pattern

Return `Err` from the closure to trigger an automatic rollback:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbError, Value};

pool.transaction(|mut tx| async move {
    let affected = tx.execute(
        "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ? AND balance >= ?",
        &[Value::Float(100.0), Value::Int(sender_id), Value::Float(100.0)],
    ).await?;

    if affected == 0 {
        // Returning Err here causes an automatic rollback
        return Err(DbError::new("insufficient funds or account not found"));
    }

    tx.execute(
        "UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?",
        &[Value::Float(100.0), Value::Int(receiver_id)],
    ).await?;

    tx.commit().await
}).await?;
```

:::note[Savepoints]
The current API does not expose SQL savepoints. For nested transaction semantics, use the closure form and handle all steps within a single `transaction` call.
:::

---

# Migrations

<https://rws8.tech/docs/database/migrations/>

The migration runner reads `*.sql` files from a directory in lexicographic order, executes any that have not already been applied, and records each run in a `_schema_migrations` table. No external tools or frameworks are required.

## How it works

1. `pool.migrate("migrations/").await` creates `_schema_migrations(version VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY, applied_at VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL)` if it does not already exist (`VARCHAR` since 18.30: MySQL can't key a `TEXT` column; a table created as `TEXT` by an earlier release keeps working).
2. It reads every `*.sql` file in the directory sorted lexicographically by filename.
3. Files whose name is already in `_schema_migrations` are skipped.
4. Each unapplied file is executed inside a `BEGIN` / `COMMIT` transaction, one statement at a time — the file is split on `;`, so a `;` inside a string literal or a trigger/function body breaks it. If the file fails, the transaction is rolled back and `migrate` returns `Err` immediately — subsequent files are not attempted.

## File naming convention

Prefix files with a zero-padded sequence number so lexicographic order matches execution order:

```
migrations/
  001_create_users.sql
  002_add_email_index.sql
  003_create_posts.sql
  004_add_posts_status_column.sql
```

The full filename (without the directory prefix) is used as the version key, so renaming a file that has already been applied will cause it to run again. Never rename applied migration files.

## Example migration files

```sql
-- migrations/001_create_users.sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    name    TEXT    NOT NULL,
    email   TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    active  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
);
```

```sql
-- migrations/002_add_email_index.sql
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);
```

```sql
-- migrations/003_create_posts.sql
CREATE TABLE posts (
    id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    user_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
    title      TEXT    NOT NULL,
    body       TEXT    NOT NULL,
    status     TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft',
    created_at TEXT    NOT NULL
);
```

```sql
-- migrations/004_add_posts_status_column.sql
ALTER TABLE posts ADD COLUMN published_at TEXT;
```

## Running migrations

Call `migrate` once at server startup, before the application begins accepting requests:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbConfig, DbPool};

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let config = DbConfig::from_env().expect("database config");
    let pool = DbPool::new(config).await.expect("connection pool");

    pool.migrate("migrations/").await.expect("migrations failed");

    // start the server ...
}
```

If all migrations have already been applied, `migrate` is a no-op and returns immediately.

## Checking migration status

`pool.migration_status(dir).await` returns a `Vec` — one entry per SQL file in the directory — without executing anything. Use it for health checks, admin endpoints, or CLI tooling.

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::MigrationStatus;

let statuses: Vec = pool.migration_status("migrations/").await?;

for s in &statuses {
    let state = if s.applied { "applied" } else { "pending" };
    println!("{}: {}", s.version, state);
}

// Check if any migrations are pending
let pending = statuses.iter().any(|s| !s.applied);
if pending {
    eprintln!("Warning: unapplied migrations exist");
}
```

`MigrationStatus` fields:

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `String` | Filename used as the version key |
| `applied` | `bool` | `true` if the migration has been run |
| `has_down` | `bool` | `true` if a companion `.down.sql` file exists, meaning this migration can be rolled back |

## Rolling back

Add a companion **down file** next to any up migration you want to be reversible: take the up file's name and replace its `.sql` extension with `.down.sql`.

```
migrations/
  001_create_users.sql
  001_create_users.down.sql
  002_add_email_index.sql
  002_add_email_index.down.sql
```

```sql
-- migrations/001_create_users.down.sql
DROP TABLE users;
```

```sql
-- migrations/002_add_email_index.down.sql
DROP INDEX idx_users_email;
```

`pool.rollback_last(dir).await` undoes the single most recently applied migration: it runs the down file's SQL and deletes the migration's row from `_schema_migrations`, both inside one transaction — rolled back together if the down SQL fails. "Most recently applied" is the highest version string among applied migrations, the same lexicographic order `migrate` uses to apply them.

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::DbPool;

let pool = DbPool::from_env().await.expect("connection pool");

match pool.rollback_last("migrations/").await {
    Ok(Some(version)) => println!("rolled back {}", version),
    Ok(None) => println!("nothing to roll back"),
    Err(e) => eprintln!("rollback failed: {}", e),
}
```

`pool.rollback(dir, n).await` rolls back up to the last `n` applied migrations, most recent first, stopping early (without error) once nothing is left to undo:

```rust
// Roll back the last 3 migrations, in reverse order they were applied.
let rolled_back = pool.rollback("migrations/", 3).await.expect("rollback failed");
for version in &rolled_back {
    println!("rolled back {}", version);
}
```

Both methods return `Err` if the migration they're trying to undo has no companion `.down.sql` file — rollback is opt-in per migration, not automatic. Migrations already rolled back before such a failure stay rolled back; each step commits independently.

:::caution[Down migrations are not automatically the inverse]
`rust-web-server` does not generate down SQL for you — you write it, the same way you write the up file. Get it right by hand: `DROP TABLE` undoes `CREATE TABLE`, `DROP COLUMN` undoes `ADD COLUMN`, and so on. A down file that doesn't actually reverse its up file will leave the schema in an inconsistent state relative to `_schema_migrations`.
:::

## Seeds

`pool.seed("seeds/").await` runs every `*.sql` file in the directory, in name order, each in its own transaction (split at `;`, like migrations), and answers the files it ran. Nothing records that a seed ran: it runs again every time, so write seeds that can — `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (PostgreSQL, SQLite), `INSERT OR IGNORE` (SQLite), `INSERT IGNORE` (MySQL). A failing file is rolled back and stops the run.

```sql
-- seeds/01_roles.sql
INSERT INTO roles (name) VALUES ('admin') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
INSERT INTO roles (name) VALUES ('member') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
```

The convention is a `seeds/` directory beside the migrations directory: `migrations/` → `seeds/`, `db/migrations/` → `db/seeds/`.

### Seeds in Rust

Rows that are easier to make in Rust — with [factories](/testing/database/), computed values, several tables at once — go in seeders (18.30.0). A seeder is a name and an async function of the pool; `pool.seed_with(dir, &seeders)` runs the `*.sql` files first, then the seeders in the order added, and answers what it ran:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbPool, Seeders};

pub fn seeders() -> Seeders {
    Seeders::new()
        .add("users", |pool: DbPool| async move {
            User::factory().create_many(10, &pool).await?;
            Ok(())
        })
        .add("admin", |pool: DbPool| async move {
            if User::query(&pool).where_eq("email", "admin@example.com").count().await? == 0 {
                User::factory().with(|u| { u.email = "admin@example.com".into(); u.admin = true; }).create(&pool).await?;
            }
            Ok(())
        })
}

let ran = pool.seed_with("seeds", &seeders()).await?; // ["01_roles.sql", "users", "admin"]
```

Like SQL seeds, seeders run every time, so write them to tolerate their rows being there (the `admin` one looks first). A seeder isn't wrapped in a transaction — use `pool.transaction(…)` in it when its rows must go in together — and a failing one stops the run with its name in the error. With seeders, a missing SQL directory means no SQL seeds rather than an error. Implement the `Seeder` trait instead of a closure when a seeder needs state of its own.

The `rws` binary can't run an app's Rust code, so `rws db seed` runs the SQL files only. Give the app's own binary the same command, with its seeders, through `db_cli::run_with_seeders`:

```rust
// src/main.rs
let args: Vec = std::env::args().collect();
if let Some(db_args) = rust_web_server::db_cli::requested(&args) {
    let code = rust_web_server::db_cli::run_with_seeders(db_args, &myapp::seeders(), &mut std::io::stdout(), &mut std::io::stderr());
    std::process::exit(code);
}
```

`cargo run -- db seed` then runs `seeds/*.sql` and the seeders (`--json`: `{"directory":…,"seeded":["01_roles.sql","users","admin"]}`); every other `db` command works as `rws db`'s.

## From the command line: `rws db`

`rws db` runs the same operations on the project in the working directory (or `--dir`), with the migrations directory from its [`rws.app.toml`](/building-apps/project-layout/) and the seeds beside it:

```bash
rws db status                    # applied / pending, and which have a .down.sql
rws db migrate                   # apply every pending migration
rws db rollback                  # undo the last one; `rws db rollback 3` the last three
rws db seed                      # run seeds/*.sql
rws db schema                    # tables: columns, primary key, indexes, foreign keys
rws db migrate --database-url postgres://app:secret@db/app --json
```

The database is `--database-url`, else `DATABASE_URL`, else the `RWS_DB_*` variables (see [the overview](/database/overview/#environment-variables)); URLs are sqlx's — `sqlite:app.db` (`sqlite:app.db?mode=rwc` creates the file), `postgres://user:password@host:5432/db`, `mysql://user:password@host:3306/db`. `--migrations <dir>` and `--seeds <dir>` override the directories. `--json` prints the result for agents: `status` is the dev MCP server's `migrations` answer (`{"directory":…,"migrations":[{"version":…,"applied":…,"has_down":…}]}`), `migrate` adds `"applied"` (the versions this run applied), `rollback` answers `{"directory":…,"rolled_back":[…]}`, `seed` `{"directory":…,"seeded":[…]}`, and a failure `{"error":…}`. Exit codes: `0` done, `1` a database or migration error (including a missing `.down.sql`), `2` bad arguments.

## The schema as data

`pool.schema().await?` reads the connected schema from the database's catalog — SQLite's `sqlite_master` and `pragma_*` functions, PostgreSQL's `information_schema` and `pg_catalog` (the `current_schema()`), MySQL's `information_schema` (the `DATABASE()`) — into a `DbSchema` (18.30.0): every table (views left out, `_schema_migrations` included) with its columns (type as the backend spells it, nullability, default, whether it is in the primary key), the primary key in key order, the indexes (columns, `unique`, `primary`; SQLite has none for an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`) and the foreign keys (columns, referenced table and columns, `on_update`, `on_delete`). It reads the primary of a [replicated pool](/database/overview/#read-replicas).

```rust
let schema = pool.schema().await?;
let users = schema.table("users").expect("migrated");
assert_eq!(vec!["id".to_string()], users.primary_key);
for fk in &schema.table("orders").unwrap().foreign_keys {
    println!("{:?} -> {}({:?}) on delete {}", fk.columns, fk.references_table, fk.references_columns, fk.on_delete);
}
println!("{}", schema.to_json());
```

`to_json()` is what `rws db schema --json` prints and the dev MCP server's `db_schema` tool answers:

```json
{"backend":"sqlite","tables":[{"name":"orders",
  "columns":[{"name":"id","type":"INTEGER","nullable":true,"default":null,"primary_key":true},
             {"name":"user_id","type":"INTEGER","nullable":false,"default":null,"primary_key":false}],
  "primary_key":["id"],
  "indexes":[{"name":"orders_by_user","columns":["user_id"],"unique":false,"primary":false}],
  "foreign_keys":[{"name":null,"columns":["user_id"],"references":{"table":"users","columns":["id"]},"on_update":"NO ACTION","on_delete":"CASCADE"}]}]}
```

Without `--json`, `rws db schema` prints a table per block: `  user_id  INTEGER  NOT NULL`, `  index orders_by_user (user_id)`, `  foreign key (user_id) references users (id) on delete CASCADE`.

The command needs a `rws` built with a database driver — `cargo install rust-web-server --features model-sqlite,model-postgres,model-mysql`; the release binaries have none, and say so.

## Startup pattern

A typical async server startup sequence:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbConfig, DbPool};
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::server::Server;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let config = DbConfig::from_env().expect("db config");

    // Create pool and run migrations
    let pool = DbPool::new(config).await.expect("connection pool");
    pool.migrate("migrations/").await.expect("migrations");

    // Pass the pool (Clone) into your app state
    let app = App::with_async_state(std::sync::Arc::new(pool))
        // register routes ...
        ;

    let (listener, thread_pool) = Server::setup().expect("server setup");
    Server::run_tls(listener, thread_pool, app).await;
}
```

:::note[One migration per file]
Each file should contain a single logical change. Splitting changes across many small files makes it easy to roll back a specific step and keeps the history readable.
:::

:::note[Idempotent DDL]
Prefer `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` and `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS` so that rerunning a migration file manually (during development) does not error. The runner itself skips already-applied files, but the guard costs nothing and prevents accidents.
:::

# Relations

<https://rws8.tech/docs/database/relations/>

The ORM provides relationship helpers for one record — `HasMany`, `HasOne`, `BelongsTo` and (18.30.0) `BelongsToMany` — and `Relation` descriptors that [load a relation for a whole result set](#eager-loading-with-with). There is no lazy loading — you call `.load(&pool).await` or `.with(…)` explicitly when you want the data.

Relation helpers are not fields of a model: `#[derive(Model)]` maps every field to a column, and a `HasMany` field has no column. Build the helper from a loaded record instead — a small method per relation keeps the call site readable.

## HasMany

`HasMany` represents a one-to-many relationship from an owner to a collection of child records. The child table has a foreign key column that holds the owner's primary key. Construct it with the owner's primary key value and the foreign key column name on the child table:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::relation::HasMany;
use rust_web_server::model::Value;
use rust_web_server::Model;

#[derive(Model, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[table(name = "users")]
pub struct User {
    #[primary_key(auto_increment)]
    pub id: i64,
    pub name: String,
}

impl User {
    pub fn posts(&self) -> HasMany {
        HasMany::new(Value::Int(self.id), "user_id")
    }
}
```

Load the related records by calling `.load(&pool).await`:

```rust
let posts: Vec = user.posts().load(&pool).await?;
```

Under the hood this issues: `SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = ?`.

## HasOne

`HasOne` represents a one-to-one relationship where the child table holds the foreign key (the inverse of `BelongsTo`).

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::relation::HasOne;

impl User {
    pub fn profile(&self) -> HasOne {
        HasOne::new(Value::Int(self.id), "user_id")
    }
}

// Loading
let profile: Option = user.profile().load(&pool).await?;
```

Under the hood: `SELECT * FROM profiles WHERE user_id = ? LIMIT 1`.

## BelongsTo

`BelongsTo` is the inverse side — the child record holds a foreign key that points to the owner's primary key.

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::relation::BelongsTo;

#[derive(Model, Debug, Clone, Default)]
#[table(name = "posts")]
pub struct Post {
    #[primary_key(auto_increment)]
    pub id: i64,
    pub title: String,
    pub user_id: i64,
}

impl Post {
    pub fn user(&self) -> BelongsTo {
        BelongsTo::new(Value::Int(self.user_id))
    }
}

// Loading
let author: Option = post.user().load(&pool).await?;
```

Under the hood: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? LIMIT 1`.

## Complete User + Post example

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbPool, Value};

let pool = DbPool::from_env().await?;

// Load a user
let user: User = pool
    .query::("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? LIMIT 1", &[Value::Int(1)])
    .await?
    .into_iter()
    .next()
    .expect("user 1");

// Load that user's posts — one extra query
let posts: Vec = user.posts().load(&pool).await?;

// Load the author of a post — one extra query
if let Some(post) = posts.first() {
    let author: Option = post.user().load(&pool).await?;
}
```


## Eager loading with `with()`

Calling `.load()` for each row of a list is one query per row (N+1). `with()` loads a relation for the whole result set in **one more query per relation**, `WHERE fk IN (…)` (18.30.0). Describe each relation once, as a `Relation`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{Order, Relation};

impl Post {
    pub fn comments() -> Relation { Relation::has_many("post_id") } // comments.post_id = posts.id
    pub fn author() -> Relation { Relation::belongs_to("user_id") }    // posts.user_id = users.id
    pub fn tags() -> Relation { Relation::belongs_to_many("post_tags", "post_id", "tag_id") }
}

impl User {
    pub fn profile() -> Relation { Relation::has_one("user_id") }
}

// Three queries, however many posts: the posts, their comments, their authors.
let posts = Post::query(&pool)
    .where_eq("published", true)
    .order_by("id", Order::Desc)
    .with(Post::comments())
    .with(Post::author())
    .fetch_all()
    .await?;

for post in &posts {
    let comments: &[Comment] = post.related(&Post::comments());
    let author: Option<&User> = post.one(&Post::author());
    println!("{} by {:?}: {} comments", post.title, author.map(|a| &a.name), comments.len());
}
```

`with()` turns the query into an `EagerQuery` whose `fetch_all`, `fetch_one` and `paginate` answer `Loaded` values. A `Loaded` derefs to the model (`post.title`); `related(&rel)` is the relation's rows (empty when there are none), `one(&rel)` the first — the row of a `belongs_to` or `has_one` — `take(&rel)` moves them out, `into_inner()` drops the relations, and `is_loaded(&rel)` says whether the query loaded it.

| Constructor | Meaning | Query |
|---|---|---|
| `Relation::has_many(fk)` | `R.fk` holds the owner's key | `SELECT * FROM r WHERE fk IN (…)` |
| `Relation::has_one(fk)` | as `has_many`, at most one row (the lowest key) | the same |
| `Relation::belongs_to(fk)` | the owner's `fk` holds `R`'s key (`NULL`: none) | `SELECT * FROM r WHERE id IN (…)` |
| `Relation::belongs_to_many(join, owner_key, related_key)` | through a join table | `SELECT r.*, j.owner_key … JOIN join j ON j.related_key = r.id WHERE j.owner_key IN (…)` |

Related rows come in primary-key order, soft-deleted ones (`#[soft_delete]`) left out. Keys go in batches of 500 (`eager::IN_BATCH`), so a larger result set costs one query per batch. A row related to several owners (a shared author, a tag) is cloned into each, so the related type must be `Clone`. The same descriptor loads without a query builder: `Post::comments().load(&pool, &post)` for one owner, `Post::comments().load_for(&pool, &posts)` for a slice (one `Vec` per owner, in order).

Nested loading (comments' authors) is a second step: collect the comments and call `Comment::author().load_for(&pool, &comments)`.

### Nested relations

A relation's own relations load with `with_nested(relation, |nested| …)` — one more query per nested relation, whatever the number of rows (18.35.0):

```rust
// Four queries: the authors, their posts, the posts' comments, the posts' labels.
let authors = Author::query(&pool)
    .with_nested(Author::posts(), |posts| posts.with(Post::comments()).with(Post::labels()))
    .with(Author::profile())
    .fetch_all()
    .await?;

for post in authors[0].related_loaded(&Author::posts()) {          // &[Loaded]
    let comments: &[Comment] = post.related(&Post::comments());
    println!("{}: {} comments", post.title, comments.len());
}
```

`related_loaded` gives the related rows with their relations; `related` still gives the plain rows. Nesting goes as deep as the closures do (`posts.with_nested(Post::author(), |a| a.with(Author::profile()))`).

## Many-to-many: `BelongsToMany`

`BelongsToMany` is one owner's links through a join table (18.30.0). It loads the linked rows and adds and removes the links:

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{BelongsToMany, Value};

// CREATE TABLE post_tags (post_id BIGINT NOT NULL, tag_id BIGINT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag_id));
impl Post {
    pub fn tag_links(&self) -> BelongsToMany {
        BelongsToMany::new(Value::Int(self.id), "post_tags", "post_id", "tag_id")
    }
}

let links = post.tag_links();
links.attach(&pool, [rust.id, web.id]).await?;          // links added: 2 (an existing link is skipped)
links.detach(&pool, [web.id]).await?;                   // links removed: 1
let changes = links.sync(&pool, [rust.id, async_.id]).await?; // exactly these: adds and removes as needed
println!("attached {:?}, detached {:?}", changes.attached, changes.detached);
let tags: Vec = links.load(&pool).await?;          // the linked rows, soft-deleted ones left out
let ids = links.ids(&pool).await?;                      // the join table's keys
links.detach_all(&pool).await?;
```

`attach` and `sync` run in a transaction (read the links, then write). They insert the two key columns only, so other join-table columns need defaults. Give the join table a primary key or unique index over both columns: the methods never link twice, but two processes attaching at once could. For a whole result set use `Relation::belongs_to_many(…)` with `with()`, above.

:::note[No lazy loading by design]
Lazy loading hides database access behind field access, making it easy to accidentally trigger hundreds of queries. Explicit `.load().await` calls and `with()` keep all I/O visible at the call site, making performance characteristics clear during code review.
:::

---

# Model admin

<https://rws8.tech/docs/database/model-admin/>

`model_admin::ModelAdmin` gives the tables you register pages to list, search, show, create, edit and delete rows — Django's admin, for a `DbPool` (any `model-*` feature). It's a middleware, so it works in front of sync and async apps alike (18.35.0).

```rust,no_run
use rust_web_server::auth_flows::CurrentUser;
use rust_web_server::model_admin::ModelAdmin;

let admins = ["ann@example.com".to_string()];
let admin = ModelAdmin::new(pool.clone())
    .title("Notes admin")
    .model::()                         // its #[table] name
    .table("rws_users")                      // or a table by name
    .allow(move |request| CurrentUser::of(request).is_some_and(|u| admins.contains(&u.email)));

// The first layer wrapped is the outermost.
let site = app(pool)
    .wrap(FlashLayer::new())                 // clears the messages the admin pages show
    .wrap(auth)                              // AuthFlows: who's asking
    .wrap(admin);
```

**Nobody gets in until `allow` says so**: without it every admin page answers `403`. The check runs for each request, after the layers outside the admin — wrap it after [`AuthFlows`](/features/auth-flows/) (inside it) to use `CurrentUser`, and after [`FlashLayer`](/building-apps/forms-uploads/#flash-messages-and-redirects) and [`CsrfLayer`](/features/csrf/) (whose token the forms carry).

## Pages

| Path | Page |
|---|---|
| `/admin` | The tables, with their row counts |
| `/admin/<table>?q=&page=` | 25 rows a page, newest key first; `q` searches the text columns (case-insensitive) |
| `/admin/<table>/new`, `POST /admin/<table>` | A new row |
| `/admin/<table>/<id>` | One row |
| `/admin/<table>/<id>/edit`, `POST /admin/<table>/<id>` | Change it |
| `POST /admin/<table>/<id>/delete` | Delete it |

`.prefix("/backoffice")` moves them. Only registered tables are served; table names are letters, digits and `_`.

## How it reads the database

The columns, their types and the primary key come from the database itself ([`DbPool::schema`](/database/migrations/#the-schema-as-data)) each time a page is drawn, so a migration shows at once — no admin code per model. Form values are converted by the column's type: integers and floats are checked, a `BOOLEAN` column is a checkbox, an empty field is `NULL` for a nullable column; `created_at` / `updated_at` are set to now when the form leaves them empty. On an edit, a column the form doesn't send keeps its value. What the database refuses — `NOT NULL`, a unique index, a foreign key — comes back as an alert on the form, through a [flash message](/building-apps/forms-uploads/#flash-messages-and-redirects) (add `FlashLayer`).

A table needs a one-column primary key to be edited; others are listed only. An integer key is left to the database when creating a row; any other key is a form field. On SQLite a column declared `INTEGER` is a number field even when it holds booleans (declare it `BOOLEAN` for a checkbox).

Values are shown as text and escaped; long ones are cut to 80 characters in the list. The pages are plain HTML with a little inline CSS and no scripts beyond a delete confirmation.

---

# In-memory SQLite

<https://rws8.tech/docs/database/in-memory/>

The `model-sqlite` feature ships an ergonomic constructor that opens a SQLite `":memory:"` database without a file path, hostname, or credentials. All operations are `async fn`.

## DbPool::memory() — isolated in-memory database

`DbPool::memory().await` creates a `sqlx::Pool` with `max_connections = 1` connected to `sqlite::memory:`. Each call returns a **separate, independent** in-memory database — ideal for tests that must not share state.

```rust
use rust_web_server::model::{DbPool, Value};

let pool = DbPool::memory().await.unwrap();

pool.execute(
    "CREATE TABLE items (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)",
    &[],
).await.unwrap();

pool.execute(
    "INSERT INTO items (name) VALUES (?)",
    &[Value::Text("apple".into())],
).await.unwrap();

let rows = pool.query_rows("SELECT name FROM items", &[]).await.unwrap();
assert_eq!(1, rows.len());
let name: String = rows[0].get("name").unwrap();
assert_eq!("apple", name);
```

## Test isolation

Each `DbPool::memory().await` call is a new, empty database. Two pools have no shared state:

```rust
async fn test_db() -> DbPool {
    let pool = DbPool::memory().await.unwrap();
    pool.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)", &[]).await.unwrap();
    pool
}

// Test A
let pool_a = test_db().await;
pool_a.execute("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)", &[Value::Text("Alice".into())]).await.unwrap();

// Test B — completely isolated
let pool_b = test_db().await;
let rows = pool_b.query_rows("SELECT * FROM users", &[]).await.unwrap();
assert!(rows.is_empty());  // Alice is only in pool_a's database
```

Use `#[tokio::test]` for async tests:

```rust
#[tokio::test]
async fn test_example() {
    let pool = DbPool::memory().await.unwrap();
    pool.execute("CREATE TABLE t (v TEXT)", &[]).await.unwrap();
    let rows = pool.query_rows("SELECT * FROM t", &[]).await.unwrap();
    assert!(rows.is_empty());
}
```

For tests, `TestDb::sqlite().migrations("migrations").await` does this with the app's migrations applied (and a connection that never expires, so the database can't vanish mid-test); `TestDb` also gives PostgreSQL and MySQL tests a rolled-back transaction each, and `#[derive(Factory)]` fills tables with models — see [Test databases and factories](/testing/database/).

## Feature requirement

`DbPool::memory()` requires the `model-sqlite` feature, which also implies `http2` (tokio runtime):

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["model-sqlite"] }
```
