# MCP Authentication

<https://rws8.tech/docs/mcp/auth/>

By default the MCP endpoint (`POST /mcp`) is open to any caller. Call `.require_bearer(token)` to gate every request behind a static Bearer token, or `.require_oauth(provider, audience)` (`sso` feature) for full per-user OAuth 2.0 / OIDC bearer JWT verification — see [OAuth 2.0 authorization](#oauth-20-authorization-mcp-2025-03-26) below.

## require_bearer

```rust
use rust_web_server::mcp::McpServer;

let mcp = McpServer::new("my-server", "1.0")
    .require_bearer(std::env::var("MCP_TOKEN").expect("MCP_TOKEN not set"));
```

Every request to `/mcp` (`POST`, the `GET` SSE stream and `OPTIONS` alike) must include:

```
Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

A missing or incorrect token produces an immediate `401 Unauthorized` before any JSON-RPC processing:

```
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
Content-Type: text/plain

Unauthorized
```

## Loading the token from an environment variable

Never hard-code the token in source code. The conventional variable is `MCP_TOKEN`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let mcp = App::new()
    .mcp("my-server", "1.0")
    .require_bearer(
        std::env::var("MCP_TOKEN").expect("MCP_TOKEN env var not set"),
    );
```

Set the variable before starting the server:

```sh
export MCP_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
cargo run
```

The bundled `rws` binary mounts its built-in MCP tools only when `MCP_TOKEN`
is set to a non-empty value (since 17.113.1): its tools change the running
server, so without a token `/mcp` answers `404`. There `/mcp` also sits behind
the access log, the IP blocklist and the global rate limit (not maintenance
mode — the `maintenance` tool is how it's switched off). An empty token passed
to `require_bearer` refuses every request rather than accepting an empty
`Authorization` header, and tokens are compared in constant time.

## One token per caller

`require_bearer_tokens` (since 18.0.0) accepts several tokens and names the
caller behind each; tools see that name as `{"sub":"<name>"}` in
[`ctx.auth_claims`](#reading-verified-claims), the same place OAuth puts the
token's claims:

```rust
let mcp = McpServer::new("team-tools", "1.0")
    .require_bearer_tokens([("token-for-alice", "alice"), ("token-for-ci", "ci")])
    // Only alice may call tools whose names start with "admin_".
    .tool_filter(|ctx, tool| {
        !tool.starts_with("admin_") || ctx.auth_claims.as_deref() == Some(r#"{"sub":"alice"}"#)
    });
```

`resource_filter(|ctx, uri_template| …)` and `prompt_filter(|ctx, name| …)` do the same for resources and prompts: hidden ones are left out of the lists and answer "not found" (since 18.9.0).

`tool_filter(|ctx, tool_name| -> bool)` decides per request which tools a
caller sees in `tools/list`; calling any other answers `Unknown tool`, as
for a tool that doesn't exist. It works with `require_oauth` too (decide
from the claims). A `require_bearer` token carries no name, so its requests
have no `auth_claims`.

## Browser clients: `Origin` and `Content-Type`

A request that carries an `Origin` header — every request a browser sends —
is refused with `403` unless that origin is listed (since 17.113.1). This is
the MCP transport's required `Origin` check: without it a web page, or a
DNS-rebinding attack, could drive a local MCP server from the visitor's
browser. Clients that send no `Origin` (CLI tools, agents, Claude Desktop)
are unaffected.

```rust
let mcp = McpServer::new("my-server", "1.0")
    .require_bearer(token)
    .allowed_origins(["https://inspector.example.com"]);
```

The `rws` binary takes the list from `MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` (comma-separated).
`POST /mcp` must carry `Content-Type: application/json` (otherwise `415`): a
form or `text/plain` body is what a page can send cross-site without a CORS
preflight.

## Configuring Claude Desktop

Add the `Authorization` header to the server entry in `claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "my-server": {
      "url": "http://localhost:7878/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer <your-token-here>"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Replace `<your-token-here>` with the value of `MCP_TOKEN`.

## Full example

```rust
use rust_web_server::server::Server;
use rust_web_server::mcp::{McpServer, McpContent};

# #[cfg(not(feature = "http2"))]
# fn main() {
let token = std::env::var("MCP_TOKEN")
    .expect("Set MCP_TOKEN before starting the server");

let mcp = McpServer::new("secure-server", "1.0")
    .require_bearer(token)
    .tool(
        "ping",
        "Returns pong",
        r#"{"type":"object","properties":{}}"#,
        |_| Ok(McpContent::text("pong")),
    );

let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().unwrap();
Server::run(listener, pool, mcp);
# }
```

## CORS preflight

`OPTIONS /mcp` answers `200 OK` with `Allow: GET, POST, OPTIONS` — but only after the auth check: with `.require_bearer()` or `.require_oauth()` configured, a preflight without a valid `Authorization` header gets `401`, like any other request to `/mcp`.

:::note[Multi-user auth]
`.require_bearer` enforces a single shared token — it is not a per-user authentication mechanism. For per-user access control validating JWT claims against a live IdP, use [`.require_oauth`](#oauth-20-authorization-mcp-2025-03-26) below instead of a custom wrapper. For anything else (e.g. checking a database), implement a custom `Application` wrapper that inspects the `Authorization` header and delegates to `McpServer` only on success:

```rust
use rust_web_server::application::Application;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::Response;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;
use rust_web_server::mcp::McpServer;

struct AuthGate {
    inner: McpServer,
}

impl Application for AuthGate {
    fn execute(&self, req: &Request, conn: &ConnectionInfo) -> Result {
        // your custom auth logic here
        self.inner.execute(req, conn)
    }
}
```
:::

## OAuth 2.0 authorization (MCP 2025-03-26)

The 2025-03-26 revision of the MCP spec defines an OAuth 2.0 authorization flow for multi-tenant or enterprise deployments, where each connecting user authenticates independently rather than sharing one static token. `.require_oauth(provider, audience)` (`sso` feature) implements this by verifying the client's bearer token as a signed JWT against a live JWKS endpoint — reusing [`sso::jwks::JwksCache`](/features/sso/#rs256es256-jwt-verification-via-jwks), the same verifier `OidcAuth` and `AuthServer` use elsewhere in this crate.

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["sso"] }
```

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::sso::OidcProvider;

let app = App::new()
    .mcp("my-server", "1.0")
    .require_oauth(OidcProvider::google(), "my-mcp-client-id");
```

`provider` supplies the issuer, JWKS URI, and (for the metadata endpoint below) the authorization/token endpoints — use a preset (`OidcProvider::google()`, `::okta(domain)`, `::keycloak(base, realm)`, etc.) or discover them live:

```rust
use rust_web_server::sso::OidcProvider;

let provider = OidcProvider::discover("https://accounts.example.com")?;
let app = mcp.require_oauth(provider, "my-mcp-client-id");
```

A request with a missing, malformed, or invalid-signature bearer token gets the same `401 Unauthorized` / `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` response `.require_bearer()` returns — only the verification underneath differs.

### Reading verified claims

On success, the verified claims (a serialized [`OidcClaims`](/features/sso/)) populate `McpContext.auth_claims` as a JSON string, readable from any `.tool_with_context()` handler:

```rust
use rust_web_server::mcp::{McpContent, McpServer};

let mcp = McpServer::new("my-server", "1.0")
    .require_oauth(rust_web_server::sso::OidcProvider::google(), "my-mcp-client-id")
    .tool_with_context("whoami", "Report the caller", "{}", |ctx, _args| {
        let claims = ctx.auth_claims.unwrap_or_default();
        Ok(McpContent::text(claims))
    });
```

### Discovery endpoint

With `.require_oauth()` configured, the server publishes RFC 9728
protected-resource metadata (MCP 2025-06-18) at
`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` (and at that path followed by the MCP
path, e.g. `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp`):

```json
{
  "resource": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp",
  "authorization_servers": ["https://accounts.google.com"],
  "bearer_methods_supported": ["header"]
}
```

A `401` points clients at it:
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"`.
The client then discovers the authorization server from its own metadata
and asks it for a token for `resource` (RFC 8707).

Pass this server's canonical URL as the audience —
`.require_oauth(provider, "https://mcp.example.com/mcp")`: tokens must carry
it in `aud`, and it is the metadata's `resource`. With a plain client id as
the audience, `resource` is built from the request's `Host` and the MCP
path. (Before 18.0.0 an authorization-server-style document was served at
`/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`; it's gone.)

If `.require_oauth()` isn't configured, these paths aren't handled specially —
they fall through to the fallback app (or the built-in `App`'s `404`) like any
other non-MCP path.

### Combining with `require_bearer`

If `.require_bearer(token)` or `.require_bearer_tokens(...)` and `.require_oauth(provider, audience)` are configured on the same server, OAuth verification takes precedence and the static token is never checked. This isn't a supported combination to actually run in production — pick one — it's just an unambiguous tie-break so the behavior isn't undefined if both happen to be set.

---

# Operate rws from an AI client

<https://rws8.tech/docs/mcp/operate/>

The `rws` binary has an MCP endpoint with 25 tools for looking at and steering
the running server: its configuration, metrics, recent requests and errors,
the response cache, the IP blocklist, maintenance mode, runtime feature flags
and config reload. An AI client connected to it can answer "why are we
throwing 500s?" from the server's own request log and act on the answer.

## Turn it on

The endpoint exists only with a token (since 17.113.1 — its tools change the
running server):

```bash
export MCP_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
rws --tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem
```

- `/mcp` then requires `Authorization: Bearer $MCP_TOKEN`. Without
  `MCP_TOKEN`, `/mcp` is `404`.
- Serve it over HTTPS (or keep the port private): the token travels in every
  request.
- Browser-based clients send an `Origin` header; list theirs in
  `MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` (comma-separated), any other origin gets `403`.
  Desktop and CLI clients send none and need nothing here.
- `/mcp` sits behind the access log, the IP blocklist and the global rate
  limit, like every other path.

In config-driven proxy mode (`[[route]]` / `[[upstream]]` in
`rws.config.toml`) the built-in tools aren't mounted.

## Connect a client

**Claude Code:**

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http rws https://www.example.com/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $MCP_TOKEN"
```

**Claude Desktop** (`claude_desktop_config.json`) and **Cursor**
(`.cursor/mcp.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "rws": {
      "url": "https://www.example.com/mcp",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer " }
    }
  }
}
```

Each tool carries behaviour hints: the 17 that only read are marked
read-only, and the ones that change something (`set_maintenance`, `block_ip`,
`unblock_ip`, `cache_clear`, `feature_set`, `reload_config`, `authz_write`,
`authz_delete`) are not, so a
client that asks before acting asks for those.

## The tools

| Look | Change |
|---|---|
| `server_config` — every active `RWS_CONFIG_*` value, secrets hidden | `reload_config` — re-read config and certificates |
| `server_metrics` — request, error, connection counters | `set_maintenance` `{"enabled": true}` — `503` for everything but health checks |
| `recent_requests` `{"n": 50}` — last requests (max 100) | `block_ip` / `unblock_ip` `{"ip": "…"}` — runtime blocklist (`403`) |
| `recent_errors` `{"n": 50}` — last 4xx/5xx | `cache_clear` — empty the response cache, or `{"path": "/p"}` / `{"prefix": "/p/"}` to purge part of it |
| `list_blocked_ips`, `maintenance_status` | `feature_set` `{"name": "…", "enabled": false}` |
| `cache_stats`, `rate_limit_config`, `check_rate_limit` `{"ip": "…"}` | |
| `cors_config`, `list_routes`, `list_static_files` | |
| `feature_flags`, `feature_list` | |
| `authz_check` `{"subject": "user:alice", "relation": "viewer", "object": "doc:42"}` — allowed, and why | `authz_write` / `authz_delete` `{"tuple": "doc:42#viewer@user:alice"}` |
| `authz_tuples` `{"object": "doc", "subject": "user:alice"}` — relationship tuples | |
| `traffic_summary` `{"hours": 24, "host": "example.com"}` (or `{"live": true}`, who is on the site now; `{"from": "2026-03-01", "country": "DE"}`, the traffic database) — who visited: people, AI agents, bots; sessions and bounce rate; where people came from and their countries, browsers and devices | |

The same operations are on the [admin API](/deployment/admin/) (since
18.10.0), which runs the same code: a tool and its admin endpoint answer
alike.

An app built on the library gets the same tools from
`rust_web_server::dev_mcp`: `ops_tools(server, routes, cache)` is what the
binary mounts (since 18.28.0), and [`app.dev_mcp()`](/mcp/dev-tools/) adds
them with `DevTools::with_ops()` next to tools for developing the app.

A call with missing or mistyped arguments comes back as an error the model
reads (`missing required property "ip"`), not a silent default.

## Playbooks

**A spike of errors.** Ask: *"Look at the last 100 errors. Is one client
responsible? If an IP is sending most of them and they look like scanning,
block it and confirm."* The client calls `recent_errors`, groups by `ip`, and
calls `block_ip`; follow-up requests from that address get `403`.
`list_blocked_ips` and `unblock_ip` undo it.

**A bad deploy.** Ask: *"Errors started a minute ago. Put the site in
maintenance mode, then show me the config."* `set_maintenance` with
`{"enabled": true}` makes every non-health path answer `503` while health
checks still pass; fix the config, ask for `reload_config`, check
`recent_errors`, and turn maintenance off again.

**Before a change.** Ask: *"What would change if I disabled the `beta-ui`
feature?"* — `feature_list`, then `feature_set` once you agree.

## What it can't do

The tools act on this process only — a second replica has its own
blocklist, maintenance switch and request log. They don't restart the
server, edit `rws.config.toml` or read files outside the static root. The
blocklist and maintenance mode are in memory: a restart clears them.

---

# Build agent tools on your app

<https://rws8.tech/docs/mcp/agent-tools/>

An app built on rws can answer AI agents with the same functions its REST
API calls. `app.mcp(name, version)` puts an MCP endpoint at `/mcp` in front
of the app; each domain function becomes a [typed tool](/mcp/tools/#typed-tools)
whose schemas come from its Rust types; everything else still reaches the
app. The runnable version is
[`examples/mcp_inventory.rs`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/mcp_inventory.rs).

```bash
MCP_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32) \
  cargo run --example mcp_inventory --features "macros serde sso openapi"
curl localhost:7878/items
claude mcp add --transport http inventory http://localhost:7878/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $MCP_TOKEN"
```

## One domain, two front doors

Keep the logic in plain functions over plain types, and let the REST
handlers and the tools both call them:

```rust
/// A stock change.
#[derive(Deserialize, JsonSchema)]
pub struct AdjustStock {
    pub sku: String,
    /// Units to add (positive) or remove (negative).
    pub delta: i64,
}

impl Inventory {
    pub fn adjust(&self, change: &AdjustStock, changed_by: Option) -> Result { /* ... */ }
}

let server = App::with_state(Arc::clone(&inventory))
    .post("/items/:sku/adjust", |request, params, _, inventory| { /* parse, inventory.adjust(..) */ })
    .mcp("inventory", "1.0")
    .typed_tool("adjust_stock", "Add or remove units of an item; fails rather than go below zero.",
        move |ctx, change: AdjustStock| inventory.adjust(&change, caller(ctx.auth_claims.as_deref())))
    .typed_tool("list_items", "List stocked items, optionally only those running low.",
        move |_, filter: ListItems| Ok(inventory.list(&filter)))
    .tool_annotations("list_items", ToolAnnotations { read_only_hint: Some(true), ..Default::default() });
```

- The doc comments on the types are what the model reads about each
  argument; write them for it.
- A domain error (`only 1 of TEE-02 on hand`) returns as an `isError`
  result the model can act on, not a protocol failure.
- Mark tools that only read with `read_only_hint`, so clients that ask
  before acting ask only for the ones that change something.

## Who is calling

`/mcp` needs a token; the REST routes keep their own rules.

- **One shared token:** `.require_bearer(token)`.
- **Your identity provider:** `.require_oauth(OidcProvider::discover(issuer)?,
  audience)`. rws checks the token's signature, issuer, expiry and audience,
  serves `/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` so clients can find the
  provider, and hands the verified claims to every tool as
  `ctx.auth_claims` — the example records the caller's e-mail on each stock
  change. The example takes the issuer and audience from `MCP_OAUTH_ISSUER`
  and `MCP_OAUTH_AUDIENCE`. See [Auth](/mcp/auth/).

## Live updates

A resource plus `notify_resource_updated` lets a client keep a view
current. The example serves `inventory://items` and, whenever the stock
changes — through a tool or through the REST API — tells every session
subscribed to it:

```rust
let notifier = server.clone();
inventory.on_change(move || notifier.notify_resource_updated("inventory://items"));
```

A client holding `GET /mcp` open (SSE) and subscribed with
`resources/subscribe` receives
`{"method":"notifications/resources/updated","params":{"uri":"inventory://items"}}`
and reads the resource again.

## Testing

`TestClient` drives the whole stack, auth included, without a socket — the
example's tests call tools over `/mcp`, then check the change through the
REST route:

```rust
let adjusted = call(&client, "adjust_stock", r#"{"sku":"TEE-02","delta":-2}"#);
assert!(adjusted.contains(r#""onHand":1"#));
assert!(client.get("/items/TEE-02").send().body_text().contains(r#""onHand":1"#));
```

`cargo test --example mcp_inventory --features "macros serde sso openapi"` runs them.

---

# Let a coding agent inspect your app

<https://rws8.tech/docs/mcp/dev-tools/>

A coding agent working on an rws app can read the code, but not what the
running app actually registered, which settings it ended up with, or why the
last request failed. `app.dev_mcp()` (since 18.28.0) puts an MCP endpoint in
front of the app that answers those questions: its routes and the
middleware around them, its effective configuration with secrets hidden, the
last requests and errors, and — with a `model-*` feature — its database
schema and migrations.

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::dev_mcp::DevMcpExt;
use rust_web_server::server::Server;

let app = App::with_state(state)
    .get("/api/items/:id", get_item)
    .post("/api/items", create_item)
    .wrap(CsrfLayer::new())
    .dev_mcp(); // /mcp in development, nothing in production
```

`dev_mcp()` works on every application type (`AppWithState`, `App`,
`WithMiddleware`, `AsyncAppWithState`, …) and returns one you serve as
before. Every path but `/mcp` still reaches the app.

## When it is mounted

| `RWS_ENV` | token set | `/mcp` |
|---|---|---|
| `dev` | no | mounted, **no authentication** |
| any | yes | mounted, requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>` |
| `test`, `prod`, unset | no | not mounted (one line on stdout says so) |

- `RWS_ENV` is `dev`, `test` or `prod` (the default; anything unrecognised
  counts as `prod`). See [environment variables](/configuration/env-vars/#environment-kind).
- The token is read from `MCP_TOKEN`, the variable the `rws` binary's
  [`/mcp`](/mcp/operate/) uses. `DevTools::token(…)` sets it in code,
  `DevTools::token_env("APP_DEV_TOKEN")` reads another variable.
- In development without a token anyone who can reach the port can call the
  tools, including the ones that change things: keep the port on
  `127.0.0.1` (`RWS_CONFIG_IP`) or set a token.
- Browser-based clients send an `Origin` header, which is refused unless it
  is listed with `DevTools::allowed_origins([…])`. CLI and desktop clients
  send none.
- Calls to the changing tools are recorded in the admin
  [audit log](/deployment/admin/#users-roles-and-the-audit-log), as for the binary.

Connect the agent while the app runs:

```bash
RWS_ENV=dev RWS_CONFIG_IP=127.0.0.1 cargo run
claude mcp add --transport http my-app http://localhost:7878/mcp
```

## The tools

| Tool | Answers |
|---|---|
| `routes` | Each route's method and pattern, in registration order, and the middleware layers around them in the order a request passes them: `{"routes":[{"method":"GET","pattern":"/api/items/:id"}],"middleware":["CsrfLayer"]}` |
| `config` | `RWS_ENV`, the compiled-in features and every `RWS_*`, `OTEL_*` and `MCP_*` setting in effect (config file and flags included). Values of settings named `*SECRET*`, `*PASSWORD*`, `*TOKEN*`, PKCS#11 PINs and passwords inside URLs (`postgres://app:(hidden)@db/app`) are hidden |
| `layout` | The app's name, its [`rws.app.toml`](/building-apps/project-layout/) (`"manifest":null` without one — the conventional layout), and for each part (`main`, `lib`, `routes`, `models`, `jobs`, `migrations`, `templates`, `tests`, `static`) its path, whether it exists and the names in it; a manifest that doesn't parse is reported in `error`. Read on every call, so new files show at once |
| `recent_requests` `{"n": 50}` | The last requests (at most 100): method, path, status, client IP, latency |
| `recent_errors` `{"n": 50}` | The last 4xx/5xx |
| `models` | With a `model-*` feature: each type registered with `DevTools::model::()` — type, table, columns, primary key; with `DevTools::database(pool)` also each column's type there, `table_exists`, `missing_columns` (model columns the table lacks) and `unmapped_columns` (table columns no field maps) |
| `db_schema` | With `DevTools::database(pool)`: every table: its columns (name, type, nullable, default, primary key), primary key, indexes and foreign keys (18.30.0; `DbPool::schema`, the JSON `rws db schema --json` prints) — SQLite, PostgreSQL (the current schema) and MySQL (the current database) |
| `migrations` | With `DevTools::migrations(dir)` too: each migration file, whether it is applied and whether it has a `.down.sql` |
| `migrations_run` | Apply the pending migrations; answers the status afterwards |
| `migrations_rollback_last` | Undo the last applied migration; answers which (`null` when none). The same operations from a shell: [`rws db`](/database/migrations/#from-the-command-line-rws-db) |
| `gen_model`, `gen_route`, `gen_migration`, `gen_test` | The [generators](#generators): write a model, routes, a migration or a test into the project, or with `dry_run` answer the plan |

The middleware listed is the stack around the app's routes (each layer's
`Middleware::layer_name()`, by default its type name); rws has no per-route
middleware to report. Routes come from `Application::registered_routes()`: the
built-in controllers behind an `AppWithState` (static files, `/healthz`, …)
aren't listed.

`dev_mcp()` records the app's requests for `recent_requests` itself. If the
app already has a `LogLayer`, pass `.record_requests(false)` so each request
is listed once.

`layout` reads the working directory unless `DevTools::app_dir(dir)` names
the project root; pass `env!("CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR")` when the app serves
static files from another directory (it is the project root in `cargo run`
and `cargo test`).

Rust can't list a program's `#[derive(Model)]` types at run time, so
`models` reports the ones you name:

```rust
let tools = DevTools::new()
    .model::()
    .model::()
    .database(pool.clone()); // compare each with its table
```

```json
{"database":true,"models":[{"type":"app::models::User","name":"User","table":"users",
  "primary_key":"id","auto_increment":true,
  "columns":[{"name":"id","primary_key":true,"db":{"type":"INTEGER","nullable":false,"primary_key":true}},
             {"name":"email","primary_key":false,"db":null}],
  "table_exists":true,"missing_columns":["email"],"unmapped_columns":[]}],"hint":null}
```

`missing_columns` is what a migration has yet to add. The same description
is `model::ModelInfo::of::()` in code.

## Generators

`gen_model`, `gen_route`, `gen_migration` and `gen_test` are
[`rws gen`](/building-apps/generators/) as tools (18.29.0): the agent asks
for a model, a resource's routes, a migration or a test and gets code pinned
to the release's API, written into the project `layout` reports (the
`app_dir`). They change files, so `.read_only()` leaves them out, as it does
`migrations_run`.

| Tool | Arguments |
|---|---|
| `gen_model` | `name` (`Post`), `fields` (`["title:String", "views:i64", "note:Option"]`), `db` (`sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`; default from `Cargo.toml`), `timestamps`, `soft_delete` (booleans, 18.30.0: `--timestamps`, `--soft-delete`), `dry_run` |
| `gen_route` | `resource` (`posts`), `fields`, `methods` (`["list", "show", "create", "update", "remove"]`, default all), `prefix` (`/api`), `dry_run` |
| `gen_migration` | `name` (`add_index_to_posts`), `dry_run` |
| `gen_test` | `resource`, `app_expr` (`app(Store::memory())` when `app` takes arguments), `dry_run` |

Each answers the plan as JSON — the same as `rws gen --json`:

```json
{"command":"rws gen migration add_index","status":"written","written":true,
 "changes":[{"path":"migrations/0001_add_index.sql","action":"create","diff":"--- /dev/null\n+++ b/migrations/0001_add_index.sql\n…"}],
 "notes":[]}
```

`dry_run: true` answers `"status":"planned"` and writes nothing. Nothing is
overwritten: a file in the way makes the call a tool error whose text is the
same JSON with `"status":"conflict"` and the diff; a bad name or type is a
tool error with `"status":"usage"`.

## Choosing what is mounted

`dev_mcp_with(DevTools)` takes the options:

```rust
use rust_web_server::dev_mcp::{DevMcpExt, DevTools};
use rust_web_server::model::DbPool;

let pool = DbPool::from_env().await?;
let app = routes
    .dev_mcp_with(
        DevTools::new()
            .database(pool.clone())
            .migrations("migrations")
            .with_ops()      // also the rws binary's 25 operations tools
            .read_only(),    // but none of the tools that change something
    );
```

| Method | Does |
|---|---|
| `.database(pool)` / `.migrations(dir)` | The database tools (`model-sqlite`, `model-postgres` or `model-mysql`) |
| `.model::()` | List the `#[derive(Model)]` type `T` in `models` (once per type) |
| `.app_dir(dir)` | The project root `layout` reads (default: the working directory) |
| `.with_ops()` | The [operations tools](/mcp/operate/#the-tools) as well: metrics, rate limits, maintenance mode, the IP blocklist, feature flags, authorization, traffic, config reload |
| `.cache(layer)` | The `cache_stats` / `cache_clear` operations tools for this response cache (a clone of the layer the app wraps); implies `.with_ops()` |
| `.read_only()` | Leaves out every tool that changes something (`migrations_run`, `migrations_rollback_last`, the generators in `dev_mcp::GEN_TOOLS` and the operations tools in `dev_mcp::OPS_WRITE_TOOLS`) |
| `.token(t)` / `.token_env(name)` | The bearer token, or the variable it is read from (default `MCP_TOKEN`) |
| `.env(RwsEnv::Dev)` | Decide as if `RWS_ENV` were this (tests) |
| `.at("/_dev/mcp")` | Another path, for an app that serves its own MCP server at `/mcp` |
| `.server_info(name, version)` | What `initialize` reports (default `rws-dev`) |
| `.record_requests(false)` | Don't record requests (the app has a `LogLayer`) |

An app that builds its own `McpServer` and gates it itself can add the same
tools with `DevTools::new().register(server)` — the routes are those of the
app the server wraps. `dev_mcp::ops_tools(server, routes, cache)` adds only
the operations tools; it is what the `rws` binary mounts.

## Testing it

The tools are ordinary MCP tools, so `TestClient` drives them:

```rust
use rust_web_server::dev_mcp::{DevMcpExt, DevTools, RwsEnv};
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

let client = TestClient::new(app().dev_mcp_with(DevTools::new().env(RwsEnv::Dev)));
let res = client
    .post("/mcp")
    .body_json(r#"{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"tools/call","id":1,"params":{"name":"routes","arguments":{}}}"#)
    .send();
assert!(res.body_text().contains("/api/items/:id"));
```

Each [starter](/getting-started/ai-agents/) has a `tests/dev_mcp.rs` that
calls `initialize`, `tools/list` and then every listed tool, failing on any
JSON-RPC or tool error (the generators with `dry_run`, since they need
arguments); CI runs it for every starter.

## Not yet

Jobs, and the same data as MCP resources, are planned.

# MCP gateway

<https://rws8.tech/docs/mcp/gateway/>

`McpGateway` (since 18.0.0) federates upstream MCP servers behind one
`/mcp`. Clients connect to the gateway with their own credentials; the
gateway calls each upstream with *its* credentials, so the tokens for your
GitHub, Jira or internal MCP servers live in one place and never reach the
agents. Which caller may use which tools is one list.

The runnable version is
[`examples/mcp_gateway.rs`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/mcp_gateway.rs):
`cargo run --example mcp_gateway` starts two upstreams in-process and the
gateway in front of them.

```rust
use rust_web_server::mcp::gateway::{McpGateway, Upstream};

let gateway = McpGateway::new("gateway", "1.0")
    .upstream(Upstream::new("github", "https://mcp.github.example/mcp")
        .header("Authorization", format!("Bearer {}", std::env::var("GITHUB_MCP_TOKEN")?)))
    .upstream(Upstream::new("jira", "http://jira-mcp.internal:8080/mcp"))
    .allow("alice", ["*"])
    .allow("ci", ["github__search_*", "jira__get_issue"])
    .build()?                                   // connects and lists every upstream's tools
    .require_bearer_tokens([
        (std::env::var("ALICE_TOKEN")?, "alice"),
        (std::env::var("CI_TOKEN")?, "ci"),
    ]);

let (listener, pool) = Server::setup()?;
Server::run_tls(listener, pool, gateway).await;
```

## From the config file

The `rws` binary runs a gateway from `rws.config.toml` with `[route.action] type = "mcp"` — upstreams, callers and their tokens (from environment variables), `allow` rules, limits and the audit log. See [the config reference](/configuration/config-file/#routeaction--mcp). The rest of this page is the Rust API it is built on.

## What callers see

- Each upstream tool appears as `<prefix>__<tool>` (`github__search_issues`),
  with the upstream's description, input and output schemas, title and
  behaviour hints.
- A call is checked against the upstream's input schema, then forwarded;
  the upstream's result comes back as it was sent — content, structured
  content, `isError`.
- When the upstream fails — it is down, answers HTTP 5xx, or returns a
  JSON-RPC error — the caller gets an `isError` result naming the upstream
  (`github: rate limited`), never a protocol error.

## Who may call what

`.allow(identity, tools)` rules add up:

| Pattern | Matches |
|---|---|
| `github__search_issues` | that tool |
| `github__*` | every tool from `github` (any prefix ending in `*`) |
| `*` | every tool |

The identity is the caller's `sub`: the name given with
[`require_bearer_tokens`](/mcp/auth/#one-token-per-caller), or the `sub`
claim of an OAuth token with [`require_oauth`](/mcp/auth/#oauth-20-authorization-mcp-2025-03-26).
`.allow("*", ...)` applies to every identified caller. A caller no rule
names sees an empty `tools/list`, and a tool it may not use answers as if
it didn't exist (`Unknown tool`) — nothing is forwarded. A plain
`require_bearer` token carries no identity, so behind it the gateway allows
nothing: use `require_bearer_tokens` or `require_oauth`.

## Prompts and resources

Upstream prompts appear as `<prefix>__<name>` with their arguments, and `prompts/get` is forwarded. Upstream resources and resource templates keep their own URIs (if two upstreams publish the same URI, the first keeps it) and `resources/read` is forwarded. Both are listed at `build()` — unlike tools, they aren't refreshed — and an upstream that has neither, or fails to list them, still federates its tools.

The rules from [`allow`](#who-may-call-what) cover them too: a caller sees a prompt when a rule matches its `<prefix>__<name>`, and a resource when one matches `<prefix>__<uri>` (so `github__*` covers everything from `github`; listing only tool names covers no prompts or resources). Hidden ones are left out of the lists and answer "not found" (since 18.9.0).

## Rate limits

`.limit(tools, max_calls, window_secs)` caps how often each caller (each `sub`) may call the tools matching `tools` — a full name, a prefix ending in `*`, or `*` — counted per tool:

```rust
use rust_web_server::mcp::gateway::{McpGateway, Upstream};

let gateway = McpGateway::new("gateway", "1.0")
    .upstream(Upstream::new("github", "http://127.0.0.1:9001/mcp"))
    .allow("*", ["*"])
    .limit("github__*", 60, 60)            // each caller: 60 calls a minute per GitHub tool
    .limit("github__create_issue", 5, 3600); // and 5 new issues an hour
```

Over a limit, the call answers a tool error saying when to retry, without reaching the upstream. A call must pass every limit that matches. Counts are kept in the gateway's process (since 18.9.0).

## Audit log

`.audit_log(true)` writes one JSON line per `tools/call` to the access log (stdout, or the file `RWS_CONFIG_ACCESS_LOG` names):

```json
{"time":"2026-10-29T12:00:00Z","event":"mcp_tool_call","sub":"alice","tool":"github__create_issue","upstream":"github","outcome":"ok","duration_ms":182.411}
```

`outcome` is `ok`, `tool_error`, `refused` (over a [rate limit](#rate-limits)) or `denied` (the caller may not use the tool). Arguments and results are not logged (since 18.9.0).

## Upstreams

- `Upstream::new(prefix, url)` — `url` is the server's Streamable HTTP
  endpoint. The prefix is letters, digits, `-` and single `_`.
- `.header(name, value)` — sent on every request to that upstream; the
  caller's `Authorization` is never passed on.
- `.header_for(name, |claims| …)` — a header computed for each tool call
  from the caller's verified claims (the `auth_claims` JSON), e.g. that
  user's own upstream token, so the upstream acts as them; `None` sends no
  header. Only `tools/call` carries a caller: listing, prompts and resources
  use the static headers (since 18.9.0).
- `.timeout_ms(ms)` — per request (default 30 s).

`McpGateway::refresh_every(Some(duration))` (default 5 minutes; `None` lists
once) re-reads every upstream's tools: new ones appear, removed ones go,
changed ones are re-published, and the gateway's clients get
`notifications/tools/list_changed`. Between refreshes `tools/list` is answered
from the gateway's copy; an upstream that can't be reached keeps the tools it
had (since 18.9.0).

The gateway initializes a session with each upstream, sends the session id
and negotiated `MCP-Protocol-Version` on later requests, reads JSON or
event-stream replies, and starts a new session once if the upstream has
forgotten its own. `build()` fails, naming the upstream and its URL, if one
can't be reached at startup.

### Protocol versions

The gateway opens a 2025-11-25 session with each upstream. An upstream that
refuses `initialize` (one that speaks only 2026-07-28) is used statelessly
instead (since 18.9.0): `server/discover` once, then every request carries
the version and an empty client capabilities object in `params._meta` and
the `MCP-Protocol-Version`, `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers, with no
session. Its results lose the 2026-only fields (`resultType`, cache hints)
on the way through, so 2025 clients of the gateway can use its tools; a
tool that asks for more input (2026 multi round-trip) answers an error.
Clients of the gateway may use either version.

## Not yet

Upstream notifications (`listChanged`, resource updates, progress) aren't followed — tools are re-read on the [refresh interval](#upstreams) instead — and tool results aren't cached. The [roadmap](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/spec/ROADMAP.md) tracks the gateway (#28).

---

# A2A agents

<https://rws8.tech/docs/mcp/a2a/>

[Agent2Agent (A2A)](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/) lets one
AI agent call another: it reads the other's **Agent Card**, sends it a
**message**, and follows the **task** that starts. MCP connects an agent to
tools; A2A connects agents to agents. `A2aServer` (since 18.17.0) serves the
A2A 1.0 JSON-RPC binding; you write what the agent does.

```rust,no_run
use rust_web_server::a2a::{A2aReply, A2aServer, AgentCard, Artifact, Message, Skill};
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let agent = A2aServer::new(
    AgentCard::new("Invoice agent", "Reads invoices and answers questions about them", "1.0.0")
        .skill(Skill::new("summarize", "Summarize an invoice", "Totals, due date, line items").tag("invoices")),
)
.on_message(|ctx, message| {
    let question = message.text();
    if question.is_empty() {
        return A2aReply::Message(Message::agent_text("Which invoice?"));
    }
    if ctx.task.is_none() && !question.contains("INV-") {
        // Ask back; the client's next message carries this task's id.
        return A2aReply::Task(ctx.input_required("Which invoice number?"));
    }
    A2aReply::Task(ctx.complete(vec![Artifact::text("summary", format!("Summary for {question}"))]))
})
.wrap(App::new()); // everything that isn't A2A goes to your app
```

## What it serves

- `GET /.well-known/agent-card.json`: the card, with its name, description,
  version, skills, input and output media types (`text/plain` by default,
  `.modes(…)` to change), and the endpoint's URL (from the request's `Host`,
  or `.url("https://…")` behind a proxy).
- `POST /a2a` (`.at("/path")` to move it): JSON-RPC 2.0 with the 1.0 method
  names:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `SendMessage` | Calls your handler. An `A2aReply::Message` answers directly; an `A2aReply::Task` is stored and returned. A message with the `taskId` of a task waiting for input continues it (`ctx.task` is that task) |
| `GetTask` | A stored task, `historyLength` most recent messages |
| `ListTasks` | Tasks, newest first, by `contextId` / `status`, `pageSize` 1–100 with `pageToken` |
| `CancelTask` | Cancels a task that isn't finished (`-32002` when it is) |
| `SendStreamingMessage` | Like `SendMessage`, as server-sent events: the task first, then each `statusUpdate` and `artifactUpdate`, ending when the task finishes or asks for input (or one `message` event) |
| `SubscribeToTask` | Follows a task that isn't finished: the task first, then its updates |

Clients must send `A2A-Version: 1.0` (header or query parameter); other
versions get `-32009`. Errors use the A2A codes (`-32001` task not found,
`-32004` unsupported operation, …) with a `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` detail.
Push notifications and the extended card are off until you turn them on
(below); the card's `capabilities` say which are on, and their methods
answer `-32003` / `-32004` while off.

## Messages and tasks

A `Message` has `parts`: text, raw bytes, a URL, or JSON data
(`Part::text`, `Part::raw`, `Part::url`, `Part::data`); `message.text()`
joins the text parts. The handler's `ctx` builds the task to return:

- `ctx.complete(artifacts)`: done, with outputs (`Artifact::text(name, text)`);
- `ctx.input_required(question)`: waiting for the client's answer;
- `ctx.fail(reason)` / `ctx.reject(reason)`;
- `ctx.task(state, message, artifacts)` for anything else.

## Long-running work

`ctx.start()` stores the task (working) and gives you a `TaskHandle` to
update it from any thread; return `A2aReply::Running(handle)`:

```rust,ignore
.on_message(|ctx, message| {
    let task = ctx.start();
    let worker = task.clone();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        worker.working(Some("reading the invoice"));
        if worker.is_canceled() { return; }           // CancelTask was called
        worker.artifact(Artifact::text("summary", "…"));
        worker.complete();                            // or fail(reason), input_required(question)
    });
    A2aReply::Running(task)
})
```

`worker.artifact_chunk(artifact, append, last_chunk)` streams an output in
pieces: chunks with `append` add their parts to the artifact with the same
id.

`SendMessage` waits until the task finishes or asks for input (A2A's
default), up to `.blocking_timeout(…)` (300 s), then answers with its state;
a client that sends `configuration.returnImmediately: true` gets the task at
once and polls `GetTask` or streams. Streams get every update as it happens.

## Authentication

```rust,ignore
let agent = A2aServer::new(card)
    .require_bearer_tokens([("token-for-billing", "billing"), ("token-for-crm", "crm")]);
```

Requests to the JSON-RPC endpoint need `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
(`401` otherwise); the card stays public and lists the bearer scheme
(`securitySchemes`, `securityRequirements`). Each token stands for an
identity, and callers only see their own tasks. `require_bearer(token)` is
the one-token form.

## Push notifications

A client that won't hold a stream open can give a webhook: in `SendMessage`
(`configuration.taskPushNotificationConfig`) or later with
`CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig` (plus `Get…`, `List…`, `Delete…`). Each
update is POSTed to it as the same JSON a stream carries (`task`,
`statusUpdate`, `artifactUpdate`), `Content-Type: application/a2a+json`,
with `Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>` from the config's
`authentication` and its `token` as `X-A2A-Notification-Token`.

```rust,ignore
let agent = A2aServer::new(card)
    .push_notifications(["https://hooks.partner.example/", "https://ci.example.com/a2a/"]);
```

Webhook URLs come from clients, so rws calls only URLs that start with a
prefix you list (requests to anywhere else, such as `169.254.169.254` or your
internal network, are refused with `-32602`) and follows no redirects.
Deliveries go out in order from one thread, 10 s timeout, three attempts
(0.5 s and 2 s apart); at most 10 webhooks per task, and credentials are
never returned by `Get…`/`List…`.

## Extended card

```rust,ignore
let agent = A2aServer::new(public_card)
    .require_bearer_tokens([("token-for-billing", "billing")])
    .extended_card(AgentCard::new("Invoice agent", "With the internal skills", "1.0.0").skill(audit));
```

Authenticated callers get the fuller card from `GetExtendedAgentCard`; the
public card says one exists (`capabilities.extendedAgentCard`).

## Gateway

The `rws` binary can also stand in front of agents that run elsewhere (any
A2A 1.0 implementation), from `rws.config.toml`:

```toml
[[route]]
  [route.match]
  path = "/agents/billing/*"
  [route.action]
  type = "a2a"
  [route.action.a2a]
  upstream = "http://10.0.0.7:9000"
  headers_env = { Authorization = "BILLING_AGENT_AUTHORIZATION" }
  [route.middleware.auth]
  type = "bearer"
  token_env = "PARTNER_TOKEN"
```

Callers read the card at `/agents/billing/.well-known/agent-card.json`; its
only interface is JSON-RPC at `/agents/billing`, so the agent's own address
stays private. Calls are forwarded with the configured headers instead of
the caller's `Authorization`, streams pass through, and with
`audit_log = true` each call is a JSON line (client, method, status,
duration). Settings: [config file](/configuration/config-file/#routeaction--a2a).

## Conformance

CI runs the official A2A compatibility kit
([a2aproject/a2a-tck](https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-tck), pinned) over
JSON-RPC against `examples/a2a_tck.rs`, which implements the kit's
scenarios. It passes every JSON-RPC check that applies (94 of 101; the rest are optional features the test agent leaves off); `ci/a2a-tck-baseline.txt` would list known failures and is empty.

## History and limits

The task's history keeps every message in order. A handler that panics
fails its task instead of the request. At most 10,000 tasks are kept (the
oldest finished ones go first), 16 streams per task, 4 MiB per request.

# Tools from OpenAPI

<https://rws8.tech/docs/mcp/openapi-tools/>

Most APIs an agent should use already describe themselves with OpenAPI.
`mcp::openapi_tools` (since 18.19.0) reads an OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 document
(JSON) and makes each operation an MCP tool: its path, query and header
parameters and its JSON body become the tool's `inputSchema`, a JSON object
response its `outputSchema`, and `request(arguments)` builds the HTTP
request for a call.

```rust
use rust_web_server::mcp::openapi_tools::{tools, ToolOptions};

let spec = r#"{"openapi":"3.1.0","info":{"title":"Billing","version":"1"},
  "paths":{"/invoices/{id}":{"get":{"operationId":"getInvoice","summary":"Get an invoice",
    "parameters":[{"name":"id","in":"path","required":true,"schema":{"type":"integer"}}]}}}}"#;
let found = tools(spec, &ToolOptions::default()).unwrap();
let call = found[0].request(r#"{"id": 42}"#).unwrap();
assert_eq!("/invoices/42", call.path_and_query);
```

## Your app's own routes

An app that describes its routes with [OpenAPI](/features/openapi/) gets
MCP tools for them in one call; each call runs the route in-process (no HTTP
round trip), through the app's middleware:

```rust,ignore
use rust_web_server::mcp::{openapi_tools::ToolOptions, McpServer};
use rust_web_server::openapi::{OpenApiConfig, Operation};

let config = OpenApiConfig::new("Invoices", "1.0")
    .operation("GET", "/invoices/:id", Operation::new("Get an invoice").operation_id("getInvoice")
        .path_param_schema("id", r#"{"type":"string"}"#, "The invoice"));
let app = App::with_state(state).get("/invoices/:id", get_invoice).post("/invoices", create_invoice);
let spec = app.openapi_spec(&config);           // `openapi` feature
let mcp = McpServer::new("invoices", "1.0")
    .openapi_tools(app.clone(), &spec, &ToolOptions::default())?
    .require_bearer_tokens([("token", "alice")])
    .wrap(app.openapi(config));                 // the HTTP API stays as it was
```

The handler sees the MCP caller's identity (the token's `sub`) in the
`X-Rws-Mcp-Caller` header. A non-2xx answer is a tool error with its status
and body. `openapi_tools` takes any `Application` and any OpenAPI document,
so it also works for apps whose document is written by hand.

## Through the MCP gateway

The `rws` binary's [MCP gateway](/mcp/gateway/) takes an API as a source next
to MCP upstreams: its operations become `<prefix>__<operation>` tools, each
call an HTTP request to `base_url` with the API's own credentials (never the
caller's token), the gateway's allow rules, limits and audit log applying as
to any tool.

```toml
[[route.action.mcp.openapi]]
prefix      = "billing"
spec        = "https://billing.internal/openapi.json"   # or a file path
base_url    = "https://billing.internal"                # calls go only here, without redirects
include     = ["getInvoice", "listInvoices"]            # operationIds; default: every GET
exclude     = []
timeout_ms  = 30000
headers_env = { Authorization = "BILLING_API_AUTHORIZATION" }
```

The document is read when the gateway starts (and on reload). A JSON object
answer is the result's `structuredContent` when the operation declares an
object response; other answers are text; a non-2xx answer is a tool error
carrying its status and body (results are cut at 1 MiB). In code:
`McpGateway::openapi(OpenApiUpstream::new(prefix, spec, base_url))`.

## What becomes a tool

- **Only `GET` operations**, unless `ToolOptions::include` lists
  operationIds: an agent changing data should be a decision you make per
  operation. `exclude` drops some.
- **Names**: the `operationId` (characters outside `A-Za-z0-9_-` become
  `_`, at most 64), else `<method>_<path>`; `prefix` adds `<prefix>__`;
  a repeated name gets `_2`, `_3`.
- **Description**: `summary`, then `description` (cut at 1 KiB).
- **Annotations**: `GET`/`HEAD` read-only, `DELETE` destructive,
  `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE` idempotent, all open-world.

## Building the request

`request(arguments)` fills path parameters (percent-encoded, so a value
can't leave its segment), adds query parameters (arrays repeat the name),
headers (control characters refused) and the `body` argument as JSON.
Cookie parameters aren't sent.

## Hostile documents

Only local `$ref`s (`#/components/...`) are followed; remote ones become
`{}` and are never fetched. A cycle, a reference chain over 24 deep, a
schema nested over 64 levels or one that would inline to more than 50,000
values (refs that fan out) stops there with `{}`. Documents over 16 MB are
refused.

# Test Client

<https://rws8.tech/docs/testing/test-client/>

`TestClient` wraps any type that implements `Application` and dispatches requests through `Application::execute` in-process. No network, no port binding, no spawned threads — tests run as fast as plain function calls.

## Creating a client

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

let client = TestClient::new(App::new());
```

Every request is dispatched on a synthetic `127.0.0.1:12345 → 127.0.0.1:7878` connection. Pass any `Application` implementation — `App`, `AppWithState`, `WithMiddleware`, `McpServer`, or your own type.

## State-aware applications

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;
use rust_web_server::routes;

struct AppState { counter: u32 }

let state = Arc::new(AppState { counter: 42 });
let app = routes! {
    App::with_state(Arc::clone(&state)),
    GET "/count" => |_req, _params, _conn, s: &Arc| {
        // ... build response
    },
};
let client = TestClient::new(app);
```

## Building requests

Each HTTP method has a corresponding builder method on `TestClient`:

```rust
client.get("/users")
client.post("/users")
client.put("/users/1")
client.patch("/users/1")
client.delete("/users/1")
client.options("/users")
```

All return a `TestRequest` that you configure with chained builder calls before calling `.send()`.

### Adding headers

```rust
let resp = client.get("/api/data")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer my-token")
    .header("Accept", "application/json")
    .send();
```

### Setting the body

```rust
// Raw bytes
let resp = client.post("/upload")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/octet-stream")
    .body_bytes(vec![0x89, 0x50, 0x4E, 0x47])
    .send();

// UTF-8 text
let resp = client.post("/echo")
    .header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
    .body_text("hello world")
    .send();

// JSON (set Content-Type yourself)
let resp = client.post("/users")
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .body_text(r#"{"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"}"#)
    .send();
```

## Reading the response

`.send()` returns a `TestResponse`:

```rust
let resp = client.get("/healthz").send();

resp.status()        // i16 — e.g. 200
resp.reason()        // &str — e.g. "OK"
resp.is_success()    // bool — true when 200–299
resp.body_text()     // &str — panics if body is not valid UTF-8
resp.body_bytes()    // &[u8] — raw body
resp.header("content-type")   // Option<&str> — case-insensitive lookup
resp.headers()       // &[Header] — all response headers
resp.is_streamed()   // bool — the body is a stream (SSE, stream_pipe), not in body_bytes()
resp.sse()           // TestSse — the body's Server-Sent Events
```

## Async apps: `send_async`

An `App::with_async_state` app can be driven from `#[tokio::test]` with `.send_async().await`, which awaits the handler rather than blocking the test's thread as `.send()` does. Prefer it whenever the handler uses something made on the test's runtime, such as a PostgreSQL or MySQL `DbPool` — see [Test databases](/testing/database/#an-app-on-a-testdb).

```rust
let resp = client.get("/notes").send_async().await;
```

## More helpers

Beside `TestClient`, the `test_client` module has:

- [WebSocket and SSE](/testing/websocket-sse/) — `client.websocket(path).connect()` runs a route's upgrade handler over an in-memory connection; `resp.sse_events(n, timeout)` reads an event stream.
- [Test databases and factories](/testing/database/) — `TestDb::sqlite().migrations("migrations")`, a transaction per test on PostgreSQL/MySQL, and `#[derive(Factory)]`.
- [OpenAPI snapshots](/testing/snapshots/) — `assert_openapi_snapshot(&client, "tests/snapshots/openapi.json")`, `RWS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1` to rewrite.

Nothing in `test_client` is on the request path. It's compiled into every build so an app's own tests reach it without a feature (`TestDb` and factories need a `model-*` feature, `#[derive(Factory)]` also `macros`).

## Testing middleware

Wrap any application with middleware before handing it to `TestClient`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::request_id::RequestIdLayer;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

let app = App::new().wrap(RequestIdLayer::new());
let client = TestClient::new(app);

// A request without an ID gets a fresh one on the response
let resp = client.get("/healthz").send();
assert!(resp.header("x-request-id").is_some());

// An incoming ID is echoed back unchanged
let resp = client.get("/healthz").header("X-Request-Id", "abc-123").send();
assert_eq!(Some("abc-123"), resp.header("x-request-id"));
```

`RateLimitLayer` (in `middleware`) uses the process-wide `rate_limit::global()`
limiter keyed by client IP, and every `TestClient` request comes from
`127.0.0.1` — so rate-limit tests share one budget across the whole test run.

## Complete CRUD test suite

```rust
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use rust_web_server::app::App;
    use rust_web_server::core::New;
    use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

    // `App::new()` has no `/users` routes: build your own app here (and
    // change the return type) — the `/users` tests below assume it has them.
    fn make_client() -> TestClient {
        TestClient::new(App::new())
    }

    #[test]
    fn health_check_returns_200() {
        let client = make_client();
        let resp = client.get("/healthz").send();
        assert_eq!(200, resp.status());
    }

    #[test]
    fn unknown_route_returns_404() {
        let client = make_client();
        let resp = client.get("/does-not-exist").send();
        assert_eq!(404, resp.status());
    }

    #[test]
    fn post_creates_resource() {
        let client = make_client();
        let resp = client
            .post("/users")
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .body_text(r#"{"name":"Alice","email":"alice@example.com"}"#)
            .send();
        assert_eq!(201, resp.status());
        assert!(resp.header("location").is_some());
    }

    #[test]
    fn get_returns_json_content_type() {
        let client = make_client();
        let resp = client
            .get("/users/1")
            .header("Accept", "application/json")
            .send();
        assert_eq!(200, resp.status());
        let ct = resp.header("content-type").unwrap_or("");
        assert!(ct.contains("application/json"), "content-type was: {ct}");
    }

    #[test]
    fn put_updates_resource() {
        let client = make_client();
        let resp = client
            .put("/users/1")
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .body_text(r#"{"name":"Alice Smith"}"#)
            .send();
        assert_eq!(200, resp.status());
    }

    #[test]
    fn delete_removes_resource() {
        let client = make_client();
        let resp = client.delete("/users/1").send();
        assert!(resp.status() == 200 || resp.status() == 204);
    }

    #[test]
    fn body_text_is_accessible() {
        let client = make_client();
        let resp = client.get("/healthz").send();
        let body = resp.body_text();
        // body is a &str; check it is non-empty or contains expected content
        assert!(!body.is_empty() || resp.status() == 200);
    }
}
```

## Isolated CORS and security-header tests

By default, `App::new()` reads CORS, CSP, and other settings from `RWS_CONFIG_*` environment variables on each request. That means tests which set those env vars can race against each other when `cargo test` runs in parallel — and any test that calls `override_environment_variables_from_config` must hold `test_env::lock()` for its duration.

For tests that only verify header behavior, the cleaner approach is `App::with_config`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::server_config::ServerConfig;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;
use rust_web_server::header::Header;

#[test]
fn cors_denied_for_unlisted_origin() {
    // No env writes → no test_env::lock() → runs safely in parallel.
    let config = ServerConfig {
        cors_allow_all: false,
        cors_allow_origins: String::new(),
        ..ServerConfig::default()
    };
    let client = TestClient::new(App::with_config(config));

    let resp = client
        .options("/static/file.png")
        .header(Header::_ORIGIN, "https://evil.example.com")
        .send();

    assert!(resp.header("access-control-allow-origin").is_none());
}

#[test]
fn cors_passes_for_listed_origin() {
    let config = ServerConfig {
        cors_allow_all: false,
        cors_allow_origins: "https://trusted.example.com".to_string(),
        cors_allow_credentials: "true".to_string(),
        ..ServerConfig::default()
    };
    let client = TestClient::new(App::with_config(config));

    let resp = client
        .options("/static/file.png")
        .header(Header::_ORIGIN, "https://trusted.example.com")
        .header(Header::_ACCESS_CONTROL_REQUEST_METHOD, "GET")
        .send();

    assert_eq!(
        "https://trusted.example.com",
        resp.header("access-control-allow-origin").unwrap_or("")
    );
}
```

`App::with_config(config)` pins the app to a fixed `ServerConfig` for the lifetime of the `App` instance — SIGHUP and `POST /admin/config/reload` do not affect it. `App::new()` (no pinned config) continues to read env vars per request, which is correct for production and for tests that specifically verify hot-reload behavior.

`AppWithState`, `AsyncAppWithState` (requires `http2`), and `ConfigDrivenApp` (config-driven proxy) each fall through to a built-in `App` for any request their own routes/rules don't handle. That fallback reads env vars per request by default, same as `App::new()` — call `.with_config(ServerConfig)` on any of them for the same parallel-test-safe pinning:

```rust
use rust_web_server::state::AppWithState;
use rust_web_server::server_config::ServerConfig;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

let config = ServerConfig { cors_allow_all: false, cors_allow_origins: String::new(), ..ServerConfig::default() };

let app = AppWithState::new(())
    .with_config(config)
    .get("/version", |_req, _params, _conn, _state| rust_web_server::response::Response::new());
let client = TestClient::new(app);
```

:::note[No TCP overhead]
Because `TestClient` bypasses the network stack entirely, tests do not need `#[tokio::test]`, `async`, or any port allocation. They run in plain `#[test]` functions and complete in microseconds.
:::

:::note[Error responses]
If `Application::execute` returns `Err(String)`, `TestClient` converts it to a synthetic `500 Internal Server Error` response whose body is the error message. This means error paths are testable with the same `resp.status()` assertions.
:::

---

# WebSocket and SSE in tests

<https://rws8.tech/docs/testing/websocket-sse/>

`TestClient` drives two kinds of long-lived responses in-process (since 18.29.0): a WebSocket route's upgrade handler, over an in-memory duplex, and a `text/event-stream` body, read as it arrives. Both wait with timeouts, so a handler that never answers fails the test instead of hanging it.

## WebSocket

`client.websocket(path).connect()` sends the opening handshake through the app. When the route answers with `WebSocket::upgrade`'s `101`, the handler runs on a thread of its own — the same handler the server would run — and you get a `TestWebSocket`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;
use rust_web_server::websocket::{Message, WebSocket};

#[test]
fn echo() {
    let app = App::with_state(()).get("/echo", |request, _params, _conn, _state| {
        WebSocket::upgrade(request, |mut ws| {
            while let Ok(Some(Message::Text(text))) = ws.recv() {
                let _ = ws.send_text(&text);
            }
        })
    });
    let client = TestClient::new(app);

    let mut ws = client.websocket("/echo").connect().expect("a 101");
    ws.send_text("hi");
    assert_eq!("hi", ws.recv_text());
    assert_eq!(Some(1000), ws.close(1000, "done")); // the handler's close code
}
```

Anything but an upgrade comes back as the `Err` response, so refusals are testable too:

```rust
let refused = client.websocket("/admin/live").connect().err().expect("refused");
assert_eq!(401, refused.status());
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `.header(name, value)` | add a handshake header (`Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, …) |
| `.timeout(d)` | how long `recv`/`close` wait for the handler (default 5 s) |
| `send_text` / `send_binary` | send a message, masked as a browser does |
| `ping(payload)` / `send(frame)` | a ping, or any `Frame` |
| `send_raw(bytes)` | bytes as they are, to test protocol errors (an unmasked frame gets close code 1002) |
| `recv()` | `Ok(Some(Message))`; `Ok(None)` once the handler sent a close (answered for you); `Err` on a timeout or a handler that returned without closing. Pings are answered and skipped, fragments joined |
| `recv_text()` / `recv_binary()` | the next message, panicking if it's anything else |
| `recv_frame()` | the next raw frame (pings and pongs included) |
| `close_code()` | the handler's close code, once it closed |
| `close(code, reason)` | the closing handshake; waits for the handler to return, returns its close code |
| `handler_finished(timeout)` | whether the handler returned |
| `handshake()` | the `101` response and its headers |

Dropping a `TestWebSocket` ends the connection: the handler's `recv` returns an error. A handler that reaches for `tokio::runtime::Handle::current()` finds the test's runtime when the test is `#[tokio::test]`.

## Server-Sent Events

`TestResponse::sse()` reads a `text/event-stream` body — streamed by `Sse::stream` (`stream_pipe`) as it arrives, or buffered by `Sse::into_response` at once — and parses it into `SseFrame { event, data, id, retry }`:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::sse::{Sse, SseEvent};
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestClient;

#[test]
fn ticks() {
    let app = App::with_state(()).get("/ticks", |_req, _params, _conn, _state| {
        let (events, response) = Sse::stream();
        std::thread::spawn(move || {
            for n in 1..=3 {
                let _ = events.send(SseEvent::data(n.to_string()).event_type("tick").id(n.to_string()));
            }
        });
        response
    });
    let client = TestClient::new(app);

    let events = client.get("/ticks").send().sse_events(3, Duration::from_secs(5));
    assert_eq!(3, events.len());
    assert_eq!("tick", events[0].event);
    assert_eq!("1", events[0].data);
    assert_eq!(Some("1"), events[0].id.as_deref());
}
```

`sse_events(n, timeout)` returns up to `n` events within `timeout` in all — fewer when the stream ends or time runs out, so assert on the count. For finer control keep the `TestSse` from `.sse()`:

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `next_event(timeout)` | the next event, or `None` (stream ended, or timed out) |
| `events(n, timeout)` | up to `n` events |
| `collect_until_end(timeout)` | every event until the stream ends (waits the whole `timeout` if it never does) |
| `is_ended()` / `error()` | whether the stream ended, and why if it was an error |
| `comments()` | comment lines seen (keep-alives) |

Parsing follows the HTML Standard's rules: lines end in CRLF, LF or CR; `data` lines join with `\n`; the event type defaults to `message`; a block without `data` isn't dispatched; `retry` must be digits. `SseParser` is the same parser on its own (`parser.feed(bytes)` returns the events those bytes completed). It refuses an event or line over 8 MiB (`sse::MAX_EVENT_BYTES`) instead of buffering without bound.

A streamed body is read on a thread of its own; it ends with the stream, or at the first read after the `TestSse` is dropped (for `Sse::stream`, the next event or keep-alive comment). `TestResponse::is_streamed()` tells whether a response has a streamed body, and `take_stream()` hands you its reader for anything that isn't SSE.

---

# Test databases and factories

<https://rws8.tech/docs/testing/database/>

Two helpers for tests that touch the database (since 18.29.0, `model-*` features): `TestDb`, a database per test that leaves nothing behind, and `#[derive(Factory)]`, which builds `#[derive(Model)]` structs with a default for every field.

## TestDb

```rust
use rust_web_server::test_client::TestDb;

#[tokio::test]
async fn notes_start_empty() {
    let db = TestDb::sqlite().migrations("migrations").await.unwrap();
    db.execute("INSERT INTO notes (text) VALUES ('hi')", &[]).await.unwrap();
    // db derefs to DbPool; db.pool() is a clone for the app's state
}
```

`TestDb::sqlite()` (and the other constructors) return a builder: `.migrations(dir)` adds a directory of `*.sql` migrations (call it again for more; relative to the package root under `cargo test`), and `.await` — or `.build().await` — connects and migrates. A failing migration is the `Err`.

| Backend | Constructor | How the test is isolated |
|---|---|---|
| SQLite | `TestDb::sqlite()` | a fresh in-memory database per `TestDb`, migrations applied; gone with the last clone of its pool. Tests run in parallel |
| PostgreSQL | `TestDb::postgres(url)`, `TestDb::postgres_from_env()` | migrations applied for real (once per process and directory); then a pool of **one connection** that starts a transaction as it connects. Nothing is committed: `db.rollback().await` rolls it back, and dropping the `TestDb` closes the connection, which the server rolls back |
| MySQL | `TestDb::mysql(url)`, `TestDb::mysql_from_env()` | the same as PostgreSQL |

The `_from_env` forms read `RWS_TEST_POSTGRES_URL` / `RWS_TEST_MYSQL_URL` (sqlx URLs, e.g. `postgres://user:password@localhost/app_test`). When the variable isn't set they print `skipped: …` and return `None`, so a test runs where a server is available and returns early elsewhere:

```rust
#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread")]
async fn orders_against_postgres() {
    let Some(db) = TestDb::postgres_from_env() else { return };
    let db = db.migrations("migrations").await.unwrap();
    // …
}
```

Limits of the transaction, the usual ones for transactional tests:

- Give tests a database of their own: the schema (migrations) persists, only data is rolled back.
- One connection: code holding two connections at once (two transactions alive together) waits for itself. `DbPool::begin`/`transaction` do work — sqlx makes them savepoints inside the test's transaction, so their `commit` commits nothing.
- Raw `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` statements end the test's transaction, and so does DDL on MySQL (`CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE` commit implicitly). Keep schema changes in migrations.
- On PostgreSQL a failed statement aborts the transaction, and every later statement in the test fails; run statements that are expected to fail inside `DbPool::transaction` (a savepoint).

### An app on a TestDb

Hand `db.pool()` to the app's state and drive it with `TestClient` as usual. From `#[tokio::test]`, an `App::with_async_state` app is best driven with `send_async().await`, which awaits the handler instead of blocking the test's thread:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::test_client::{TestClient, TestDb};

#[tokio::test]
async fn counts_notes() {
    let db = TestDb::sqlite().migrations("migrations").await.unwrap();
    let client = TestClient::new(my_app::app(db.pool()));
    let response = client.get("/notes").send_async().await;
    assert_eq!(200, response.status());
}
```

`send()` works too (the handler runs on rws's long-lived `rws-async` runtime, so the pool keeps its connection), but it blocks the test's thread while it waits: on the default single-threaded test runtime nothing else runs meanwhile, so a pool whose connections belong to that runtime — PostgreSQL and MySQL, made in the test — would wait for it forever. SQLite connections don't depend on a runtime.

## Factories

Add `Factory` next to `Model`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::{Factory, Model};

#[derive(Model, Factory, Debug, Clone)]
#[table(name = "users")]
pub struct User {
    #[primary_key(auto_increment)]
    pub id: i64,
    pub name: String,      // "name-1", "name-2", …
    pub email: String,     // "email-1@example.com", …
    pub age: Option<i32>,  // None
    pub admin: bool,       // false
}
```

`User::factory()` returns a `ModelFactory`:

```rust
let unsaved = User::factory().build();
let ann = User::factory().with(|u| u.name = "Ann".into()).create(&db).await?;
assert!(ann.id > 0); // read back after the INSERT
let admins = User::factory().with(|u| u.admin = true).create_many(3, &db).await?;
let five = User::factory().build_many(5);
```

| Method | What it does |
|---|---|
| `.with(\|m\| …)` | change each built instance (after the defaults and earlier `with`s) |
| `.build()` / `.build_many(n)` | instances, not saved |
| `.create(&pool).await` | one instance `INSERT`ed (whatever its key) and read back with its id |
| `.create_many(n, &pool).await` | `n` of them |

Defaults per field type: numbers `0`, `bool` `false`, `Option` `None`, `String` the field's name and a sequence number (with `@example.com` for a field whose name contains `email`), so unique columns stay unique. An `auto_increment` key is `0` (the database picks it); any other key is the sequence number. `#[ignore]` fields, and field types with no `FactoryValue` impl, get `Default::default()` — implement `test_client::factory::FactoryValue` for your own column types to choose their default.

The sequence is per model type and shared by every test in the process, in whatever order they run: assert on the values a factory returns rather than on `name-1`.

`#[derive(Factory)]` needs `rws-macros` 17.30 (the `macros` feature) and reads the same attributes as `#[derive(Model)]`.

# OpenAPI snapshots

<https://rws8.tech/docs/testing/snapshots/>

`assert_openapi_snapshot` (since 18.29.0) compares an app's OpenAPI document with a file committed beside the tests, so a change to the API shows up in review as a change to that file:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::openapi::OpenApiConfig;
use rust_web_server::test_client::{assert_openapi_snapshot, TestClient};

#[test]
fn api_matches_the_snapshot() {
    let app = my_app::app().openapi(OpenApiConfig::new("Shop", "1.0.0"));
    assert_openapi_snapshot(&TestClient::new(app), "tests/snapshots/openapi.json");
}
```

The first argument is anything the document can be read from: a `TestClient` whose app serves `GET /openapi.json` (`AppWithState::openapi`), a `TestResponse` of it, or the JSON text itself (`app.openapi_spec(&config)`). A document that isn't JSON or has no `openapi` field fails — a `404` page is no snapshot.

Both sides are normalized before comparing — parsed, object keys sorted, printed with two-space indentation — so key order and whitespace don't count. A mismatch fails with a line diff (`-` the snapshot, `+` now, three lines of context):

```text
the document differs from the snapshot tests/snapshots/openapi.json (- snapshot, + now):
  …
            "200": {
-             "description": "OK"
+             "description": "Found"
            }
  …
If the change is intended, run the test with RWS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 and commit the file.
```

## Updating

```bash
RWS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 cargo test     # write the current documents
git diff tests/snapshots/             # review what changed, then commit
```

With `RWS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS` set (to anything but empty, `0` or `false`) the assertion writes the normalized document — creating the file and its directory — and passes. Without it a missing file fails with that hint, so CI never passes by writing its own snapshot. `RWS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS` is read by the test helpers only; it isn't a server setting.

Relative paths are relative to the working directory, which under `cargo test` is the package root.

`assert_json_snapshot(json, path)` does the same for any JSON document — a JSON Schema, an MCP `tools/list` result, a response body.

# Docker

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/docker/>

## Prebuilt image

Every release publishes a multi-arch image (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) to
[Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/r/bohdaq/rws) as `bohdaq/rws` and to the
GitHub Container Registry as `ghcr.io/bohdaq/rws`, tagged with the full
version (`17.113.0`), the major version (`17`), and `latest`:

```bash
# Serve the current directory
docker run -p 7878:7878 -v "$PWD:/srv:ro" bohdaq/rws

# Pin a version (recommended in production)
docker run -p 7878:7878 -v "$PWD:/srv:ro" bohdaq/rws:17.113.0
```

The image is `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot` plus the static musl `rws` binary (about 12 MB) — no shell, no package manager, runs as a non-root user. The working directory is `/srv`: mount static content there, or put an `rws.config.toml` there to run as a config-driven proxy. Configure with `RWS_CONFIG_*` environment variables, e.g. `-e RWS_CONFIG_PORT=8080`. Each release image is started and checked (`/healthz`, the served page, `--version`) before it's published.

### Automatic HTTPS in Docker

`rws` writes the Let's Encrypt certificate, its key and the ACME account key
to `/data` (owned by the image's user). Mount a volume there so restarts reuse
the certificate instead of requesting a new one:

```bash
docker run -d --name rws -p 80:80 -p 443:443 -p 443:443/udp \
  -v "$PWD:/srv:ro" -v rws-data:/data bohdaq/rws
```

with an `[acme]` section in the mounted `rws.config.toml` (see
[Automatic HTTPS](/features/acme/)). `443/udp` carries HTTP/3.

Build your own image with the Dockerfile below if you need non-default Cargo features or your own application code.

## Multi-stage Dockerfile

The recommended Dockerfile uses a two-stage build: a `rust:1.99` builder compiles the binary, then a slim Debian image carries only the final executable.

```dockerfile
# ── Stage 1: build ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM rust:1.99 AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Cache dependencies before copying source.
COPY Cargo.toml Cargo.lock ./
# Build a dummy main to prime the dependency cache.
RUN mkdir src && echo 'fn main(){}' > src/main.rs && cargo build --release && rm src/main.rs

# Now copy real source and build.
COPY . .
RUN cargo build --release

# ── Stage 2: runtime ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FROM debian:bookworm-slim

# Runtime dependencies for TLS (ca-certificates) and diagnostics (curl).
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates curl \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY --from=builder /app/target/release/rws /usr/local/bin/rws

# TCP port (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2)
EXPOSE 7878
# UDP port (HTTP/3 / QUIC) — only relevant with the http3 feature
EXPOSE 7878/udp

HEALTHCHECK --interval=15s --timeout=3s --start-period=5s \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:7878/healthz || exit 1

CMD ["rws"]
```

:::note[Dependency cache layer]
The dummy `src/main.rs` trick builds and caches all Cargo dependencies before the real source is copied. Subsequent builds that only change application code skip the full `cargo build` of your dependencies.
:::

## Image sizes by feature flag

The default `cargo build --release` enables the `http3` feature, which includes QUIC, HTTP/2, TLS (`rustls`), and the `quinn`/`h3` stacks. Lighter builds are available:

| Feature flag | TLS | HTTP/2 | HTTP/3 | Approx. final image |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `http1` (no-default) | No | No | No | ~3 MB |
| `http2` (no-default) | Yes (rustls) | Yes | No | ~7 MB |
| `http3` (default) | Yes (rustls) | Yes | Yes | ~12 MB |

To build with the `http1`-only feature (smallest image):

```dockerfile
RUN cargo build --release --no-default-features --features http1
```

## Exposed ports

| Port | Protocol | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `7878` | TCP | HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TLS upgrade via ALPN) |
| `7878/udp` | UDP | HTTP/3 / QUIC (only active when a TLS cert is configured) |

Change the port at runtime with `RWS_CONFIG_PORT`.

## Environment variable injection

All `RWS_CONFIG_*` variables can be passed via `docker run -e` or a `.env` file:

```bash
docker run \
  -e RWS_CONFIG_IP=0.0.0.0 \
  -e RWS_CONFIG_PORT=8080 \
  -e RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT=8 \
  -e RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=json \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  my-rws-image
```

## docker-compose with TLS

Mount your certificate files as a read-only volume and pass the paths via environment variables:

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
version: "3.9"

services:
  rws:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "443:7878"
      - "443:7878/udp"   # QUIC / HTTP/3
      - "80:7879"         # HTTP → HTTPS redirect port
    environment:
      RWS_CONFIG_IP: "0.0.0.0"
      RWS_CONFIG_PORT: "7878"
      RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE: "/run/secrets/cert.pem"
      RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE: "/run/secrets/key.pem"
      RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT: "7879"
      RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT: "json"
    volumes:
      - ./certs/cert.pem:/run/secrets/cert.pem:ro
      - ./certs/key.pem:/run/secrets/key.pem:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fk", "https://localhost:7878/healthz"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s
    restart: unless-stopped
```

:::note[SIGHUP hot-reload inside Docker]
Send `docker kill --signal=SIGHUP <container>` to reload TLS certificates, CORS rules, rate limits, and log format without restarting the container. The server's `/admin/config/reload` endpoint does the same over HTTP.
:::
