# Kubernetes

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/kubernetes/>

## Health endpoints

`rust-web-server` exposes one endpoint per Kubernetes probe:

| Endpoint | Probe | `200` when |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /livez` (also `GET /healthz`) | Liveness | Every liveness check passes — with none registered, while the process answers |
| `GET /readyz` | Readiness | The server is up and not shutting down, and every readiness check passes; `503` during startup and the SIGTERM drain |
| `GET /startupz` | Startup | Every startup check has passed once (then it stays `200`) |

### Health checks

Register what "alive", "ready" and "started" mean for your app with the `health` module (18.35.0):

```rust
use rust_web_server::health;

health::database("db", pool.clone());                    // readiness: SELECT 1 (model-* features)
health::readiness("payments-api", || ping_payments());   // Err(message) takes the pod out of the Service
health::startup("search-index", || if index_loaded() { Ok(()) } else { Err("loading".into()) });
health::liveness("worker", || if worker_alive() { Ok(()) } else { Err("the worker thread died".into()) });
```

Checks run concurrently, each within `health::set_timeout` (default 2 s; a slower check fails), off the event loop, so a check may block. `?verbose` gives one line per check, as the Kubernetes API server's own probes do:

```text
$ curl -s localhost:7878/readyz?verbose
[+]db ok
[-]payments-api failed: connection refused
readyz check failed
```

Without `?verbose` the body is `OK`, or the failed checks. `health::register_async(probe, name, || async { … })` takes an async check; `health::report(probe)` runs them from code. Keep liveness checks to what a restart fixes: a database outage belongs in readiness, or every pod restarts at once.

## Graceful shutdown

When Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM`, the server:

1. Clears `SERVER_READY` — `/readyz` begins returning `503`, Kubernetes stops sending new traffic.
2. Keeps accepting for `shutdown_delay_secs` (default 5, since 18.27.0): endpoint removal reaches kube-proxy and ingress controllers a moment after the pod is told to stop, and until then they still send it requests. Before 18.27 rws stopped accepting at once and those got a `502`/`503` from the load balancer.
3. Stops accepting new TCP connections.
4. Waits for the requests whose handlers are still running, at most `shutdown_timeout_secs` (default 25, since 18.35.0; `RWS_CONFIG_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_SECS`) — the thread pool's drain on `http1`. Before 18.35 the async servers returned at once and a handler still running was cut off when the process exited. Idle keep-alive connections don't hold it up.
5. Exits cleanly.

Ctrl+C (SIGINT) skips the delay and the wait. Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to at least the delay plus the timeout (`30` with the defaults) to give in-flight requests time to complete before Kubernetes sends `SIGKILL`.

## Generate the manifests

`rws gen deploy --image <image>` writes `deploy/k8s/` for the app in the current project (18.35.0): a Deployment with the startup, readiness and liveness probes above, `POD_NAME`/`POD_NAMESPACE` from the downward API, a 35 s grace period for the shutdown, a non-root read-only container; a Service; a PodDisruptionBudget; a HorizontalPodAutoscaler; a ServiceAccount; and a `kustomization.yaml`:

```sh
rws gen deploy --image ghcr.io/acme/notes:1.4.0 [--port 7878] [--replicas 2] [--max-replicas 10] [--out deploy/k8s]
kubectl apply -k deploy/k8s
```

The name comes from `rws.app.toml` (or `Cargo.toml`). The files are yours to change; like every generator it never overwrites one (`--dry-run` shows them first). For an app that uses the Kubernetes API see [Using the Kubernetes API](/deployment/kubernetes-api/); an operator prints its own RBAC ([Operators](/deployment/kubernetes-operators/#manifests)).

:::tip[Helm chart]
The manifests below are also a Helm chart, published with every release (since 18.2.0):

```bash
kubectl create secret tls rws-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
helm install my-rws oci://ghcr.io/bohdaq/charts/rws --version 18.2.0
```

It renders the same `Deployment`, `Service`, `PodDisruptionBudget` and `HorizontalPodAutoscaler`, plus an optional `Ingress` and prometheus-operator `ServiceMonitor`; CI installs it into a kind cluster with TLS on and off. Its values are documented in [`helm/rws/README.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/tree/main/helm/rws).

Routes, upstreams and middleware come from `rws.config.toml`; give it to the chart as `configFile` (since 18.27.0). The chart mounts it from a ConfigMap and sets `RWS_CONFIG_FILE`. A new value rolls the pods; with `watch = true` in the file, an edit of the ConfigMap itself is applied in place, within a minute (the kubelet's sync).

```bash
helm install my-rws oci://ghcr.io/bohdaq/charts/rws --set tls.enabled=false --set quic.enabled=false \
  --set-file configFile=rws.config.toml
```
:::

## Deployment YAML

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rws
  labels:
    app: rws
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rws
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rws
      annotations:
        # Prometheus scrape annotations — tells Prometheus to scrape this pod.
        prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
        prometheus.io/path: "/metrics"
        prometheus.io/port: "7878"
        prometheus.io/scheme: "https"   # the pod serves TLS
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: rws
          image: ghcr.io/bohdaq/rws:18
          ports:
            - name: https
              containerPort: 7878
              protocol: TCP
            - name: quic
              containerPort: 7878
              protocol: UDP
          env:
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_IP
              value: "0.0.0.0"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_PORT
              value: "7878"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT
              value: "4"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT
              value: "json"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE
              value: "/tls/tls.crt"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE
              value: "/tls/tls.key"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tls
              mountPath: /tls
              readOnly: true
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 7878
              scheme: HTTPS   # the port serves TLS; plain-HTTP probes would fail
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 3
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: 7878
              scheme: HTTPS   # the port serves TLS; plain-HTTP probes would fail
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 2
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "64Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
      volumes:
        - name: tls
          secret:
            secretName: rws-tls
```

Every `RWS_CONFIG_*` variable can come from a ConfigMap or Secret. Settings that name a file, such as `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE`, take a path, so mount the Secret as a volume (as above) rather than putting its contents in the variable:

```yaml
envFrom:
  - configMapRef:
      name: rws-config   # e.g. RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT, RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT
```

## PodDisruptionBudget

Keep at least two pods running during rolling updates or node drains:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: rws-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rws
```

## HorizontalPodAutoscaler

Scale on CPU utilisation, or on requests per second per pod. rws exports the
counter `rws_requests_total` at `/metrics`; the
[Prometheus Adapter](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prometheus-adapter)
turns it into the per-pod rate `rws_requests_per_second` in the custom
metrics API. Install it with the rule in
[`helm/prometheus-adapter-values.yaml`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/helm/prometheus-adapter-values.yaml):

```bash
helm install prometheus-adapter prometheus-community/prometheus-adapter \
  -n monitoring -f helm/prometheus-adapter-values.yaml   # set prometheus.url first
kubectl get --raw "/apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/pods/*/rws_requests_per_second"
```

The rule:

```yaml
rules:
  custom:
    - seriesQuery: 'rws_requests_total{namespace!="",pod!=""}'
      resources:
        overrides:
          namespace: {resource: namespace}
          pod: {resource: pod}
      name:
        matches: "^rws_requests_total$"
        as: "rws_requests_per_second"
      metricsQuery: 'sum(rate(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}[2m])) by (<<.GroupBy>>)'
```

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: rws-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: rws
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
    # Requests per second per pod, from the Prometheus Adapter rule above.
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric:
          name: rws_requests_per_second
        target:
          type: AverageValue
          averageValue: "500"
```

With the Helm chart: `--set autoscaling.enabled=true --set autoscaling.customMetric.enabled=true`.
(Until 18.2.0 this page used an `External` metric named `rws_route_requests_total`, which nothing served.)

## Structured logging for Kubernetes

Access logs are JSON by default (`RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=json`, or `log_format = 'json'` in `rws.config.toml`; `combined` gives Combined Log Format, `off`/`none` disables the access log). Kubernetes log aggregators (Fluentd, Fluent Bit, Vector) can then parse and index each field:

```json
{"time":"2026-07-02T12:00:00Z","remote_addr":"10.0.0.1","method":"GET","path":"/api/users","protocol":"HTTP/1.1","status":200,"bytes":1024}
```

:::note[Log to stdout]
`rust-web-server` writes all access logs to stdout (buffered per thread, written at least every 100 ms). Let the container runtime and your log aggregator handle collection and rotation — this is the Kubernetes-native approach.
:::

## Prometheus scraping

With the `prometheus.io/*` annotations on the pod (`prometheus.io/scheme: "https"` when the pod serves TLS), a Prometheus using annotation-based discovery scrapes `GET /metrics` automatically; with the prometheus-operator, enable the chart's `metrics.serviceMonitor` instead. The endpoint returns server-wide counters and — if `MetricsLayer` is enabled — per-route histograms in Prometheus text format. Circuit-breaker state (`rws_circuit_breaker_state{backend}`) is included automatically. The full metric list is on the [Metrics](/features/metrics/) page.

See the [Observability](/deployment/observability) page for example Grafana queries.

# Kubernetes Ingress

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/kubernetes-ingress/>

`KubernetesIngressWatcher` watches the Kubernetes API server for Ingress resources and maintains a live route table in memory. `IngressRouter` implements `Application` and uses that table to forward requests to the correct upstream service.

## How it works

1. `KubernetesIngressWatcher` does a full `GET /apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/{ns}/ingresses` on an interval (default 30 s, configurable) as a resync safety net, **and** opens a long-lived `?watch=true` streaming connection alongside it — any `ADDED`/`MODIFIED`/`DELETED` event on that stream triggers an immediate re-list instead of waiting for the next interval. On a quiet cluster the watch connection just sits blocked on a read, costing nothing; if the API server doesn't support watch for some reason, the interval resync alone keeps things working, just at up-to-30s latency instead of near-instant.
2. Each Ingress rule is parsed into an `IngressRule` containing `host`, `path`, `path_type`, `service_name`, `service_port`, and `namespace`.
3. `IngressRouter` matches incoming requests (host header + path, per `path_type` — see [Path matching](#path-matching)) against the live rule table and proxies to `{service_name}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local:{service_port}` over HTTP/1.1.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Required | Example | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RWS_K8S_API_SERVER` | Yes (for `from_env()`) | `http://localhost:8001` | Base URL of the Kubernetes API (plain HTTP) |
| `RWS_K8S_TOKEN` | No | `eyJhbGci…` | Bearer token for API authentication |
| `RWS_K8S_NAMESPACE` | No | `production` | Namespace to watch (default: `default`; use `all` for all namespaces) |

:::note[Two ways to reach the API server]
`from_env()` talks plain `http://` to the Kubernetes API — the simplest option, and the only one that needs no extra Cargo feature. The recommended setup for local development or a sidecar is `kubectl proxy`:

```sh
kubectl proxy &
export RWS_K8S_API_SERVER=http://localhost:8001
export RWS_K8S_TOKEN=
export RWS_K8S_NAMESPACE=default
```

For a pod that wants to talk to the in-cluster API server directly — no sidecar — use [`from_service_account()`](#connecting-directly-from-inside-a-pod) instead, which connects over TLS to `https://kubernetes.default.svc` and requires the `http-client` or `http2` feature.
:::

## Quick start

```rust
use rust_web_server::ingress::{IngressRouter, KubernetesIngressWatcher};
use rust_web_server::server::Server;

fn main() {
    let watcher = KubernetesIngressWatcher::from_env()
        .expect("Set RWS_K8S_API_SERVER before starting");
    watcher.start(); // spawns background polling thread

    let app = IngressRouter::new(watcher);
    let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().unwrap();
    Server::run(listener, pool, app);
}
```

## Configuration options

```rust
let watcher = KubernetesIngressWatcher::from_env()
    .unwrap()
    .namespace("production")     // override namespace
    .ingress_class("rws")        // only watch Ingress objects with spec.ingressClassName: rws
    .poll_interval_secs(15);     // resync every 15 s instead of 30 (watch still runs alongside)

let app = IngressRouter::new(watcher)
    .connect_timeout_ms(2_000)  // TCP connect to upstream (default 5 000 ms)
    .read_timeout_ms(60_000);   // response read timeout   (default 30 000 ms)
```

### IngressClass filtering

On a single-controller cluster, `.ingress_class(...)` doesn't need to be set — the watcher picks up every Ingress object regardless of `spec.ingressClassName` by default, matching the pre-filtering behavior this crate has always had. On a **multi-controller** cluster (e.g. `rws` running alongside `nginx-ingress`), set `.ingress_class("rws")` so this watcher only builds routes from Ingress objects meant for it — an Ingress with no `ingressClassName` at all never matches a configured filter, so it needs one explicitly to be picked up.

## Path matching

`IngressRule::matches` implements the two Kubernetes `pathType` values that carry real routing semantics:

- If `host` is non-empty, the incoming `Host` header must match (case-insensitive).
- Any query string on the request URI is ignored for path matching.
- **`Prefix`** (the default when `pathType` is absent, and how `ImplementationSpecific` is also treated) matches on whole path *segments*, not raw bytes: rule path `/foo` matches `/foo`, `/foo/`, and `/foo/bar`, but **not** `/foobar`.
- **`Exact`** requires the request path to equal the rule's path exactly (ignoring the query string).

The first matching rule wins. Rules are evaluated in the order they are returned by the API server.

Upstream addresses are resolved as:

```
{service_name}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local:{service_port}
```

## RBAC requirements

The pod's service account needs read access to Ingress resources. Apply the following manifests:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress
  namespace: default
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["networking.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["ingresses"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress-reader
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: rws-ingress-reader
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: rws-ingress
    namespace: default
```

## Deployment example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress-controller
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rws-ingress-controller
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rws-ingress-controller
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: rws-ingress
      containers:
        - name: rws
          image: your-registry/rust-web-server:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 7878
          env:
            - name: RWS_K8S_API_SERVER
              value: "http://localhost:8001"
            - name: RWS_K8S_TOKEN
              value: ""
            - name: RWS_K8S_NAMESPACE
              value: "default"
        # kubectl proxy sidecar exposes the API over plain HTTP
        - name: kubectl-proxy
          image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
          args: ["proxy", "--port=8001", "--address=127.0.0.1"]
```

## Connecting directly from inside a pod

`from_service_account()` (requires the `http-client` or `http2` feature — both already pull in `rustls`) reads the token, namespace, and CA certificate from the files Kubernetes mounts into every pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/`, and finds the API server via the `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST`/`KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT` environment variables every pod also has injected automatically — the same mechanism every other Kubernetes client library uses. No `kubectl proxy` sidecar needed:

```rust
use rust_web_server::ingress::{IngressRouter, KubernetesIngressWatcher};

let watcher = KubernetesIngressWatcher::from_service_account()
    .expect("not running inside a pod, or the http-client/http2 feature isn't enabled");
watcher.start();

let app = IngressRouter::new(watcher);
```

The connection is TLS, trusting **only** the cluster's own CA certificate (`.../ca.crt`) — not the public root store `http_client` uses elsewhere in this crate, since the API server's certificate is signed by that private, cluster-specific CA. Building without the `http-client`/`http2` feature leaves `from_service_account()` returning a clear error pointing back at the `kubectl proxy` + `from_env()` path above, rather than silently failing at connect time.

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["http-client"] }
```

# Kubernetes Gateway API

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/kubernetes-gateway-api/>

:::note[Conformance]
rws passes the Gateway API v1.7.0 conformance suite (standard channel) for the GATEWAY-HTTP, GATEWAY-GRPC, GATEWAY-TLS, GATEWAY-TCP and GATEWAY-UDP profiles with every standard-channel extended feature, in both deployment modes; CI runs the suite on every change (`.github/workflows/gateway-api.yml`). Experimental-channel features (destination-port matching, listener filters, ClusterTrustBundle, address routability) aren't claimed yet. Design and history: [`spec/GATEWAY_API.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/spec/GATEWAY_API.md).
:::

The Linux release binaries and the container image (`ghcr.io/bohdaq/rws`, `bohdaq/rws`) are built with the `gateway-api` feature; macOS and Windows binaries aren't (build those with `--features gateway-api`). With it and `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_ENABLED=true`, rws watches the cluster's Gateway API objects, serves the Gateways whose GatewayClass names its controller, and reports what it accepted in their status. Every replica serves traffic; one, holding the `rws-gateway-controller` Lease, writes status and manages Services.

## What it serves

- **GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, ReferenceGrant** status: acceptance, listener conditions (protocol, route kinds, certificates, conflicts), attached-route counts, route parent conditions (listener allowance by namespace, hostname intersection, `sectionName`/`port`), backend resolution (Service kind, ReferenceGrants, existence), `observedGeneration`.
- **A Service per Gateway** (`rws-<gateway>`, `LoadBalancer` by default), in the Gateway's namespace: one port per listener port, each mapped to a container port from `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_PORT_RANGE`. A Service only selects pods in its own namespace, so it has no selector: rws writes its EndpointSlice (`rws-<gateway>-ipv4`, and `-ipv6` when pods have IPv6 addresses) with its own serving pods — those in its namespace matching `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_POD_SELECTOR` — and their readiness. The Service's load-balancer address becomes the Gateway's `status.addresses`; `spec.infrastructure` labels and annotations are put on it.
- **HTTP and HTTPS listeners**, the latter with the certificate from the listener's TLS Secret (by SNI between listeners).
- **HTTPRoute routing**: hostnames, `Exact`/`PathPrefix` paths, exact header and query-parameter matches, methods, the spec's precedence between routes and rules (between routes on one listener, the route's own hostname decides — an exact name before a wildcard — not its intersection with the listener's), weighted backends over the Services' ready endpoints. The client's `Host` is kept.
- **HTTPRoute filters**, applied in the order listed: `RequestHeaderModifier` and `ResponseHeaderModifier` (`set` replaces, `add` appends, `remove` drops — names case-insensitive), `RequestHeaderModifier` and `URLRewrite` on a `backendRef` (only for requests sent to that backend; a `ReplacePrefixMatch` there replaces the rule's matched prefix), `RequestRedirect` (scheme, hostname, port, `ReplaceFullPath`/`ReplacePrefixMatch` path, status 301/302/303/307/308; the port defaults to the scheme's well-known port when the scheme is set, else the listener's, and a well-known port isn't written into `Location`), `URLRewrite` (hostname, path) and `CORS` (preflights answered with `204` by rws, actual requests get `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and the exposed headers; `*` in an origin matches one or more labels). An `ExtensionRef` or unknown filter answers `500`, as the spec requires.

- **Timeouts and retries**: `timeouts.request` bounds the whole exchange, retries included, and `timeouts.backendRequest` each attempt; past either the client gets `504`, and `0s` turns a timeout off. `retry.attempts` is the number of retries (the first try isn't counted) on the listed `retry.codes`, on connection errors and on backend timeouts, `retry.backoff` apart (25 ms when unset).

- **Backend protocols**: a Service port with `appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c` is reached over cleartext HTTP/2 (prior knowledge); WebSocket and other `Upgrade` requests are forwarded on a connection of their own, and a backend's `101` turns the client's connection into a byte relay with it.

The GatewayClass's `status.supportedFeatures` lists what rws claims; the conformance job checks the same list.

- **Mirroring**: each `RequestMirror` filter sends a copy of the request, as the rule's other request filters left it, to one ready endpoint of its Service, for `percent` or `fraction` of requests (all when neither is set); the copy's response is dropped and never delays the client's.

- **GRPCRoute**: attached like HTTPRoutes (HTTP and HTTPS listeners carry both), matched on `method` (`Exact` service and/or method; `RegularExpression` isn't supported) and headers, with the header-modifier and mirror filters, weighted backends reached over h2c with trailers passed through. A call no rule matches gets HTTP `404`, which gRPC clients report as `UNIMPLEMENTED`.

- **TLSRoute** on `TLS` listeners: in `Passthrough` mode rws reads the ClientHello's SNI, picks the route whose hostname matches best and relays the still-encrypted stream (the backend presents its own certificate); in `Terminate` mode (the default) it decrypts with the listener's certificate and relays the plaintext over TCP. Listeners of both modes can share a port when their hostnames differ: the ClientHello's SNI picks the listener, then its mode.
- **TCPRoute** on `TCP` listeners and **UDPRoute** on `UDP` listeners: bytes, or datagrams, relayed to a backend of the route's first rule by weight. When several routes attach to one listener, the oldest serves it (TLSRoutes: the best hostname match first). Each UDP client gets its own socket to the backend, closed after 60 s without traffic.

- **ListenerSet**: a Gateway whose `spec.allowedListeners` admits a ListenerSet's namespace (`Same`, `All`, `Selector`; the default admits none) serves its listeners after its own, older sets first, on the Gateway's Service. A set's listener that conflicts with an earlier one (same port and hostname, or another protocol on the port) isn't accepted; the set is accepted while any of its listeners is, and the Gateway counts the attached sets in `status.attachedListenerSets`. Routes reach a set's listeners only with a `ListenerSet` parentRef.

- **Misdirected requests**: over HTTPS, a request whose `Host` belongs to a different listener than the one its SNI chose (and whose certificate it was given) is answered `421 Misdirected Request`.
- **Client certificates** (`spec.tls.frontend`): the validation for a listener's port (`perPort`, else `default`) names ConfigMaps whose `ca.crt` holds the CA certificates (another namespace needs a ReferenceGrant). In `AllowValidOnly` mode (the default) the handshake requires a client certificate those CAs signed; `AllowInsecureFallback` asks for one but lets the connection through either way, and the Gateway reports `InsecureFrontendValidationMode`. A reference that doesn't resolve leaves the listener unaccepted (`NoValidCACertificate`) — rws never serves a port without the validation it was asked for. The controller also watches ConfigMaps for this.

- **BackendTLSPolicy**: a Service (or one of its ports, by `sectionName`) a policy targets is reached over TLS, trusting the CA certificates in the referenced ConfigMaps' `ca.crt` (or the platform's roots with `wellKnownCACertificates: System`), with `hostname` as SNI and as the name checked — or, when `subjectAltNames` are listed, any of those (`Hostname` or `URI`) instead. Between two policies for the same target the older wins and the other is `Conflicted`; a port's own policy beats one for the whole Service. A policy that can't be used (a missing or wrong-kind CA reference) turns its backends' requests into `500`s rather than plaintext. Status is reported per Gateway whose routes reach a targeted Service. A Gateway's `spec.tls.backend.clientCertificateRef` (a TLS Secret, or one in another namespace a ReferenceGrant opens) is the client certificate its connections to these backends present; a reference that doesn't resolve is reported in the Gateway's `ResolvedRefs`.

- **Static addresses** (`spec.addresses`): the first `IPAddress` is asked of the load balancer as the Service's `loadBalancerIP`; the Gateway is programmed once every requested address is the Service's (else `AddressNotUsable`). Another address type isn't accepted (`UnsupportedAddress`). An address with only a type asks for any address.


## Deployment modes

- **shared** (`RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_MODE=shared`, the default): the pods of the rws Deployment that runs the controller serve every Gateway. One Deployment, scaled as one.
- **provisioned** (`provisioned`; Helm `gatewayAPI.mode: provisioned`): each Gateway gets its own Deployment, `rws-gw-<namespace>-<name>`, in the controller's namespace, with the controller's image (`RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_IMAGE`) and ServiceAccount; the Gateway's `spec.infrastructure` labels and annotations go on its pods. Those pods (started with `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_GATEWAY=<namespace>/<name>`) watch the cluster like the controller but serve only their Gateway and never write; the controller's own pods serve nothing. Gateways don't share pods, so one's load or failure doesn't reach another. A Gateway's Deployment is deleted with it (by the controller: an object can't own one in another namespace).

Either way the Gateway's Service lists the serving pods in its EndpointSlice.

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_ENABLED` | `false` | Run the controller |
| `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_CONTROLLER_NAME` | `rws8.tech/gateway-controller` | The GatewayClasses' `controllerName` to handle |
| `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_POD_SELECTOR` | `app.kubernetes.io/name=rws` | Labels of the rws pods, selected by every Gateway's Service |
| `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_PORT_RANGE` | `10000-10999` | Container ports for listeners |
| `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_SERVICE_TYPE` | `LoadBalancer` | Type of each Gateway's Service |
| `RWS_CONFIG_GATEWAY_API_LEASE_NAMESPACE` | the pod's namespace | Where the leader Lease lives |

Also as `[gateway_api]` in `rws.config.toml` ([Config file](/configuration/config-file/)).

## Permissions

The controller needs to list and watch GatewayClasses, Gateways, HTTPRoutes, GRPCRoutes, TLSRoutes, TCPRoutes, UDPRoutes, ReferenceGrants, BackendTLSPolicies, ListenerSets, Services, EndpointSlices, Namespaces, Secrets and ConfigMaps; patch the status of GatewayClasses, Gateways and every route kind; create and patch Services and EndpointSlices; read its own namespace's Pods; and get, create and update Leases in its namespace. The Gateway API CRDs (standard channel, v1.6 or v1.7) must be installed in the cluster first.

## Benchmarks

rws 18.8.1 against five other Gateway API implementations, each at its chart defaults with one data-plane replica, in one kind cluster on one GitHub Actions runner (run [40681376798](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/actions/runs/40681376798)). The same HTTPRoute sends every request to the same nginx backend; [oha](https://github.com/hatoo/oha) loads it for 20 s per row with keep-alive and no compression, from the runner. CPU is what the gateway's pods (controller and data plane) used per request, from the kubelet. Runner hardware varies between runs, so compare rows of this run only. The harness is `bench/gateway/run.sh` (workflow `gateway-bench.yml`, manual).

Versions: Envoy Gateway v1.9.2, NGINX Gateway Fabric 2.7.2, Traefik (chart 41.7.1), kgateway v2.4.6, Istio 1.30.5.

Requests per second, and p99 latency in ms (64 connections unless noted):

| Scenario | rws | kgateway | Istio | Traefik | Envoy Gateway | NGINX GF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| HTTP/1.1, 1 KiB | **38 501** · 5.8 | 20 225 · 9.5 | 16 274 · 9.3 | 17 539 · 14 | 16 685 · 15 | 10 951 · 20 |
| HTTP/1.1, 1 KiB, 256 conns | **39 230** · 23 | 21 103 · 36 | 17 795 · 23 | 18 484 · 45 | 17 757 · 67 | 10 814 · 86 |
| HTTP/1.1, 1 MiB | **2 467** · 71 | 2 009 · 93 | 2 057 · 186 | 1 879 · 81 | 1 556 · 191 | 841 · 200 |
| HTTPS, 1 KiB | **34 792** · 5.3 | 19 085 · 10 | 15 946 · 6.7 | 17 941 · 13 | 16 372 · 16 | 10 121 · 22 |
| HTTP/2 + TLS, 1 KiB | **32 120** · 5.5 | 17 226 · 11 | 14 063 · 7.6 | 13 158 · 14 | 14 817 · 15 | 9 419 · 25 |
| Header modifiers + rewrite, 1 KiB | **36 821** · 5.0 | 19 573 · 8.9 | 16 272 · 6.7 | 18 004 · 14 | 16 907 · 16 | —¹ |

CPU µs per request:

| Scenario | rws | kgateway | Istio | Traefik | Envoy Gateway | NGINX GF |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| HTTP/1.1, 1 KiB | **40** | 106 | 116 | 96 | 80 | 117 |
| HTTP/1.1, 1 KiB, 256 conns | **19** | 82 | 66 | 175 | 171 | 191 |
| HTTP/1.1, 1 MiB | 928 | 1182 | 1254 | **597** | 1098 | 1365 |
| HTTPS, 1 KiB | **33** | 73 | 64 | 165 | 121 | 171 |
| HTTP/2 + TLS, 1 KiB | **63** | 152 | 209 | 178 | 188 | 292 |
| Header modifiers + rewrite, 1 KiB | **27** | 129 | 77 | 96 | 116 | —¹ |

Every gateway answered every request with 200 except as noted. Memory (working set of the gateway's pods after the runs): rws 42–118 MiB (mimalloc keeps freed memory, so it stays at its peak after the 1 MiB run), NGINX Gateway Fabric 60–74, the others 70–200.

¹ NGINX Gateway Fabric answered 404 through the rewriting route in this setup, so the row isn't comparable; it also had 160 cancelled requests over HTTP/2.

What this doesn't measure: many routes or Gateways, configuration churn, connection setup (every scenario reuses connections), and real backends.

# Using the Kubernetes API

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/kubernetes-api/>

The `k8s` feature (18.35.0) gives an app running in Kubernetes the API itself: configuration that changes without a restart, secrets read where they live, the pods behind a Service, and one replica at a time for singleton work. It builds on [kube-rs](https://kube.rs), which `rust_web_server::k8s` re-exports (`kube`, `k8s_openapi`, `schemars`).

```toml
rust-web-server = { version = "18.35", features = ["k8s"] }
```

## A client

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::client;

let kube = client::client().await?;          // in a pod: its service account; elsewhere: ~/.kube/config
let ns = client::current_namespace();        // POD_NAMESPACE, the service account's, the kubeconfig's, else "default"
```

`client::from_kubeconfig(path)` reads a given file; `client::offline()` is a client that never connects (for an operator's `--manifests`, which describes its controllers without a cluster); `client::identity()` is this replica's name (`POD_NAME`, else `HOSTNAME`). [`rws gen deploy`](/deployment/kubernetes/#generate-the-manifests) sets `POD_NAME` and `POD_NAMESPACE` from the downward API.

## ConfigMaps and Secrets

`config::ConfigWatch` keeps one ConfigMap's or Secret's data current through a watch — no volume mount, no restart, and a change arrives in a second or two:

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::config::ConfigWatch;

let settings = ConfigWatch::config_map(kube.clone(), &ns, "app-settings").await?;   // fails if it can't be read now
let page_size: usize = settings.get("page_size").and_then(|v| v.parse().ok()).unwrap_or(20);
settings.on_change(|data| println!("now: {data:?}"));

// RWS_CONFIG_* keys become rws's own settings, re-read after each change:
settings.apply_to_env("RWS_CONFIG_");

let credentials = ConfigWatch::secret(kube.clone(), &ns, "db-credentials").await?;
```

| Method | What |
|---|---|
| `get(key)`, `snapshot()` | The value now, every key now |
| `on_change(f)` | Called with the new data after each change |
| `apply_to_env(prefix)` | Keys with `prefix` as environment variables, now and on change, then `server_config::invalidate()` |
| `exists()` | `false` once the object was deleted (the last data is kept) |

Binary data is included when it's UTF-8. A clone shares the watch; it stops when the last clone is dropped.

### `k8s://` secret references

```rust
let password = rust_web_server::k8s::config::resolve(&kube, "k8s://prod/db-credentials#password").await?;
```

`k8s://<namespace>/<secret>#<key>` (or `k8s://<secret>#<key>` for the current namespace) reads one key of a Secret, as `vault://`, `aws-sm://` and `azkv://` read [other stores](/features/secrets/).

## Service discovery

The ready endpoints of a Service, from its EndpointSlices, kept current in a [`BackendPool`](/proxy/service-discovery/) — for a `ReverseProxy`, or to reach each pod of a headless Service:

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::discovery;

let pool = discovery::service_endpoints(kube.clone(), &ns, "orders", Some("http")).await?;
pool.backends();    // ["10.42.0.17:8080", "10.42.1.9:8080"]
```

Endpoints whose `ready` condition is `false` are left out; `Some("http")` picks the Service port of that name (`None`: the first). IPv6 addresses come as `[addr]:port`.

## Leader election

`leader::LeaderElector` holds a `coordination.k8s.io/v1` Lease so one replica at a time does singleton work — a scheduler, a cleanup loop:

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::leader::LeaderElector;

let elector = LeaderElector::new(kube.clone(), &ns, "report-scheduler");
let mut leader = elector.handle();
tokio::spawn(elector.run());

loop {
    leader.wait_until_leader().await;
    // … work while leader.is_leader() …
}
```

The holder renews every 5 s; another replica takes over when a renewal is 15 s old (`.timing(duration, renew)`). Writes carry the Lease's `resourceVersion`, so two replicas can't both win. `release()` hands it over at once (on shutdown). Controllers get this built in: [`Operator::leader_election`](/deployment/kubernetes-operators/#leader-election).

## Permissions

The pod's service account needs:

| For | Rules |
|---|---|
| `ConfigWatch::config_map` / `secret`, `k8s://` | `get`, `list`, `watch` on `configmaps` / `secrets` in the namespace |
| `discovery::service_endpoints` | `list`, `watch` on `endpointslices` (`discovery.k8s.io`) |
| `LeaderElector` | `get`, `create`, `update` on `leases` (`coordination.k8s.io`) |

`manifests::Rbac` writes them: see [Manifests](/deployment/kubernetes-operators/#manifests).

# Operators

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/kubernetes-operators/>

An operator watches custom resources and makes the cluster match them. To start from a working one — a custom resource, a controller, webhooks, `--manifests`, tests — generate the starter:

```sh
cargo generate --git https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server starters/operator
```

 The `k8s` feature (18.35.0) has the parts on top of [kube-rs](https://kube.rs)'s controller runtime: controllers with finalizers and status, an operator that runs them under leader election with metrics and a readiness check, admission and conversion webhooks with their certificate, CRD and RBAC manifests generated from the code, and tests against a real API server.

## A custom resource

A resource's types are Rust structs; `#[derive(CustomResource)]` (kube) makes the kind and its CRD:

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::{kube::CustomResource, schemars::JsonSchema};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(CustomResource, Deserialize, Serialize, Clone, Debug, JsonSchema)]
#[kube(group = "example.com", version = "v1", kind = "Backup", namespaced, status = "BackupStatus")]
pub struct BackupSpec {
    pub schedule: String,
    pub database: String,
}

#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize, Clone, Debug, Default, JsonSchema)]
pub struct BackupStatus {
    pub last_run: Option,
}
```

## Controllers

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::time::Duration;
use rust_web_server::k8s::controller::{Action, Context, Controller, Operator};
use rust_web_server::k8s::kube::api::Api;
use rust_web_server::k8s::Error;
use k8s_openapi::api::batch::v1::CronJob;

async fn reconcile(backup: Arc, ctx: Arc) -> Result {
    ctx.apply_owned(&*backup, cron_job_for(&backup)).await?;                 // owned: deleted with it
    ctx.patch_status(&*backup, serde_json::json!({ "last_run": null })).await?;
    ctx.event(&*backup, false, "Scheduled", "the CronJob is up to date").await?;
    Ok(Action::requeue(Duration::from_secs(300)))
}

let kube = rust_web_server::k8s::client::client().await?;
Operator::new(kube.clone(), "backup-operator")
    .leader_election(&rust_web_server::k8s::client::current_namespace(), "backup-operator")
    .controller(
        Controller::new(Api::::all(kube.clone()))
            .owns(Api::::all(kube.clone()))          // a change to its CronJob reconciles the Backup
            .reconcile(reconcile)
            .finalizer("example.com/cleanup", |backup, ctx| async move { delete_backups_of(&backup).await }),
    )
    .run()
    .await;
```

| `Controller` | What |
|---|---|
| `new(api)` | Watch `api`'s objects (`Api::all` or `Api::namespaced`) |
| `watching(config)` | Only those a label or field selector picks |
| `owns(api)` | Also reconcile when an object it owns (owner reference) changes |
| `reconcile(f)` | `async fn(Arc, Arc) -> Result`: make the world match, answer when to look again (`Action::requeue(d)`, `Action::await_change()`) |
| `finalizer(name, cleanup)` | Add the finalizer to each object; on deletion run `cleanup`, then remove it |
| `on_error(delay)` | First retry delay after a failed reconcile (5 s), doubling per failure of the same object up to 5 min |
| `rule(rule)` | An extra RBAC rule the reconcile needs |

`Context` has the `client` and helpers: `patch_status(obj, json)` (merge into the status subresource), `apply_owned(owner, child)` (server-side apply with an owner reference, field manager = the operator's name) and `event(obj, warning, reason, note)` (a Kubernetes Event, shown by `kubectl describe`).

### The operator

`Operator::run` runs every controller and registers a readiness check (`/readyz`, see [health checks](/deployment/kubernetes/#health-checks)). Serve it beside the probes:

```rust
let operator = tokio::spawn(operator.run());
let (listener, pool) = Server::setup()?;
Server::run_tls(listener, pool, App::new()).await;     // /livez, /readyz, /metrics
```

`/metrics` gets `rws_controller_reconciles_total` and `rws_controller_reconcile_errors_total` per controller.

### Leader election

With `.leader_election(namespace, lease)` the controllers run only on the replica holding the Lease; the others wait. A replica that loses the Lease exits, and Kubernetes restarts it as a follower — kube's controllers can't be stopped and restarted in place, and an exit is the safe way to never reconcile on two replicas.

## Webhooks

`webhook::Webhooks` is an rws application answering the API server's AdmissionReview and ConversionReview requests:

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::webhook::{Webhooks, WebhookCertificate};

let webhooks = Webhooks::new()
    .validate::("/validate-backups", |request| match &request.object {
        Some(b) if b.spec.schedule.is_empty() => Err("spec.schedule is required".into()),
        _ => Ok(()),
    })
    .mutate::("/mutate-backups", |mut backup| {
        backup.labels_mut().insert("example.com/managed".into(), "true".into());
        Ok(backup)
    })
    .convert("/convert-backups", |object, desired_version| v1_to_v2(object, desired_version))
    .wrap(App::new());                                       // probes and metrics on the same server

// The API server only calls webhooks over TLS it trusts.
let cert = WebhookCertificate::shared(&kube, &namespace, "backup-operator-webhook-tls", "backup-operator").await?;
cert.install("/tmp/tls")?;                                    // RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE / KEY_FILE
cert.patch_ca_bundle(&kube, Some("backup-operator"), None, None).await?;
Server::run_tls(listener, pool, webhooks).await;
```

| Builder | The handler gets | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `validate::(path, f)` | The request: `operation`, `object`, `old_object`, `user_info`, `name`, `namespace` | `Ok(())` allows, `Err(message)` denies (kubectl shows the message) |
| `mutate::(path, f)` | The object (on create and update) | The object changed; the JSON patch from old to new is computed for you |
| `convert(path, f)` | Each object and the desired `apiVersion` | The object in that version (`apiVersion` set for you) |

With more than one replica, use `WebhookCertificate::shared(&client, namespace, secret, service)`: the first replica makes the certificate and stores it in a `kubernetes.io/tls` Secret, the others read it (a create race is settled by the API server) — replicas each making their own would overwrite each other's `caBundle`, and the API server would reject every replica but one. The pod needs `get` and `create` on `secrets`; `to_secret`/`from_secret` convert (cert-manager's Secrets have the same keys).

`WebhookCertificate::generate(service, namespace)` makes a CA and a serving certificate for `<service>.<namespace>.svc` (`generate_for(name, dns_names)` for others); `install(dir)` writes `tls.crt`, `tls.key`, `ca.crt` and points rws's TLS settings at them; `patch_ca_bundle` puts the CA into the webhook configurations (and a CRD's conversion webhook) at startup, so no cert-manager is needed. With cert-manager, mount its Secret and set the TLS settings instead.

## Manifests

The CRDs, RBAC and webhook configurations come from the code, so they never drift from it:

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::manifests::{self, Rbac, WebhookRule, WebhookTarget};

manifests::print_on_request(|| {                // `backup-operator --manifests | kubectl apply -f -`
    let rbac = Rbac::new("backup-operator", "backups").rules(operator.rules());
    let target = WebhookTarget { service: "backup-operator".into(), namespace: "backups".into(), port: 443, path: "/validate-backups".into(), ca_pem: ca.clone() };
    let mut docs = vec![manifests::crd::()];
    docs.extend(rbac.documents());
    docs.push(manifests::webhook_configuration("backups", false, &target, &[WebhookRule::new("example.com", "v1", "backups", &["CREATE", "UPDATE"])], true));
    docs
});
```

| Function | Writes |
|---|---|
| `crd::()` | The CustomResourceDefinition from the type's schema |
| `with_conversion_webhook(crd, target)` | The CRD with `conversion.strategy: Webhook` |
| `Rbac::new(name, ns).rules(…).documents()` | ServiceAccount, ClusterRole (rules merged per resource), ClusterRoleBinding; `.leader_election()` adds the Lease rule |
| `Operator::rules()` | What its controllers need: their kinds and status, what they own, events, the Lease |
| `webhook_configuration(name, mutating, target, rules, fail_closed)` | A Validating/MutatingWebhookConfiguration |
| `to_yaml(&docs)` | A YAML stream: each document as JSON (which YAML accepts) after a `---` line |

## Testing against a real API server

A fake API server doesn't run admission, garbage collection, finalizers or status subresources — the things operators get wrong. `testing::TestCluster` uses a real one (kind, k3d, or envtest's `kube-apiserver`) from `RWS_TEST_KUBECONFIG`, with a namespace of its own per test:

```rust
use rust_web_server::k8s::testing::{eventually, TestCluster};

#[tokio::test]
async fn backups_get_a_cron_job() {
    let Some(cluster) = TestCluster::from_env().await else { return };   // skipped without a cluster
    cluster.install_crd::().await.unwrap();                       // applied, then waited for
    let ns = cluster.namespace("backup").await.unwrap();                  // backup-<random>, labelled rws-test=true
    tokio::spawn(operator(cluster.client.clone()).run());
    ns.api::().create(&Default::default(), &Backup::new("nightly", spec())).await.unwrap();
    let job = eventually(Duration::from_secs(30), || async { ns.api::().get_opt("nightly").await.ok().flatten() }).await;
    assert!(job.is_some());
    ns.delete().await;
}
```

```sh
kind create cluster --name test --kubeconfig /tmp/kubeconfig
RWS_TEST_KUBECONFIG=/tmp/kubeconfig cargo test
```

With `RWS_TEST_REQUIRE_KUBERNETES` set, a missing cluster fails the test instead of skipping it — for CI. rws's own CI runs its Kubernetes tests this way on kind, and deploys the operator starter into the cluster (`ci/e2e/operator.sh`): the API server calls its webhooks over TLS, its controller reconciles, one of two replicas leads. Never point it at a cluster that matters: the tests create and delete namespaces and cluster-wide CRDs.
