# Observability

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/observability/>

## Metrics

### Built-in Prometheus endpoint

`GET /metrics` is always available and returns metrics in the Prometheus text exposition format. No configuration is required.

Server-wide counters updated by the request loop:

| Metric | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `rws_requests_total` | Counter | Total HTTP requests received |
| `rws_errors_total` | Counter | Connections whose handling ended in an error (I/O or application error, or a panicked handler) — not a count of 5xx responses |
| `rws_active_connections` | Gauge | Number of currently open connections |
| `http_server_request_duration_seconds` | Histogram | OpenTelemetry `http.server.request.duration` by method, status, scheme and protocol version — a [native histogram](/features/metrics/#native-histograms) for a protobuf scrape |

### Per-route metrics with MetricsLayer

Add `MetricsLayer` to any application to record per-route counters and latency histograms:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::metrics::MetricsLayer;

let app = App::new().wrap(MetricsLayer);
```

`MetricsLayer` adds:

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rws_route_requests_total` | Counter | `method`, `path`, `status` | Requests per route and status code |
| `rws_route_duration_seconds` | Histogram | `method`, `path` | Response time distribution |

### Circuit breaker state

Present automatically — no `MetricsLayer` or other opt-in needed — for every backend known to [`circuit_breaker::global()`](/proxy/circuit-breaker/):

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rws_circuit_breaker_state` | Gauge | `backend` | `0`=closed, `1`=half_open, `2`=open |

Wire `ReverseProxy::with_circuit_breaker(Arc::new(circuit_breaker::global()))` to get this metric for free alongside [automatic breaker integration](/proxy/circuit-breaker/#automatic-reverseproxy-wiring).

### TLS

`rws_tls_handshakes_total{tls_protocol_version,tls_cipher,tls_group}`, `rws_tls_handshake_failures_total` and `rws_tls_certificate_expiry_timestamp_seconds{name}` — see [TLS metrics](/features/metrics/#tls). Alert on `rws_tls_certificate_expiry_timestamp_seconds - time() < 14 * 86400`.

### Upstreams

Config-file proxies export `rws_upstream_requests_total`, `rws_upstream_request_duration_seconds`, `rws_upstream_retries_total`, `rws_upstream_backend_up` and `rws_upstream_circuit_breaker_state` per `upstream` and `backend` — see [Upstream metrics](/features/metrics/#upstream-metrics).

### OTLP metrics export

`http.server.request.duration` can also be pushed to an OpenTelemetry Collector (or any OTLP/HTTP endpoint: Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, Datadog's OTLP intake) — the same data `/metrics` serves, so the two never disagree. The `rws` binary starts the exporter when an endpoint is set:

```bash
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318   # metrics go to /v1/metrics, spans to /v1/traces
export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=edge-1                                   # default rws
export OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL=15000                          # ms, default 60000
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="api-key=secret"               # optional, key=value,…
rws
```

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | Collector base URL; `/v1/metrics` and `/v1/traces` are appended |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` | Full metrics URL, used as is (wins over the base) |
| `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL` | Milliseconds between exports (default `60000`) |
| `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` | `none` turns metrics export off |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_HEADERS` | Request headers, `key=value` pairs separated by commas (values percent-decoded) |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `service.name` resource attribute |

Each export is an OTLP/HTTP JSON `ExportMetricsServiceRequest` with cumulative temporality and the convention's explicit buckets, attributes `http.request.method`, `http.response.status_code`, `url.scheme`, `network.protocol.name` and `network.protocol.version`. A last export is sent on SIGTERM/SIGINT. From Rust: `otel::metrics::start(MetricsExportConfig { .. })` or `otel::metrics::start_from_env()`, and `otel::shutdown()` before exit.

### Grafana / PromQL queries

```promql
# Request rate (requests per second over 1 m)
rate(rws_requests_total[1m])

# Error rate
rate(rws_errors_total[1m])

# p99 latency per route
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(rws_route_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# Top routes by request count
topk(10, sum by (path) (rate(rws_route_requests_total[5m])))

# Backends currently tripped open
rws_circuit_breaker_state == 2
```

## Logs

### JSON structured logs (default)

By default the server writes one newline-delimited JSON object per request to stdout:

```json
{"time":"2026-07-02T12:00:00Z","remote_addr":"203.0.113.9","method":"GET","path":"/docs/","protocol":"HTTP/2.0","status":200,"bytes":14384,"host":"example.com","user_agent":"Mozilla/5.0 …","referer":"https://www.google.com/"}
```

`host`, `user_agent` and `referer` come last, each only when the request
sent the header (since 18.15.0). JSON logs are well-suited for ingestion by Loki, Fluentd, Datadog, and other structured-log collectors.

### Combined Log Format

Set `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=combined` (via environment variable or `rws.config.toml`) for Apache Combined Log Format (CLF):

```
127.0.0.1 - - [02/Jul/2026:12:00:00 +0000] "GET /healthz HTTP/1.1" 200 2
```

This format is compatible with GoAccess, AWStats, and most log-analysis tools.

To produce the same line yourself — in your own middleware or a custom server loop — call `Log::combined`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::log::Log;

// request: &Request, response: &Response, peer_addr: &SocketAddr
let line = Log::combined(&request, &response, &peer_addr);
println!("{}", line);
// 192.168.1.1 - - [29/Jun/2026:14:23:05 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 1234
```

`RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=off` writes no access log at all.

### Buffered writes

Access-log lines are buffered per worker thread and written to stdout by a
background thread every 100 ms — at once when a thread's buffer passes
32 KiB, when a thread exits, and when the process exits normally (including
a graceful shutdown on `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`). Writing each line with its own
`write` under the process-wide stdout lock cost about a sixth of a small
request's CPU. A line can therefore appear up to 100 ms after its request;
lines from one thread keep their order, and every line carries its own
timestamp. Code that ends the process some other way can call
`Log::flush_access_log()` first.

### Writing to a file

Set `access_log` (`RWS_CONFIG_ACCESS_LOG`, since 18.1.0) to write the access
log to a file instead of stdout:

```toml
log_format          = "combined"
access_log          = "/var/log/rws/access.log"
access_log_max_size = "100M"    # rotate past 100 MiB (the default since 18.15.0)
access_log_keep     = 5         # access.log.1 … access.log.5
```

- Lines are appended; the file and its directory must be writable by rws.
- **Rotation by rws** (the default): past `access_log_max_size` (100 MiB
  unless set) the file is renamed `access.log.1` (older ones shift up, the
  oldest past `access_log_keep` is deleted) and a new one is started — at
  most 600 MiB with the defaults. Before 18.15.0 the default was `0`,
  never rotating.
- **Rotation by logrotate:** set `access_log_max_size` to `0` and have
  logrotate send `SIGUSR1` after moving the file; rws reopens the path
  before its next write:

  ```
  /var/log/rws/access.log {
      daily
      rotate 14
      compress
      delaycompress
      missingok
      notifempty
      postrotate
          systemctl kill -s USR1 rws.service
      endscript
  }
  ```

  Without an access-log file `SIGUSR1` keeps its default action (it ends
  the process), so don't send it to an rws logging to stdout.

### Disk safety

A busy server writes a lot: at 10,000 requests a second an access log
grows by about 170 GB a day. Everything rws writes is bounded:

| What | Bound |
|---|---|
| Access log in a file | rotated at `access_log_max_size` (100 MiB) × `access_log_keep` (5) |
| Disk cache | `[route.middleware.cache] max_size` (256 MiB), oldest out |
| Any of them, whatever the settings | `min_free_disk` (below) |

**`min_free_disk`** (`RWS_CONFIG_MIN_FREE_DISK`, since 18.15.0): before
writing the access-log file or a disk-cache entry, rws checks the free
space of that filesystem (at most every 5 s). Under the floor it stops
writing there — the lines are dropped and counted, the cache serves what it
has — logs one warning, and resumes when space is back. A full disk then
costs log lines, never the server, a database or a mail spool on the same
disk.

```toml
min_free_disk = "2G"     # or "5%"; default: the larger of 1% and 1 GiB; "0" turns it off
```

The space counted is what an unprivileged process may use, so the root
reserve most filesystems keep is already set aside. `/metrics` has
`rws_disk_free_bytes{dir}`, `rws_disk_low{dir}`,
`rws_access_log_dropped_lines_total` and `rws_cache_skipped_writes_total`;
the admin API's `/status` lists each directory, and the admin UI's Overview
warns while one is low.

**Logging to stdout** leaves the bound to what collects it:

- **journald** keeps at most `SystemMaxUse` (default 10% of the
  filesystem, up to 4 GiB) and drops lines past `RateLimitBurst` per
  `RateLimitIntervalSec`. For a busy server set them in
  `/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/rws.conf`:

  ```ini
  [Journal]
  SystemMaxUse=2G
  RateLimitIntervalSec=0
  ```

  (`RateLimitIntervalSec=0` stops journald dropping rws's lines; the size
  cap still holds.)
- **Docker**: the default `json-file` driver never rotates — set
  `--log-opt max-size=100m --log-opt max-file=5` (or the same in
  `daemon.json`).
- **Kubernetes** rotates container logs at 10 MiB × 5 by default
  (`containerLogMaxSize`, `containerLogMaxFiles`).

If you don't read every line, `log_format = "off"` writes none; metrics and
the admin API keep working.

### Log aggregation in Kubernetes

The server writes all logs to stdout. Kubernetes log aggregation pipelines pick them up automatically:

```sh
# View logs in real time
kubectl logs -f deployment/my-rws-app

# Ship to Loki via Promtail — no application config required; just label the pod
```

### Anonymised addresses and redaction

Since 18.33.0 the access log can leave out what it doesn't need to keep
about people. All of it is off by default, and then every line is byte for
byte what it was; the settings are hot-reloadable.

```toml
access_log_anonymize_ip     = "truncate"            # or "hash"; default "off"
# access_log_ip_hash_secret = "…"                   # the key for "hash"
log_redact_query            = ["token", "api_key"]  # query parameter values → REDACTED
log_redact_headers          = ["x-api-key"]         # header values → REDACTED
```

- **`access_log_anonymize_ip`**: `truncate` writes an IPv4 address as its
  /24 and an IPv6 address as its /48 (`203.0.113.0`, `2001:db8:1::`), as
  Google Analytics and nginx `map` recipes do. `hash` writes 16 hex digits
  of HMAC-SHA256(`access_log_ip_hash_secret`, address) instead: one client
  keeps one pseudonym, so you can still count and follow a client, but the
  address can't be recovered without the key (and an IPv4 address space is
  too small to hash without one — with no secret `hash` truncates). It
  applies to the client address in JSON and combined lines, including the
  one taken from a trusted proxy's `X-Forwarded-For`, to
  [OTLP log records](#otlp-logs) and to the `recent_requests` list.
  [Traffic insights](/deployment/traffic/) keep no addresses either way; the
  [IP blocklist](/features/ip-filter/) and rate limits still see real ones.
- **`log_redact_query`**: the values of these query parameters (any case)
  are written as `REDACTED` in the logged path and `Referer`:
  `/login?user=ann&token=REDACTED`.
- **Headers.** An access-log line carries three request headers: `Host`,
  `User-Agent` and `Referer` (JSON only). `Authorization`,
  `Proxy-Authorization`, `Cookie` and `Set-Cookie` are never written —
  not in the access log, not in `recent_requests`, and shown as `REDACTED`
  in `Log::request_response`'s debugging dump. `log_redact_headers` adds
  names whose values are written as `REDACTED` wherever a header is logged
  (`user-agent`, `referer`, or your own in the dump).

### Syslog

`access_log_syslog` (since 18.33.0) sends every access-log line to a syslog
server too, besides stdout or the [file](#writing-to-a-file):

```toml
log_format                 = "json"                 # what SIEMs parse best
access_log_syslog          = "tcp://siem.internal:6514"   # or udp://host:514, unix:///dev/log
access_log_syslog_facility = "local0"               # default; any facility name or 0–23
```

Each line is one RFC 5424 message, severity `info`, APP-NAME `rws`, MSGID
`access`, the host name from `HOSTNAME` (else `/etc/hostname`):

```
<134>1 2026-11-04T12:00:00Z web-1 rws 4242 access - {"time":"2026-11-04T12:00:00Z","remote_addr":"203.0.113.0",…}
```

Over TCP messages are framed by octet counting (RFC 6587: `LEN SP MSG`),
which rsyslog, syslog-ng, Splunk and Graylog accept; over UDP and Unix
sockets each is one datagram. Nothing is sent on the request path: the
background thread that flushes the access log every 100 ms hands each
batch to the thread `rws-syslog`. While the server is unreachable up to
8 MiB of lines wait, then lines are dropped; a TCP connection is re-made
on the next batch. Read at startup; plain TCP only (put a local relay in
front for TLS).

### OTLP logs

With `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp` (since 18.33.0) every access-log record also
goes to an OpenTelemetry collector as an OTLP/HTTP JSON log record
(`/v1/logs`), next to [metrics](#otlp-metrics-export) and
[traces](#tracing):

```bash
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318   # logs go to /v1/logs
export OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=otlp
rws
```

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` | `otlp` turns log export on (off by default) |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT` | Full logs URL, used as is; else the base URL + `/v1/logs`, else `http://localhost:4318/v1/logs` |
| `OTEL_BLRP_SCHEDULE_DELAY` | Milliseconds between exports (default `1000`) |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_HEADERS` | Request headers, `key=value,…` |

A record's body is the access-log line (in `log_format`; JSON when that is
`off`, so you can ship only OTLP), with the settings above applied. Its
attributes are `http.request.method`, `url.path`,
`http.response.status_code`, `client.address` and
`network.protocol.version`; its severity INFO, WARN for 4xx and ERROR for
5xx. When the request was traced (the binary traces when an OTLP endpoint
is set), the record carries the server span's `traceId` and `spanId`, so a
backend links each log line to its trace. Records are formatted into a
buffer per thread and sent by the thread `rws-otlp-logs`; a thread with more
than 1 MiB unsent drops records while the collector is down. The rest goes
out on SIGTERM. From Rust: `otel::logs::start(LogsExportConfig { .. })` or
`otel::logs::start_from_env()`.


## Tracing

### OtelLayer

`OtelLayer` implements `Middleware` and propagates W3C `traceparent` headers. Add it to your application and configure an OTLP exporter:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::otel::{self, ExporterConfig, OtelLayer, TracingConfig};

otel::setup(TracingConfig {
    service_name: "my-service".to_string(),
    exporter: ExporterConfig::Otlp {
        endpoint: "http://tempo:4318".to_string(),
    },
    ..TracingConfig::default()
});

let app = App::new().wrap(OtelLayer);
```

The layer reads the incoming `traceparent` header, creates a span for each request (a child of the caller's span when one was sent), and exports completed spans to the configured OTLP endpoint. Start nested spans inside a request with `otel::span(name)` / `otel::client_span(name)` — see [Distributed Tracing](/features/tracing/#child-spans).

The `rws` binary adds `OtelLayer` and exports spans by itself when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set — see [Environment variable setup](/features/tracing/#environment-variable-setup).

### Supported backends

- **Grafana Tempo** — point `endpoint` at the OTLP HTTP port (default `4318`)
- **Jaeger** — enable the OTLP receiver and point at port `4318`
- **OpenTelemetry Collector** — use as a fan-out proxy to multiple backends

### Distributed tracing across services

Include the `traceparent` header in outbound requests using the synchronous HTTP client:

```rust
use rust_web_server::http_client::Client;

let response = Client::new()
    .get("http://downstream-service/api/data")
    .header("traceparent", incoming_traceparent)
    .send()?;
```

Inside a traced request rws does this itself: the HTTP client, the proxies and database statements get client spans, and `traceparent` plus [`baggage`](/features/tracing/#baggage) are sent on — see [Automatic client spans and propagation](/features/tracing/#automatic-client-spans-and-propagation).

## Health endpoints

Two health endpoints are built into every server instance without any configuration:

### GET /healthz — liveness

Returns `200 OK` as long as the binary is running. Use this as the Kubernetes liveness probe:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 7878
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
```

### GET /readyz — readiness

Returns `200 OK` during normal operation. Returns `503 Service Unavailable` during graceful shutdown (after `SIGTERM` is received, while in-flight requests are being drained). Use as the Kubernetes readiness probe:

```yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: 7878
  initialDelaySeconds: 3
  periodSeconds: 5
```

The readiness gate ensures the load balancer stops routing new traffic to a pod as soon as it begins draining, giving in-flight requests time to complete before the pod terminates.

---

# Admin API

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/admin/>

The admin API (since 18.10.0) lets you inspect a running server without editing files or restarting it. It runs on a listener of its own, which is off by default and never mixed into the public routes, and every request needs a bearer token.

## Turning it on

```toml
[admin]
listen          = "127.0.0.1:9901"           # off when unset
token_env       = "RWS_ADMIN_TOKEN"          # env var holding the token (this is the default)
allowed_origins = ["https://ops.example.com"] # browser origins besides the listener's own
```

```sh
export RWS_ADMIN_TOKEN="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
rws
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $RWS_ADMIN_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:9901/admin/api/v1/status
```

The token lives in the environment, never in the file. When the variable is unset or empty the admin listener doesn't start (the server still does, and logs why), and `rws --check` reports it as an error. `rws --check` also warns when `listen` is reachable from other hosts.

Keep it on loopback and reach it through an SSH tunnel (`ssh -L 9901:127.0.0.1:9901 host`). If you must listen on another address, firewall the port: the token is the only protection.

## From the command line: `rws ctl`

`rws ctl` (since 18.20.0) drives the same API from a shell. The deb and rpm
packages also install it as `rwsctl`, and the binary run under that name acts
the same.

```text
rws ctl status                         # version, uptime, listeners, disks
rws ctl reload                         # waits; prints the errors and exits 1 on a bad config
rws ctl drain <upstream> <backend> [--undo]
rws ctl maintenance [on|off]
rws ctl block <ip> | unblock <ip> | blocklist
rws ctl purge <cache> [--path /p | --prefix /p/]
rws ctl caches | upstreams
rws ctl certs [renew]                  # expiry and ACME state; renew orders now
rws ctl logs [-n 100] [-f]             # recent access-log lines; -f follows
rws ctl traffic [--week | --month | --hours N] [--host example.com]
rws ctl whoami                         # the token's user and role
rws ctl audit [-n 50]                  # recent changes: who, what, when
rws ctl audit --verify [FILE]          # check the audit log's hash chain (18.33.0)
```

It finds the server the way the server finds its settings: `--admin
http://127.0.0.1:9901` if given, else `[admin] listen` in `RWS_CONFIG_FILE` or
`./rws.config.toml` (a `0.0.0.0` listener is reached on loopback), else
`127.0.0.1:9901`. The token comes from `--token-file <path>`, else the variable
`[admin] token_env` names, else `RWS_ADMIN_TOKEN`. There is no `--token`: an
argument shows up in `ps` and shell history.

```sh
# on the server, next to its config
sudo -u rws env RWS_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/rws/rws.config.toml rwsctl status
# from a laptop, through a tunnel
ssh -fNL 9901:127.0.0.1:9901 web1
rws ctl --admin 127.0.0.1:9901 --token-file ~/.config/rws/web1.token certs
```

Output is for people (aligned tables, one line per change); `--json` prints the
API's JSON instead. Exit codes: `0` done, `1` the server refused or the
operation failed (a reload with errors, an unknown backend or cache), `2` bad
arguments, the admin API unreachable, or the token refused — so a deploy script
can run `rwsctl reload || rollback`.

## The web UI

Open `http://127.0.0.1:9901/admin/` (through the SSH tunnel on a remote host) and paste the token. It shows:

- **Overview**: uptime, request and error counters, a live requests-per-second chart, the listeners and the build.
- **Traffic**: who visited, people, AI agents and bots, over a day, week or 30 days (18.15.0; see [Traffic insights](/deployment/traffic/)).
- **Upstreams**: every backend's health and circuit breaker, with a switch to drain it.
- **Certificates**: what the server presents and when it expires, and ACME's renew button.
- **Controls**: maintenance mode, reload, the response caches (purge everything, a path or a prefix), authorization tuples (add, remove, check), the IP blocklist and feature flags.
- **Config**: every setting in effect, filterable, secrets hidden.
- **Logs**: the access log as it's written, with pause.

The token stays in the browser tab (`sessionStorage`), and the page talks only to the API below with it. The UI's own files (`/admin/`, `/admin/admin.js`, `/admin/admin.css`) are served without the token: they hold no data. They are built into the binary, so there is nothing to deploy, and they're served with a strict `Content-Security-Policy` (scripts and connections to the listener itself only, no framing).

## Users, roles and the audit log

Since 18.22.0 a team can share the admin API without sharing one token.
The `token_env` token is user `admin` with role `admin`; `users` adds
named tokens, each in its own environment variable:

```toml
[admin]
listen    = "127.0.0.1:9901"
token_env = "RWS_ADMIN_TOKEN"                    # user "admin", role admin
users     = ["deploy-bot:RWS_ADMIN_DEPLOY:operator", "grafana:RWS_ADMIN_GRAFANA:viewer"]
audit_log = "/var/log/rws/audit.log"             # also keep the audit log in a file
```

| Role | May |
|---|---|
| `viewer` | read everything: status, config (secrets hidden), metrics, logs, traffic, upstreams, certificates, the audit log |
| `operator` | also reload, drain backends, switch maintenance mode, block IPs, flip feature flags, purge caches, renew certificates |
| `admin` | also add and remove authorization tuples |

A refused request is `403` saying which role it needs. Tokens must be at
least 16 characters; `rws --check` names an entry that isn't
`name:ENV_VAR:role` or whose variable is unset.

Every change — through the API, the UI, `rws ctl` or the built-in MCP tools
(user `mcp`) — and every refused attempt is recorded: time, user, role, how
they signed in, source address, method, path, the request body with
anything that looks like a secret redacted, and the result. The last 1000
are kept in memory: `GET /admin/api/v1/audit?n=100`, `rws ctl audit`, and the
**Audit** page. With `audit_log` they're also appended to that file as JSON
lines (one per change, for your log shipper). Reads aren't recorded.
`GET /admin/api/v1/whoami` (`rws ctl whoami`) says who a token is.

### A tamper-evident audit log

Since 18.33.0 every line rws appends to `audit_log` ends with two more
fields, which make the file a hash chain:

```json
{"at":1793793600,"time":"…","user":"deploy-bot",…,"node":"web-1","prev":"9f86d0…","hash":"3a7bd3…"}
```

`prev` is the SHA-256 (hex) of the whole line before it in the file (64
zeros for a new file's first line); `hash` is the SHA-256 of this line
without its `,"hash":"…"`. Editing an entry breaks its `hash`; deleting,
inserting or reordering entries breaks the next one's `prev`. Check a file:

```sh
rws ctl audit --verify                 # the server's audit_log, via GET /admin/api/v1/audit/verify
rws ctl audit --verify audit.log.3     # a copy or an archived file, here, without the API
# /var/log/rws/audit.log: intact — 1204 entries, 1204 chained
# /var/log/rws/audit.log: BROKEN at line 731: the entry doesn't match its hash: it was changed
```

`--verify` exits 1 when the chain is broken (`--json` prints the report).

- **Existing files** keep working: lines written before 18.33 have no hash
  and are accepted until the first chained line, whose `prev` covers the last
  of them. A line without a hash *after* the chain started is reported.
- **Restarts** continue the chain from the file's last line. rws keeps the
  hash of what it last wrote in memory, so an edit to the last line while
  it runs is caught by the next entry.
- **Rotation**: the first line of a new file has the last line of the old
  one as its `prev`; the report says `continues_from` (offline, check the
  old file too). Truncating the end of a file can't be detected from the
  file alone — ship it to a log store as it is written (it's JSON lines) and
  keep `rws ctl audit --verify` output alongside.
- One rws process per file: replicas writing one shared file would
  interleave two chains.

### Single sign-on for the admin UI

People can sign in with your identity provider instead of pasting a token,
their role coming from their groups:

```toml
[admin]
listen                 = "127.0.0.1:9901"
oidc_issuer            = "https://id.example.com/realms/main"  # or oidc_provider = "google" | "microsoft" | "github"
oidc_client_id         = "rws-admin"
oidc_client_secret_env = "RWS_ADMIN_OIDC_SECRET"
oidc_cookie_secret_env = "RWS_ADMIN_COOKIE_SECRET"   # ≥ 32 characters; sign-ins survive restarts
oidc_roles             = ["rws-admins=admin", "sre=operator", "*=viewer"]
# oidc_role_claim      = "groups"                    # the ID-token claim with the groups
```

Register `http://127.0.0.1:9901/admin/auth/callback` (or the address you
reach the UI at) as the redirect URI. The login page then shows **Sign in
with single sign-on**. `oidc_roles` maps a group, an email address or `*`
(anyone who can sign in) to a role; a user matching several gets the
highest, one matching none is refused. The session is a signed `HttpOnly`
cookie on the admin origin, valid 12 hours; changes made with it also need
the `X-Rws-Admin` header the UI sends (and pass the origin check), so
another site can't make them. Tokens keep working for scripts and
`rws ctl`. Needs the `sso` feature (in the release binaries).

## Security

- Every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, on loopback too. A missing or wrong token gets `401`, whatever the path, and the token is compared in constant time.
- A browser request whose `Origin` is neither the listener's own nor in `allowed_origins` gets `403`, so a page on another site can't use a token the browser holds.
- Admin requests are served on threads of their own (at most 32 connections at once), apart from the server's workers, so an overloaded server can still be inspected.
- Responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store`.

## Endpoints

All under `/admin/api/v1/`, JSON in and out.

| Method and path | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /status` | Version, process id, uptime, readiness, compile-time features, the main, redirect and admin listeners, and `disk`: each directory rws writes to with `free_bytes`, `total_bytes` and `low` (under `min_free_disk`, 18.15.0) |
| `GET /whoami` | The caller: `{"user":"deploy-bot","role":"operator","via":"token"}` (`via`: `token` or `oidc`; 18.22.0) |
| `GET /audit?n=100` | The newest changes and refused attempts, newest first (at most 1000): `at`, `time`, `user`, `role`, `via`, `address`, `method`, `path`, `detail` (body, secrets redacted), `status`, `node` |
| `GET /audit/verify` | Check the `audit_log` file's [hash chain](#a-tamper-evident-audit-log) (18.33.0): `{"file":…,"ok":true,"entries":12,"chained":10,"unchained":2,"continues_from":null,"broken":null}`; when broken, `"broken":{"line":7,"reason":"…"}`. `404` without an `audit_log` file |
| `GET /auth` | Without credentials: how to sign in, `{"token":true,"oidc":false}` (the UI's login page) |
| `GET /config` | Every `RWS_CONFIG_*` setting in effect; values of names with `SECRET`, `PASSWORD` or `TOKEN` read `(hidden)` |
| `POST /reload` | Reload the configuration and certificates, as `SIGHUP` does, and wait for it (up to 10 s): `{"reloaded":true,"applied":true,"reloads":3,"errors":[]}`. With errors (a config file that doesn't validate) `applied` is `false`, `errors` lists them and the running configuration stays. `503` while the server starts or stops, `504` when it didn't finish |
| `GET /metrics` | Request, error and connection counters, thread-pool queue, readiness (`/metrics` on the main port has the full Prometheus set) |
| `GET /build` | Compile-time features as `{"http3":true,…}` |
| `GET /rate-limit` | The global limit: `configured`, `max_requests`, `window_secs` |
| `GET /rate-limit/check?ip=…` | That address's remaining quota (counts as one request) |
| `GET /cors` | The CORS settings in effect |
| `GET /maintenance`, `PUT /maintenance` `{"active":true}` | Maintenance mode: `503` for everything but health checks |
| `GET /blocklist`, `POST /blocklist` `{"ip":"…"}`, `DELETE /blocklist/<ip>` | The runtime IP blocklist (`403`), for static files and config-file proxy routes alike (proxy routes since 18.20.1). Addresses are checked; the admin listener isn't behind the blocklist |
| `GET /flags`, `PUT /flags/<name>` `{"enabled":true}` | Runtime feature flags |
| `GET /cache`, `DELETE /cache` | Response-cache hits, misses and size; clear it. `404` when the server has no cache |
| `GET /caches` | Every response cache (18.11.0): `name` (`app` for the binary's own, `route:<name>` per config route, `route:#N` for unnamed ones), `kind` (`memory` or `disk`), `entries`, `bytes` (disk only, else `null`), `hits`, `misses` |
| `DELETE /caches/<name>?path=/p` or `?prefix=/p/` | Purge one target (every `Vary` variant) or a prefix; without either, everything. Answers `{"name":…,"purged":n}`; `404` for an unknown name |
| `GET /authz` | The authorization schema (18.14.0): `{"types":{"doc":["owner","viewer"],…}}`. `404` without authorization configured |
| `GET /authz/tuples?object=&relation=&subject=&limit=` | Relationship tuples; `object` is `doc:42` or just a type (`doc`); at most `limit` (100, up to 1000) |
| `POST /authz/tuples` `{"tuple":"doc:42#viewer@user:alice"}` | Add a tuple (checked against the schema): `{"tuple":…,"written":true}` (`false`: already there); `400` when the schema doesn't allow it |
| `DELETE /authz/tuples?tuple=…` (or the same JSON body) | Remove a tuple: `{"tuple":…,"deleted":true\|false}` |
| `POST /authz/check` `{"subject":"user:alice","relation":"viewer","object":"doc:42"}` | `{"allowed":true,"path":[…]}` — the path that allowed it |
| `GET /traffic?hours=24&host=` (or `?from=YYYY-MM-DD&to=YYYY-MM-DD`) | Visitors, page views and requests for people, AI agents and bots over the last `hours` (1–2160), the period before, a series and the top lists (18.15.0, [Traffic insights](/deployment/traffic/)). `404` when counting is off |
| `GET /traffic/query?from=&to=&host=&path=&country=&channel=&utm_source=&utm_campaign=&browser=&os=&device=` | Page views from the traffic database (`[traffic] database_url_env`) for any days and filters (18.31.0, [Traffic insights](/deployment/traffic/#keeping-every-page-view-in-postgresql-optional)). `404` without a database, `400` for a bad date |
| `GET /traffic/owner` | The owner link's path (`/_rws/me?k=<key>`) and the configured sites to open it on; a browser that opens it counts as the owner's (18.35). `404` when counting is off |
| `GET /traffic/live?host=` | People on the site in the last 5 minutes, page views per minute for 30 minutes, current pages and countries (18.31.0). `404` when counting is off |
| `GET /routes` | The application's routes (method and pattern) |
| `GET /requests?n=20`, `GET /errors?n=20` | The last requests, or the last 4xx/5xx (at most 100) |
| `GET /upstreams` | The config file's `[[upstream]]`s: each backend's `url`, `weight`, `healthy` (passing its health checks), `breaker` (`closed`, `open`, `half_open`, or `null` without a circuit breaker) and `drained` |
| `PUT /upstreams/<name>/drain` `{"backend":"http://10.0.0.5:8080","drained":true}` | Take a backend out of rotation, or put it back (`false`). New requests skip it, requests already on it finish, its health checks go on. With every backend drained the route answers `503`. Kept across reloads, not restarts. `404` for an unknown upstream or backend |
| `GET /certificates` | Every certificate served (`default` for the main one, virtual hosts and on-demand names by name): `not_after`, `expires`, `days_left`, `source`; and `acme`: whether its renewal loop runs and its last check (`renewed`, `current`, or the error) |
| `GET /logs?n=100` | The last access-log lines (up to 500 kept), oldest first, each as a string: in the `json` log format each is a JSON document |
| `GET /logs/stream` | New access-log lines as they're written, as server-sent events (`data: <line>`), batched every 100 ms. A client that falls behind misses lines rather than slowing the server; at most 8 follow at once (`503` past that) |
| `POST /certificates/renew` | Order a new ACME certificate now, through the renewal loop (`202`); it is hot-swapped when issued, as a scheduled renewal is. `404` without ACME |

Follow the log from a terminal:

```sh
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $RWS_ADMIN_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:9901/admin/api/v1/logs/stream
```

Lines are kept only while the admin API runs, and come from the access log (`log_format = "off"` leaves them empty). Lines over 8 KiB are cut.

To reload certificates from files (after replacing them yourself), use `POST /reload`: it reloads them as `SIGHUP` does.

A typical backend rollout: drain it, wait for its in-flight requests (`rws_upstream_requests_total` stops moving), deploy, check `GET /upstreams` shows it `healthy`, undrain.

Maintenance mode applies in proxy mode too (the binary puts the maintenance check in front of config-file routes since 18.10.0; while it's off, proxy routes keep their non-blocking forwarder).

Changes made here are in memory: they last until the process restarts (a reload doesn't undo them). The binary's [MCP tools](/mcp/operate/) run the same code, so both answer alike.

Library users: the admin API reports the cache and routes registered with `admin::ops::register_cache` and `register_routes`.

Example `GET /status`:

```json
{"version":"18.10.0","pid":4242,"uptime_secs":3605,"ready":true,"features":["http2","http3","acme","auth","mimalloc"],"listeners":{"main":{"address":"0.0.0.0:443","tls":true},"redirect":"80","admin":"127.0.0.1:9901"}}
```

`POST /admin/config/reload` on the main listener (the older reload endpoint) is unchanged.

---

# Several replicas

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/cluster/>

Most of rws's configuration is the config file, so replicas agree by
running the same file. Changes made at runtime through the
[admin API](/deployment/admin/), `rws ctl` or the MCP tools are different:
on their own they stay on the replica that took them. Point the replicas at
one Redis (since 18.22.0) and those changes reach every replica within
about a second:

```toml
[cluster]
redis  = "10.0.0.20:6379"     # defaults to [acme] redis when that's set
# redis_password = "…"        # or RWS_CONFIG_CLUSTER_REDIS_PASSWORD (never printed)
# prefix = "rws:cluster:"     # key prefix, when several clusters share a Redis
# node   = "web-1"            # this replica's name (default: the host name)
```

Shared: the IP blocklist, maintenance mode, drained upstream backends,
feature flags, and purges of named caches (each replica purges its own).
Not shared: anything in the config file (deploy the same file), ACME
certificates (use [`[acme] redis`](/features/acme/) for those, which can be
the same Redis), rate-limit counters, sessions.

```sh
rws ctl --admin web-1:9901 block 203.0.113.9     # refused on every replica
rws ctl --admin web-2:9901 status
# cluster   node web-2 · Redis up · 3 node(s): web-1, web-2, web-3
```

How it works: one JSON document in Redis (`<prefix>state`) holds the shared
state and a version number. A change applies on the replica that took it,
then a Lua script applies the same change to the document inside Redis, so
changes made at the same moment on different replicas don't overwrite
each other. Every replica reads the document once a second and makes its own
state match when the version moved. Each replica also writes a heartbeat
(`<prefix>nodes`); `GET /admin/api/v1/status` lists the replicas seen in
the last minute.

When Redis is unreachable, changes still apply on the replica that took
them, `rws ctl status` shows them as waiting, and they're sent when Redis is
back. A Redis that comes back empty is filled again from the replicas' own
state, so nothing they agreed on is undone. A replica started later adopts
the document. Audit-log entries name the replica (`node`).

Redis needs Lua scripting (every Redis since 2.6, Valkey, KeyDB, managed
Redis services); run it on a private network or with a password.

---

# Fleet config

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/fleet/>

Since 18.23.0 an instance can fetch its configuration instead of having it
copied onto it. Point it at a source, give it the public key the configs
are signed with, and it keeps itself up to date:

```toml
[fleet]
source        = "https://config.example.com/rws/{node}.toml"   # or s3://bucket/key, git+https://…#branch:path
public_key    = "kJ0pQ…base64…="       # from `rws fleet keygen` (or a path to the .pub file)
interval_secs = 30                     # how often to look (at least 5)
report_url    = "https://config.example.com/rws/report"   # optional: each outcome is POSTed here
# s3_endpoint = "https://minio.internal:9000"              # S3-compatible storage other than AWS
# insecure    = true                   # skip signatures (only for testing)
```

`{node}` is the node name (`[cluster] node`, else the host name), so each
instance can get its own file, or all can share one.

## What happens each round

1. Fetch the config — HTTP with `If-None-Match`, so an unchanged file costs
   a `304`; S3 with the standard AWS credentials (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`,
   `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_REGION`); git with a shallow clone in
   `.rws/fleet/git`, fetched and reset each round (needs `git` installed).
2. Fetch the signature next to it (`<source>.sig`) and check it against
   `public_key`. A missing or wrong signature: refused. The signature
   carries a serial, and a config whose serial isn't above the applied one
   is refused — so whoever can serve files (a bucket, a mirror) can't roll
   instances back to an older signed config (since 18.24.0; the serial is
   kept in `.rws/fleet/serial` across restarts).
3. Check the config as `rws --check` does, on this machine (certificate
   files, secrets in the environment), and that its `[fleet]` table is the
   same as the local file's: the fleet can't change where it pulls from, the
   key, or `insecure`. Errors: refused.
4. Write it over the local config file (atomically) and reload, as `SIGHUP`
   does. A reload that reports errors: refused, and the previous file is put
   back, so a restart doesn't load what the running server refused.
5. POST `{"node":…,"rws":…,"applied":true,"config":"<sha-256>"}` — or
   `"applied":false` with the `error` — to `report_url`.

A refused config never replaces the running one. `GET
/admin/api/v1/status` (and `rws ctl status`) shows the source, the
applied config's hash, the last check and the last error.

## Signing

```sh
rws fleet keygen ops            # ops.key (secret, 0600) and ops.pub
rws fleet sign web-1.toml --key ops.key   # writes web-1.toml.sig — refuses a config that fails rws --check
# the serial defaults to the current Unix time; --serial N sets it
aws s3 cp web-1.toml s3://ops-config/rws/ && aws s3 cp web-1.toml.sig s3://ops-config/rws/
```

Signatures are Ed25519 over a domain tag, the serial and the file's exact
bytes; the `.sig` file is one line, `rws-fleet-sig v2 <serial> <base64>`.
18.23's format (the body alone, no serial) is still accepted until an
instance has applied a v2 file, but it can't stop a rollback — re-sign with
18.24. Keep `ops.key` in your
CI's secret store and sign as the last step of the pipeline that reviewed
the change; instances only need `ops.pub`.

## What reloads and what doesn't

The fetched file replaces the whole config file, so it carries the same
`[fleet]` table as the instance's file (or put the fleet settings in the
environment as `RWS_CONFIG_FLEET_*` and leave them out of both). A reload applies what `SIGHUP` applies: routes,
upstreams, middleware, CORS, rate limits, log format and certificates.
Listen addresses, the admin listener, `[fleet]` itself and switching
between serving files only and config-driven routes (the first `[[route]]`)
take a restart — start instances with at least one route if their configs
will have routes.

The fleet config is the declared layer. Runtime changes through the admin
API — blocks, drains, maintenance — are the live layer, shared across
replicas by [`[cluster]`](/deployment/cluster/), and aren't overwritten by
a fleet update.

---

# Traffic insights

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/traffic/>

The admin UI's **Traffic** page (since 18.15.0) shows who visited your sites
over the last day, week or 30 days, in four groups:

- **People**: browsers that load the page's styles, scripts or fonts, as a
  browser does for a person.
- **Apps** (since 18.35): your native apps and browser extensions calling
  the server. They never load a page, so they'd otherwise look like bots.
- **AI agents**: AI crawlers, AI search and assistants fetching a page for
  someone (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, ChatGPT-User…).
- **Bots**: search engines, SEO tools, monitors, link previews, scanners
  probing for `/.env` or `/wp-login.php`, libraries like `curl`, and anything
  that claims to be a well-known crawler from outside that crawler's network.

Your own visits are counted apart, so the groups show everyone else (since
18.35, [Your own visits](#your-own-visits)).

rws counts this from the requests it already serves: no JavaScript on your
pages, no cookies, nothing sent anywhere.

## Turning it on

It is on whenever the [admin API](/deployment/admin/) is. Open the admin UI
and pick **Traffic**. To turn counting off, or tune it:

```toml
[traffic]
enabled        = true                       # false: not counted, no page
retention_days = 30                         # 1–90
persist        = "/var/lib/rws/traffic.json" # default: traffic.json beside the certificate; "off": memory only
exclude        = ["/healthz", "/readyz", "/metrics"]
```

The counts are saved every five minutes and at shutdown (written to a
temporary file and renamed, readable by its owner only, and only while
the disk has room), so restarts
and upgrades keep them. Without a certificate and without `persist` they live
in memory only.

## What the page shows

Since 18.32.0 the page is an overview with tabs:

- **The bar at the top**: the period (*Today*, *7 days*, *30 days* or a
  *Custom* range of whole UTC days), **who** — *Humans* (the analytics
  below), *Apps*, *AI agents*, *Bots* or *All* side by side — the site when
  there is more than one (the sites your `[[route]]`s match first, then
  other `Host` names seen; picking one shows only that site's numbers,
  lists and visitors),
  **Compare** (the period before, drawn grey in the chart and as the change
  under each number), and how many people are online now.
- **Overview**: visitors, page views, sessions, bounce rate and session
  length — click one to chart it (per hour for *Today*, else per day) —
  then a line of how sure the count of people is — **Verified** (ran the
  [script](#the-first-party-script-optional)), **Likely** (loaded the page's
  assets), **Page only** and **Server networks** (browser `User-Agent`s
  counted as bots: no asset loaded, or a cloud network) — and how many of
  your own page views were left out, then cards of top pages, sources, a
  **world map** of countries, devices, and *Right now*.
  A card's **All →** opens its tab.
- **Visitors** (since 18.35): the last visits, newest first — country,
  device, how they arrived (channel, referring site, campaign), the pages
  in order, events, **Verified**, and *Visit 2 today* when someone came
  back. Up to 300 are kept across days, with no address or `User-Agent`.
- **Pages**: top, entry and exit pages, paths answered `404`, **landing
  pages by source** (the first page of visits from outside, per channel)
  and **downloads** (installers, packages, archives and `install.sh`
  fetched in full, by who fetched them).
- **Sources**: channels, referring sites and UTM campaigns.
- **Audience**: countries, browsers, operating systems and devices, with
  their share.
- **Behaviour**: what the [first-party script](#the-first-party-script-optional)
  reports — time on page, goals, events, scroll depth, screen sizes.
- **AI agents** (the switch, not a tab): requests, agents and pages they
  fetched with the change from the period before, a chart, the agents
  (with **Verified** when the request came from the network its operator
  publishes), the pages they read and what for (training, search,
  assistants). **Apps**: app users by app and platform, versions, the
  events apps sent and downloads. **Bots**: the same numbers, bots by kind
  and by name, the paths answered `404`, **crawlers** (named crawlers'
  pages and 404s) with the **404s they hit**, **probes** (the paths
  scanners asked for) and where they came from (country and network).
  **All**: humans, apps, AI agents and bots in one chart and their share of
  requests.

**Click a row to filter** the page by it: by site always; by page, country,
channel, campaign, browser, system or device with the
[traffic database](#keeping-every-page-view-in-postgresql-optional), which
can answer any combination (the filters show as chips; ✕ removes one).
Page names drop the site when only one is shown. The map's country shapes
are [Natural Earth](https://www.naturalearthdata.com)'s (public domain),
built into the page; clicking a country filters like its row.

## The first-party script (optional)

What the server can't see — how long a page stays open, how far it's
scrolled, screen sizes, route changes in a single-page app, and your own
events — comes from a small script rws serves itself (since 18.31.0). It
reports to the same server, sets no cookie and stores nothing in the
browser, so it needs no consent banner either. Turn it on:

```toml
[traffic]
script = true
goals  = ["/thanks/", "/docs/*", "event:signup"]   # optional conversions
```

and add it to your pages:

```html
<script defer src="/_rws/t.js"></script>
```

Send an event from your own code, with up to four string properties:

```js
rws.track("signup", { plan: "pro" });
```

rws then answers `GET /_rws/t.js` (about 1.6 KB, 0.8 KB compressed, cached for an hour) and
`POST /_rws/t` (reports of at most 2 KB, from the same origin only); every
other request passes through untouched. `/_rws/` is reserved for rws.
Reports count only for a visitor already counted as a person, and at most
500 per session. A **goal** is a page path (exact, or a prefix ending in
`*`) or `event:<name>`; the page shows how many sessions reached it and the
share of all sessions. The **Behaviour** section shows time on page, scroll
depth (up to 25/50/75/100 %), screen widths, events and their properties,
and goals. Browsers driven by automation (`navigator.webdriver`) don't
report.

## Keeping every page view in PostgreSQL (optional)

The page's counts are kept small on purpose: hourly totals and the top
entries of each list, for `retention_days`. To keep every page view — for
longer history, or filters the counts can't answer ("visitors from Germany
who read `/docs/*` on a phone, from the spring campaign") — give rws a
PostgreSQL database (since 18.31.0):

```toml
[traffic]
database_url_env = "TRAFFIC_DATABASE_URL"   # the variable holding the URL
```

```sh
TRAFFIC_DATABASE_URL=postgres://rws:secret@db.internal/analytics rws
```

rws creates two tables if they're missing, `rws_traffic_pageviews` (one row
per person's page view: time, site, path, the day's visitor hash, session
start, referring site, channel, UTM values, country, browser family, OS,
device class) and `rws_traffic_reports` (the script's reports), and writes
them in batches from a background thread — every 10 seconds or 500 rows.
Rows hold no IP address and no `User-Agent`; the visitor hash changes every
day and at every restart. If the database is slow or down, rows queue (up
to 20,000) and then are dropped rather than slowing requests. rws never
deletes rows: keep or prune them as your policy says.

The Traffic page then filters by any row you click (country, page,
channel, campaign, device… in any combination) over any dates, and so does
the API:

`GET /admin/api/v1/traffic/query?from=2026-03-01&to=2026-05-31&country=DE&path=/docs/*&device=mobile`

Filters: `host`, `path` (exact, or a prefix ending in `*`), `country`,
`channel`, `utm_source`, `utm_campaign`, `browser`, `os`, `device`; `from`
and `to` are UTC days, inclusive (default: the last 30 days). The answer
has page views, visitors (per day), sessions, bounces, page views per day
and the top pages, countries, channels, referrers, campaigns, browsers,
systems and devices. `404` without a database. The tables are plain SQL, so
any other tool can read them too.

The release binaries include PostgreSQL support (the `model-postgres`
feature), except the FIPS build: the database client's TLS brings crypto
outside the validated module.

## Your own visits

Since 18.35 rws leaves the owner's visits out of everyone's numbers (and
shows how many it left out). A client is yours when:

- it made a **successful admin API call** — the admin UI does, signed in,
  whether you opened it on the admin listener or through a route that
  proxies it. From then on that day, its address and `User-Agent` are
  yours on every site;
- its address is in **`owner_networks`**:

  ```toml
  [traffic]
  owner_networks = ["203.0.113.7", "198.51.100.0/24"]
  ```

- its browser has the **owner cookie**. *Exclude a browser…* on the
  Overview lists a link per site, `https://<site>/_rws/me?k=<key>`: open it
  in each browser and on each phone you use. It sets `rws_me` on that site
  for a year (`HttpOnly`); `/_rws/me?off` removes it. The key is derived
  from the admin token, so it changes when the token does (with OIDC
  sign-in only, it's made at start and a restart ends it). Keep the links
  private: anyone opening one is counted as you.

Recognition starts when it happens: what you did earlier that day stays
where it was counted. `GET /admin/api/v1/traffic/owner` returns the link's
path and the sites.

## Apps and extensions

Native apps and browser extensions call your server without loading a
page, so the browser test would count them as bots. Since 18.35 they are
**Apps**, from:

- **`apps`**: `name=pattern` pairs. A pattern with `://` matches the start
  of the request's `Origin` (an extension); any other pattern is looked for
  in the `User-Agent` (case doesn't matter), and after a pattern ending in
  `/` the version is read:

  ```toml
  [traffic]
  apps = [
    "HITOP=HITOP/",                                   # HITOP/2.3.1 CFNetwork/… Darwin/…
    "HITOP=chrome-extension://abcdefghijklmnopabcdefghijklmnop",
    "HITOP=safari-web-extension://",
  ]
  ```

- **the platform**, for anything unnamed: an extension `Origin`
  (`chrome-extension://`, `moz-extension://`, `safari-web-extension://`),
  Apple's networking stack (`CFNetwork/… Darwin/…`, `NetworkingExtension/…`),
  Android's (`Dalvik/`) and Electron. These are counted as *iOS/macOS app*,
  *Chrome extension* and so on: a request can claim any name, so only
  configured names are kept as names. `okhttp` isn't taken as an app —
  scrapers use it too; name your Android app's `User-Agent` in `apps`.

An app user is a client counted once a day, like a visitor. Apps can also
report **events** — no script, any origin, nothing stored on the device:

```sh
curl -X POST https://example.com/_rws/e \
  -d '{"app":"HITOP","v":"2.3.1","p":"ios","n":"request_sent"}'
```

`app` must be one of `apps`' names (else `403`); `n` is the event (≤ 64
characters), `v` the version (≤ 32), `p` the platform (`ios`, `ipados`,
`macos`, `visionos`, `watchos`, `android`, `windows`, `linux`, `chrome`,
`edge`, `firefox`, `safari`, `web`; else `other`). `204` when taken, `400`
when malformed; at most 500 events per client a day count. It answers
`OPTIONS` and sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so an extension or a
web view can post too. `/_rws/e` and `/_rws/me` are answered whenever
traffic is counted, `script` or not.

Referrals from app stores (App Store, Google Play, Chrome Web Store,
Firefox and Edge add-ons, Microsoft Store, Snapcraft, Flathub, F-Droid) are
their own channel, **App stores**. A goal can be any request a person
makes, not only a page: `goals = ["req:/api/proxy"]` counts the visits
that used a web app, not just opened it.

## Downloads, probes and crawlers

- **Downloads**: `GET`s answered `200` for `.dmg`, `.pkg`, `.zip`,
  `.tar.gz`, `.tgz`, `.tar.xz`, `.exe`, `.msi`, `.msix`, `.deb`, `.rpm`,
  `.AppImage`, `.apk`, `.aab`, `.ipa`, `.vsix`, `.xpi`, `.crx`, `.flatpak`,
  `.snap`, `.7z`, `install.sh` and `install.ps1`, per file and by who
  fetched them (people, apps, bots and tools, AI, you).
- **Probes**: the paths scanners asked for, and where from — country and
  network (the hosting provider, or `-`). `probe_addresses = true` adds
  each scanner's address, to block it; no other address is ever kept.
- **Crawlers**: each named crawler's (Googlebot, Bingbot, GPTBot…) page
  fetches and `404`s, and the paths that answered them `404` — the ones
  to fix or redirect.

## Sessions

A person's page views 30 minutes or less apart are one **session**; a
longer pause, or midnight (UTC), starts the next. A **bounce** is a
session of one page view. **Session length** runs from the first page
view to the last, so a one-page session is 0 seconds long — the server
can't see how long the last page stayed open. Sessions still going count
as if they ended now. Sessions are counted on the day they began.

## Sources and audience

Sources are counted once per session, from its first page view. That
page view **arrives from outside** when it has no `Referer` (*direct*),
a `Referer` from another site, or UTM tags; moving between the site's own
pages isn't counted as an arrival. The channel is *campaign* when the URL
has `utm_*` values, else from the referring site: *search* (Google, Bing,
DuckDuckGo, …), *social* (X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Reddit, Hacker News, …),
*AI assistants* (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, …) or
*other sites*.

Browser, system and device come from the `User-Agent`, and from the
`Sec-CH-UA-Platform` / `Sec-CH-UA-Mobile` client hints Chromium browsers
send, which win. Only the family is kept (Chrome, not Chrome 141). iPad
Safari presents itself as a Mac, so it counts as desktop.

The country comes from a table built into the binary, **IP Geolocation by
[DB-IP](https://db-ip.com)** ("IP to Country Lite", CC BY 4.0, ~700 KB,
refreshed each release): the lookup happens on the server, nothing is sent
anywhere, and only the country is counted — the address isn't kept.
Private and reserved addresses are *Unknown*. To use a newer table, build
one with `ci/gen_geo.py --update` and point `[traffic] geo_db` at it.
Building without the `geo` feature (on by default) leaves the table out;
countries are then *Unknown*, and `geo_db` isn't read either (decoding a
table needs the feature).

Nothing is stored in the visitor's browser — no cookie, no local storage —
so no consent banner is needed for these counts. The cost is that a
person who comes back the next day is a new visitor.

## How visitors are told apart

From each request's address, `User-Agent` and path, in this order:

1. Loopback is this machine (health checks, the admin UI) and isn't counted.
2. An address in a published crawler network (Google, Bing, Apple,
   DuckDuckGo, OpenAI, Perplexity, Common Crawl) is that crawler, verified.
3. A `User-Agent` that claims one of those crawlers from anywhere else is
   **spoofed**, a bot.
4. Paths only scanners ask for are scanners.
5. A browser `User-Agent` from a cloud or server hosting network (AWS,
   Google Cloud, Azure, OVHcloud, Hetzner, DigitalOcean… — since 18.35) is a
   program — a link scanner, a preview, a headless crawler — and a bot of
   kind **hosting**, named after the provider, even when it loads assets and
   runs the script. The networks come from a table built into the binary
   (**[DB-IP](https://db-ip.com)** "IP to ASN Lite", CC BY 4.0, ~60 KB,
   refreshed each release with `ci/gen_hosting.py`). Consumer VPN and CDN
   egress (Cloudflare WARP, iCloud Private Relay, VPN services) isn't
   hosting: people browse from it. `[traffic] hosting_networks = false`
   counts these browsers as people again.
6. Known AI agents ([ai.robots.txt](https://github.com/ai-robots-txt/ai.robots.txt))
   and crawlers ([crawler-user-agents](https://github.com/monperrus/crawler-user-agents))
   by name. Both lists and the networks are bundled and refreshed each release.
7. A browser `User-Agent` waits: once it loads a `.css`, `.js`, `.mjs` or font
   it is a person and its earlier requests count as one. Without one within
   two minutes or 32 requests it is a bot ("browser, no assets").

A visitor is a hash of a per-process secret, the day, the site, the address
and the `User-Agent`. The secret and the hashes are never saved: no addresses
or `User-Agent`s are kept, in memory or in the file. A restart within a day
can count a returning visitor once more.

**Sites and unknown hosts** (since 18.35.2): when your `[[route]]`s match
sites by `host`, those are the sites. `www.<site>` counts as `<site>`, and
every other `Host` — addresses, `localhost`, no `Host`, names no route
serves, and the names in `hide_hosts` — counts as one **Unknown hosts**
entry, so scanners' junk headers don't fill the site list. Counts saved
under such names move there when rws starts.

```toml
[traffic]
hide_hosts = ["mail.example.com", "mta-sts.example.com"]
```

**Sites and unknown hosts** (since 18.35.2): when your `[[route]]`s match
sites by `host`, those are the sites. `www.<site>` counts as `<site>`, and
every other `Host` — addresses, `localhost`, no `Host`, names no route
serves, and the names in `hide_hosts` — counts as one **Unknown hosts**
entry, so scanners' junk headers don't fill the site list. Counts saved
under such names move there when rws starts.

```toml
[traffic]
hide_hosts = ["mail.example.com", "mta-sts.example.com"]
```

Counting costs about 170 ns per request; the country, device and hosting
network are worked out once per visitor per day. Memory and the file are
bounded: every site a `[[route]]` matches by `host` (up to 238) plus 16 other
`Host` names (the rest count as `other`), and 200 entries per list per day
(the rest as `(other)`; 100 are saved). Before 18.35 the first 16 names seen
took the slots, so a site added later could end up in `other`; its counts
from then stay there, while its pages and sessions show under the site.

## From the API or an AI client

`GET /admin/api/v1/traffic?hours=168&host=example.com` returns the page's data
(`hours` 1–2160, default 24; `host` optional); `404` when counting is off.
`hosts` lists the sites to pick from, the configured ones (also in
`configured`) first.
`?from=2026-10-01&to=2026-10-07` (UTC days, inclusive; `to` defaults to
today) asks for those days instead. Views over two days cover whole days.
Besides the totals and lists, the answer has `series` (per hour or day:
requests per group and people's `pages`), `previous_series` (the period
before, at the same times) and `days` (people's visitors, sessions and
bounces per day, and the period before's). The
`GET /admin/api/v1/traffic/live?host=example.com` (since 18.31.0) returns
the live view: `visitors` (people in the last 5 minutes), `views_5m`, a
`series` of page views per minute for 30 minutes, the `pages` and
`countries` of the people active now.

Since 18.35 the answer also has `totals.apps` and `totals.owner` (and in
`series`), `tiers` (`verified`, `page_only`, `hosting` visitors), `apps`
(`users`, `versions`, `events`: `app\tplatform`, `app\tversion`,
`app\tevent`), `probes` (`paths`, `sources`), `crawl` (`name`, `pages`,
`not_found`), `crawl_404`, `entries` (`host/path\tchannel`), `downloads`
(`host/path\tgroup`), `owner_pages` and `visits` (the last 100: `start`,
`end`, `host`, `views`, `pages`, `country`, `browser`, `os`, `device`,
`channel`, `referrer`, `campaign`, `verified`, `number`, `events`).

MCP tool `traffic_summary` `{"hours": 24}` answers the same, so an AI client
connected to the server can tell you who has been visiting; `{"live": true}`
gives the live view, and `{"from": "2026-03-01", "country": "DE", …}` a
database query.

# systemd

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/systemd/>

On a Linux host without containers, run `rws` as a systemd service. The unit
below runs it as an unprivileged user that can bind ports 80 and 443, sees
the system read-only except for its own state and log directories, and
reloads its configuration on `systemctl reload`.

## Install from a package

Since 18.2.0 rws has `.deb` and `.rpm` packages for x86_64 and arm64, from
signed repositories (so `apt upgrade` / `dnf upgrade` bring new releases) or
from each [GitHub release page](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/releases).
They install the binary as `/usr/bin/rws` (and `/usr/bin/rwsctl`, [`rws ctl`](/deployment/admin/#from-the-command-line-rws-ctl)), the unit below, a configuration
in `/etc/rws/rws.config.toml` and a placeholder page in `/var/www/rws`,
create the `rws` user, and start the service on port 7878.

Debian, Ubuntu:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://rws8.tech/apt/rws.gpg | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/rws.gpg >/dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rws.gpg] https://rws8.tech/apt stable main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/rws.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install rws
curl localhost:7878/                           # rws is running
```

Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma (packages and repository metadata are signed):

```bash
sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/yum.repos.d/rws.repo https://rws8.tech/rpm/rws.repo
sudo dnf install rws
```

A downloaded package installs the same way: `sudo apt install ./rws_18.2.0_amd64.deb`,
`sudo dnf install ./rws-18.2.0-1.x86_64.rpm`. The repositories hold the
newest release only; older ones stay on the release pages.

Put your site in `/var/www/rws`, change settings in
`/etc/rws/rws.config.toml` (an upgrade keeps your edits) and apply them with
`sudo systemctl reload rws`. To serve on port 80, set `port = 80` — the unit
already grants the capability.

## Install by hand

```bash
sudo install -m 0755 rws /usr/bin/rws
sudo useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --home-dir /var/lib/rws --shell /usr/sbin/nologin rws
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rws /var/www/rws
sudo cp rws.config.toml /etc/rws/
sudoedit /etc/systemd/system/rws.service      # the unit below
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now rws
```

## The unit

The packages install this file as `/usr/lib/systemd/system/rws.service`
([`packaging/linux/rws.service`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/packaging/linux/rws.service)):

```ini
[Unit]
Description=rws web server
Documentation=https://rws8.tech
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
# rws says when it serves (after listeners and certificates), around
# reloads and at shutdown, and pings the watchdog while it runs.
Type=notify
NotifyAccess=main
WatchdogSec=30
User=rws
Group=rws
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/rws
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/rws/rws.config.toml
# ACME certificates and account key in /var/lib/rws (StateDirectory below).
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CERT_PATH=/var/lib/rws/cert.pem
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_ACME_KEY_PATH=/var/lib/rws/key.pem
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ACCOUNT_KEY_PATH=/var/lib/rws/acme_account.key
ExecStart=/usr/bin/rws
# Re-read the config and certificates without dropping connections.
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2s
LimitNOFILE=65536

# Ports 80/443 without root.
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes

# Writable: /var/lib/rws (state) and /var/log/rws (access log) only.
StateDirectory=rws
LogsDirectory=rws
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/www/rws /etc/rws
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
ProtectProc=invisible
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
LockPersonality=yes
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
SystemCallArchitectures=native
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallFilter=~@privileged @resources
UMask=0027

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

`systemd-analyze security rws.service` rates it "OK" or better; check it on
your host after installing.

## Access log

Write the access log under `/var/log/rws` (the unit's `LogsDirectory`) in
`/etc/rws/rws.config.toml`:

```toml
access_log = "/var/log/rws/access.log"
```

Rotate it with logrotate, which tells rws to reopen the file with
`systemctl kill -s USR1 rws.service` — see
[Writing to a file](/deployment/observability/#writing-to-a-file) for the
logrotate snippet, or set `access_log_max_size` and let rws rotate it.
Without `access_log`, lines go to stdout and land in the journal
(`journalctl -u rws`).

## Readiness and the watchdog

With `Type=notify` (since 18.20.0) systemd counts rws as started only once
it serves: listeners bound, certificates loaded (ACME included). `systemctl
start` and `restart` wait for that and fail if rws doesn't get there.
`systemctl reload` waits for the reload to finish (`RELOADING=1`, then
`READY=1`), and `systemctl status` shows rws's status line. With
`WatchdogSec=` rws pings systemd from its event loop at half the interval;
a hung process stops pinging and is restarted. An older unit with
`Type=simple` keeps working: rws only notifies when systemd asks for it
(`NOTIFY_SOCKET`).

## Socket activation

The packages also install `rws.socket`. Enabled, systemd opens the ports
and hands them to rws, so a restart refuses nothing (connections wait in
the socket's queue) and rws doesn't need `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`:

```sh
sudo systemctl enable --now rws.socket
sudo systemctl restart rws        # no refused connections
```

```ini
[Socket]
ListenStream=443
FileDescriptorName=https
ListenStream=80
FileDescriptorName=redirect
ListenDatagram=443
FileDescriptorName=quic
Service=rws.service
```

rws takes each listener from systemd when one matches by name (`https` or
`http` for the main port, `redirect`, `quic`, `admin`) or by port, and
binds the rest itself. With per-core runtimes every runtime accepts on its
own copy of the inherited socket. Startup prints which sockets systemd
passed.

## Day to day

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Check a config change before applying it | `rws --check /etc/rws/rws.config.toml` |
| Apply it (config, routes, certificates) | `sudo systemctl reload rws` |
| Logs and errors | `journalctl -u rws -f` |
| Reopen the access log | `sudo systemctl kill -s USR1 rws` |
| Restart | `sudo systemctl restart rws` |

# Windows

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/windows/>

The `rws.exe` in each release's `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` zip on the
[GitHub release page](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/releases)
runs as it does elsewhere: it serves the current directory on port 7878.

```powershell
Expand-Archive rws-18.2.0-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip C:\rws
cd C:\www
C:\rws\rws-18.2.0-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\rws.exe
```

## As a Windows service

`rws.exe --windows-service=<directory>` runs under the Service Control
Manager (since 18.2.0): it serves `<directory>` and reads
`<directory>\rws.config.toml` if there is one. Stopping the service — or
shutting Windows down — stops rws gracefully, finishing requests in flight.

In an administrator PowerShell:

```powershell
New-Service -Name rws -DisplayName "rws web server" -StartupType Automatic `
  -BinaryPathName '"C:\rws\rws.exe" --windows-service="C:\www"'
Start-Service rws
curl.exe http://localhost:7878/healthz
```

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Stop / start | `Stop-Service rws`, `Start-Service rws` |
| Apply a config change | `Restart-Service rws` — there is no SIGHUP on Windows. With `watch = true` rws reloads settings and routes by itself ([Hot reload](/features/hot-reload/)); a new certificate still needs a restart |
| Remove | `Stop-Service rws; sc.exe delete rws` |

The directory is required: a service starts in `C:\Windows\System32`, and
rws serves its working directory. Keep only what should be public in it
(rws never serves `rws.config.toml`, `*.pem` or `*.key`).

A service has no console, so its access log goes nowhere unless you write it
to a file — in `<directory>\rws.config.toml`:

```toml
access_log = 'C:\rws\logs\access.log'
access_log_max_size = 104857600   # rotate at 100 MiB
```

The service runs as LocalSystem by default; to run it as a less privileged
account, set one with `sc.exe config rws obj= "NT AUTHORITY\LocalService"`
and give that account read access to the directory and write access to the
log directory.
