# WASM Guest Component

<https://rws8.tech/docs/deployment/wasm/>

`rws-wasm-shim` is a separate workspace package that runs the same `App`/`Router`/middleware logic you use natively — but hosted inside a WASM component instead of a `TcpListener`. The host (Wasmtime, Spin, Fastly Compute) owns the listening socket and TLS termination; it calls the guest once per request through the standard [`wasi:http/proxy`](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-http) world.

This is the "Foundation + Phase 1 + most of Phase 2" slice of the project tracked in [`spec/WASM_SHIM.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/spec/WASM_SHIM.md) in the repository — read that file for the full multi-phase plan and every verification detail. Everything on this page was tested against a real `wasmtime serve` process, not just compiled.

## Why not just compile the whole server to WASM?

`rws`'s normal accept loop uses `std::thread` (`ThreadPool`) and `rustls`/`aws-lc-rs` for TLS — neither compiles for `wasm32-wasip2`. Rather than trying to port sockets and TLS into the sandbox, the guest component reuses the existing seam every controller and middleware layer already goes through:

```rust
pub trait Application {
    fn execute(&self, request: &Request, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Result;
}
```

`Request` and `Response` are plain data structs with no socket handle anywhere in them, so the same `App::execute()` call that runs natively behind a `TcpListener` also runs unchanged behind a `wasi:http` incoming request.

## Building and running

```bash
rustup target add wasm32-wasip2   # wasm32-wasip2 is Tier 2 since Rust 1.82
cd rws-wasm-shim
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2
wasmtime serve target/wasm32-wasip2/release/rws_wasm_shim.wasm
```

In another shell:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/
```

The build output (`rws_wasm_shim.wasm`) is already a valid WASM component on this target — no separate `wasm-tools component new` step is needed.

The adapter is a small `Guest::handle` implementation (full version in `rws-wasm-shim/src/lib.rs`):

```rust
use wasip2::exports::http::incoming_handler::Guest;
use wasip2::http::types::{IncomingRequest, ResponseOutparam};
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::application::Application;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

wasip2::http::proxy::export!(Shim);
struct Shim;

impl Guest for Shim {
    fn handle(request: IncomingRequest, response_out: ResponseOutparam) {
        // translate `request` into a rust_web_server::request::Request,
        // call App::new().execute(&request, &connection), and write the
        // Response back through `response_out`.
    }
}
```

## What runs inside the guest

Only the parts of `rust-web-server` that don't touch a socket or spawn a thread are compiled for `wasm32-wasip2` — everything else is behind `#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]`. This list grew substantially past the initial "core only" slice — outbound HTTP now works, which unblocks everything built on top of it:

| Available in the guest | Native-only (excluded for `wasm32`) |
|---|---|
| `App`, `Router`, `Controller`, extractors | `Server`, `ThreadPool` |
| In-memory middleware (CORS, CSRF, rewrite, IP filter, request ID, in-memory rate limit/cache) | `ReverseProxy`, `H2ReverseProxy`, `GrpcProxy`, `TcpProxy`, `UdpProxy`, `WsProxy` |
| `Response::json`/`::text`, static-file serving (streamed for large files too) | `WebSocket`, `mailer` (raw SMTP — no `wasi:http` equivalent for arbitrary TCP protocols) |
| `http_client::Client` — **both HTTP and HTTPS**, via a `wasi:http` `outgoing-handler` backend (TLS terminated by the host, not `rustls`) | `otel`, `log`, `Scheduler` (background jobs), `redis_protocol`, `circuit_breaker`, `canary`, `service_discovery`'s DNS/etcd/Consul/Docker sources, `ingress`, `timeout`, `proxy_config` (config-driven proxy) |
| `auth` (`BasicAuthLayer`, `JwtLayer`, `ForwardAuthLayer`), `auth-asymmetric`, `csrf`, `crypto`, `webhook`, `rewrite-regex` | `model` (async ORM — needs real DB wire protocols) |
| `sso`, `sso-server`, `sso-saml`, `secrets`, `storage-s3`, `storage-azure` — all work because they only ever used `http_client::Client`, no code changes needed | |

## Three real limitations (confirmed, not theoretical)

All of these were empirically verified against a real `wasmtime serve` process, not inferred from the spec:

1. **Stateful middleware does not survive across requests.** `wasmtime serve` instantiates a **fresh guest per request** — confirmed by making an adapter call a request counter five times per invocation and watching it read back exactly `5` on every single request, never `10` or `15`. `RateLimiter`, `CacheLayer`, in-memory sessions, and metrics counters all silently reset every request under this host. Other hosts (Fastly Compute, Spin) are widely understood to behave the same way for the same isolation reasons, though only `wasmtime serve` was directly tested here. There is no in-crate fix for this — it needs either a host-provided KV binding (the `wasi-keyvalue` proposal, still pre-1.0) or accepting that stateful middleware requires a specific instance-reuse-guaranteeing host.
2. **Filesystem access needs an explicit host grant.** Unlike outbound HTTP (part of the `wasi:http/proxy` world's base contract), filesystem access is opt-in — `wasmtime serve` requires `--dir HOST_DIR::.` to expose any directory to the guest. Without it, static-file controllers silently fall back to `rws`'s built-in embedded default pages for every path, with no error — easy to miss in testing. With `--dir` granted, real files (including a 9 MB file exercised through the streaming code path) serve correctly.
3. **No real client IP or TLS SNI hostname.** The host already accepted the TCP connection and terminated TLS before ever invoking the guest, and the `wasi:http` incoming-request type has no field for either. `ConnectionInfo` gets a placeholder address and `sni_hostname: None`.

## Dependency notes

- The static-file/directory-listing controllers that ship with `App` depend on the [`file-ext`](https://crates.io/crates/file-ext) crate for path handling. `file-ext` 12.1.0 added `wasm32` support (path separator, temp folder, and a `remove_dir_all`-based recursive delete in place of shelling out to `rm`, which has no equivalent in a WASI guest) — an older `file-ext` version will fail to compile for this target.
- `rustls`'s own `aws-lc-rs` crypto-backend feature compiles C/asm that doesn't build for `wasm32-wasip2`. The root `Cargo.toml` moves `rustls`/`webpki-roots` into a `[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dependencies]` table so enabling `http-client` (or `sso`/`secrets`/`storage-s3`/`storage-azure`, which depend on it) on `wasm32` never pulls that broken dependency in — the wasm32 build gets its TLS from the host instead, via the `outgoing-handler` interface.

## What's still open

- An automated CI job that builds the component and drives a `wasmtime serve` smoke test in scripted form (the manual verification above, scripted).
- Verification against hosts other than `wasmtime serve` (Spin, Fastly Compute) — architecturally expected to behave the same way, but untested.
- A documented, supported answer for stateful middleware under per-request instantiation (a host-provided KV binding, most likely) — currently just a documented limitation, not a workaround.

See `spec/WASM_SHIM.md` in the repository for the complete, itemized history of what was built and verified.

---

# API Reference

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/api/>

Full rustdoc documentation is published at [docs.rs/rust-web-server](https://docs.rs/rust-web-server).

This page is a quick-reference index — click through to docs.rs for the complete method-level API. Module paths are relative to `rust_web_server::`; a feature in parentheses means the item is compiled only with that Cargo feature.

## Application layer

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Application` | `application` | Trait implemented by all app types: `execute(&Request, &ConnectionInfo) -> Result`. `runs_inline(request, connection)` (default `false`) lets the async servers run a request on the event loop instead of the blocking pool — only for work that never waits. `registered_routes()` / `middleware_names()` (default empty, 18.28.0) describe the app for tools; wrappers forward them. See [Async handlers](/building-apps/async-handlers/) |
| `AsyncResponse` | `application` (`http2`) | Return type of the optional `Application::execute_async`, awaited on the connection's task instead of holding a blocking-pool thread |
| `Controller` | `controller` | Trait with `is_matching(request, connection)` and `process(request, response, connection)`. See [Controllers](/building-apps/controllers/) |
| `App` | `app` | Zero-config application with all built-in controllers. `App::with_config(ServerConfig)` pins it to a fixed config (no env reads per request — the lock-free pattern for parallel tests) |
| `AppWithState` | `state` | State-aware app with `.get/.post/.put/.patch/.delete` route builders; state shared as `Arc`. Entry point `App::with_state(S)`; `.with_config(ServerConfig)` pins the fallback `App`. See [State](/building-apps/state/) |
| `AsyncAppWithState` | `async_state` (`http2`) | Same with `async fn` handlers. Entry point `App::with_async_state(S)` |
| `Middleware` | `middleware` | Layer trait: `handle(request, connection, next)`. `runs_inline` / `is_passthrough` (default `false`) declare a layer non-blocking or a no-op for a request. `layer_name()` (default: the type's name, 18.28.0) is how tools list it. See [Middleware](/building-apps/middleware/) |
| `WithMiddleware` | `middleware` | Wraps any `Application` with a layer stack; `app.wrap(layer)`, first-pushed is outermost |
| `k8s::client` / `k8s::config::ConfigWatch` / `k8s::config::resolve` | `k8s` (`k8s`) | A Kubernetes client (in-cluster or kubeconfig); a ConfigMap's or Secret's data kept current by a watch (`get`, `on_change`, `apply_to_env`); `k8s://ns/name#key` secrets (18.35.0). See [Using the Kubernetes API](/deployment/kubernetes-api/) |
| `k8s::discovery::service_endpoints` / `k8s::leader::LeaderElector` | `k8s` (`k8s`) | A Service's ready endpoints as a `BackendPool`; leader election over a Lease (`handle`, `wait_until_leader`, `release`) (18.35.0) |
| `k8s::controller::{Controller, Operator, Context}` | `k8s` (`k8s`) | Controllers (`reconcile`, `owns`, `finalizer`, `on_error`) run by an `Operator` (leader election, metrics, readiness); `Context::patch_status`, `apply_owned`, `event` (18.35.0). See [Operators](/deployment/kubernetes-operators/) |
| `k8s::webhook::{Webhooks, WebhookCertificate}` | `k8s` (`k8s`) | Validating, mutating and conversion webhooks as an rws app; a CA + serving certificate, `install`, `patch_ca_bundle` (18.35.0) |
| `k8s::manifests` (`Rbac`, `Rule`, `crd`, `webhook_configuration`, `to_yaml`, `print_on_request`) | `k8s` (`k8s`) | CRDs, RBAC and webhook configurations from the code (18.35.0) |
| `k8s::testing::{TestCluster, TestNamespace, eventually}` | `k8s` (`k8s`) | Tests against a real API server from `RWS_TEST_KUBECONFIG`, a namespace per test (18.35.0) |
| `generator::plan_deploy` / `DeploySpec` | `generator` | `rws gen deploy`: Kubernetes manifests for the app (18.35.0). See [Generate the manifests](/deployment/kubernetes/#generate-the-manifests) |
| `health` (`Probe`, `Registry`, `Report`) | `health` | Liveness, readiness and startup checks for `/livez`, `/readyz`, `/startupz`: `readiness(name, f)`, `liveness`, `startup`, `register_async`, `database(name, pool)`, `report`, `set_timeout` (18.35.0). See [Health checks](/deployment/kubernetes/#health-checks) |
| `Container` | `di` | `TypeId`-keyed dependency injection container: `register::`, `provide::<dyn Trait>`, `*_named`, `get`. Pass it directly to `App::with_state(container)` — not `into_arc()`, which double-wraps. See [Dependency injection](/building-apps/dependency-injection/) |
| `Lifecycle` | `di` | `start`/`stop` for services registered with `Container::register_managed`; `Container::on_start`/`on_stop`/`start`/`stop`/`is_started` (18.35.0). See [Lifecycle hooks](/building-apps/dependency-injection/#lifecycle-hooks) |
| `ErrorPages` | `error_pages` | Middleware: panics and app errors as a detailed page / problem details in `dev`/`test`, a bare `500` in `prod` (`from_env`, `detailed`) (18.35.0). See [Error pages](/building-apps/error-handling/#error-pages) |
| `ValueCache` | `cache` | In-memory values with per-entry TTL: `fetch_or`, `try_fetch_or`, `fetch_or_async`, `invalidate_prefix` (18.35.0). See [Caching values](/features/caching/#caching-values-fetch_or) |
| `AppManifest` | `app_manifest` | `rws.app.toml`, parsed: `name`, `paths`, `file`, `warnings`; `load(dir)` (conventional when absent; name from `Cargo.toml`), `parse(text)` / `FromStr`, `conventional(name)`, `layout(dir)` (18.28.0). See [Project layout](/building-apps/project-layout/) |
| `Generate` / `plan` / `Plan` | `generator` | `rws gen model|route|migration|test` as a library (18.29.0): `Generate::{Model, Route, Migration, Test}` (`Model`'s `timestamps` / `soft_delete`, 18.30.0), `plan(dir, &request)` reads the project and answers a `Plan` (`changes`, `notes`, `status()`, `has_conflicts()`, `render(diffs)`, `to_json(written)`), `Plan::apply(dir)` writes it — never overwriting a file; `run(args, out, err)` is the command line (`EXIT_OK`/`EXIT_CONFLICT`/`EXIT_USAGE`). See [Generators](/building-apps/generators/) |
| `plan_model_migration` / `ExistingColumns` | `generator` | The additive migration from the models to a database's tables and columns: `rws gen migration <name> --from-models` (18.35.0). See [Migrations from the models](/building-apps/generators/#migrations-from-the-models) |
| `db_cli::run` / `run_with_seeders` / `requested` | `db_cli` | `rws db migrate|rollback [N]|status|seed|schema` (18.30.0): `run(args, out, err)` answers the exit code (`EXIT_OK`, `EXIT_FAILED`, `EXIT_USAGE`); `--database-url` / `DATABASE_URL` / `RWS_DB_*`, `--dir`, `--migrations`, `--seeds`, `--json`; `run_with_seeders(args, &Seeders, out, err)` for an app's own binary, whose `db seed` runs Rust seeders after the SQL files. See [`rws db`](/database/migrations/#from-the-command-line-rws-db) |
| `FileChange` / `ChangeKind` / `GenError` | `generator` | One file of a plan (`path`, `kind` — `Create`, `Edit`, `Unchanged`, `Conflict` — `content`, `original`, `diff`); why a generator refused (`usage`, `message`, `to_json()`) |
| `Field` / `FieldType` / `BaseType` / `Db` / `RouteAction` | `generator` | `name:type` (`Field::parse`, `parse_fields`; types `i64`, `i32`, `f64`, `bool`, `String`, `Option`); the database a migration is written for (`sqlite`, `postgres`, `mysql`); the routes `gen route` writes (`List`, `Show`, `Create`, `Update`, `Remove`; `parse_list("list,show")`) |
| `AppPaths` / `LayoutEntry` / `EntryKind` / `ManifestError` | `app_manifest` | Where each part lives (`main`, `lib`, `routes`, `models`, `jobs`, `migrations`, `templates`, `tests`, `static_files`; `Default` = the conventional layout; `entries()`, `get(role)`); one role as found on disk (`role`, `path`, `kind` file/dir, `exists`); a parse error (`line`, `message`) |
| `TeraEngine` | `template` (`tera`) | Jinja2-style templates: `from_dir`, `from_raw`; global `template::init(dir)` / `template::render(name, &ctx)` / `template::reload()` (also run on `SIGHUP`); view helpers `url_for`, `vite`, `vite_asset` and `template::page_context(request)` (flash, CSRF field, path; 18.35.0). See [Templates](/building-apps/templates/) |

## Macros

| Item | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `routes!` | `macros` | Declarative routing table — builds `AppWithState`, `AsyncAppWithState` or `Router` from `METHOD "path" => handler` lines. See [Routing](/building-apps/routing/) |
| `#[route]`, `#[get]`, `#[post]`, `#[put]`, `#[patch]`, `#[delete]` | crate root (`macros`) | On a classic handler, a `Route:` doc comment; on one with extractor arguments (18.28.0), a unit struct implementing `handler::Handler`/`AsyncHandler`/`RouteSpec`, registered with `.route(h)`, the pattern's parameters checked against the `Path` argument at compile time. See [Routing](/building-apps/routing/#typed-handlers-get-with-extractors) |
| `#[derive(FromPath)]` | crate root (`macros`) | `handler::FromPath` for a struct with one `FromStr` field per route parameter, by name (18.28.0) |
| `#[derive(FromRequest)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Derives `FromRequest` for a named-field struct, extracting fields in order and stopping at the first error |
| `#[derive(JsonSchema)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Derives `schema::JsonSchema` for a named-field struct or unit enum, following its `#[serde]` renames (18.0.0). See [Typed tools](/mcp/tools/#typed-tools) |
| `#[derive(Validate)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Derives `Validate` from `#[validate(length, range, email, required, url)]` field annotations |
| `#[derive(Config)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Typed env-var binding: generates `load() -> Result`; `#[config(env, default, prefix)]`. See [Config binding](/features/config-binding/) |
| `#[derive(Model)]` | crate root (`macros` + a `model-*` feature) | Maps a struct to a table (`#[table]`, `#[primary_key(auto_increment)]`, `#[column]`, `#[ignore]`) and generates `T::repository(&pool)` / `T::query(&pool)` |
| `#[derive(Factory)]` | crate root (`macros` + a `model-*` feature) | Beside `Model`: `test_client::factory::Factory` and `T::factory()` for tests (18.29.0, rws-macros 17.30). See [Factories](/testing/database/#factories) |

## HTTP primitives

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Request` | `request` | Parsed HTTP request: method, URI, version, headers, body bytes. `request.header(name)` is a case-insensitive, allocation-free lookup; `Request::is_supported_method` checks a method token |
| `Response` | `response` | HTTP response: status code, headers, body as `Vec`. `Response::json(status, bytes)` / `Response::text(status, &str)` are one-line builders; `response.header(name)` looks a header up |
| `STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE` | `response` | Every HTTP status code as a typed constant |
| `Header` | `header` | Name/value pair (`Cow<'static, str>` fields since 18.0.0; build with `Header::new(name, value)`, read via deref); constants for all standard header names. See [Migrating to 18.0](/reference/migrating-18/) |
| `HTTP` | `http` | Version constants; `HTTP::is_supported_version` |
| `MimeType` | `mime_type` | MIME type constants and detection from a file extension |
| `Range` / `ContentRange` | `range` | Byte ranges and the body parts of a `Response` (bytes, files, multipart) |
| `URL` | `url` | Parse and build URLs; percent-encode/decode |
| `FormUrlEncoded` | `body::form_urlencoded` | Parses `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies. See [Forms & uploads](/building-apps/forms-uploads/) |
| `FormMultipartData` | `body::multipart_form_data` | Parses `multipart/form-data` uploads |
| `Json` | `json` (`serde`) | Serde JSON extractor and responder. See [JSON](/building-apps/json/) |
| `CookieJar` | `cookie` | Parses the `Cookie` request header. See [Cookies](/building-apps/cookies/) |
| `SetCookie` | `cookie` | Builds `Set-Cookie` values with all RFC 6265 attributes |
| `signed_cookie` / `verify_signed_cookie` | `cookie` (`crypto`) | HMAC-SHA256 tamper-evident cookie value `"<value>.<hex-signature>"`; verification returns `None` on tampering |
| `encrypted_cookie` / `decrypt_cookie` | `cookie` (`crypto`) | AES-256-GCM confidential cookie value; fresh nonce per call, `None` on tampering or wrong key |

| `ConnectionInfo` | `server` | Client/server IP, port, and SNI hostname per connection |

| `UserStore` / `AuthUser` / `MemoryUserStore` / `DbUserStore` | `auth_flows` (`DbUserStore`: a `model-*` feature) | Where accounts live: your own table, memory, or `rws_users` (18.35.0) |
| `BasicAuthLayer` | `auth` (`auth`) | HTTP Basic authentication via a closure or `from_htpasswd_file` (plain or rws's `{SHA256}` scheme — not Apache `{SHA}`/`$apr1$`/bcrypt). See [Auth](/features/auth/) |
| `JwtLayer` | `auth` (`auth`) | HS256 Bearer JWT validation; `::rs256`/`::es256` verify against a static public key (`auth-asymmetric`) |
| `Identity` / `with_identity` / `scope_identity` | `authz` | The authenticated caller (`user:alice`), set by every authenticator for the rest of the request — not a header; `Identity::current()` (18.14.0). See [Authorization](/features/authorization/) |
| `Authorizer` / `Schema` / `Tuple` / `TupleStore` / `MemoryStore` | `authz` | Relationship-based access control: a schema of relations (`user \| group#member \| owner \| parent->viewer`), tuples (`doc:42#editor@user:alice`), `check` / `explain` with depth and read limits (18.14.0). | `SqlStore` | `authz::sql` (`model-*`) | Relationship tuples in SQLite / Postgres / MySQL (`rws_authz_tuples`), 1 s read cache, own runtime (18.14.0). See [Authorization](/features/authorization/#storing-tuples-in-a-database) |
| `AuthzLayer` / `ObjectTemplate` | `authz` | Middleware: the caller needs a relation on an object named from the request (`doc:{path:2}`, `{query:k}`, `{header:H}`); 401 / 403 (18.14.0). See [Authorization](/features/authorization/#protecting-routes) |
| `ForwardAuthLayer` | `auth::forward` (`auth`) | Delegates allow/deny to an external HTTP service; verbatim pass-through on non-2xx, 502 if unreachable |
| `IpFilter` | `ip_filter` | IPv4/IPv6 address or CIDR allowlist/denylist; `ip_filter::is_valid_entry` checks an entry; `ip_filter::client_ip` / `request_scheme` give the client's address and scheme behind a trusted proxy. See [IP filter](/features/ip-filter/) |
| `Blocklist` | `blocklist` | Runtime IP blocklist: `blocklist::global().block(ip)` / `.unblock` / `.is_blocked` / `.list` / `.clear` |
| `BlocklistLayer` | `blocklist` | Answers `403` for blocked client IPs |
| `MaintenanceLayer` / `MAINTENANCE_MODE` | `maintenance` | While the `AtomicBool` is `true`, answers `503` for everything but `/healthz` and `/readyz` |
| `RequestLog` | `request_log` | In-memory buffer of recent requests (`request_log::global()`, capacity 1000); `.recent(n)` / `.recent_errors(n)` |
| `LogLayer` | `request_log` | Records each request into `RequestLog` |
| `EarlyHintsLayer` / `early_hints::send` | `early_hints` | `103 Early Hints` with `Link` values before the response, on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (HTTP/1.1 opt-in) (18.12.0). See [Early Hints](/features/early-hints/) |
| `traffic::classify` / `Class` / `Kind` / `Group` | `traffic` | Who a client is from its address, User-Agent and path: person (browser), AI (training, search, assistant), bot (search engine, SEO, monitoring, preview, scanner, spoofed crawler, tool); crawler networks verified by their published IP ranges (18.15.0) |
| `traffic::device::parse` / `Device` | `traffic` | A browser's family, operating system and device class from its `User-Agent` and client hints (18.31.0) |
| `traffic::TrafficScriptLayer` | `traffic` | Serves the first-party traffic script (`/_rws/t.js`) and takes its reports (`/_rws/t`) when `[traffic] script` is on; passes every other request through (18.31.0) |
| `traffic::geo::country` | `traffic` | The country of an address from the built-in DB-IP Lite table (`geo` feature) or `[traffic] geo_db` (18.31.0) |
| `traffic::hosting::provider` | `traffic` | The cloud or server hosting provider of an address (`"AWS"`, `"other hosting"`) from the built-in DB-IP ASN Lite table (`geo` feature); browsers from one count as bots (18.35) |
| `traffic::apps::detect` / `App` / `set_apps` / `configured` | `traffic` | A native app or browser extension from its `User-Agent` and `Origin`: a configured `[traffic] apps` name, or a platform name (Apple or Android networking, Electron, extension origins); counted as **Apps**, not bots (18.35) |
| `traffic::owner` (`in_networks`, `has_cookie`, `key`, `is_admin_call`) | `traffic` | Whether a request is the site owner's: a successful admin API call, `[traffic] owner_networks`, or the `rws_me` cookie set by `/_rws/me?k=<key>`; the owner's visits are counted apart (18.35) |
| `traffic::configure_sites` / `traffic::record::set_configured_hosts` | `traffic` | The sites the configuration's routes match, counted separately and listed first on the Traffic page (18.35) |
| `RequestIdLayer` | `request_id` | Correlation-ID middleware — echoes or generates `X-Request-Id` (`generate_request_id()`, UUID-v4-shaped, not crypto-random). See [Request ID](/features/request-id/) |
| `CsrfLayer` | `csrf` (`csrf`) | Double-submit cookie CSRF protection; 403 on mismatch. See [CSRF](/features/csrf/) |
| `CsrfToken` | `csrf` (`csrf`) | Extractor for the current token in a GET handler; implements `Display` |
| `TimeoutLayer` | `timeout` | Wraps a whole `Application` with a deadline (`504`). See [Timeouts](/features/timeouts/) |
| `with_timeout` / `with_timeout_state` / `with_timeout_async` | `timeout` | Per-handler timeouts. The sync ones bound the client's wait but can't cancel the work; `with_timeout_async` (`http2`) cancels the future |
| `FeatureStore` | `feature` | Runtime feature toggles: `feature::global().set(name, bool)` / `.is_enabled` / `.list` |

| `ModelRepository` | `model` | `Repository` implementation from `T::repository(&pool)`, for `ID` = `i64`, `i32`, `String`, `Uuid` (18.30.0); `save` inserts when an auto-increment key is 0 or another key isn't in the table, else updates; `insert`, `query()`, and for soft-delete models `restore`, `force_delete_by_id`, `find_by_id_with_deleted`. See [Keys, timestamps, soft delete, locking](/database/conventions/) |
| `PrimaryKey` | `model` | The key types `ModelRepository` implements `Repository` for: `i64`, `i32`, `String`, `Uuid` (sealed, 18.30.0) |
| `Timestamp` | `model` | A UTC instant in microseconds: `now()`, `parse`, `to_rfc3339`, `to_value(backend)`, `FromColumn`/`ToColumn`, `serde` as RFC 3339; the type of `#[timestamps]` / `#[soft_delete]` fields (18.30.0). See [Timestamps](/database/conventions/#timestamps) |

| `DbError` / `DbErrorKind` | `model` | The model layer's error (its message in `.0`); `kind()` — `StaleVersion` (a `#[version]`ed `save` of a stale copy), `NotFound`, `Other` — and `is_stale_version()` / `is_not_found()` (18.30.0). | `QueryBuilder` | `model` | Fluent query builder: `where_eq`, `filter`, `order_by`, `limit`, `fetch_all`, `count`, `paginate`, `paginate_after`; `with_deleted`, `only_deleted`, `force_delete`, `restore` for soft-delete models; `where_in`, `where_null`, `where_not_null`, `scope(f)`, `with(relation)` (18.30.0). | `HasMany` / `HasOne` / `BelongsTo` | `model` | Explicit-load relations with `.load(&pool).await` — no hidden N+1. See [Relations](/database/relations/) |
| `BelongsToMany` / `SyncChanges` | `model` | One owner's many-to-many links through a join table: `load`, `ids`, `attach`, `detach`, `detach_all`, `sync` (answers the `SyncChanges`: `attached`, `detached`) (18.30.0). See [Many-to-many](/database/relations/#many-to-many-belongstomany) |
| `Relation` / `RelationKind` | `model` (`model::eager`) | How `O` reaches `R`: `has_many(fk)`, `has_one(fk)`, `belongs_to(fk)`, `belongs_to_many(join, owner_key, related_key)`; `load(&pool, &owner)`, `load_for(&pool, &owners)` — one query per 500 keys (18.30.0). See [Eager loading](/database/relations/#eager-loading-with-with) |
| `EagerQuery` / `Loaded` | `model` (`model::eager`) | From `QueryBuilder::with(relation)`: `.with(…)` more, `fetch_all` / `fetch_one` / `paginate` answer `Loaded` — derefs to the model; `related(&rel)`, `one(&rel)`, `take(&rel)`, `is_loaded(&rel)`, `into_inner()` (18.30.0) |
| `Nested` | `model` | The relations to load for a relation's rows: `with_nested(relation, \|n\| n.with(…))` on `QueryBuilder`/`EagerQuery`; read with `Loaded::related_loaded` (18.35.0). See [Nested relations](/database/relations/#nested-relations) |
| `ModelAdmin` | `model_admin` (a `model-*` feature) | Middleware: list, search, create, edit and delete rows of registered tables, from the live schema; `allow(check)` required (18.35.0). See [Model admin](/database/model-admin/) |
| `MigrationStatus` | `model` | Applied/pending state from `DbPool::migration_status`. See [Migrations](/database/migrations/) |
| `ModelInfo` | `model` | What a `Model` type maps to — `type_name`, `table`, `columns`, `primary_key`, `auto_increment`; `ModelInfo::of::()`, `short_name()` (18.28.0). What `DevTools::model::()` reports. See [dev tools](/mcp/dev-tools/) |
| `Page` | `pagination` (re-exported from `model`) | Offset page: totals, `has_next`/`has_prev`, `.map(f)`, `.link_header(base_url)`; usable without the model layer. See [Pagination](/database/pagination/) |
| `CursorPage` | `pagination` (re-exported from `model`) | Keyset page with `next_cursor`, `.link_header(base_url, cursor_param)` |

# Troubleshooting

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/troubleshooting/>

## Starting the server

### `unable to set up TCP listener: Permission denied (os error 13)`

Ports below 1024 need privileges. Use a higher port (`--port=7878`), or run
with `sudo` / as Administrator. In a container, the release image runs as a
non-root user, so map a high container port to 80/443 instead.

### `unable to set up TCP listener: Address already in use`

Another process holds the port. Find it:

```bash
sudo lsof -i :7878     # macOS and Linux
sudo fuser 7878/tcp    # Linux
```

### `Cannot assign requested address (os error 99)`

The `--ip` you passed isn't assigned to any local interface. List them with
`ip addr` (Linux) or `ifconfig`, or bind to all of them with `--ip=0.0.0.0`.

### `sudo rws` says `command not found`

`~/.cargo/bin` (or `/usr/local/bin`) isn't on root's `PATH`. Use the full
path: `sudo ~/.cargo/bin/rws`.

## Reaching the server

### Other machines can't connect

- Bound to `127.0.0.1`? That only accepts local connections. The default is
  `0.0.0.0`; pass `--ip=0.0.0.0` if you overrode it.
- `Connection refused` from another host with the right IP: a firewall is
  blocking the port.

### Serving on IPv6

`rws --ip=::` listens on IPv6 (and IPv4-mapped addresses). Link-local
`fe80::…` addresses need a zone id that browsers rarely accept; connect with
the machine's IPv4 address or a global IPv6 address instead.

### HTTPS, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 isn't working

No certificate is configured, so `rws` falls back to plain HTTP/1.1. Provide
one ([HTTPS / TLS](/features/https-tls/)) or let `rws` get one
([ACME](/features/acme/)):

```bash
rws --tls-cert-file=/path/to/cert.pem --tls-key-file=/path/to/key.pem
```

### `TLS setup failed: failed to read cert file …`

The path is wrong, the process can't read it, or the file isn't PEM. Both the
certificate (chain) and the key must be PEM.

### The browser warns about the certificate

Self-signed certificates aren't trusted. For local development add yours to
the system trust store (or use `mkcert`); in production use a public CA,
for example through [ACME](/features/acme/).

### Malformed-request errors (`400`)

The server received something that isn't an HTTP request — a port scanner,
TLS sent to a plain-HTTP port, or garbage. The client gets a `400 Bad Request`;
it's safe to ignore.

### A directory shows a file listing

A directory without `index.html` is shown as a listing. Add an `index.html` to
serve that instead.

## Logs and metrics

### I want the Combined Log Format, not JSON

Set `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=combined` (or `log_format = "combined"` in
`rws.config.toml`); `off` disables the access log. JSON is the default. Lines
are buffered and written within 100 ms — see
[Observability](/deployment/observability/).

### Scraping metrics

`GET /metrics` serves Prometheus text format; see [Metrics](/features/metrics/)
for the metric names and a scrape config.

## Kubernetes

### Probes fail with `Connection refused`

The kubelet probes the pod IP, so `rws` must not be bound to `127.0.0.1`.
The default `0.0.0.0` works; check for an `ip = "127.0.0.1"` override.

### `/readyz` returns `503` right after start

Expected: it returns `503` until startup finishes, then `200`. If it stays at
`503`, startup failed — check the logs. Give slow starts an
`initialDelaySeconds`:

```yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: 7878
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
```

### Requests are dropped on `SIGTERM`

`rws` stops accepting on `SIGTERM` and finishes in-flight requests. Requests
can still arrive while the load balancer hasn't noticed yet; delay
termination with a `preStop` sleep (Kubernetes 1.30+ — the release image has
no shell for an `exec` hook):

```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    sleep:
      seconds: 5
```

More in [Kubernetes](/deployment/kubernetes/).

## Building from source

### `linker 'cc' not found`

Install a C toolchain (needed by `aws-lc-rs` and other native dependencies):

```bash
sudo apt-get install build-essential        # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo dnf group install "Development Tools"  # Fedora/RHEL
sudo pacman -S base-devel                   # Arch
```

### `found crate … compiled by an incompatible version of rustc`

Stale build artifacts from another toolchain: `cargo clean && cargo build`.

### `error: package … requires rustc 1.99`

The minimum supported Rust version is 1.99: `rustup update stable`.

### `failed open - '…/FETCH_HEAD' is locked: Permission denied`

The Cargo registry was written by `sudo cargo …` once. Fix the ownership
(`sudo chown -R $USER ~/.cargo`) rather than building as root.

---

# Error responses

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/errors/>

Since 18.17.0 the errors rws produces itself, rather than your application,
answer with [RFC 9457](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457) problem
details:

```http
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Retry-After: 5

{"type":"about:blank","title":"Service Unavailable","status":503,"detail":"every backend is out of rotation"}
```

`type` is `about:blank`, so `title` is the status's reason phrase, and
`detail` (when there is one) says what happened. Status codes and other
headers (`Retry-After`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `Allow`) are unchanged.

## Which errors

| Status | When | `detail` |
|---|---|---|
| `400` | A request rws can't parse; a body an extractor rejects | The parse error |
| `401` | Basic / JWT / bearer auth, `PURGE` without the purge token, authorization without an identity | — or the reason |
| `403` | IP filter, blocklist, CSRF, authorization denied | — |
| `404` | No matching ingress rule; no matching Gateway API route | — |
| `408` | The request head took longer than 30 s | How long it may take |
| `413` | A body over `max_body_size` | The declared or reached size and the limit |
| `417` | An `Expect` value other than `100-continue` | The value |
| `421` | A Gateway API request for a host the connection isn't for | — |
| `429` | A rate limit | — |
| `431` | A request head over 64 KiB | The limit |
| `500` | An SSO callback that fails, a failing WASM plugin, a handler that errs | The reason |
| `501` | A method no built-in handles | The method |
| `502` | An upstream that can't be reached or answers garbage; an unreachable forward-auth service | — or the reason |
| `503` | Every backend out of rotation; maintenance mode; a route whose auth or plugin is misconfigured | The reason |
| `504` | An upstream or a handler that took too long | — |

Not affected:

- The 404 page for a missing static file (your `404.html`, or the
  built-in one): that's your site's content.
- APIs with their own error format: the admin API, MCP (JSON-RPC errors),
  the LLM proxy (OpenAI-style errors), the OAuth server (RFC 6749 errors),
  validation errors (`422` with the field list).
- HTTP/2 `413`/`431` sent while the request is still arriving: those are
  headers only.

`AppError::into_response()` uses the same shape, so your own errors match
rws's.

## Plain text instead

```toml
error_format = "text"   # RWS_CONFIG_ERROR_FORMAT
```

brings back the bodies of earlier releases: `502 Bad Gateway`,
`503 Service Unavailable: every backend is out of rotation`, and so on, as
`text/plain`.

---

# Migrating to 18.0

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/migrating-18/>

18.0 has a handful of breaking changes; most applications only meet the first and the `Request.body` type. If you are coming from 17.113.0 or earlier, also read [the patch-release changes](#coming-from-171130-or-earlier).

## `Header` fields are `Cow<'static, str>`

`Header { name, value }` used to be two `String`s; now both are
`Cow<'static, str>`, so the standard headers on every response are borrowed
instead of allocated.

```rust
use rust_web_server::header::Header;

// 17.x
let h = Header { name: Header::_LOCATION.to_string(), value: url };

// 18.0 — a &'static str is borrowed, a String is owned
let h = Header::new(Header::_LOCATION, url);
let h = Header::new("X-Static", "fixed");
let h = Header { name: "X-Static".into(), value: "fixed".into() }; // fields are still public
```

Reading:

| 17.x | 18.0 |
|------|------|
| `h.value.as_str()` | `&*h.value` or `h.value.as_ref()` (`as_str` isn't stable on the 1.88 MSRV) |
| `h.value.clone()` (a `String`) | `h.value.to_string()` |
| `h.value.push_str(..)` | `h.value.to_mut().push_str(..)` |
| `h.name == "Content-Type"` | unchanged (`Cow<str>` compares with `&str`) |

To find a request header, prefer `request.header("content-type")` — a
case-insensitive lookup that returns `Option<&Header>` without allocating.

## Default response headers

| Header | 17.x | 18.0 |
|--------|------|------|
| `Accept-CH`, `Critical-CH`, client hints in `Vary` | always | only with `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS=true` |
| `Vary` | `Origin` + the client-hint headers | `Origin` |
| `Cache-Control` on static files | `no-store, …` | `no-cache` (`RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL`) |
| `Last-Modified` on static files | non-standard | standard HTTP date |
| `Date` | — | on every response |
| `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy` | always | only with `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true` |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `default-src 'self'` unless `RWS_CONFIG_CSP` | `RWS_CONFIG_CSP`, or the default with `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true` |
| `Date-Unix-Epoch-Nanos`, `Last-Modified-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` | always | only with `RWS_CONFIG_NANOS_HEADERS=true` |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (+ `-Credentials: true`) for any `Origin` | always (`cors_allow_all` defaulted to `true`) | only with `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=true` or a listed origin |

What it means:

- **Browsers now keep static files** and revalidate them (`If-None-Match` /
  `If-Modified-Since` → `304`). To get the old behaviour set
  `RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL=` (empty). For fingerprinted asset names,
  set something like `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. Responses from
  your handlers still default to `no-store, …`.
- **Security headers**: to keep sending `X-Frame-Options`,
  `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy` and the default CSP, set
  `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true` (`security_headers = true`). A CSP set
  with `RWS_CONFIG_CSP` is sent either way.
- **Nanosecond timestamps**: clients that read `Date-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` or
  `Last-Modified-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` need `RWS_CONFIG_NANOS_HEADERS=true`
  (`nanos_headers = true`).
- **Client hints**: if your app reads `Sec-CH-*` request headers, set
  `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS=true` (or `client_hints = true` in
  `rws.config.toml`).
- **CORS**: a browser app on another origin that calls `rws` needs its origin
  in `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` (`[cors] allow_origins`), plus
  `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=true` if it sends cookies. Setting
  `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=true` restores the old echo-any-origin
  behaviour; avoid it for anything with logins.
- **ACME renewal**: certificates renew at two-thirds of their lifetime (or
  when the CA's renewal information says), not 30 days before expiry; set
  `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_BEFORE_DAYS=30` to keep the old margin. Code that
  builds an `AcmeConfig` by hand sets `renew_before_days: None` (or
  `Some(days)`) and `profile: None`.
- **`CacheLayer`** no longer stores `no-cache` responses, responses to `Range`
  requests, or responses whose `Vary` names a request header outside its key.
  Static files are therefore not cached by it (they were never meant to be).

## RSA public keys

`rws` verifies RS256 JWTs and SAML signatures itself now (the `rsa` crate had
an unfixed advisory, RUSTSEC-2023-0071). Two signatures change:

- `auth::verify_jwt_rs256(token, &key)` takes a `&rsa_key::RsaPublicKey`.
- `SamlIdpMetadata.signing_key` is an `rsa_key::RsaPublicKey`.

`JwtLayer::rs256(pem)` and the SSO/JWKS code are unchanged for callers.

```rust
use rust_web_server::rsa_key::RsaPublicKey;

let key = RsaPublicKey::from_public_key_pem(&pem)?; // BEGIN PUBLIC KEY or BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY
let key = RsaPublicKey::from_public_key_der(&der)?; // SPKI
let key = RsaPublicKey::from_components(&n_bytes, &e_bytes)?;
```

Keys under 2048 bits are rejected; a JWKS key that can't be used is skipped.

## `Request.body` is a `Body`

`Request.body` was a `Vec<u8>`; it is a `request::Body`, which can also be a
stream of a body still arriving. It dereferences to `&[u8]`, so reading
code mostly compiles unchanged. What to change:

| 17.x | 18.0 |
|---|---|
| `body: vec![]` | `body: Default::default()` |
| `body: bytes` (a `Vec<u8>`) | `body: bytes.into()` |
| `request.body.clone()` where a `Vec<u8>` is wanted | `request.body.to_vec()` |
| `String::from_utf8(request.body)` | `String::from_utf8(request.body.to_vec())` |
| `request.body = vec` | `request.body = vec.into()` |
| `assert_eq!(b"x".to_vec(), request.body)` | unchanged (`Vec<u8> == Body` works) |

## The `rws` binary runs one runtime per core

The `rws` binary now starts one single-threaded runtime per core, each
accepting on its own `SO_REUSEPORT` socket, like nginx's workers
(`RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME=per-core`, Unix). On fast CPUs this serves more
requests per second; on slower ones it can cost more CPU per small request.
To keep 17.x behaviour, set `runtime = "shared"` in `rws.config.toml` or
`RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME=shared`. Applications built on the library are
unchanged: they stay `shared` unless they set it.

## 18.9: `ConnectionInfo.tls`

`ConnectionInfo` has a new public field, `tls: bool` (the client connected
over TLS), which proxies use for `X-Forwarded-Proto`. A struct literal that
builds a `ConnectionInfo` must now set it. To stop field additions breaking
your code, use the constructor or `Default`:

```rust,ignore
// 18.8
let connection = ConnectionInfo { client, server, request_size: 10_000, sni_hostname: None };
// 18.9
let connection = ConnectionInfo { tls: false, ..ConnectionInfo::new(client, server) };
let connection = ConnectionInfo::default(); // in tests
```

## Coming from 17.113.0 or earlier

18.0 carries the 17.113.1 security fixes and the 17.113.2 conformance fixes.
If you skipped those releases, these refuse or change what you may rely on:

- **Static files:** paths with `..`, dot-files (`.git/`, `.env`; set
  `RWS_CONFIG_SERVE_DOTFILES=true` to serve them), `*.pem`, `*.key` and
  `rws.config.toml` are not served. Request paths are percent-decoded, so a
  file whose name contains a literal `%` is requested as `%25`.
- **ACME** keeps its keys in `.rws/acme/` by default (files at the old
  default paths are moved there on start).
- **The `rws` binary** mounts `/mcp` only when `MCP_TOKEN` is set.
- **HTTP/1.1 requests** without `Host` or with two, with a lower-case method,
  a folded header line or whitespace before a header's colon get `400`; an
  HTTP/1.0 connection closes after each response unless the client sends
  `Connection: keep-alive`.
- **CORS** origins match whole: list each origin, a part of one no longer
  matches.

## Also new in 18.0 (not breaking)

- A request head that doesn't complete within 30 s of its first byte gets
  `408 Request Timeout`.
- `[[upstream]] tls_ca_file` trusts a private CA for `https://` upstreams.
- Inline tables in settings: `rate_limit = { max_requests = 100 }`.

The full list is in [`CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

## 18.27: the client behind a trusted proxy

Behind a `trusted_proxies` load balancer, the rate limit, `allow_ips` /
`deny_ips`, blocklist, WAF IP rules, `ip_hash` and the logs now see the
client from `X-Forwarded-For` instead of the balancer. An allowlist written
against the balancer's address (e.g. `allow_ips = ["10.0.0.5"]`) now meets the
real clients: list them, or set `client_ip = "peer"` (`RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_IP`)
for the old behaviour. See [The client address](/proxy/reverse-proxy/#the-client-address).

`GET /metrics` now answers only loopback and private-range clients
(`metrics_allow`). A Prometheus that scrapes rws over a public address gets
`404`: add it, `metrics_allow = ["203.0.113.7"]`, or `"*"` for the old
behaviour.

## 18.24: trusted proxies

Not a breaking release, but one default changed: an incoming
`X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host` or `Forwarded` is believed only from
`trusted_proxies` (loopback and private ranges by default). If rws sits
behind a load balancer or CDN with a public address, list it:
`trusted_proxies = ["203.0.113.0/24"]` — or `"*"` to keep 18.23's behaviour.

# Architecture

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/architecture/>

`rws` is one crate: the server, the reverse proxy and the application
framework share one request type and one handler trait. HTTP/1.1 parsing,
routing, middleware, JSON, WebSocket, SSE and the HTTP/2 server are written
in-crate (the `h2` crate is only the proxies' HTTP/2 client); HTTP/3 uses
`h3` + `quinn`, TLS `rustls`.

## Builds

| Build | Runtime | Listeners |
|-------|---------|-----------|
| `http3` (default) | tokio | HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN), HTTP/3 over QUIC on the same port, optional HTTP → HTTPS redirect |
| `http2` | tokio | as above without QUIC |
| `http1` | none — a thread pool | plain HTTP/1.1 |

Without a certificate the async builds serve plain HTTP/1.1 on the same port.

## A request's path

```
TcpListener / QUIC endpoint
  └─ connection task (async builds) or pool thread (http1)
       ├─ TLS handshake, ALPN → HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2      (10 s deadline)
       ├─ read head (≤ 64 KiB, 30 s from its first byte), then the body
       │     (Content-Length or chunked; Expect: 100-continue; body limit → 413)
       ├─ Request::parse → Request + ConnectionInfo (addresses, SNI)
       ├─ Application::execute(&request, &connection) → Response
       │     middleware layers → router / controllers / proxy
       ├─ gzip if the client accepts it and it pays off
       └─ write head + body (one write, writev, sendfile, or chunked stream)
```

- **HTTP/1.1** connections are keep-alive loops with pipelining; one handler
  serves plain TCP and TLS. Every read has a 30 s idle timeout.
- **HTTP/2 and HTTP/3** translate each stream into the same `Request`, call the
  same `Application`, and translate the `Response` back into frames. Large
  bodies stream in 64 KiB chunks within flow-control limits.
- **Where handlers run.** Handlers are synchronous. In the async builds a
  request runs on tokio's blocking pool, unless the application says it is
  cheap (`Application::runs_inline` — `App` does for GET and HEAD), in which
  case it runs on the connection task. Async handlers
  (`App::with_async_state`) and config-file proxy routes without middleware
  are awaited without tying up a thread.

## Applications and middleware

Everything that answers requests implements one trait:

```rust
pub trait Application {
    fn execute(&self, request: &Request, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Result;
}
```

- `App` — the built-in controllers (health, metrics, static files, …).
- `App::with_state(S)` / `App::with_async_state(S)` — your routes plus shared state.
- `Router` — path routing with `:params` and `*wildcards`, usable inside any application.
- `McpServer`, `ConfigDrivenApp` (the config-file proxy) — also applications.

Middleware wraps an application (`app.wrap(layer)`); the first layer added is
the outermost. Rate limiting, auth, CORS, caching, metrics, tracing, rewriting
and the reverse proxy itself are all `Middleware`, so one model covers a web
app, a gateway and a mix of both.

## Static files

A GET for a regular file takes a fast path: the open file handle, its size
and modification time, small files' contents (≤ 64 KiB) and their gzip
output are cached per file version, so a hit costs one `fstat`. An edit in
place is served at once (strict mode, the default). Files over 256 KiB
stream from disk; on plain TCP, downloads use `sendfile` with the response
head in the same TCP segment. Responses carry `ETag` and `Last-Modified` and
answer `304` to revalidation.

## Reverse proxy

Upstream HTTP/1.1 connections are pooled per backend (64 idle, 25 s — under
the 30 s after which an rws backend closes an idle keep-alive connection).
Before a pooled connection is reused it is checked without blocking; one the
backend has closed is dropped and the request goes out on a new connection,
whatever its method. A request whose connection fails before any response
byte is retried only when it is idempotent (it may have reached the backend). A
config-file route without middleware is forwarded entirely on the event loop;
others go through the blocking path with the same pool. Responses over 1 MB,
chunked or SSE are streamed through instead of buffered. Health checks,
load-balancing strategies, retries and circuit breakers sit around the pool.
See [Reverse proxy](/proxy/reverse-proxy/) and [Config-driven proxy](/proxy/config-driven/).

## Configuration

Settings are layered — built-in defaults, environment variables,
`rws.config.toml`, command-line flags — and all end up as `RWS_CONFIG_*`
environment variables at startup. Request handling reads a typed snapshot
(`ServerConfig::current()`), rebuilt when the configuration changes; `SIGHUP`
reloads CORS, rate limits, log format, proxy routes and TLS certificates
without a restart. See [Configuration](/configuration/overview/).

# Benchmarks

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/benchmarks/>

`rws` is measured against Caddy and nginx on the same machine, with the same
files and the same load. The numbers below come from one run (40243377254) of the
[Benchmark workflow](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/.github/workflows/bench.yml)
on a 4-CPU GitHub Actions runner (Linux x86_64), with the load generator on the
same machine.

**Load:** [`oha`](https://github.com/hatoo/oha), 64 keep-alive connections,
20 seconds per scenario after a 2-second warm-up, HTTP/1.1, no compression
(`--disable-compression`: the Caddy and nginx configs don't compress, and
`rws` compresses text by default), access logs off everywhere. `rws` is the
release build (`--features "acme auth mimalloc"`), Caddy 2.11.7, nginx from Ubuntu with
`sendfile`, `open_file_cache` and upstream keep-alive enabled. nginx's
`open_file_cache_valid 1s` trusts a cached file's size and modification time
for a second; `rws` runs with the equivalent `open_file_cache_strict = false`
(its default re-checks them with an `fstat` on every request, so an edit in
place is served at once).

| Scenario | Server | Requests/s | p50 (ms) | p99 (ms) | CPU/request (µs) | Peak memory (MiB) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Static file, 1 KiB | rws | 96,670 | 0.61 | 1.65 | 16.9 | 33.5 |
| | Caddy | 18,592 | 2.73 | 13.49 | 154.4 | 66.1 |
| | nginx | 81,161 | 0.59 | 3.10 | 25.1 | 23.2 |
| Static file, 1 MiB | rws | 9,511 | 6.26 | 14.00 | 209.8 | 33.5 |
| | Caddy | 2,398 | 19.03 | 124.03 | 1,194.7 | 69.4 |
| | nginx | 9,767 | 6.42 | 14.05 | 216.2 | 23.4 |
| Reverse proxy, 1 KiB | rws | 34,260 | 1.79 | 3.89 | 44.6 | 35.5 |
| | Caddy | 13,402 | 4.16 | 14.17 | 190.6 | 66.7 |
| | nginx | 33,942 | 1.74 | 4.51 | 47.1 | 24.2 |

CPU/request is the server's user + system CPU time over the run (including
worker processes) divided by the requests it served.

Every request in every scenario returned `200 OK`.

### Extended scenarios

The same run, with the extended scenarios (`EXTENDED=1`, see
[Reproduce](#reproduce)):

| Scenario | Server | Requests/s | p50 (ms) | p99 (ms) | CPU/request (µs) | Peak memory (MiB) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 26 KiB JS file, gzip | rws | 86,327 | 0.69 | 1.87 | 20.9 | 41.8 |
| | Caddy | 5,729 | 8.51 | 51.96 | 606.3 | 109.2 |
| | nginx | 1,802 | 35.26 | 71.94 | 2,063.6 | 27.3 |
| Static 1 KiB, access log on | rws | 88,643 | 0.66 | 1.81 | 20.2 | 41.6 |
| | Caddy | 15,964 | 2.97 | 18.12 | 191.7 | 65.6 |
| | nginx | 75,518 | 0.62 | 3.16 | 28.6 | 23.2 |
| Static 1 KiB, HTTPS | rws | 70,372 | 0.82 | 2.22 | 25.9 | 49.4 |
| | Caddy | 25,555 | 2.22 | 9.57 | 112.6 | 69.4 |
| | nginx | 63,752 | 0.75 | 3.75 | 33.5 | 41.7 |
| Static 1 KiB, HTTP/2 | rws | 66,141 | 0.90 | 2.44 | 27.4 | 63.7 |
| | Caddy | 13,604 | 4.04 | 14.20 | 216.0 | 66.9 |
| | nginx | 51,416 | 0.84 | 4.46 | 37.9 | 42.2 |
| Static 1 MiB, HTTPS | rws | 1,602 | 35.23 | 49.34 | 923.7 | 65.7 |
| | Caddy | 1,460 | 38.13 | 108.27 | 1,483.6 | 68.0 |
| | nginx | 1,311 | 45.19 | 101.34 | 1,639.9 | 42.3 |

`rws` compresses a static text file once per version and serves the cached
result; nginx and Caddy compress on every request, which is why the gzip row
differs by two orders of magnitude (level 6 everywhere). HTTP/2 is served by
`rws`'s own implementation (since 18.0.0): with the `h2` crate, framing and
HPACK cost more per request than all of nginx's own code, and nginx led this
scenario by 23–41%. Large files over TLS were slow on AMD
EPYC 7763 runners until 18.0.0: rustls copies each record's plaintext into
a buffer 5 bytes past a page boundary, and with the file buffer page-aligned
too, glibc's `rep movsb` ran that copy at 2.8 instead of 40 GB/s (4 KiB
aliasing). The file buffer now starts mid-page; that scenario went from
nginx +9% to `rws` −35 to −50%.

On a 10-core Mac (same tools and configuration, `oha` on the same machine):
1 KiB static — rws 107k, nginx 100k; 1 MiB static — 9.8k vs 9.4k; proxy —
49.0k vs 48.9k requests per second.

## Reading the numbers

- **Against Caddy:** `rws` serves 4.0× (large) to 5.2× (small) as many file
  requests, 2.6× as many proxied and 4.9× as many HTTP/2 requests per
  second, using a quarter to a ninth of the CPU per request, with a p99
  three to nine times lower and about half the memory.
- **Against nginx:** less CPU per request in every scenario — small files
  −33%, large files −3%, proxying −5%, HTTP/2 −28%, HTTPS −23%, large files
  over HTTPS −44%, with an access log −29%, with gzip a hundredth — more
  requests per second in all but large plain files (−3%), and the lower p99
  everywhere. This run used an AMD EPYC runner. On the fastest (Intel)
  runner type nginx keeps 6–8% more plain-HTTP requests per second and
  about the same CPU for large files and proxying (run 40209996636);
  `RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME=per-core` narrows that (run 40242045036). The load
  generator shares the runner's 4 CPUs, so the CPU/request column is the
  comparison to read.
- **Memory:** release builds allocate with mimalloc, which costs about 5%
  less CPU per request than the system allocator but holds more memory —
  34–66 MiB here, against nginx's 23–42. Built without the `mimalloc`
  feature, `rws` peaks at 9–17 MiB.
- The gap depends on the runner's hardware; same-run A/Bs (`base_ref`,
  below) are how changes are judged.
- Shared CI runners are noisy: absolute numbers vary by a factor of two
  between runs. Compare servers within one run, not numbers across runs.
- Compression matters: with `Accept-Encoding: gzip` sent and only `rws`
  compressing, the comparison measures `gzip`, not the servers. Compare like
  for like.

## Why it's fast

- **Open files are reused** (an open-file cache like nginx's): a request for
  a hot file costs one `fstat`; files up to 64 KiB are served from memory,
  and the response head and body go out in one write.
- **Quick requests run on the event loop.** Static files, health checks and
  metrics skip the hand-off to a blocking thread pool, as in nginx. Handlers
  that may block (your routes) still get a pool thread, so a slow handler
  can't stall other connections. See
  [`runs_inline`](/building-apps/middleware/#running-on-the-event-loop-runs_inline).
- **Proxying holds no thread.** Proxy routes without middleware, to HTTP or
  HTTPS backends, wait for the backend on the connection's task, over pooled
  keep-alive connections.
- **One idle timer per connection**, pushed back on each read without a lock.
- **`sendfile` for downloads** over plain HTTP on Linux and macOS: the kernel
  copies file pages straight to the socket, with the response head in the
  same segment (`TCP_CORK` on Linux, `sendfile`'s header vector on macOS).
- **Configuration is a cached snapshot**, not read from the environment on
  every request; a reload replaces it.
- **Few allocations per request.** The standard response headers are
  borrowed `&'static str`s (`Header` fields are `Cow<'static, str>`), so
  attaching them copies nothing; request heads and upstream response heads
  are parsed in one pass over the bytes; numbers are formatted on the stack;
  the file check is one `fstat`.

## Reproduce

Run the workflow from the repository's Actions tab ("Benchmark" → "Run
workflow"), or locally:

```bash
cargo build --release --bin rws --features "acme auth"
RWS=target/release/rws OHA=oha CADDY=caddy NGINX=nginx bench/run.sh
```

`CADDY` and `NGINX` are optional; the proxy scenario needs `NGINX`, which also
serves as the shared backend for every proxy under test. `DURATION` (default
`15s`) and `CONNECTIONS` (default `64`) tune the load. The script prints a
Markdown table and writes `bench-results.md` and `bench-results.json`.

`EXTENDED=1` (on by default in the workflow) adds the paths real deployments
hit that the three scenarios above leave out, each with equivalent settings
on every server: `text-gzip` (a 26 KiB JavaScript file with
`Accept-Encoding: gzip`, gzip level 6 everywhere), `log-1k` (an access log
written to a file), `https-1k` and `h2-1k` (TLS over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2),
and `https-1m` (a 1 MiB file over TLS, where `sendfile` doesn't apply). The
script makes a self-signed certificate with `openssl`, and skips a TLS
scenario for an nginx built without its ssl or http2 module.

## Profile

To see where `rws` spends its CPU, run the workflow with **profile** checked:
it builds with frame pointers and samples `rws` with `perf` during each
scenario, and nginx's workers too (`nginx-<scenario>` reports; the distro
nginx has no symbols, but its kernel time is comparable with `rws`'s). The job summary lists the hottest symbols, and the `bench-profile`
artifact has flat and call-tree reports plus `perf script` output for flame
graphs (`inferno-collapse-perf | inferno-flamegraph`). Locally, on Linux:

```bash
RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes" cargo build --release --bin rws --features "acme auth"
PERF_DIR=perf RWS=target/release/rws OHA=oha NGINX=nginx bench/run.sh
perf report -i perf/static-1k.data --no-children
```

Sampling slows `rws` down, so take throughput numbers from an unprofiled run.

## Compare two builds

Runner hardware differs from run to run (nginx itself varies threefold), so
a change can only be judged against its baseline in the same run. Give the
workflow a **base_ref** (a branch, tag or commit) and it also builds that
ref and benches it as `rws-base`, right after `rws`; locally, set
`RWS_BASE=<binary>`. **base_workers** (`RWS_BASE_WORKERS`) runs `rws-base`
with that many tokio workers — with no base ref, the same build again — to
compare worker counts, and **base_runtime** (`RWS_BASE_RUNTIME`) does the same
for `RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME` (shared or per-core). (Fewer workers than CPUs raises the measured
requests per second only because the load generator shares the runner's
CPUs; on a dedicated server one worker per core is right.)

---

# rws vs nginx vs Caddy

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/compare/>

**Short answer:** pick **rws** if you want one binary that serves files, gets
its own certificates, load balances and adds auth from one TOML file, with
the same engine available as a Rust library. Pick **Caddy** for the same
"HTTPS by default" experience with a large Go plugin ecosystem. Pick
**nginx** when you need the most battle-tested server, the lowest memory use,
or modules only nginx has.

Facts about nginx and Caddy were checked against their documentation on
2026-11-06 ([sources](#sources)). Tell us on
[GitHub](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/issues) if something
has changed.

## At a glance

| | rws | Caddy | nginx |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automatic HTTPS | Built in: HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01, DNS-01 (RFC 2136, Cloudflare, Route 53, exec), wildcards, on-demand TLS | Built in and on by default: HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01, DNS-01 via plugins, on-demand TLS, a local CA for localhost | Official `nginx-acme` dynamic module (HTTP-01, TLS-ALPN-01; no DNS-01), or certbot |
| Config | One `rws.config.toml`; `rws --check`; hot reload on SIGHUP or file change; admin API | Caddyfile or JSON; `caddy validate`; admin API | `nginx.conf`; `nginx -t`; reload; Control API since 1.31.5 (off by default) |
| HTTP/3 (QUIC) | On by default with TLS | On by default | Yes, since 1.25.0 (marked experimental) |
| Load balancing | Round robin, random, least connections, IP hash, weights, sticky cookies, circuit breaker, retries, active health checks | Random, round robin, weighted, least connections, IP/URI/header/cookie hash, active and passive health checks, retries | Round robin, least connections, least time, hash, random, sticky (1.29.6+); active health checks in NGINX Plus |
| Auth | Bearer, JWT, basic, forward auth, OIDC sign-in; fails closed when misconfigured. SAML in the library | Basic, forward auth; more via plugins | Basic, `auth_request`; JWT and OIDC in NGINX Plus |
| Observability | Prometheus metrics with native histograms, OpenTelemetry traces, metrics and logs, JSON access log, admin UI with traffic analytics (people, AI agents, bots) | Prometheus metrics (HTTP metrics opt-in), OTLP metrics, OpenTelemetry tracing, structured JSON logs | `stub_status`, OpenTelemetry tracing module; full metrics API in NGINX Plus |
| Kubernetes | Gateway API controller (v1.6.3 conformance, all five Gateway profiles), Helm chart | Ingress controller (caddyserver/ingress, work in progress); no Gateway API implementation | NGINX Gateway Fabric (Gateway API), NGINX Ingress Controller |
| Extending | A Rust crate: routes, middleware, MCP server, ORM; WASM plugins | Go plugins compiled in (xcaddy) | C modules, njs, Lua via OpenResty |
| License | MIT | Apache-2.0 | BSD-2-Clause |

## Speed

Measured on one 4-CPU GitHub Actions runner, 64 keep-alive connections, no
compression, access logs off. The method and every number are on the
[benchmarks page](/reference/benchmarks/). In short: rws and nginx lead on
requests per second and CPU per request in most scenarios; nginx uses the
least memory in every scenario.

## When to choose which

- **rws**: a small team's whole front door in one file (static site,
  automatic certificates, a few proxied apps, auth and rate limits), or a
  Rust app that wants a production HTTP server inside it.
- **Caddy**: you want automatic HTTPS and already rely on a Caddy plugin.
- **nginx**: very high traffic on minimal memory, an existing nginx setup, or
  a module only nginx has.

## Moving from nginx or Caddy

- [Quick start](/getting-started/quick-start/): static files and a proxy in five minutes
- [Automatic HTTPS](/features/acme/)
- [Config-driven proxy](/proxy/config-driven/)

# Roadmap

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/roadmap/>

These features are planned. Each appears as a callout on the relevant docs page.

:::caution[Coming Soon]
**Baggage and automatic child spans**

W3C baggage propagation, and spans created automatically for each database query and outbound call. Child spans already work when started by hand with `otel::span` / `otel::client_span` — see [Distributed Tracing](/features/tracing/#child-spans).
:::

:::caution[Coming Soon]
**Admin UI**

`GET /admin` — a browser-based dashboard showing live metrics, current configuration, and a tail of the access log. Requires authentication.
:::

:::caution[Coming Soon]
**Access log rotation**

Built-in log-file rotation (by size or time) so the server can write logs to disk without an external `logrotate` configuration.
:::

---

**WebAssembly guest component** — shipped. `App`/`Router`/middleware now run inside a `wasi:http/proxy` WASM component (Wasmtime, Spin, Fastly Compute) via the separate `rws-wasm-shim` package. See [WASM Guest Component](/deployment/wasm/). Larger follow-up phases (streaming bodies, outbound HTTP from the guest) remain open — tracked in `spec/WASM_SHIM.md` in the repository.

---

The full ordered list of open work is [`spec/ROADMAP.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/spec/ROADMAP.md); track progress and open issues at [github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/issues).

# Support policy

<https://rws8.tech/docs/reference/support-policy/>

## Release lines

rws follows [semver](https://semver.org/). Minor releases (18.21, 18.22, …)
are additive: a configuration and an app that work on one 18.x work on
every later 18.x. Breaking changes wait for a major release and are listed
on a migration page ([Migrating to 18](/reference/migrating-18/)).

| Line | Gets | For how long |
|---|---|---|
| **Current** — the newest minor | every fix | until the next minor |
| **LTS** — one minor every six months | security fixes and critical bug fixes | 12 months from its release |
| Everything else | nothing | — |

LTS lines so far:

| Line | Released | Supported until | Branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18.20 | 2026-11-01 | 2027-11-01 | `18.20.x` |

"Critical" means data loss, a crash or hang reachable by clients, a
regression that stops a documented configuration from working, or a broken
certificate renewal. New features never go to an LTS line.

## Security fixes

Reports go through GitHub's private advisories (see
[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/SECURITY.md)).
Targets: an answer within 3 working days, an assessment within 7 days, and
fixed releases for critical and high issues within 14 days — on the current
line and every supported LTS line at once — published with a GitHub
security advisory and a CVE.

## Upgrading

Within a major version, upgrade to the newest minor: read the changelog's
**Changed** and **Security** entries, run `rws --check` on your
configuration with the new binary, then replace it (the
[packages](/deployment/systemd/) and the container images make this one
step). Staying on an LTS line trades features for fewer changes: patch
releases on it (`18.20.1`, `18.20.2`) contain only fixes.

## Verifying what you run

Release binaries have build-provenance attestations, container images are
signed with Sigstore cosign, and each release ships a CycloneDX SBOM — see
[Installation](/getting-started/installation/) for the commands.
